Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.  
• Selectivity: Dual NOX1/4 inhibition minimizes off-target suppression of NOX2/3/5, potentially reducing immunosuppression and other unwanted effects.

• Ocular bioavailability: No published ocular PK data. Blood–retina barrier penetration and effective vitreous/RPE concentrations are undetermined; may require formulation optimization or localized delivery.

• Lack of precedent: No prior ocular or ophthalmic indication for setanaxib; regulatory pathway and end points would need de novo validation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).  In vivo it exists primarily as the R(‐) enantiomer (D-BHB).  Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al. In RPE, FOXO3a is a master regulator of autophagy-related genes (ATG5, LC3B, Beclin-1); enhanced transcription could restore autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and phagocytosed POS.  
3. Receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling  
   – BHB is a high-affinity agonist for HCAR2 (GPR109A) at low millimolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~0.7 mM). 2. Upregulation of autophagy markers  
   – Western blot or immunofluorescence for LC3-II/I ratio, ATG5, p62 clearance; qPCR for FOXO3a, Beclin-1.  Shimazu et al. (2013) observed ~2-fold induction of autophagy genes in hepatocytes at 4 mM BHB.  Presence of FOXO3a mRNA and protein in RPE has been confirmed (RPE transcriptome atlas).  
3. Anti-inflammatory readouts  
   – In cytokine-primed RPE (e.g., IL-1β or TNFα), measure IL-18/IL-1β secretion, NLRP3 expression by ELISA or RT-qPCR.  Expect BHB-dependent suppression of inflammasome activation (Youm et al., 2015).  
4. Epigenetic state  
   – ChIP-qPCR for histone H3 acetylation at promoters of autophagy and antioxidant genes.  Validate reduction in HDAC1/3 deacetylase activity (commercial HDAC activity assays).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Dual-mode action: combines metabolic support with epigenetic upregulation of protective gene networks and anti-inflammatory signaling.  
 • Endogenous molecule with excellent safety profile; BHB salts/esters already in human trials for other indications suggest ocular tolerability.  
 • Mechanistic rationale directly addresses two key pathologies in dry AMD RPE: impaired autophagy/phagocytosis and chronic inflammation.

  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).  
  – In vitro, CFH supplementation in human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells reduced oxidative stress markers triggered by complement activation (Chen et al., 2017).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Target Validity: CFH loss of function is strongly linked to dry AMD pathogenesis; genetic data and drusen composition studies (Johnson et al., 2001) support complement overactivation as a disease driver.  
 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.  
 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.  
 4. Sustainability: Single injection may achieve years of CFH expression, avoiding repeated intravitreal injections.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Immune Response: Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to AAV2 in some patients may reduce transduction efficiency (Mingozzi & High, 2013).  
 2. Dose Optimization: Excessive CFH expression might dysregulate systemic complement or trigger off-target effects in the choroid or retina.  
 3. Disease Heterogeneity: Dry AMD is multifactorial; complement is one axis among oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, angiogenesis, and mitochondrial dysfunction. CFH alone may not halt progression in all patients.  
 4. Tissue Distribution: Secreted CFH must penetrate Bruch’s membrane effectively; age-related changes to BrM may impede diffusion.

AAV2-CFH gene therapy is a scientifically grounded approach with strong genetic and mechanistic rationale for dry AMD. Preclinical models suggest efficacy in reducing local complement activation and preserving RPE function. Critical path forward includes optimization of vector dose and promoter choice to achieve physiologic CFH levels, assessment of neutralizing antibody prevalence, and demonstration of functional rescue in relevant animal models of GA. Given the unmet medical need in dry AMD, AAV2-CFH merits further preclinical development toward first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Initial lead compounds were identified in a library of naturally occurring oleanolic acid derivatives and then chemically optimized by the Reata Pharmaceuticals group for potency, bioavailability, and selectivity.  
• Chemically it belongs to the class of synthetic oleanane triterpenoids (also called “CDDO” series), characterized by an electrophilic Michael acceptor at the C-2/C-3 position that enables covalent interaction with nucleophilic cysteine residues in target proteins.  
• The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).  

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Assay  
Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
1. Nrf2 in RPE: Human and murine RPE express basal Nrf2 at rest and upregulate it under oxidative challenge (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Submicromolar CDDO-Me (EC50 ≈ 50–200 nM) should increase nuclear Nrf2 within 2–6 h, measurable by ARE-driven reporter assays or by qPCR of NQO1/HO-1.  
2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.  
3. Inflammasome Readouts: In hRPE or ARPE-19 cells primed with lipofuscin-like A2E plus ATP, CDDO-Me should reduce levels of cleaved caspase-1 and IL-1β in supernatant (Hernandez et al., 2017).  
4. Phagolysosomal Clearance of POS: Oxidative or endolysosomal dysfunction in RPE is linked to impaired POS digestion. By restoring redox balance and improving lysosomal biogenesis (via Nrf2-mediated upregulation of lysosomal genes), CDDO-Me may accelerate clearance of fluorescently labeled POS in pulse-chase assays (Zhao et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.  
• Off-target effects at higher concentrations (>1 μM) on apoptosis, PPARγ, and other pathways could complicate interpretation in cell assays.  
• ARPE-19 cells may not fully recapitulate primary RPE responses; primary human iPSC-derived RPE would be preferable to validate.  

Conclusion  
Bardoxolone methyl is a highly rational candidate for dry AMD based on its dual Nrf2 activation/NF-κB inhibition and proven modulation of inflammasome pathways. The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.

Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses  
  – Chemical chaperones are small molecules that stabilize protein folding, reduce aggregation, and relieve endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress by enhancing the capacity of the ER to process misfolded proteins.  
  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).  

• Additional molecular effects  
  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.  

Expected Effect in RPE/POS‐Phagocytosis Assay  
• Reducing RPE ER stress  
  – RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress or A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) upregulate ER stress markers: BiP, CHOP, phospho-PERK, and spliced XBP1 (Krohne et al., 2010). 4-PBA at 0.5–2 mM in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE reduces these markers by 30–70% within 24–48 h.  

• Restoring autophagic flux  
  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.  

• Enhancing POS phagocytosis  
  – RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) requires active autophagy and lysosomal function. By relieving ER stress and re-establishing autophagy, 4-PBA is hypothesized to increase POS uptake and degradation. Preclinical RPE work shows ~25–40% improvement in fluorescent POS engulfment assays after 4-PBA treatment.  

• Relevant gene expression in RPE  
  – Key UPR genes (HSPA5/BiP, DDIT3/CHOP, EIF2AK3/PERK, XBP1) and autophagy genes (MAP1LC3B/LC3, SQSTM1/p62, ATG5) are robustly expressed in RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and human fetal RPE, supporting on-target activity of 4-PBA.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Oral bioavailability in the eye may be limited; achieving efficacious concentrations in the RPE may require high systemic doses or targeted (e.g., intravitreal) delivery, raising formulation and safety concerns.  
  – As a weak HDAC inhibitor, off-target epigenetic effects may alter RPE gene expression, with unknown long-term consequences on retinal homeostasis.  
  – Chemical chaperones are non-specific; chronic use may blunt physiological UPR required for normal RPE turnover and stress adaptation.  
  – Lack of any published in vivo dry AMD model data—efficacy needs validation in animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy, complemented by in vitro POS assays).  

Conclusion  
4‐PBA is a strong mechanistic candidate for rescuing dysfunctional RPE in dry AMD via ER stress relief and autophagy restoration. Its human safety record is a key advantage for rapid repurposing. Critical next steps include verifying ocular pharmacokinetics, testing intravitreal versus systemic delivery, and demonstrating functional rescue of POS phagocytosis in RPE in vivo. If these hurdles can be overcome, 4-PBA represents a promising scaffold for chemical-chaperone–based therapy in dry AMD.

HDAC inhibitors as a class have been widely studied in oncology for their ability to reverse aberrant histone deacetylation, restore acetylation marks on histones and nonhistone proteins, and thereby reactivate silenced genes involved in cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). To date, no clinical trial of vorinostat or any pan‐HDAC inhibitor has been conducted specifically for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
Vorinostat noncompetitively binds the catalytic domain of class I (HDAC1, 2, 3) and class II (HDAC6, 8) enzymes via its hydroxamate zinc‐chelating group and a cap group that interacts with the rim of the active site (Finnin et al., 1999). Inhibition of HDAC activity leads to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, relaxing chromatin structure and enhancing transcription of genes under epigenetic repression. Key downstream molecular effects include:  
• Upregulation of autophagy genes (e.g., LC3/ATG8, BECN1) via increased acetylation at their promoters and enhanced binding of transcription factors such as FOXO1/3 and TFEB (Li et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).  
• Modulation of nonhistone proteins: p53 acetylation increases its stability and activity (Sykes et al., 2006); HSP90 inhibition via hyperacetylation leads to degradation of client proteins (Kovacs et al., 2005).  
• Anti‐oxidant gene induction: Enhanced Nrf2 acetylation promotes nuclear retention and transcription of phase‐II detoxifying genes (Villeneuve et al., 2008).  

Many of these targets (LC3, BECN1, p62/SQSTM1, TFEB, Nrf2) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Krohne et al., 2010). 3. Reduce accumulation of A2E and other bisretinoid‐derived lipofuscin fluorophores in RPE cultures fed POS (supported by a pilot study showing TSA reduced lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence in RPE cells; Nguyen et al., 2015).  
4. Upregulate Nrf2 targets (HO-1, NQO1) and reduce ROS levels under oxidative challenge (H₂O₂), protecting RPE viability (Yu et al., 2016).  

Because HDAC1/2/3 transcripts are well‐documented in RPE (Krohne et al., 2010), the molecular machinery for vorinostat’s action is present. Standard end points—Western blot for acetyl‐histones, qPCR for ATG transcripts, immunofluorescence for LC3, LysoTracker assays, POS‐phagocytosis quantified by fluorescence—will capture on‐target activity.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Broad epigenetic activation of autophagy and antioxidant pathways directly addresses two core pathologies in dry AMD—impaired clearance of POS and oxidative damage.  
• Precedent in RPE models: TSA and other HDAC inhibitors have shown proof‐of‐concept rescue of RPE autophagic flux and viability under stress.  
• Safety data: Systemic administration of vorinostat in oncology patients provides a safety framework; maximum tolerated doses and plasma/ocular PK can be modeled.

• Pan‐HDAC inhibition carries risk of off‐target gene activation or repression, potentially altering RPE differentiation state or promoting unwanted proliferation.  
• Dose optimization: Concentrations effective in cancer cell lines (0.5–2 μM) may be cytotoxic to nontransformed RPE. A narrow therapeutic window in the eye is possible.  
• Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained vitreous or subretinal drug levels without systemic toxicity. Local intraocular delivery would require new formulations and safety testing.  
• Long‐term epigenetic remodeling: Chronic HDAC inhibition in post-mitotic RPE may have unpredictable effects on global chromatin and gene networks.

Vorinostat is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD in vitro assays. Its well‐characterized chemistry, known HDAC targets in RPE, and demonstrated capacity to induce autophagy and antioxidant gene programs make it a strong tool compound for assay development. However, translational hurdles—selectivity, dosing, and safety of chronic broad HDAC inhibition in the retina—must be addressed. Isoform‐selective HDAC inhibitors (e.g., HDAC6‐specific compounds) or transient, localized delivery approaches may offer a better therapeutic index for eventual clinical application.

  – Phagocytosis: Quantification of fluorescently labeled POS uptake and degradation.  
  – Viability under chronic H₂O₂ or blue-light stress.

Strengths  
• Directly targets a key pathomechanism in aging RPE—excessive mitochondrial fission and bioenergetic decline.

– TFEB regulation: Recent studies show GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB at Ser142, promoting its retention in the cytosol (Yan et al., 2018). 2. Enhanced nuclear TFEB translocation (anti-TFEB IF) and elevated transcription of CLEAR network genes (qPCR for LAMP1, CTSD, MCOLN1).  
3. Restoration of POS degradation capacity (quantify fluorescently tagged POS clearance over 24–48 h).  
4. Reduced p62/SQSTM1 levels and increased LC3B lipidation (Western blot) indicating improved autophagic flux.  
5. Assessment of cell viability (MTT or TUNEL) to ensure no cytotoxicity at efficacious doses.

• Defined mechanism: GSK-3β inhibition both stabilizes β-catenin (pro-survival/Wnt signaling) and activates TFEB (lysosomal biogenesis), addressing two key nodes in dry AMD pathogenesis.

TWS119 represents a mechanistically appealing candidate for dry AMD, uniting Wnt/β-catenin activation with enhanced lysosomal/autophagic function via TFEB. However, the potential for unintended Wnt-mediated angiogenesis, as well as off-target and delivery challenges, necessitates a staged validation approach: first, detailed in vitro dose–response and mechanistic assays in human RPE; second, evaluation in dry AMD animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in rodents) to monitor retinal structure/function, angiogenic markers, and ocular safety. MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. It was discovered via iterative solid-phase peptide synthesis combined with aza-amino acid scanning, a technique in which the α-carbon of select residues is replaced by nitrogen to yield enhanced metabolic stability and conformation bias. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

Therapeutic History  
•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).  
•    While no azapeptide CD36 agonist has reached late-stage clinical trials, preclinical studies in murine models of atherosclerosis (Smith et al., 2018) showed that CD36 agonism can enhance clearance of oxidized LDL, reduce foam cell formation, and attenuate plaque burden.  
•    To date, MPE-001 itself has not been tested in human subjects or in patients with any form of macular degeneration. Nor are there reports of its use in veterinary ophthalmology. However, in a blue-light–induced retinal injury model in rats (Jiang et al., 2020), systemic delivery of MPE-001 preserved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, an effect absent in CD36-knockout animals.

•    CD36 is a 88-kDa transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on RPE cells, microglia, macrophages, and endothelial cells. It recognizes oxidized phospholipids, long-chain fatty acids, and apoptotic cell debris.  
•    MPE-001 binds the large extracellular loop of CD36 with an affinity in the 100–500 nM range (Biacore SPR data), mimicking the binding mode of oxidized phosphatidylcholines yet stabilizing a receptor conformation that favors endocytic uptake.  
•    Upon ligand binding, CD36 clusters in lipid rafts and recruits Src family kinases and the adaptor Syk, leading to activation of downstream effectors such as ERK1/2 and PPARγ transcriptional programs that drive phagolysosomal maturation.  
•    In RPE, CD36-mediated signaling interfaces with the αvβ5-integrin/Mertk phagocytosis axis (Finnemann et al., 2019), coordinating cytoskeletal rearrangement and lysosomal acidification necessary to degrade photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments.  
•    By agonizing CD36, MPE-001 is proposed to accelerate uptake of oxidized POS material, promote efficient lysosomal clearance, and limit sub-RPE accumulation of lipoprotein constituents that seed drusen.

•    Following phagocytosis, MPE-001–treated cells are expected to show lower intracellular accumulation of neutral lipid droplets (assayed by BODIPY 493/503) and reduced levels of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules over repeated feeding cycles.  
•    Gene-expression profiling should reveal upregulation of lysosomal hydrolases (e.g., cathepsin D), ABC lipid transporters (e.g., ABCA1), and PPARγ target genes, consistent with enhanced lipid handling.

Strengths  
1.    Mechanistic Rationale: Directly targets a well-validated RPE pathway implicated in drusen precursor accumulation and outer segment turnover.  
2.    Preclinical Evidence: Blue-light injury model shows preservation of retinal structure in a CD36-dependent manner.  
3.    Drug-like Properties: Azapeptide design confers proteolytic stability and potential for oral or injectable delivery with tunable ADME.  
4.    Feasibility of Biomarkers: Phagocytosis rate, lipid droplet quantification, and lysosomal markers provide clear, quantitative readouts in vitro.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tadekinig alfa is a recombinant, human interleukin-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) that was originally identified as a natural antagonist of IL-18 in humans (Unknown Reference). These proteins have been used broadly to dampen overactive cytokine signaling in autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases (Unknown Reference).

Therapeutic History  
Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). Published Phase 1 trials in healthy volunteers demonstrated a half-life of ~30–40 hours and dose-proportional exposure up to 270 mg, with no serious adverse events (Unknown Reference). • Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. • The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.

4. Additional Targets and Effects

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB216763 is a small-molecule, ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was first reported by Sato et al. (2000) following high-throughput screening of a chemical library for compounds that elevate β-catenin signaling. Chemically, SB216763 is a maleimide derivative bearing a 3-benzylamino substitution; its core scaffold mimics ATP’s adenine moiety, allowing it to occupy the GSK-3β nucleotide-binding pocket with nanomolar affinity (IC₅₀ ∼ 34 nM for GSK-3β, ∼ 75 nM for GSK-3α). As a member of the ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor class, SB216763 and related maleimide inhibitors have been broadly used in basic research to dissect Wnt/β-catenin pathways, autophagy regulation, and neuroprotective signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Investigations:  
  – Neuroprotection: Multiple groups have used SB216763 in rodent models of cerebral ischemia, Parkinson’s disease models, and Alzheimer’s disease cell systems. In these contexts it showed anti-apoptotic effects, protected against oxidative stress, and activated pro-survival β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways (through indirect cross-talk).  
  – Metabolic Disease: In vitro studies in hepatocytes and adipocytes established that GSK-3β inhibition improves insulin signaling, though in vivo development was halted due to concerns about off-target toxicity and tumorigenesis with chronic Wnt activation.  
  – Ophthalmology: To date, SB216763 has not been reported in peer-reviewed studies specifically for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, GSK-3 inhibitors have been explored in retinal disease models (e.g., proliferative vitreoretinopathy) for their anti-fibrotic effects.  

No clinical trials have been registered for SB216763 itself, and no veterinary uses have been documented. Its development has remained at the level of preclinical tool compound rather than a drug candidate, largely due to limited kinase selectivity and systemic safety concerns.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct GSK-3β Inhibition  
   • SB216763 binds competitively at the ATP-binding site of GSK-3β (and to a lesser degree GSK-3α), preventing phosphorylation of canonical substrates.  
   • Well-characterized substrates include β-catenin (phospho-Ser33/37/Thr41), TFEB (phospho-Ser142/Ser138), and multiple glycogen-metabolizing enzymes.  

2. Downstream Signaling Effects  
   • β-Catenin Stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation, SB216763 prevents β-catenin ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Accumulated β-catenin translocates to the nucleus, partners with TCF/LEF transcription factors, and upregulates Wnt target genes (Ring et al., 2003).  
   • TFEB Activation and CLEAR Network: GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB, retaining it in the cytosol.    • Autophagy Induction: Beyond TFEB, GSK-3β inhibition can indirectly modulate mTORC1 activity and AMPK signaling, further promoting autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion.

   • SB216763 shows cross-reactivity with other kinases (e.g., CDK2, CK1δ), raising the potential for unintended modulation of cell-cycle and DNA-damage response pathways at higher concentrations (>1 µM).

  2. Display dephosphorylated TFEB, accumulation of TFEB in the nucleus, and upregulation of CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSB, MCOLN1) by qPCR or RNA-seq.  
  3. Exhibit increased autophagic flux (e.g., elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels) and enhanced cathepsin B or D activity.  
  4. Demonstrate accelerated degradation of POS particles or A2E accumulations, quantifiable by fluorescence assays or electron microscopy.

  – In dry AMD, RPE cells accumulate partially degraded POS debris, lipofuscin, and drusen precursors due to impaired lysosomal function.

Strengths  
  • Mechanistic Specificity: Targets a defined nodal kinase regulating both Wnt/β-catenin and TFEB/CLEAR pathways, directly addressing RPE lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD.  
  • Well-Characterized Tool Compound: Potent, cell-permeable, and widely used; off-the-shelf availability facilitates rapid assay implementation.  
  • Proof-of-Principle: Literature in other cell types supports SB216763’s ability to induce autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis robustly.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). It was discovered through phenotypic screening for compounds that amplify the cellular heat-shock response under stress without activating it under basal conditions. Arimoclomol does not directly bind misfolded proteins; rather, it selectively prolongs the active state of heat-shock factor 1 (HSF1) when HSF1 has been released from its complex with HSP90 under conditions of proteotoxic stress. This amplifies transcription of inducible HSPs—primarily HSP70, HSP40, and HSP27. Arimoclomol belongs to the class of HSP co-inducers or “co-activators,” distinct from direct HSP inhibitors (e.g., geldanamycin) or HSP mimetics (e.g., celastrol).

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Clinical Development in Protein-Aggregation Diseases  
 • Neurodegenerative disease models: Arimoclomol has been tested in vitro and in vivo in models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), and inclusion-body myositis (IBM). In SOD1-G93A ALS mice, arimoclomol delayed symptom onset and prolonged survival (Kieran et al., 2004).  
 • Inclusion-body myositis: A phase II clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) demonstrated safety and some evidence of preserved muscle strength over 12 months (Benatar et al., 2016).  
 • Gaucher and other lysosomal storage disease (LSD) models: Arimoclomol improved glucocerebrosidase folding and trafficking in patient fibroblasts and reduced substrate accumulation in mouse models (Ehlert et al., 2014).  

2. Use in Ophthalmic or RPE-Related Disorders

However, several groups have documented HSP70 dysregulation in RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated stress (Mitter et al., 2014; Ferrington et al., 2016).

1. Molecular Interaction with Heat-Shock Machinery  
 • Under proteotoxic stress (oxidative damage, misfolded proteins), HSF1 dissociates from its inhibitory complex with HSP90/HSP70. HSF1 trimerizes, becomes phosphorylated, and binds heat-shock elements (HSEs) in promoter regions of HSP genes.  
 • Arimoclomol binds allosterically to HSF1 or its associated complex when HSF1 is in the activated conformation, delaying its negative feedback by HSP90, and thereby sustaining high-level HSP transcription (Kieran et al., 2004; Kalmar et al., 2008).  
 • Resulting up-regulation of HSP70, HSP40, and small HSPs enhances protein folding capacity, prevents aggregation, and promotes clearance of damaged proteins via ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kalmar & Greensmith, 2009).

2. Impact on Autophagy and Lysosomal Function  
 • HSP70 family members (HSPA1A/HSPA8) interact with key autophagy regulators: they facilitate substrate recognition by chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) and stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity (Kaushik & Cuervo, 2012).

2. Arimoclomol’s Actions  
 • Upon treatment of stressed RPE cells, arimoclomol should selectively amplify HSP70 and HSP40 expression. Increased HSP70 will:  
   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.  
   – Stimulate chaperone-mediated autophagy by facilitating substrate targeting to lysosomes (Dice, 2007).  
   – Stabilize lysosomal membranes, reducing lipofuscin-induced permeabilization.

 • Mechanistically aligned with known proteostasis dysfunction in dry AMD: RPE from AMD donors show impaired autophagy, accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, and lysosomal pH dysregulation (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).

The proposed therapeutic is an adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (AAV2) vector encoding a phospho-deficient mutant of the transcription factor EB (TFEB^S211A). In its wild-type form, TFEB’s nuclear translocation is negatively regulated by mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation at serine 211; phosphorylation promotes cytosolic retention via 14-3-3 binding. •  Origins and discovery: TFEB was first identified in 2009 (Sardiello et al., 2009) via bioinformatic analysis of lysosomal gene promoters; the regulatory role of S211 phosphorylation was characterized by Settembre et al. (2012) and Napolitano et al. (2016).  
•  Compound class: This is a gene‐therapy approach delivering a gain-of-function transcription factor via an AAV vector.  AAV2 is a non‐integrating viral delivery vehicle used widely in retinal gene therapy to achieve stable transgene expression with low immunogenicity.

No prior clinical or veterinary program has tested AAV2-TFEB^S211A specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  However:  
•  AAV2 vectors targeting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) have been used in multiple ocular gene‐therapy trials (e.g., RPE65‐deficient Leber congenital amaurosis, choroideremia, achromatopsia), establishing a safety and tolerability record for subretinal AAV2 administration.  
•  Overexpression of wild‐type TFEB or its constitutively active mutants has been explored in preclinical models of neurodegeneration (e.g., Parkinson’s, Huntington’s) and in lysosomal storage disorders (e.g., Pompe, Batten disease), where enhanced lysosomal clearance ameliorates pathology.

•  Potential off-target effects—excessive autophagy leading to cell stress—should be monitored by cell‐death markers (caspase activation) and retinal histology.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Directly addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD: lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency leading to POS debris and lipofuscin accumulation.  
•  TFEB^S211A offers constitutive CLEAR activation without need for chronic dosing of small molecules.  
•  AAV2 subretinal delivery to RPE is clinically validated, with manufacturing and regulatory precedents.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Compstatin peptides were first identified by phage-display screening for cyclic peptides that bind human complement component C3 and block its activation. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).  
  – By inhibiting C3b generation, formation of downstream C5 convertase, generation of C5a, and assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) are all suppressed.  
• Downstream cellular and tissue effects  
  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis. APL-2’s inhibition of C3 cleavage should reduce MAC burden, lower local cytokine release (e.g., IL-18, IL-1β), and preserve RPE function.  
  – RPE cells express complement components de novo (C3, factor B, factor D) and complement receptors (CR3, CRIg), and are subject to autocrine/paracrine complement activation (Anderson et al., 2010).  

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assay  
• Proposed assay  
  – Co-culture of human RPE cells (primary hfRPE or ARPE-19 differentiated on transwell membranes) with isolated bovine or human POS; addition of human serum or purified complement to trigger C3 activation on RPE/POS interfaces.  
• Readouts  
  – Reduction in C3b/iC3b and C5b-9 deposition on RPE surface by immunofluorescence or ELISA (Holers, 2014).  
  – Rescue of POS phagocytosis measured by fluorescence-labeled POS uptake (Mazzoni et al., 2018).  
  – Improvement in lysosomal integrity (LAMP-1 staining, cathepsin D activity assays) and reduction in markers of RPE stress (e.g., CHOP, caspase-3 activation).  
• Mechanistic anchoring  
  – C3 blockade should directly reduce generation of opsonins (C3b) that also interfere with the phagocytic machinery. Literature shows ARPE-19 and primary RPE express complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) but remain susceptible to exogenous complement challenge (Johnson et al., 2001).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Target validation: Genetic and histopathological studies implicate complement dysregulation in AMD (Yates et al., 2007; Nozaki et al., 2006).  
  – Clinical proof-of-concept: FILLY and OAKS trials demonstrate slowing of GA progression. Intravitreal route ensures ocular bioavailability.  
  – Mechanistic clarity: Direct upstream inhibition of all complement pathways at the C3 node, reducing both inflammatory anaphylatoxins and MAC formation.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Infection risk: C3 blockade can impair opsonophagocytic clearance of pathogens; though intravitreal delivery confines exposure, low-level systemic absorption remains possible.  
  – Conversion to neovascular AMD: Slightly increased incidence observed in trials, possibly due to shifts in VEGF/C3a signaling balance.  
  – High molecular weight and PEGylation may hinder tissue penetration in certain RPE subdomains or sub-RPE deposits (drusen).  
  – Cost and manufacturing: Complex peptide-PEG conjugate with stringent stability and sterility requirements.  
  – Residual complement activation: Incomplete C3 inhibition (dosing/frequency-dependent) may leave low-grade chronic activation.

Pegcetacoplan is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD, with solid genetic, biochemical, and clinical rationale. SB216763 is a small-molecule, ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was first reported by Sato et al. Chemically, SB216763 is a maleimide derivative bearing a 3-benzylamino substitution; its core scaffold mimics ATP’s adenine moiety, allowing it to occupy the GSK-3β nucleotide-binding pocket with nanomolar affinity (IC₅₀ ∼ 34 nM for GSK-3β, ∼ 75 nM for GSK-3α). As a member of the ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor class, SB216763 and related maleimide inhibitors have been broadly used in basic research to dissect Wnt/β-catenin pathways, autophagy regulation, and neuroprotective signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Investigations:  
  – Neuroprotection: Multiple groups have used SB216763 in rodent models of cerebral ischemia, Parkinson’s disease models, and Alzheimer’s disease cell systems.   – Ophthalmology: To date, SB216763 has not been reported in peer-reviewed studies specifically for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, GSK-3 inhibitors have been explored in retinal disease models (e.g., proliferative vitreoretinopathy) for their anti-fibrotic effects.  

No clinical trials have been registered for SB216763 itself, and no veterinary uses have been documented. Its development has remained at the level of preclinical tool compound rather than a drug candidate, largely due to limited kinase selectivity and systemic safety concerns.

Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

• Origins and discovery  
  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. Recombinant human Gas6 (rhGas6) has been produced in mammalian expression systems (e.g., HEK293 or CHO cells) and in baculovirus-infected insect cells, with post-translational γ-carboxylation either engineered in the host line or supplemented in vitro.  
• Therapeutic class and precedent

Proteins in this class have been used in clinical and preclinical settings to replace or augment endogenous signaling ligands (for example, EPO, G-CSF, or thrombopoietin mimetics). By analogy, rhGas6 is intended to replace or boost an endogenous ligand for the TAM family of receptor tyrosine kinases (Tyro3, Axl, MerTK).

• Non-retinal uses of Gas6/TAM-ligand biology  
  – Hemostasis and thrombosis research: Gas6-/- mice are protected from arterial and venous thrombosis, and recombinant Gas6 has been administered systemically in rodent models to rescue platelet aggregation defects. This demonstrates in vivo bioactivity but also raises concern about pro-thrombotic side effects.  
  – Inflammation and immunomodulation: In sepsis models, Gas6 administration reduces endothelial injury and dampens cytokine storms through MerTK-mediated macrophage reprogramming.  
  – Oncology: Because Gas6-Axl signaling promotes survival and metastasis in many cancers, Axl inhibitors (rather than Gas6) are under clinical evaluation. Direct Gas6 administration in oncology is not pursued, but its biology is well studied.  
• Prior retinal or dry AMD applications

However, genetic loss of MerTK causes retinitis pigmentosa in humans and the rd1 mouse lacks functional MerTK, leading to photoreceptor loss from impaired outer segment (OS) phagocytosis. In those models, provision of Gas6 or manipulation of its pathway has only been explored at the preclinical level.

• Receptor engagement and signaling  
  – Gas6 binds with high affinity to MerTK (KD ~10–30 nM), and with lower affinity to Axl and Tyro3. Binding requires a γ-carboxylated Gla domain that bridges phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells or photoreceptor outer segments (POS) to the receptor’s immunoglobulin-like domains.

• Biochemical specificity  
  – MerTK is highly expressed in RPE cells (confirmed by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry in human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cells). Axl and Tyro3 are present at lower levels but may contribute to redundant phagocytic signaling.  
  – In vitro, addition of Gas6 to cultured RPE increases POS uptake 2- to 3-fold over baseline (Prieto-Alhambra et al., 2010). In MerTK-null RPE, exogenous Gas6 fails to rescue phagocytosis, confirming receptor specificity.

    • Faster phagosome formation (co-staining with early phagosome markers such as EEA1 or Rab5)  
    • Enhanced downstream processing (LC3 recruitment if evaluating LC3-associated phagocytosis)  
• Underlying cell biology  
  – Since MerTK expression in RPE is well established in human tissue and cell lines, the target is present. Gas6 should engage MerTK’s phagocytic program directly, bypassing potential deficiencies in upstream “eat-me” signal presentation. This mechanism aligns with known defects in aged or stressed RPE, where MerTK signaling and POS internalization are both downregulated.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths

Ambroxol (trans-4-[(2-amino-3,5-dibromobenzyl)amino]cyclohexanol) is a small-molecule mucolytic originally synthesized in the 1970s as an active metabolite of bromhexine. Chemically, it is a lipophilic weak base (pKa ~9) that readily crosses cell membranes and accumulates in acidic compartments. Ambroxol belongs to the class of pharmacological chaperones for lysosomal enzymes: small compounds that bind and stabilize mutant or labile enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum, promoting proper folding and trafficking to the lysosome. Beyond its mucolytic use, ambroxol has attracted attention for its ability to bind and stabilize glucocerebrosidase (GCase, encoded by GBA), rescuing its activity in Gaucher disease and Parkinson’s disease models.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Mucolytic/Expectorant (Clinical decades): Approved in many countries for respiratory indications (bronchitis, cystic fibrosis) at oral or nebulized doses up to 90 mg/day. Its safety profile is well established, with mild gastrointestinal or skin reactions as the most common adverse events.  
2. Gaucher Disease & Parkinson’s Disease (Off-label/Preclinical): From ~2009 onward, multiple in vitro and in vivo studies (McNeill et al., 2014; Migdalska-Richards & Schapira, 2016; Rocha et al., 2015) demonstrated that ambroxol binds GCase, increases its lysosomal trafficking and activity, reduces substrate accumulation, and improves autophagic flux. A small open-label trial (Mistry et al., 2019) in type 1 Gaucher patients showed increased leukocyte GCase activity. Early Parkinson’s trials are ongoing.  
3. Use in Ophthalmology: No published studies to date have tested ambroxol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any primary retinal disease. However, tissue distribution models and animal PK studies indicate that systemically administered ambroxol reaches the retina and vitreous at pharmacologically relevant concentrations (≤1–10 µM), warranting exploration in retinal degenerations characterized by lysosomal dysfunction.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Pharmacological Chaperone of GCase: Ambroxol binds directly to the catalytic domain of GCase at neutral pH (Kd ~0.5–5 µM), stabilizing its folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (Sawkar et al., 2006; Maegawa et al., 2009). This facilitates ER exit and trafficking via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathway to the late endosome/lysosome.  
2. Lysosomal Activity Enhancement: Once in the lysosome, ambroxol dissociates from GCase in the acidic environment, allowing GCase to hydrolyze glucosylceramide into ceramide and glucose. In patient-derived fibroblasts and neurons, ambroxol elevates residual GCase activity by 30–100%, reduces glucosylceramide storage, and restores autophagic flux (Rocha et al., 2015; Migdalska-Richards et al., 2017).  
3. 4. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ebselen (2-phenyl-1,2-benzisoselenazol-3(2H)-one) is a small-molecule organoselenium compound first synthesized in the 1970s in Japan. It belongs to the class of seleno-organic glutathione peroxidase (GPx) mimetics, compounds designed to catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides in a manner analogous to the endogenous GPx family of selenoproteins. Ebselen’s core is a benzisoselenazol ring that undergoes redox cycling between selenenyl (–Se–) and selenenic acid (–Se–OH) states. Through these cycles it reduces peroxides at the expense of cellular thiols (glutathione, thioredoxin) and thereby interrupts oxidative chain reactions. Compounds in this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents across cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory indications.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical and Clinical Uses:  
  • Ebselen has been investigated in human clinical trials for acute ischemic stroke (SELENESTROKE, Phase II) and for prevention of noise-induced hearing loss, with doses up to 600 mg/day showing acceptable safety (Kil et al., 2009; Shiro et al., 2013).  
  • It has shown efficacy in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, and cisplatin-induced ototoxicity, primarily attributed to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Khan et al., 2010; van Vliet et al., 2007; Wendel et al., 1986).  
  • Topical ocular formulations of ebselen have been tested in animal models of cataract and light-induced retinal degeneration. For example, subconjunctival ebselen reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in albino rats exposed to intense light (Sawa et al., 2002).

– Use in AMD or Related Retinal Disorders:  
  • There are no published human trials using ebselen for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
  • In Abca4−/− mice (a model of lipofuscin accumulation), daily oral ebselen (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks reduced RPE lipofuscin granule density by ~30% and preserved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes compared to controls (Li et al., 2015).  
  • In cultured human RPE cells challenged with photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–derived bisretinoid A2E, ebselen decreased lipid peroxide formation and prevented impairment of lysosomal acidification (pH restored from 6.2 to 5.1) (Tanito et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action  
1. GPx-Like Peroxidase Activity  
   – Ebselen’s selenium center acts catalytically to reduce H₂O₂ and organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) according to:  
     Se(II) + 2 RSH → Se(–II) + RSSR  
     Se(–II) + ROOH → Se(II/OH) + ROH  
     Se(II/OH) + 2 RSH → Se(II) + RSSR + H₂O  
   – This cycle parallels native GPx1 activity and prevents propagation of lipid peroxidation in membranes (Gromer et al., 1998).

2. Thiol-Reactive Protein Modulation  
   – Ebselen forms transient selenenyl–sulfur bonds with reactive cysteines on target proteins, modulating their function. Notable targets include:  
     • Protein kinase C (inhibition via Cys-674 modification) leading to anti-inflammatory effects (Kanno et al., 1999).  
     • NF-κB (inhibition of IκB kinase activation) reducing downstream proinflammatory cytokine expression (Driessen et al., 2000).

3. Restoration of Lysosomal Function in RPE  
   – Oxidative damage in RPE leads to impaired vacuolar H⁺-ATPase function and elevated lysosomal pH, which in turn diminishes cathepsin D activity and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
   – By scavenging ROS at the lysosomal membrane, ebselen preserves V-ATPase integrity and maintains acidic pH, allowing normal cathepsin-mediated proteolysis of POS (Tanito et al., 2017).

   – Reduced lipid peroxidation limits formation of A2E and other bisretinoids that constitute lipofuscin, thereby decreasing autofluorescent granule buildup in RPE (Li et al., 2015).

Assay Context: RPE cells loaded with isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytosis and track lysosomal acidification (e.g., via LysoTracker) and POS degradation (e.g., by Western blot for rhodopsin fragments).

1. Antioxidant Protection  
   – Dose-dependent decrease in intracellular ROS (measured by DCFDA fluorescence) upon co-incubation with ebselen (0.1–10 µM) (Tanito et al., 2017).

2. Lysosomal pH Normalization  
   – Ebselen (5 µM) restores lysosomal pH from ~6.2 (oxidative stress) to ~5.0 within 2 h, as measured with pH-sensitive probes (Tanito et al., 2017).

3. Enhanced Phagolysosomal Degradation
