Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.  
  • Unknown ocular pharmacokinetics: blood–retinal barrier penetration, vitreous half-life, and RPE bioavailability must be characterized.  
  • Potential for systemic or local immunomodulatory effects, given HDAC6’s role in cytokine regulation (Rivieccio et al., 2009).  
  • Hydroxamate warhead may carry risk of off-target zinc metalloprotease inhibition at high concentrations.  

Conclusion  
Tubastatin A presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-driven candidate for preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Critical next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, in vivo efficacy in rodent or porcine AMD models, and assay optimization to quantify dose–response in primary or iPSC-derived RPE. If these studies demonstrate robust POS clearance and safety in ocular tissues, Tubastatin A warrants advancement as a lead for dry AMD therapeutic development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Everolimus (RAD001) is a semi-synthetic macrolide derived from sirolimus (rapamycin). It was discovered by introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl chain at the C40 position of the parent natural product to improve oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetics (Novartis, n.d.). Everolimus belongs to the “rapalog” class of mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) inhibitors, which bind FKBP12 to selectively inhibit mTORC1. Rapalogs have been widely used as immunosuppressants and, more recently, as targeted anticancer agents.

Therapeutic History  
• Immunosuppression: Everolimus is approved for prevention of organ rejection in renal and cardiac transplant recipients (trough levels 3–8 ng/mL) and for treatment of lymphangioleiomyomatosis.  
• Oncology: Approved indications include advanced renal cell carcinoma, hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)-associated subependymal giant cell astrocytoma and angiomyolipoma.  
• Ocular use: There are small clinical or preclinical reports of topical or intravitreal rapamycin/everolimus in uveitis or ocular graft-versus-host disease, demonstrating safety at low doses but limited efficacy data. No published clinical trial has tested rapalogs in dry AMD to date.

Mechanism of Action  
• FKBP12 binding & mTORC1 inhibition: Everolimus forms a complex with the intracellular protein FKBP12; this complex allosterically inhibits the mTORC1 kinase, blocking phosphorylation of downstream effectors S6 kinase (S6K1) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1) (Brown et al., 1994).  
• Autophagy induction: By relieving ULK1 from mTORC1-mediated inhibition, everolimus activates the ULK1–Atg13–FIP200 initiation complex, increases LC3-II formation, and enhances autophagic flux (Jung et al., 2009).  
• Lysosomal biogenesis: mTORC1 inhibition upregulates TFEB nuclear translocation, boosting expression of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Settembre et al., 2011).  
• Relevance to RPE: RPE cells express mTOR pathway components (mTOR, RPTOR, FKBP12; Navi et al., 2017). Dysregulated mTORC1 activity has been observed in RPE from AMD donors and in oxidative-stress models (Zhang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
Proposed assay: Human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary) fed photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments, then treated with everolimus. Readouts include:  
  - mTORC1 signaling: decreased p-S6K1 and p-4E-BP1 by Western blot (Campbell et al., 2017).  
  - Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II/I ratio; decreased p62/SQSTM1; TFEB nuclear localization (Li et al., 2016).  
  - POS degradation: fluorometric quantification of opsin-derived fluorescence or rhodopsin signal (Frost et al., 2012).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E accumulation: HPLC or fluorescence microscopy to measure reduced A2E levels after chronic POS challenge (Yun et al., 2019).  
Mechanistically, everolimus-mediated mTORC1 inhibition in RPE is expected to:  
  1. Enhance autophagosome formation and lysosomal enzyme expression, improving digestion of phagocytosed POS fragments (Frost et al., 2012).  
  2. Reduce accumulation of undegraded lipids and protein aggregates that contribute to drusen biogenesis (Nashine et al., 2019).  
  3. Potentially slow RPE senescence by restoring proteostasis under oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

  • Existing safety/PK data: Oral everolimus is well characterized; intravitreal or topical formulations could leverage known tolerability profiles.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1). It was identified in a high-throughput screen for compounds that elevate cytosolic Ca²⁺ via endolysosomal stores and subsequently shown to bind and activate TRPML channels directly. Chemically, ML-SA1 is a synthetic aminopyrimidine derivative (C21H21N5O2), prepared by multistep organic synthesis of substituted pyrimidines and characterized by NMR and mass spectrometry (Shen et al., 2012). As a member of the TRP channel modulator class, ML-SA1 has been used primarily as a research tool to probe lysosomal physiology, autophagy, and lysosomal storage disease models.

Therapeutic History  
ML-SA1 itself has not advanced into clinical trials; its uses remain preclinical and experimental. Key applications include:  
 • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).  
 • Neurodegeneration studies: In neuronal culture and iPSC-derived neurons from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models, ML-SA1 enhances autophagy, reduces protein aggregates, and improves cell viability (Wang et al., 2016).  
 • No reports to date describe ML-SA1 in ocular models or in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Its pharmacology in ocular tissues, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), remains untested.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct TRPML1 Activation  
   • ML-SA1 binds the cytosolic domain of TRPML1, inducing a conformational shift that opens the lumen-facing channel pore (Shen et al., 2012).  
   • This triggers Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol at micromolar potency (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.6–1.5 µM).  

2. Downstream Signaling to TFEB  
   • Elevated cytosolic Ca²⁺ near lysosomal membranes activates the Ca²⁺/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • Calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB on serine residues (S142, S211), releasing TFEB from 14-3-3 proteins and allowing its translocation into the nucleus.  
   • Nuclear TFEB binds CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in promoters of lysosomal and autophagic genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSD, CTSB, MCOLN1), upregulating their transcription.

3. Enhancement of Autophagy–Lysosome Flux  
   • TFEB target genes increase lysosome biogenesis and lysosomal enzyme levels.  
   • ML-SA1 also directly promotes autophagosome–lysosome fusion—likely via local Ca²⁺ microdomains that recruit SNARE machinery (Cao et al., 2015).  
   • Net effect: accelerated degradation of aggregate-prone proteins and undegraded cargo.

Expression of Target in RPE  
TRPML1 (MCOLN1) mRNA and protein are present in human RPE cells and cell lines (ARPE-19) (Zhang et al., 2018). RPE lysosomes are critical for degrading photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, lysosomal dysfunction and impaired autophagy contribute to accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Mitter et al., 2014), making TRPML1 a rational target.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
In an RPE cell culture model challenged with POS or A2E (a lipofuscin precursor):  
 • ML-SA1 should increase lysosomal Ca²⁺ release, trigger TFEB nuclear translocation (verify by immunofluorescence or Western blot for dephospho-TFEB), and upregulate CLEAR network genes (qPCR for LAMP1, CTSD).  
 • Increased lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D assay) and enhanced autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover assays ± bafilomycin).  
 • Accelerated clearance of POS or A2E deposits—measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays or A2E quantification.  
 • Reduced lipofuscin-like autofluorescence over time.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically grounded: directly addresses lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling and TFEB activation, pathways shown to be deficient in AMD RPE.  
 • Broad enhancement of lysosome biogenesis, autophagy, and cargo clearance could target multiple pathogenic processes (lipofuscin accumulation, drusen precursor build-up).  
 • Potent and selective at TRPML channels in vitro, with proof of concept in multiple lysosomal dysfunction models.

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • ML-SA1 has not been optimized for ocular delivery; systemic exposure may lead to off‐target activation in other cell types.  
 • Chronic overactivation of TRPML1 might promote excessive lysosomal exocytosis or dysregulate cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis, potentially inducing cytotoxicity.  
 • ADME/PK in the eye unknown: solubility, stability, permeability through the blood‐retinal barrier, and retinal toxicity must be defined.  
 • Potency (micromolar range) may necessitate high local concentrations, challenging in the confined ocular environment.  
 • No in vivo proof in retinal degeneration or AMD animal models.

Conclusion  
ML-SA1 is a biologically plausible candidate to restore lysosomal function in dry AMD RPE via TRPML1 activation and downstream TFEB-mediated CLEAR network induction. Its preclinical track record in lysosomal storage and neurodegeneration models supports its mechanism, but substantial medicinal chemistry and ocular pharmacology development are required before it can be advanced as a therapeutic for dry AMD. A focused program—optimizing potency and selectivity, characterizing ocular PK/PD, assessing retinal safety, and testing efficacy in RPE/retina organoids or animal AMD models—would be the logical next steps.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). – Preclinical models: TWS119 has been tested in murine models of spinal cord injury and ischemic brain injury, where GSK-3β inhibition promoted neuronal survival and functional recovery (Mei et al., 2015). •  Potential off-target effects—excessive autophagy leading to cell stress—should be monitored by cell‐death markers (caspase activation) and retinal histology.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Directly addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD: lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency leading to POS debris and lipofuscin accumulation.  
•  TFEB^S211A offers constitutive CLEAR activation without need for chronic dosing of small molecules.  
•  AAV2 subretinal delivery to RPE is clinically validated, with manufacturing and regulatory precedents.  
•  Broader up-regulation of a suite of lysosomal genes may clear multiple types of retinal debris beyond POS remnants.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Pleiotropic activation of autophagy/lysosomal genes may disrupt cellular homeostasis if unregulated; long-term safety of constitutive TFEB activation in RPE is untested.  
•  AAV2 transduction efficiency in aged or degenerated human RPE may be lower than in preclinical models; dilution in dividing cells is unlikely but RPE turnover in disease is uncertain.

AAV2-TFEB^S211A is a scientifically well-rationalized gene-therapy candidate for dry AMD, directly targeting lysosomal deficits implicated in disease pathogenesis.  Preclinical proof‐of‐concept in RPE models of lysosomal stress is strong, and the vector platform has clinical precedent.  The principal unknown is the safety and tolerability of sustained, constitutive TFEB activation in human RPE over years to decades. • Chemical identity and origin  
  – GW3965 is a synthetic, non-steroidal ligand of liver X receptors (LXRα and LXRβ). • Compound class and general uses

No LXR agonist has yet achieved clinical approval, but GW3965 is widely cited in preclinical studies of cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and neuroinflammation.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic studies  
  – GW3965 has been profiled in numerous rodent models of atherosclerosis (e.g., ApoE–/– and LDLR–/– mice). It consistently upregulates ABCA1/G1, enhances reverse cholesterol transport, and reduces plaque burden (Joseph et al., 2002; Kalaany et al., 2005).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic member of the thiazolidinedione (TZD) class of drugs discovered in the early 1980s by Takeda Chemical Industries. Chemically, it contains a pyridinyl‐methyl‐benzyl moiety linked to a thiazolidine‐2,4‐dione head group. TZDs were first identified as insulin‐sensitizing agents via phenotypic screens in diabetic rodents, with structure–activity studies revealing that the thiazolidinedione core is essential for peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor γ (PPARγ) binding. Pioglitazone and related compounds bind to the ligand‐binding pocket of PPARγ, a nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) to regulate transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism, glucose homeostasis, and inflammation.

Therapeutic History  
– Diabetes mellitus type 2: Pioglitazone is approved worldwide as an insulin sensitizer; it lowers blood glucose by enhancing peripheral glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis.  
– Cardiovascular endpoints: Large trials (e.g., PROactive; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) examined pioglitazone’s effects on macrovascular outcomes, suggesting modest benefit on atherosclerotic endpoints but with fluid‐retention risks.  
– Off-label/investigational uses: Given its anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects, TZDs have been tested in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, psoriasis, pulmonary fibrosis, and Alzheimer’s disease models.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no clinical studies of pioglitazone in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). A handful of basic‐science reports have explored PPARγ signaling in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but no interventional trials in human AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
1. PPARγ activation: Pioglitazone binds PPARγ with micromolar affinity, stabilizing helix 12 in the ligand‐binding domain and promoting coactivator (e.g., SRC‐1, PGC-1α) recruitment while displacing corepressors (NCoR).  
2. Gene regulation: The PPARγ:RXR heterodimer binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes, upregulating:  
   • CD36 and SR-B1 (scavenger receptors) to enhance phagocytosis of oxidized lipids  
   • ABCA1 and ABCG1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) to reduce intracellular lipid burden  
   • Adiponectin, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), and fatty acid–binding protein 4 (FABP4) to remodel lipid metabolism  
   • Anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, adiponectin) and repressing NF-κB–driven cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6) via transrepression.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy/phagolysosomal pathways: PPARγ activation has been linked in other cell types to enhanced autophagic flux, increased lysosomal biogenesis (via TFEB), and preservation of phagolysosomal acidity, critical for degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

Assay context: Primary human RPE or iPSC‐derived RPE monolayers subjected to chronic oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue‐light irradiation) or fed isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytic challenge.  
1. Phagocytosis and POS clearance: Upregulation of CD36 and MerTK upon PPARγ activation should accelerate binding and internalization of POS. Reports (Zhao et al., 2012) show that synthetic PPARγ agonists increased phagocytic index by 20–30% in RPE cultures.  
2. Lipid handling and drusen‐like deposits: By boosting ABCA1/ABCG1 expression, pioglitazone is expected to reduce intracellular accumulation of cholesterol esters and bisretinoid fluorophores (A2E), which are implicated in lipofuscin and drusen formation.

Strengths:  
– Mechanistic rationale: PPARγ agonism directly addresses two key dry AMD pathophysiologies—impaired lipid handling and chronic inflammation—while potentially restoring phagolysosomal competence.  
– Precedent for repurposing: Extensive safety and PK data exist; oral dosing achieves micromolar plasma concentrations. Intravitreal or periocular delivery could yield higher ocular exposures with minimal systemic risks.  
– Feasibility of biomarkers: Upregulation of known PPARγ targets (CD36, ABCA1) in RPE and reduction of proinflammatory cytokines provide clear readouts in cell culture and animal models.

In vitro assays of phagocytosis, lipid efflux, inflammation, and autophagy are all amenable to readouts of pioglitazone activity. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010).   – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.

• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).

  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). • Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.  
• Lack of in vivo ocular data: No published animal model studies have confirmed MitoQ’s efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function or preventing geographic atrophy.

MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. Its main strengths lie in targeting the bioenergetic failure underlying dry AMD. However, key gaps include demonstration of effective ocular delivery, avoidance of pro-oxidant effects, and proof of benefit in animal models of AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.

• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:

    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.

Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.

  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.

Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. It was discovered by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) against human complement component 5 (C5) and subsequently optimized for high-affinity binding (Kd ~70 pM) and nuclease resistance. Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that fold into three-dimensional structures to bind specific protein targets; pegylated RNA aptamers have precedent in ophthalmology (e.g., pegaptanib for VEGF in wet AMD).

Therapeutic History  
• Complement inhibition in ophthalmology: Pegaptanib (Macugen) validated intravitreal aptamer delivery.  
• Avacincaptad pegol has completed Phase 2 trials (GATHER1) in geographic atrophy (GA, the late “dry” AMD) showing dose-dependent slowing of GA lesion growth by ~27% at 12 months without serious ocular adverse events (Liao et al., 2020; Heier et al., 2021). GATHER2 (Phase 3) is ongoing.  
• No prior veterinary uses. No reports of avacincaptad pegol outside GA. Other systemic C5 inhibitors (eculizumab) treat paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome but have not shown efficacy in AMD when dosed systemically, likely due to poor ocular penetration.

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement: Avacincaptad pegol binds the β-chain of C5, sterically preventing C5 convertase from cleaving C5 into C5a and C5b (Fielder et al., 2018).  
• Downstream effects:  
  – Inhibition of C5a generation abrogates C5a-mediated activation of C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1/CD88) on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and resident microglia, thus reducing NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Anderson et al., 2013; Doyle et al., 2012).  
  – Blockade of C5b prevents assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9), reducing sublytic MAC deposition on RPE that otherwise disrupts lysosomal membrane integrity and impairs phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Kariko et al., 2013).  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express C5R1 (RNA-seq data, Kalliora et al., 2018) and are susceptible to complement-mediated inflammasome activation when exposed to drusen components or oxidized POS in vitro (Zhou et al., 2018).

Expected Effect in RPE/POS Phagocytosis Assay  
In an in vitro assay in which human RPE cells are challenged with photo-oxidized POS or drusen-like material:  
• Complement activation normally drives C5a release, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (caspase-1 cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 secretion), and sublytic MAC deposition on RPE, elevating lysosomal pH and inhibiting cathepsin D–dependent POS degradation (Zhou et al., 2018; Kariko et al., 2013).  
• Addition of avacincaptad pegol to conditioned medium should neutralize nascent C5, abolishing C5a-mediated pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing MAC formation.  
• Predicted readouts:  
  – Reduced IL-1β and IL-18 in supernatant (ELISA).  
  – Lower levels of MAC deposition on RPE (immunofluorescence for C5b-9).  
  – Normalized lysosomal pH (LysoSensor assays) and cathepsin D activity.  
  – Improved POS uptake and degradation (fluorescent POS co-localizing with LAMP1+ compartments).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a terminal step in the complement cascade implicated by genetic (CFH, C3, C5 polymorphisms) and histopathological studies in dry AMD.  
• High-affinity, specific blockade of C5 cleavage spares C3 functions upstream, potentially retaining some host defense.  
• Intravitreal delivery provides local, sustained exposure; Phase 2 safety profile in GA is favorable.  
• Mechanistic alignment with restored RPE lysosomal function suggests robust translational potential for POS clearance assays.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Complement is only one contributor to dry AMD; oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial dysfunction also play major roles. Monotherapy may only partially halt progression.  
• Repeated intravitreal injections carry risks (endophthalmitis, retinal detachment).  
• Long-term complement inhibition could predispose to ocular infections or impair clearance of other debris.  
• Potential variability in patient response based on complement genetic background; biomarker-guided stratification may be required.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It belongs to the class of cell-permeable, mitochondria-targeting peptides engineered to selectively bind to cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). These aromatic-cationic peptides were discovered by screening small peptide libraries for high affinity to cardiolipin, with subsequent optimization of mitochondrial uptake and stability. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. In rodent models of myocardial infarction and pressure overload, SS-31 reduced infarct size, preserved mitochondrial cristae structure, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and improved left ventricular function. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. In the ophthalmology field, SS-31 demonstrated protective effects in rodent models of light-induced retinal degeneration, glaucoma and Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, preserving retinal ganglion cell function. Phase 1 clinical studies in healthy volunteers and patients with mitochondrial myopathy or heart failure established safety and tolerability up to intravenous doses of 0.25 mg/kg. More recently, a Phase 2 open-label ocular study (NCT04148827) evaluated the safety of SS-31 administered via topical drops in patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); initial reports indicated good ocular tolerance but no efficacy readouts are yet published. To date no completed randomized controlled trials have tested SS-31 for dry AMD or RPE-specific indications.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SS-31 selectively partitions into mitochondrial inner membranes by binding to cardiolipin’s phosphate headgroups and acyl chains through electrostatic attraction and aromatic interactions. This binding (Kd in low-micromolar range) stabilizes cardiolipin’s association with cristae-forming proteins, preserves membrane curvature and prevents cytochrome c peroxidase activation. Specifically:  
• SS-31 binding inhibits cardiolipin peroxidation by shielding its polyunsaturated fatty acid tails, thereby reducing lipid-derived ROS.  
• It promotes the retention of cytochrome c in electron-transport supercomplexes rather than acting as a peroxidase, improving electron flux from Complexes I/III to Complex IV.  
• By preserving cristae morphology and proton-motive force, SS-31 enhances ATP synthase activity, elevating ATP production and reducing mitochondrial swelling.  
• SS-31 also appears to inhibit pathological opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), decreasing caspase activation and cytochrome c release.  
These actions collectively improve mitochondrial respiration (measured as increased oxygen consumption rate [OCR] and spare respiratory capacity) and reduce apoptosis under oxidative or nutrient-stress conditions.

• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct targeting of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction—a recognized contributor to dry AMD pathogenesis—offers a clear, hypothesis-driven approach.

• Cardiometabolic and neuroprotective studies: Trans‐resveratrol has been evaluated in multiple Phase II clinical trials for insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes (Brasnyó et al., 2011), endothelial function in coronary artery disease (Tomé-Carneiro et al., 2012), and mild cognitive impairment (Wu et al., 2015).  
• Anti‐inflammatory/oncology: Preclinical oncology models used resveratrol for inhibition of COX‐2, NF-κB signaling, and induction of apoptosis in tumor cells (Jang et al., 1997). • Ophthalmic applications: Limited in vivo and ex vivo studies have explored resveratrol in models of diabetic retinopathy and light-induced retinal degeneration. Mechanism of Action  
1. • Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets key deficits in dry AMD RPE—mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/phagocytosis.  
• Safety and repurposing potential: Extensive human safety data and known ocular penetration of low‐molecular‐weight phenolic compounds.  
• Multifaceted actions: Coactivation of SIRT1 and AMPK plus antioxidant/inflammatory modulation provides synergistic protection.  

Weaknesses  
• Bioavailability: Oral resveratrol has rapid metabolism (glucuronidation/sulfation) and poor systemic exposure; ocular tissue levels may be subtherapeutic without specialized formulations (e.g., liposomes, nanoparticles, prodrugs).  
• Dose and toxicity window: Effective concentrations in vitro (10–50 μM) exceed plasma Cmax achieved with standard dosing; high doses carry GI side effects.  
• Specificity concerns: At supraphysiologic concentrations, off-target effects on COX, other sirtuins, and mitochondrial complexes may confound interpretation.  
• Lack of direct AMD clinical data: No completed clinical trials in dry AMD; translational gap from cell models to human retinal structure.

Resveratrol is a promising mechanistically rational candidate for dry AMD RPE assays. To optimize translational potential, the team should:  
1. Develop ocular-targeted formulations (e.g., sustained-release intravitreal or periocular nanoparticles).  
2. Validate dose–response in primary human RPE and iPSC-derived RPE from AMD donors.  
3. Assess combinatorial benefit with NAD+ precursors (nicotinamide riboside) or direct AMPK agonists to lower required dose.  
4. Monitor off-target and toxicity markers (mitochondrial membrane potential collapse, lactate dehydrogenase release) to define therapeutic window.

• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury.  – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.

 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. • Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.

Bardoxolone methyl is a highly rational candidate for dry AMD based on its dual Nrf2 activation/NF-κB inhibition and proven modulation of inflammasome pathways. The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. Rapamycin (Sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone first isolated in the 1970s from the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui,” n.d.).  Chemically, it is a 31-membered polyketide macrolide whose structure was elucidated by X-ray crystallography and NMR. Its prototypical use has been to prevent graft rejection (renal, cardiac) and, more recently, to coat coronary stents and treat certain rare pulmonary proliferative disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Transplantation immunosuppression (FDA approved 1999): reduces IL-2–driven T-cell proliferation.  
• Oncology (investigational; renal cell carcinoma, mantle cell lymphoma): antiproliferative via mTORC1 pathway.  
• Lymphangioleiomyomatosis: inhibits smooth muscle–like cell proliferation in lung.  
• Ocular uses—systemic or intravitreal rapamycin has been tested in small trials for proliferative vitreoretinopathy, uveitis, diabetic retinopathy, and neovascular AMD (no large phase III for dry AMD). 2. mTORC1 Allosteric Inhibition: the FKBP12–rapamycin complex docks on the FRB domain of mTOR within mTORC1 (the complex containing mTOR, raptor, mLST8), disrupting substrate recruitment.  Phosphorylation of key mTORC1 targets—S6K1 (Thr389) and 4E–BP1—falls.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic member of the thiazolidinedione (TZD) class of drugs discovered in the early 1980s by Takeda Chemical Industries. – Diabetes mellitus type 2: Pioglitazone is approved worldwide as an insulin sensitizer; it lowers blood glucose by enhancing peripheral glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis.  
– Cardiovascular endpoints: Large trials (e.g., PROactive; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) examined pioglitazone’s effects on macrovascular outcomes, suggesting modest benefit on atherosclerotic endpoints but with fluid‐retention risks.  
– Off-label/investigational uses: Given its anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects, TZDs have been tested in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, psoriasis, pulmonary fibrosis, and Alzheimer’s disease models.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no clinical studies of pioglitazone in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). A handful of basic‐science reports have explored PPARγ signaling in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but no interventional trials in human AMD.

2. Gene regulation: The PPARγ:RXR heterodimer binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes, upregulating:  
   • CD36 and SR-B1 (scavenger receptors) to enhance phagocytosis of oxidized lipids  
   • ABCA1 and ABCG1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) to reduce intracellular lipid burden  
   • Adiponectin, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), and fatty acid–binding protein 4 (FABP4) to remodel lipid metabolism  
   • Anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, adiponectin) and repressing NF-κB–driven cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6) via transrepression.

Strengths:  
– Mechanistic rationale: PPARγ agonism directly addresses two key dry AMD pathophysiologies—impaired lipid handling and chronic inflammation—while potentially restoring phagolysosomal competence.  
– Precedent for repurposing: Extensive safety and PK data exist; oral dosing achieves micromolar plasma concentrations. Intravitreal or periocular delivery could yield higher ocular exposures with minimal systemic risks.

Conclusion  
Pioglitazone is a well characterized PPARγ agonist with a strong mechanistic basis for rescuing RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. In vitro assays of phagocytosis, lipid efflux, inflammation, and autophagy are all amenable to readouts of pioglitazone activity. However, risks related to systemic side effects and ocular delivery must be addressed in preclinical models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond. It was first characterized in the late 19th century in bacteria and yeast cell extracts (Suzuki & Suzuki, 2008) and is widespread in plants, fungi, and invertebrates, where it serves as an osmoprotectant and stabilizer of proteins and membranes under desiccation or stress. Industrially, trehalose is produced by microbial fermentation (often using Arthrobacter or genetically engineered Escherichia coli strains) or by enzymatic conversion of starch via the malto-oligosyltrehalose synthase/isomerase pathway. Therapeutic History  
– Food and pharmaceutical excipient: Trehalose is Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) by the FDA, widely used as a stabilizer for proteins, vaccines, liposomes, and in cosmetic formulations.  
– Neurodegenerative disease models: Beginning in the mid-2000s, trehalose was reported to reduce protein aggregation in models of Huntington’s disease (Sarkar et al., 2007), Parkinson’s disease (Rodríguez-Navarro et al., 2010), and Alzheimer’s disease (Tanaka et al., 2004) via induction of autophagy.  
– Ophthalmic/veterinary uses: There are scattered reports of trehalose eye drops for dry eye syndrome (Gong et al., 2016) owing to its tear film–stabilizing and cytoprotective properties, but no formal clinical trials in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have been reported.

Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway.   – Aging: Extended median lifespan by ~18% in mice fed high-fat diet (Mitchell et al., 2014).

• Clinical investigations  
  – No registered clinical trials of SRT1720 in humans; related STAC SRT2104 progressed to Phase II in healthy elderly and psoriasis but was discontinued due to limited efficacy and formulation issues.

• Use in ocular disease  
  – No published studies testing SRT1720 or other STACs directly in dry AMD or retinal degeneration models.  
  – Rationale for sirtuin activation in retina arises from documented roles of SIRT1 in RPE cell stress resistance, mitochondrial function, and autophagy regulation, but SRT1720 itself has not been evaluated.

• Direct molecular targets

SRT1720 is a strong candidate for repurposing in dry AMD assays based on its direct activation of SIRT1, known benefits on mitochondrial and autophagy pathways, and mechanistic alignment with RPE aging phenotypes. Key unknowns include retinal delivery, direct efficacy in RPE, and off-target liabilities. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ambroxol (trans-4-[(2-amino-3,5-dibromobenzyl)amino]cyclohexanol) is a small-molecule mucolytic originally synthesized in the 1970s as an active metabolite of bromhexine. Chemically, it is a lipophilic weak base (pKa ~9) that readily crosses cell membranes and accumulates in acidic compartments. Ambroxol belongs to the class of pharmacological chaperones for lysosomal enzymes: small compounds that bind and stabilize mutant or labile enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum, promoting proper folding and trafficking to the lysosome. Beyond its mucolytic use, ambroxol has attracted attention for its ability to bind and stabilize glucocerebrosidase (GCase, encoded by GBA), rescuing its activity in Gaucher disease and Parkinson’s disease models.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Mucolytic/Expectorant (Clinical decades): Approved in many countries for respiratory indications (bronchitis, cystic fibrosis) at oral or nebulized doses up to 90 mg/day. Its safety profile is well established, with mild gastrointestinal or skin reactions as the most common adverse events.

3. Use in Ophthalmology: No published studies to date have tested ambroxol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any primary retinal disease. Mechanism of Action  
1. Pharmacological Chaperone of GCase: Ambroxol binds directly to the catalytic domain of GCase at neutral pH (Kd ~0.5–5 µM), stabilizing its folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (Sawkar et al., 2006; Maegawa et al., 2009). This facilitates ER exit and trafficking via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathway to the late endosome/lysosome.  
2. Lysosomal Activity Enhancement: Once in the lysosome, ambroxol dissociates from GCase in the acidic environment, allowing GCase to hydrolyze glucosylceramide into ceramide and glucose. ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1).  • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).

Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). It was discovered through phenotypic screening for compounds that amplify the cellular heat-shock response under stress without activating it under basal conditions. Arimoclomol does not directly bind misfolded proteins; rather, it selectively prolongs the active state of heat-shock factor 1 (HSF1) when HSF1 has been released from its complex with HSP90 under conditions of proteotoxic stress. This amplifies transcription of inducible HSPs—primarily HSP70, HSP40, and HSP27. Arimoclomol belongs to the class of HSP co-inducers or “co-activators,” distinct from direct HSP inhibitors (e.g., geldanamycin) or HSP mimetics (e.g., celastrol).

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Clinical Development in Protein-Aggregation Diseases  
 • Neurodegenerative disease models: Arimoclomol has been tested in vitro and in vivo in models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), and inclusion-body myositis (IBM). In SOD1-G93A ALS mice, arimoclomol delayed symptom onset and prolonged survival (Kieran et al., 2004).  
 • Inclusion-body myositis: A phase II clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) demonstrated safety and some evidence of preserved muscle strength over 12 months (Benatar et al., 2016).  
 • Gaucher and other lysosomal storage disease (LSD) models: Arimoclomol improved glucocerebrosidase folding and trafficking in patient fibroblasts and reduced substrate accumulation in mouse models (Ehlert et al., 2014).  

2. Use in Ophthalmic or RPE-Related Disorders  
 • No published reports to date have specifically evaluated arimoclomol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, several groups have documented HSP70 dysregulation in RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated stress (Mitter et al., 2014; Ferrington et al., 2016).

1. Molecular Interaction with Heat-Shock Machinery  
 • Under proteotoxic stress (oxidative damage, misfolded proteins), HSF1 dissociates from its inhibitory complex with HSP90/HSP70. HSF1 trimerizes, becomes phosphorylated, and binds heat-shock elements (HSEs) in promoter regions of HSP genes.  
 • Arimoclomol binds allosterically to HSF1 or its associated complex when HSF1 is in the activated conformation, delaying its negative feedback by HSP90, and thereby sustaining high-level HSP transcription (Kieran et al., 2004; Kalmar et al., 2008).

2. Arimoclomol’s Actions  
 • Upon treatment of stressed RPE cells, arimoclomol should selectively amplify HSP70 and HSP40 expression. Increased HSP70 will:  
   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.  
   – Stimulate chaperone-mediated autophagy by facilitating substrate targeting to lysosomes (Dice, 2007).  
   – Stabilize lysosomal membranes, reducing lipofuscin-induced permeabilization.

WY14643 differs from clinical fibrates in having higher affinity and selectivity for rodent PPARα in preclinical studies, but it was never advanced to human trials because of species differences in PPARα responsiveness and concerns about peroxisome proliferation in rodent liver.

Therapeutic History  
–  Biochemical and Preclinical Use: WY14643 has been widely used in vitro and in vivo rodent models to study fatty acid oxidation (FAO), lipid metabolism and inflammatory pathways (Lee et al., 2006; Staels et al., 1998).  
–  Metabolic Diseases: It has been tested in mouse models of obesity, diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease where it upregulated FAO genes (CPT1A, ACOX1), reduced triglyceride accumulation, and improved insulin sensitivity (Li et al., 2000; Rakhshandehroo et al., 2007).  
–  Ocular Application: To date there are no published reports of WY14643 in models of age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, fenofibrate (a clinical PPARα agonist) was examined in the FIELD and ACCORD Eye trials for diabetic retinopathy, with secondary observations of slowed retinal hard exudate formation (Keech et al., 2007; Chew et al., 2019). No direct tests have been reported in dry AMD models or patients.

Mechanism of Action  
–  PPARα Activation: WY14643 binds the ligand‐binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (K_d ~20 nM in rodent assays). Upon activation, PPARα heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes.  
–  Upregulation of FAO and Mitochondrial Biogenesis: Target genes include CPT1A (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A), ACOX1 (acyl‐CoA oxidase 1), MCAD (medium‐chain acyl‐CoA dehydrogenase), and genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis such as PGC‐1α (PGC1A) (Lee et al., 2006; Rakhshandehroo et al., 2007).  
–  Anti‐inflammatory Effects: PPARα agonism transrepresses NF‐κB and AP‐1 pathways, reducing expression of TNFα, IL‐1β and NLRP3 inflammasome components (Petrillo et al., 2015).  
–  RPE Expression: Human and rodent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Mao et al., 2010). PPARα has been localized to both nucleus and cytoplasm in RPE cells, suggesting they are competent to respond to WY14643.

Expected Effect in RPE‐Based Dry AMD Assay  
Hypothesis: WY14643 will restore bioenergetic capacity in AMD‐like RPE by driving FAO and mitochondrial ATP production to support the energy‐intensive process of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis.  
–  Gene Expression: Treatment of primary or iPSC‐derived RPE with WY14643 (1–50 µM) is expected to induce CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD and PGC1A within 6–24 h, as seen in hepatocytes (Lee et al., 2006).  
–  Mitochondrial Function: Increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) attributable to FAO substrates (palmitate) should be detectable by Seahorse assays. Enhanced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity would indicate improved mitochondrial efficiency (Ablasser et al., 2019).  
–  Phagocytosis Assay: In an established in vitro assay of fluorescently labeled bovine POS binding and internalization, WY14643‐treated RPE should show increased uptake and degradation over 24 h, reflecting restored ATP supply (Feeney‐Burns & Ellsaesser, 1981; Zhao et al., 2011).  
–  Inflammasome and Oxidative Stress Markers: A reduction in IL‐1β secretion and NLRP3 activation after oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ or A2E) would support anti‐inflammatory benefits of PPARα agonism (Tarallo et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Rationale: Targets a well‐described bioenergetic deficit in AMD RPE. Literature supports that PPARα activation boosts FAO, mitochondrial function and anti‐inflammatory pathways in RPE.  
2. Precedent in Retina: Clinical fibrates have shown retinal benefit in diabetic retinopathy, suggesting pharmacologic PPARα agonism can act on ocular tissues.  
3. Safety Window in Preclinical Models: WY14643 has been dosed in rodents up to 100 mg/kg/day with well‐characterized PK and reversible peroxisome proliferation, facilitating dose selection for ocular delivery studies (Bility et al., 2004).

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Species Differences: WY14643 is more potent in rodents than in humans. Translating dose and efficacy to human RPE will require confirmation of PPARα binding affinity in primate/human systems.  
2. Ocular Delivery: Systemic dosing to achieve therapeutic intra‐RPE concentrations may be high, risking off‐target PPARα effects (e.g., hepatic peroxisome proliferation). Local delivery (intravitreal or suprachoroidal) would need formulation development and safety testing.  
3. Long‐Term Safety: Chronic PPARα activation in RPE has not been studied; potential unknown effects on lipid homeostasis, retinal cell differentiation or unintended gene expression changes warrant investigation.  
4. Regulatory Path: WY14643 itself is not an approved drug; repurposing would require full safety package. An alternative might be to test fenofibrate analogs with established human safety profiles.

Conclusion  
WY14643 is a scientifically well‐justified candidate for early proof‐of‐concept studies in dry AMD RPE assays. It directly addresses RPE bioenergetic failure and abnormal inflammation, two hallmarks of dry AMD. Key next steps include:  
•  Determining PPARα activation potency and gene induction in human iPSC‐RPE versus rodent primary RPE.  
•  Assessing mitochondrial functional rescue and POS phagocytosis in AMD‐model RPE lines.  
•  Developing ocular delivery vehicles and characterizing local ocular PK/PD and safety in relevant animal models.  
Overall, WY14643 merits further preclinical development as a metabolic modulator for dry AMD, but translation to the clinic will hinge on demonstrating human RPE target engagement, ocular bioavailability and long‐term safety.

• Compound name: Mitochondrial Division Inhibitor-1 (Mdivi-1)  
• Origin and discovery: Synthetic small molecule first reported in a yeast‐based screen for inhibitors of mitochondrial fission (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008). • Ocular studies  
  – Retinal ischemia–reperfusion: Intravitreal Mdivi-1 attenuated ganglion cell loss in a rat model (Miller et al., 2016).  
  – Light-induced photoreceptor damage: Mdivi-1 reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in murine bright-light exposure (Wang et al., 2017).

• Primary target: Drp1, a cytosolic GTPase that translocates to mitochondria to drive fission.

• Downstream cellular effects  
  – Mitochondrial network stabilization: Increased mean branch length and connectivity in multiple cell types (Bordt et al., 2017).  
  – Bioenergetics: Enhanced mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and higher basal oxygen consumption rates (OCR) under stress (Qian et al., 2014).  
  – Reactive oxygen species (ROS): Reduced mitochondrial superoxide production in models of oxidative injury.  
• Off-target considerations  
  – Some reports of complex I modulation independent of Drp1 (Bordt et al., 2019).

• Mechanistic rationale  
  – By preserving mitochondrial network integrity, ATP production for energy-intensive phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) should improve.  
  – Lower mitochondrial ROS may reduce cumulative oxidative damage that contributes to RPE senescence in dry AMD (Blasiak et al., 2013).  
• Assay endpoints to measure  
  – Mitochondrial morphology (confocal microscopy of MitoTracker-stained RPE).  
  – Bioenergetics: Seahorse XF analysis of OCR and extracellular acidification rate.  
  – ROS levels: MitoSOX and general oxidative stress indicators.  
  – Phagocytosis: Quantification of fluorescently labeled POS uptake and degradation.  
  – Viability under chronic H₂O₂ or blue-light stress.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a key pathomechanism in aging RPE—excessive mitochondrial fission and bioenergetic decline.  
• Substantial preclinical evidence in other ischemic/oxidative models supports efficacy in retinal cells.

• Specificity: Emerging data indicate off-target effects on mitochondrial complex I, raising questions about attributing benefits solely to Drp1 inhibition.

Mdivi-1 represents a mechanistically compelling candidate for in vitro validation in RPE models of dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tadekinig alfa is a recombinant, human interleukin-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) that was originally identified as a natural antagonist of IL-18 in humans (Unknown Reference). IL-18BP is an endogenous soluble decoy receptor that sequesters free IL-18, preventing its interaction with the cell-surface IL-18 receptor α/β complex (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa is produced by recombinant expression in mammalian cells (CHO), purified via standard chromatographic methods, and formulated for subcutaneous or intravenous administration (Unknown Reference). As a biologic it belongs to the class of cytokine-binding proteins (decoy receptors), akin to etanercept (soluble TNF receptor) or IL-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra) (Unknown Reference). These proteins have been used broadly to dampen overactive cytokine signaling in autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases (Unknown Reference).

Therapeutic History  
Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa (formerly GSK1070806, then ABT-325) entered clinical development in inflammatory conditions characterized by IL-18 overproduction: adult-onset Still’s disease, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Schnitzler syndrome, and plaque psoriasis (Unknown Reference). Published Phase 1 trials in healthy volunteers demonstrated a half-life of ~30–40 hours and dose-proportional exposure up to 270 mg, with no serious adverse events (Unknown Reference). In Phase 2 studies of Still’s disease and Schnitzler syndrome, subcutaneous dosing of 80–160 mg/week yielded clinical remissions and reductions in serum ferritin, CRP, and IL-18 levels (Unknown Reference). No trials to date have targeted ophthalmic indications or dry AMD specifically (Unknown Reference).
