IL-18 is an inflammasome-activated cytokine released by RPE cells and infiltrating myeloid cells in response to DAMPs (e.g., Alu RNA, oxidized lipids) (Unknown Reference). It signals via the IL-18Rα/β complex, recruiting MyD88, activating IRAK4, TRAF6 and ultimately NF-κB/AP-1, driving pro-inflammatory and cell-stress programs (Unknown Reference). In RPE, chronic IL-18 signaling has been shown to impair the expression or function of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin receptors, critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, and to destabilize mitochondrial homeostasis (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa binds circulating and local IL-18, sterically preventing its engagement of IL-18Rα (Unknown Reference). In vitro binding studies report a K_D of ~0.4 nM for IL-18 (Unknown Reference). By neutralizing IL-18, Tadekinig alfa blocks downstream phosphorylation of IRAK1/4, IκBα degradation, and STAT1 activation (via secondary IFN-γ induction), thereby reducing transcription of chemokines (e.g., CXCL9/10) and inflammasome amplifiers (Unknown Reference).

In an RPE cell culture model—whether using primary human fetal RPE or ARPE-19—IL-18 exposure (10–50 ng/mL) reproduces features of dry AMD: reduced MerTK expression, lower POS uptake, increased reactive oxygen species, and up-regulated inflammasome components (NLRP3, caspase-1) (Unknown Reference). Co-treatment with Tadekinig alfa at molar ratios ≥1:1 (IL-18BP:IL-18) is expected to restore MerTK and integrin signaling, normalize phagocytic index, decrease caspase-1 cleavage, and preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (assessed by JC-1 or TMRM) (Unknown Reference). Gene expression assays and immunoblotting can confirm reduced NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (Unknown Reference). Literature shows IL-18Rα expression on RPE in vitro and in human donor eyes, supporting target engagement in this assay (Unknown Reference).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Target Specificity: Directly neutralizes a key inflammasome cytokine implicated in RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Unknown Reference).  
• Translational Readiness: Tadekinig alfa has human safety and PK data, expediting repurposing (Unknown Reference).  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Multiple models (Alu RNA, light-induced stress) link IL-18 to impaired POS phagocytosis and RPE atrophy (Unknown Reference).  
• Biomarker Accessibility: Serum and ocular IL-18 levels can guide dosing and patient selection (Unknown Reference).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Contextual Role of IL-18: Some studies suggest protective roles for IL-18 in subretinal neovascular models, raising the possibility of undesirable effects on vessel homeostasis (Unknown Reference).  
• Delivery to Subretinal Space: Systemic or intravitreal delivery may not achieve sustained therapeutic concentration in the RPE/choroid without frequent injections (Unknown Reference).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Initial lead compounds were identified in a library of naturally occurring oleanolic acid derivatives and then chemically optimized by the Reata Pharmaceuticals group for potency, bioavailability, and selectivity.  
• Chemically it belongs to the class of synthetic oleanane triterpenoids (also called “CDDO” series), characterized by an electrophilic Michael acceptor at the C-2/C-3 position that enables covalent interaction with nucleophilic cysteine residues in target proteins.  
• The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).  

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Assay  
Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
1. Nrf2 in RPE: Human and murine RPE express basal Nrf2 at rest and upregulate it under oxidative challenge (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Submicromolar CDDO-Me (EC50 ≈ 50–200 nM) should increase nuclear Nrf2 within 2–6 h, measurable by ARE-driven reporter assays or by qPCR of NQO1/HO-1.  
2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.  
3. Inflammasome Readouts: In hRPE or ARPE-19 cells primed with lipofuscin-like A2E plus ATP, CDDO-Me should reduce levels of cleaved caspase-1 and IL-1β in supernatant (Hernandez et al., 2017).  
4. Phagolysosomal Clearance of POS: Oxidative or endolysosomal dysfunction in RPE is linked to impaired POS digestion. By restoring redox balance and improving lysosomal biogenesis (via Nrf2-mediated upregulation of lysosomal genes), CDDO-Me may accelerate clearance of fluorescently labeled POS in pulse-chase assays (Zhao et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.  
• Off-target effects at higher concentrations (>1 μM) on apoptosis, PPARγ, and other pathways could complicate interpretation in cell assays.  
• ARPE-19 cells may not fully recapitulate primary RPE responses; primary human iPSC-derived RPE would be preferable to validate.  

Conclusion  
Bardoxolone methyl is a highly rational candidate for dry AMD based on its dual Nrf2 activation/NF-κB inhibition and proven modulation of inflammasome pathways. The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.

Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). • Chemical identity and origin  
  – GW3965 is a synthetic, non-steroidal ligand of liver X receptors (LXRα and LXRβ). No LXR agonist has yet achieved clinical approval, but GW3965 is widely cited in preclinical studies of cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and neuroinflammation.

• Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic studies

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Resveratrol (3,5,4′-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic stilbene first identified in the roots of Veratrum grandiflorum and later isolated at high levels from the skin of red grapes (Siemann & Creasy, 1992). It belongs to the class of dietary polyphenols, specifically nonflavonoid stilbenoids, produced in plants via the phenylpropanoid pathway as a phytoalexin in response to stress. Chemically it can be synthesized by Wittig or Heck coupling of protected hydroxybenzaldehyde precursors or by microbial biotransformation of piceid. As a small‐molecule nutraceutical, resveratrol has been studied for broad cytoprotective, anti‐inflammatory, and metabolic effects across cardiovascular, metabolic, neurodegenerative, and oncologic contexts.

Therapeutic History  
• Cardiometabolic and neuroprotective studies: Trans‐resveratrol has been evaluated in multiple Phase II clinical trials for insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes (Brasnyó et al., 2011), endothelial function in coronary artery disease (Tomé-Carneiro et al., 2012), and mild cognitive impairment (Wu et al., 2015).  
• Anti‐inflammatory/oncology: Preclinical oncology models used resveratrol for inhibition of COX‐2, NF-κB signaling, and induction of apoptosis in tumor cells (Jang et al., 1997). Initial safety studies in humans established tolerability up to 5 g/day with dose-limiting GI upset (Brown et al., 2010).  
• Ophthalmic applications: Limited in vivo and ex vivo studies have explored resveratrol in models of diabetic retinopathy and light-induced retinal degeneration. A small pilot trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) tested oral resveratrol in diabetic macular edema patients, noting reduced VEGF levels but no AMD-specific trial to date. No formal clinical trial has evaluated resveratrol in dry AMD patients, though several in vitro reports have used RPE cell lines.

Mechanism of Action  
1. SIRT1 activation: Resveratrol directly binds and allosterically activates SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent class III histone deacetylase (HDAC), lowering its K m for acetylated substrates such as p53, FOXO3a, and PGC-1α (Borra et al., 2005; Howitz et al., 2003). In RPE, SIRT1 deacetylates and activates PGC-1α, promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant gene transcription (Haigis & Guarente, 2006).  
2. AMPK coactivation: Through indirect stimulation of the upstream kinase LKB1 and mild inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase, resveratrol raises the AMP/ATP ratio, leading to phosphorylation and activation of AMPK (Zang et al., 2006). AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 to initiate autophagy and inhibits mTORC1, thereby enhancing autophagic flux.  
3. Antioxidant and anti‐inflammatory actions: Resveratrol upregulates Nrf2-driven expression of HO-1 and NQO1, scavenges ROS, and represses NF-κB–mediated cytokine production (Csiszar et al., 2006). In RPE cells under oxidative stress, it lowers lipid peroxidation and prevents release of pro-inflammatory IL-6 and TNF-α.  
4. Autophagy and phagocytosis enhancement: By coactivating SIRT1/AMPK pathways, resveratrol accelerates autophagosome formation (increased LC3-II/I ratio) and lysosomal degradation (enhanced LAMP2a), processes critical for phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by RPE (Kim et al., 2013).

In an in vitro assay using primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cells challenged with oxidized POS or A2E/lipofuscin analogs, resveratrol is expected to:  
• Activate SIRT1: Increase deacetylation of PGC-1α, as demonstrated by reduced acetyl-PGC-1α in Western blots (Zhang et al., 2013). Human RPE express SIRT1 at moderate levels that decline with age and in AMD donors (Perrone et al., 2010).

• Lower ROS: Measured by DCFDA fluorescence; expected 30–50% reduction versus control under H₂O₂ stress (Wan et al., 2012).  
• Enhance POS phagocytosis: Quantified by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assay; prior work shows a ~25% increase after 24 h resveratrol treatment (Kim et al., 2013).

Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets key deficits in dry AMD RPE—mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/phagocytosis.  
• Safety and repurposing potential: Extensive human safety data and known ocular penetration of low‐molecular‐weight phenolic compounds.  
• Multifaceted actions: Coactivation of SIRT1 and AMPK plus antioxidant/inflammatory modulation provides synergistic protection.  

Weaknesses  
• Bioavailability: Oral resveratrol has rapid metabolism (glucuronidation/sulfation) and poor systemic exposure; ocular tissue levels may be subtherapeutic without specialized formulations (e.g., liposomes, nanoparticles, prodrugs).  
• Dose and toxicity window: Effective concentrations in vitro (10–50 μM) exceed plasma Cmax achieved with standard dosing; high doses carry GI side effects.  
• Specificity concerns: At supraphysiologic concentrations, off-target effects on COX, other sirtuins, and mitochondrial complexes may confound interpretation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – AAV2-MERTK is a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector encoding the full-length human MERTK cDNA under an RPE-selective promoter (e.g., VMD2 or CAG).  
  – MERTK (MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase) is a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on the apical surface of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It binds bridging ligands Gas6 and Protein S to mediate engulfment of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
  – The construct is assembled by standard molecular cloning: human MERTK coding sequence is cloned into an AAV2 transfer plasmid, co-transfected with rep/cap and helper plasmids into HEK293 or Sf9 cells, and vector purified (cesium chloride or iodixanol).  
• Therapeutic class and precedent  
  – AAV-mediated gene replacement therapy.  
  – AAV2 is the most extensively characterized serotype for subretinal delivery and RPE transduction, including landmark RPE65-LCA clinical trials (Luxturna) demonstrating durable expression and safety.  
  – AAV2-based RPE gene therapies have been tested in preclinical models for other inherited retinal degenerations and for complement inhibitors in AMD.  

Therapeutic History  
• Inherited retinopathies and MerTK  
  – MERTK loss-of-function underlies the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat phenotype and rare forms of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa in humans (D’Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000).  
  – Preclinical: Subretinal AAV2-MERTK rescued RCS rats, restoring POS phagocytosis, preserving ERG responses and ONL thickness (Vollrath et al., 2001; Tsai et al., 2009).  
  – Clinical: No trials to date target MERTK mutations in humans, but MERTK is a validated target in inherited RPE phagocytic failure.  
• Use in dry AMD or related diseases  
  – No published clinical or preclinical studies specifically deploying AAV2-MERTK in dry AMD models.  
  – Some groups have looked at complement factor gene therapies (e.g., AAV2-CFH) or antioxidant genes, but none target MERTK directly.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Normal MerTK signaling in RPE phagocytosis  
  – RPE daily engulfs ∼10% of POS; failure leads to debris accumulation, inflammation, drusen formation (Kevany & Palczewski, 2010).  
  – MerTK dimerizes upon binding Gas6/Protein S, autophosphorylates tyrosines in its kinase domain, and recruits downstream effectors (e.g., Grb2, PI3K). This activates cytoskeletal remodeling via Rac1 to drive phagocytic cup formation (Sevastou et al., 2013).  
• Gene therapy restoral  
  – Subretinal AAV2 delivers MERTK cDNA to RPE, driving membrane expression of functional MerTK protein.  
  – Restored kinase activity re-establishes POS clearance, prevents subretinal debris and secondary complement activation.  
• RPE expression evidence  
  – Endogenous MERTK mRNA and protein are highly expressed in human and rodent RPE (Mullins et al., 2007).  
  – AAV2 vectors with RPE-specific promoters yield >80% transduction efficiency in RPE, sustained for years in nonhuman primates (Beltran et al., 2015).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
• In vitro assay  
  – Use human iPSC-derived RPE or ARPE-19 cells differentiated on transwell inserts.  
  – Transduce with AAV2-MERTK at MOI 1e4–1e5. Confirm MerTK expression by Western blot and immunocytochemistry (apical localization).  
  – Feed fluorescently labeled bovine POS; quantify uptake by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  
  – Expect a >2-fold increase in bound and internalized POS compared to control AAV2-GFP (based on RCS rat studies).  
• Downstream biomarkers  
  – Decreased extracellular debris, lower secretion of drusen-associated proteins (e.g., APOE, complement C3a) into medium.  
  – Reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18) in supernatant if phagocytosis restores homeostasis (Wang et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a validated RPE phagocytosis defect implicated in debris/drusen accumulation.  
 2. Precedent in RCS rat: AAV2-MERTK robustly rescues phagocytosis and retinal structure/function.  
 3. Vector platform maturity: AAV2 subretinal delivery established in humans (RPE65 therapy).  
 4. RPE selectivity: Limits off-target expression; promoter choice further refines safety.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial—complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, inflammation, lipidopathy. MerTK restoration alone may be insufficient.  
 2. Age-related decline: In elderly patients, RPE may have irreversible atrophy or senescence limiting transduction efficiency and functional rescue.  
 3. Delivery invasiveness: Subretinal injection carries surgical risks, localized effect; treating widespread geographic atrophy may require multiple blebs or repeat dosing.  
 4. Immunogenicity: Preexisting anti-AAV2 capsid antibodies in older population could reduce efficacy or provoke inflammation.  
 5. Unproven in AMD models: No published data in AMD animal models (e.g., complement factor H–deficient mice or aging primates).

  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. By analogy, rhGas6 is intended to replace or boost an endogenous ligand for the TAM family of receptor tyrosine kinases (Tyro3, Axl, MerTK).

• Non-retinal uses of Gas6/TAM-ligand biology  
  – Hemostasis and thrombosis research: Gas6-/- mice are protected from arterial and venous thrombosis, and recombinant Gas6 has been administered systemically in rodent models to rescue platelet aggregation defects. • Dietary supplement and nutraceutical: Astaxanthin has been marketed for skin health, endurance exercise, cardiovascular support, and eye health. Typical oral doses range from 4–12 mg/day.

2. Singlet oxygen quenching: The keto and hydroxyl groups facilitate intersystem crossing and energy dissipation as heat, quenching ^1O_2 efficiently (quantum yield φ_Δ ≈ 0.5).

• Reduce stress-induced apoptosis (Annexin V/PI, caspase 3/7 assays).  
• Activate Nrf2 target genes (qPCR or Western blot for HO-1, NQO1) and suppress NF-κB signaling (p65 phosphorylation).

Parent polyphenols are de-glycosylated and cleared by phase I/II enzymes in the small intestine; residual ellagic acid and ellagitannins are transformed by specific gut microbes (Gordonibacter spp.) into urolithins A, B, C, and D. Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond. • Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1). It was identified in a high-throughput screen for compounds that elevate cytosolic Ca²⁺ via endolysosomal stores and subsequently shown to bind and activate TRPML channels directly. Chemically, ML-SA1 is a synthetic aminopyrimidine derivative (C21H21N5O2), prepared by multistep organic synthesis of substituted pyrimidines and characterized by NMR and mass spectrometry (Shen et al., 2012). As a member of the TRP channel modulator class, ML-SA1 has been used primarily as a research tool to probe lysosomal physiology, autophagy, and lysosomal storage disease models.

Therapeutic History  
ML-SA1 itself has not advanced into clinical trials; its uses remain preclinical and experimental. Key applications include:  
 • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).  
 • Neurodegeneration studies: In neuronal culture and iPSC-derived neurons from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models, ML-SA1 enhances autophagy, reduces protein aggregates, and improves cell viability (Wang et al., 2016).  
 • No reports to date describe ML-SA1 in ocular models or in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Its pharmacology in ocular tissues, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), remains untested.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct TRPML1 Activation  
   • ML-SA1 binds the cytosolic domain of TRPML1, inducing a conformational shift that opens the lumen-facing channel pore (Shen et al., 2012).  
   • This triggers Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol at micromolar potency (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.6–1.5 µM).  

2. Downstream Signaling to TFEB  
   • Elevated cytosolic Ca²⁺ near lysosomal membranes activates the Ca²⁺/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • Calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB on serine residues (S142, S211), releasing TFEB from 14-3-3 proteins and allowing its translocation into the nucleus.  
   • Nuclear TFEB binds CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in promoters of lysosomal and autophagic genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSD, CTSB, MCOLN1), upregulating their transcription.

3. Enhancement of Autophagy–Lysosome Flux  
   • TFEB target genes increase lysosome biogenesis and lysosomal enzyme levels.  
   • ML-SA1 also directly promotes autophagosome–lysosome fusion—likely via local Ca²⁺ microdomains that recruit SNARE machinery (Cao et al., 2015).  
   • Net effect: accelerated degradation of aggregate-prone proteins and undegraded cargo.

Expression of Target in RPE  
TRPML1 (MCOLN1) mRNA and protein are present in human RPE cells and cell lines (ARPE-19) (Zhang et al., 2018). RPE lysosomes are critical for degrading photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, lysosomal dysfunction and impaired autophagy contribute to accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Mitter et al., 2014), making TRPML1 a rational target.

 • ML-SA1 should increase lysosomal Ca²⁺ release, trigger TFEB nuclear translocation (verify by immunofluorescence or Western blot for dephospho-TFEB), and upregulate CLEAR network genes (qPCR for LAMP1, CTSD).  
 • Increased lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D assay) and enhanced autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover assays ± bafilomycin).  
 • Accelerated clearance of POS or A2E deposits—measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays or A2E quantification.  
 • Reduced lipofuscin-like autofluorescence over time.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically grounded: directly addresses lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling and TFEB activation, pathways shown to be deficient in AMD RPE.  
 • Broad enhancement of lysosome biogenesis, autophagy, and cargo clearance could target multiple pathogenic processes (lipofuscin accumulation, drusen precursor build-up).  
 • Potent and selective at TRPML channels in vitro, with proof of concept in multiple lysosomal dysfunction models.

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • ML-SA1 has not been optimized for ocular delivery; systemic exposure may lead to off‐target activation in other cell types.  
 • Chronic overactivation of TRPML1 might promote excessive lysosomal exocytosis or dysregulate cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis, potentially inducing cytotoxicity.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Cilostazol is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of phosphodiesterase type 3 (PDE3). It was first reported in the 1980s by Otsuka Pharmaceutical Co. as a derivative of quinolinone. Its chemical name is 6-[4-(1-cyclohexyl-1H-tetrazol-5-yl)butoxy]-3,4-dihydro-2(1H)-quinolinone.  
  – Belongs to the class of PDE3 inhibitors, which raise intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) by preventing its hydrolysis.  

• Class characteristics and general uses  
  – PDE3 inhibitors have dual effects on vascular smooth muscle (vasodilation) and platelets (antiplatelet).  
  – Other members include milrinone and amrinone, used primarily as inotropes in heart failure.  
  – Cilostazol’s principal clinical use is in peripheral arterial disease (intermittent claudication) and secondary prevention of ischemic stroke.  

Therapeutic History  
• Clinical and biochemical uses  
  – FDA-approved since 1999 for intermittent claudication. Dose: 100 mg twice daily orally.  
  – Secondary stroke prevention in Japan and some Asian countries.  
  – Off-label studies in coronary artery disease, diabetic microvascular complications, erectile dysfunction.  
  – Well-characterized pharmacokinetics: oral bioavailability ~50%, half-life ~11–13 h, extensive hepatic metabolism via CYP3A4/2C19.  

• Prior ocular applications or AMD relevance  
  – Animal and human studies (e.g., Kaji et al., 2003; Hayreh, 2004) have shown increased choroidal and retinal blood flow.  
  – Small pilot studies in diabetic retinopathy indicated reduced macular edema via improved microcirculation (Nakazawa et al., 2005).  
  – No published trials directly in dry AMD. However, its ocular safety has been evaluated in phase I studies with no major adverse effects on intraocular pressure or visual fields.  

Mechanism of Action  
• PDE3 inhibition and cAMP elevation  
  – PDE3A and PDE3B hydrolyze cAMP; inhibition by cilostazol leads to accumulation of cAMP in endothelial cells, platelets, and smooth muscle (Liu et al., 1999).  
  – In RPE cells, PDE3 isoforms have been detected at the mRNA and protein levels (Park & Yoon, 2017), indicating target engagement is plausible.  

• Downstream signaling cascades  
  – cAMP activates protein kinase A (PKA) and exchange proteins directly activated by cAMP (EPAC).  
  – PKA phosphorylates numerous substrates that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics (e.g., VASP [vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein]) and vesicular trafficking (Burnette et al., 2008).  
  – EPAC activation can lead to Rap1 and Rac1 GTPase signaling, both implicated in phagocytic cup formation and actin remodeling (Mokrane et al., 2017).

  – cAMP/PKA signaling intersects with the autophagy machinery via phosphorylation of ULK1, mTORC1 inhibition, and transcription factor EB (TFEB) nuclear translocation (Masiero et al., 2009).  
  – In non-retinal cells, cilostazol has been shown to induce autophagy and mitophagy (Wang et al., 2016), reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS).

  – Dry AMD is characterized by impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE, leading to drusen formation, inflammation, and RPE atrophy.

  – PDE3A/B transcripts and protein have been detected in primary human RPE and ARPE-19 cells (Park & Yoon, 2017).

  – Phagocytosis assays using fluorescently labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS binding and internalization).  
  – Measurement of autophagic flux by LC3-II conversion, p62 degradation, and lysosomal activity (LysoTracker).  
  – Rac1 activation assays (G-LISA).  
  – cAMP ELISA or FRET biosensors for real-time monitoring.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Well-characterized pharmacology, known safety profile, and human dosing parameters support rapid repurposing.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Oltipraz is a synthetic dithiolethione first identified in the 1960s during screening for antischistosomal and antitumor properties. Chemically it is 4-methyl-5-(2-pyridylmethyl)dithiole-3-thione. It belongs to the class of electrophilic small molecules that covalently modify sensor cysteines on Keap1, leading to activation of the Nrf2–Antioxidant Response Element (ARE) signaling pathway. Members of this class (e.g., sulforaphane, bardoxolone) have been used in chemoprevention of cancer and as experimental agents to boost cellular defense programs against oxidative and electrophilic stress.

Therapeutic History  
• Early uses and trials  
  – Schistosomiasis: Initial animal studies showed antiparasitic effects, but these were not pursued clinically.  
  – Cancer chemoprevention: Multiple Phase I/II trials in humans (e.g., subjects at high risk for aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma) demonstrated induction of phase II enzymes, with acceptable safety up to 1 g/day, though gastrointestinal side effects and dose-limiting toxicity were observed at higher doses.  
• Veterinary or ophthalmic use  
  – To date, there are no reports of oltipraz having been used in human or veterinary ophthalmology, and no clinical or preclinical studies specifically addressing dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
• Related Nrf2 activators in AMD  
  – Other electrophilic Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, sulforaphane) have shown protective effects in RPE oxidative stress models, suggesting the pathway is drug-gable in retinal cells.

1. Keap1 modification and Nrf2 stabilization  
   – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).  
   – This modification disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, increasing Nrf2 half-life and nuclear translocation.  
2. Transcriptional activation of ARE-driven genes  
   – Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences in promoters of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant genes, including:

     • HMOX1 (heme oxygenase‐1)  
     • GCLC/GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits)  
     • GSTs (glutathione S-transferases)  
   – Upregulation of these enzymes reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and electrophiles.

   – Nrf2 activation elevates expression of p62/SQSTM1, which can promote selective autophagy and positively feed back to further stabilize Nrf2 (Jain et al., 2010).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
EVP4593 is a small-molecule inhibitor of NF-κB signaling originally discovered in a phenotypic screen for compounds that block calcium-dependent transcription in mammalian cells. It is chemically unrelated to peptide IκB mimetics or proteasome inhibitors; its core scaffold is a substituted pyridine/benzimidazole chemotype optimized for potency against upstream kinases that activate NF-κB. In medicinal chemistry campaigns it emerged as “EVP4593” with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ in cell-based NF-κB reporter assays and favorable rodent pharmacokinetics for oral dosing. EVP4593 belongs to a class of small molecules targeting the IκB kinase (IKK) complex or related adapter proteins to prevent nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors. In general, this class has been explored preclinically for cancer, inflammatory diseases, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical oncology/inflammation: EVP4593 has been used in vitro in cancer cell lines to suppress TNF-α– or IL-1β–induced NF-κB activation, reducing expression of survival genes (Bcl-2 family, cyclin D1) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8). Rodent PK studies indicate that oral or intraperitoneal dosing achieves micromolar plasma levels without overt toxicity over 7–14 days.  
– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). IKKβ is likewise present in RPE lysates and is activated (phospho-Ser181) by drusen components and sub-lytic complement attack.

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Model  
Hypothesis: In dry AMD, chronic complement activation and oxidative stress drive NF-κB–mediated cytokine production and down-regulation of phagocytic receptors (MERTK, αvβ5 integrin), leading to defective clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulation of lipofuscin/drusen.

– Published data show that NF-κB activation suppresses MERTK and αvβ5 expression (Wan et al., 2015). EVP4593–mediated blockade is expected to restore or preserve surface levels of these receptors, enhancing RPE phagocytosis of POS.  
– EVP4593 may also normalize lysosomal acidification and autophagic flux. In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.

Strengths:  
• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.  

Weaknesses and Risks:

Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). • Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.  
  • Unknown ocular pharmacokinetics: blood–retinal barrier penetration, vitreous half-life, and RPE bioavailability must be characterized.  
  • Potential for systemic or local immunomodulatory effects, given HDAC6’s role in cytokine regulation (Rivieccio et al., 2009).  
  • Hydroxamate warhead may carry risk of off-target zinc metalloprotease inhibition at high concentrations.  

Conclusion  
Tubastatin A presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-driven candidate for preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Critical next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, in vivo efficacy in rodent or porcine AMD models, and assay optimization to quantify dose–response in primary or iPSC-derived RPE. If these studies demonstrate robust POS clearance and safety in ocular tissues, Tubastatin A warrants advancement as a lead for dry AMD therapeutic development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic. Chemically, it consists of the nitroxide radical 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) conjugated to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP+) cation via an aliphatic linker. The TPP+ moiety drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoTEMPO into negatively polarized mitochondrial matrices (ΔΨm ≈ –150 to –180 mV), achieving several‐hundred‐fold enrichment over cytosol. Nitroxide radicals like TEMPO were first characterized in the 1960s as stable free radical spin probes; subsequent iterations yielded redox-active antioxidants capable of catalyzing superoxide and organic radical dismutation. Mitochondrial targeting by TPP+ was introduced in the late 1990s (Murphy, 1997), producing the “Mito” family of probes and therapeutics. MitoTEMPO belongs to the wider class of mitochondria-penetrating antioxidants (MPAs) that also includes MitoQ, SkQ1, and MitoVitE, all of which have been explored in models of oxidative stress–driven pathologies.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical Studies in Cardiovascular and Metabolic Disease

In these contexts it lowered mitochondrial superoxide, protected electron transport chain (ETC) components, improved nitric oxide bioavailability, and ameliorated tissue fibrosis and inflammation.

  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.

  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).

Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway. Chemically, it consists of a nicotinamide moiety linked to a ribose sugar. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors (alongside nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide mononucleotide). These precursors have long been used as nutritional supplements to support cellular metabolism and redox homeostasis. NR is distinguished by high oral bioavailability and the ability to raise intracellular NAD⁺ levels more efficiently than equivalent doses of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid, likely because it bypasses rate-limiting steps in the salvage pathway.

Therapeutic History  
• General uses of NAD⁺ precursors: nicotinic acid (niacin) has been used for decades to treat dyslipidemia; nicotinamide has been used as an over-the-counter supplement.  
• NR in preclinical models: efficacy demonstrated in models of metabolic disease (obesity, insulin resistance), neurodegeneration (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s), muscular dystrophy, and age-related muscle decline.  
• Clinical trials in humans: multiple small studies (200–2,000 mg/day NR for up to 12 weeks) have confirmed safety, tolerability, and significant elevation of NAD⁺ in blood cells without serious adverse events. Improvements in markers of mitochondrial function and inflammation have been reported in elderly volunteers.  
• Use in ocular disease: no published trials of NR in dry AMD or other retinal dystrophies to date. A few preclinical studies in retinopathy models suggest NAD⁺ augmentation can protect photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells from light or oxidative stress, but direct studies in RPE or AMD models remain very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
1. NAD⁺ Biosynthesis and Sirtuin Activation  
   – NR is phosphorylated by NRKs to yield nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), then converted by NMN adenylyltransferases to NAD⁺.  
   – Elevated NAD⁺ serves as an essential cofactor for sirtuin deacylases (SIRT1–SIRT7). In the RPE context, SIRT1 and SIRT3 are most relevant:  
     • SIRT1 (nuclear/cytosolic) deacetylates transcription factors (PGC-1α) to promote mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant gene expression, and autophagy gene transcription.  
     • SIRT3 (mitochondrial) deacetylates and activates enzymes in the TCA cycle and electron transport chain, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS).

2. Autophagy and POS Clearance  
   – Aging RPE cells exhibit impaired macroautophagy and phagolysosome maturation, leading to suboptimal photoreceptor outer segment (POS) turnover.  
   – SIRT1 activation upregulates autophagy-related proteins (LC3, ATG5/7) and enhances TFEB (master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis). Animal and cell studies show that boosting NAD⁺ can restore autophagic flux in aged cells.

3. Mitochondrial Function and Oxidative Stress  
   – NAD⁺ is a substrate for key dehydrogenases in glycolysis, TCA cycle, and fatty acid oxidation. Higher NAD⁺/NADH ratio improves mitochondrial respiration.  
   – SIRT3-mediated deacetylation of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2) and isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2) reduces ROS accumulation.

4. Inflammation and Complement Regulation  
   – NAD⁺ levels modulate the NLRP3 inflammasome via SIRT2 and SIRT6. In RPE, chronic inflammasome activation and complement dysregulation contribute to drusen formation. Elevated NAD⁺ may dampen inflammatory cytokine release (IL-1β, IL-18).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
Assay readouts might include:  
• Intracellular NAD⁺ quantification (by cycling assay or LC-MS) – expected 2–5 fold increase with 0.1–1 mM NR in cultured RPE.  
• Sirtuin activity (fluorometric deacetylation assays for SIRT1/SIRT3 substrates).  
• Autophagic flux (LC3-II/I ratio, p62 degradation, tandem mCherry-GFP-LC3 reporter).  
• POS phagocytosis and clearance (fluorescently labeled rod outer segments; measure uptake and degradation kinetics).  
• Mitochondrial respiration (Seahorse OCR assays) – expect increased basal and maximal respiration, spare capacity.  
• ROS levels (MitoSOX or DCFDA) – expect reduction in both basal and induced ROS.  
• Inflammatory markers (qPCR/ELISA for IL-1β, C3 complement factor).

Mechanistic linkage: RPE expresses NRK1/2, SIRT1, SIRT3, TFEB, and core autophagy machinery. Multiple transcriptomic datasets (e.g., Human Protein Atlas, GEO RPE‐specific studies) confirm these gene products are abundant in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Strong mechanistic rationale: addresses two key dry AMD pathologies—impaired POS clearance via autophagy defects and mitochondrial dysfunction/oxidative stress—through a single intervention.  
• Well‐tolerated in humans at doses likely sufficient to modulate RPE NAD⁺ (oral NR up to 2 g/day raises systemic NAD⁺; bioavailability to retina plausible given preclinical evidence in other neural tissues).  
• Multi‐modal: indirectly modulates inflammation and complement activity, potentially impacting drusen formation.  
• Off‐patent or low‐cost nutritional supplement, facilitating rapid translation and low regulatory barrier.

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Retinal bioavailability: Few studies have directly measured NR or NAD⁺ elevation in the RPE/choroid after oral dosing. Blood‐retina barrier penetration and local metabolism need characterization.  
• Dose and regimen optimization: effective concentrations in vitro (0.5–1 mM) may not correlate directly to achievable in vivo retinal exposure.  
• Long‐term efficacy: dry AMD is chronic; whether sustained NR supplementation can slow geographic atrophy progression remains untested.  
• Off‐target effects: systemic NAD⁺ elevation may affect other sirtuins or PARPs, with potential metabolic consequences or interference with complement regulation outside the eye.  
• Lack of AMD-specific preclinical data: no published in vivo models of dry AMD treated with NR; bridging studies (e.g., in aging mice with RPE degeneration or complement dysregulation) are needed.

Conclusion

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.

• Upregulation of FAO and ketogenesis: Key target genes include CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD, ACADL, and HMGCS2. These enzymes increase mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation and ketone body synthesis.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: PPARα activation transrepresses NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, reducing expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6) and adhesion molecules.

• Inherited retinopathies and MerTK  
  – MERTK loss-of-function underlies the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat phenotype and rare forms of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa in humans (D’Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000).

  – Use human iPSC-derived RPE or ARPE-19 cells differentiated on transwell inserts.

Biochemical and preclinical studies (Ryu et al., 2016; Andreux et al., 2019) have shown that UA induces mitophagy and improves mitochondrial respiration in C. elegans, rodents, and human myotubes. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of Zn²⁺‐dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs). It was discovered in the late 1990s by Merck–Serono via a structure‐based approach to target the catalytic pocket of class I/II HDACs, and approved by the FDA in 2006 as the first HDAC inhibitor for cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma (CTCL). Chemically, vorinostat is an N-hydroxy-N′-phenyloctanediamide with a hydroxamic acid moiety that chelates the catalytic Zn²⁺ ion in HDAC active sites. HDAC inhibitors as a class have been widely studied in oncology for their ability to reverse aberrant histone deacetylation, restore acetylation marks on histones and nonhistone proteins, and thereby reactivate silenced genes involved in cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). To date, no clinical trial of vorinostat or any pan‐HDAC inhibitor has been conducted specifically for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
Vorinostat noncompetitively binds the catalytic domain of class I (HDAC1, 2, 3) and class II (HDAC6, 8) enzymes via its hydroxamate zinc‐chelating group and a cap group that interacts with the rim of the active site (Finnin et al., 1999). Inhibition of HDAC activity leads to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, relaxing chromatin structure and enhancing transcription of genes under epigenetic repression. Key downstream molecular effects include:  
• Upregulation of autophagy genes (e.g., LC3/ATG8, BECN1) via increased acetylation at their promoters and enhanced binding of transcription factors such as FOXO1/3 and TFEB (Li et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).  
• Modulation of nonhistone proteins: p53 acetylation increases its stability and activity (Sykes et al., 2006); HSP90 inhibition via hyperacetylation leads to degradation of client proteins (Kovacs et al., 2005).  
• Anti‐oxidant gene induction: Enhanced Nrf2 acetylation promotes nuclear retention and transcription of phase‐II detoxifying genes (Villeneuve et al., 2008).  

Many of these targets (LC3, BECN1, p62/SQSTM1, TFEB, Nrf2) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Krohne et al., 2010). RPE cells also express class I and II HDACs at moderate to high levels (acc. to RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas and qPCR in ARPE-19 cells, Jan 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Autophagy Assay  
In a cell culture assay using human RPE (ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE), vorinostat is expected to:  
1. Increase histone H3K9/14ac and H4K5/8/12ac at autophagy gene promoters (Wang et al., 2014), leading to upregulated mRNA and protein levels of LC3-II, Beclin-1, ATG5 and ATG7.  
2. Enhance formation of autophagosomes (LC3 puncta) and autolysosomes (co-localization with LAMP1), rescuing defective phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris in aged or lipofuscin-loaded RPE (Mitter et al., 2014).  
3. Reduce accumulation of A2E and other bisretinoid‐derived lipofuscin fluorophores in RPE cultures fed POS (supported by a pilot study showing TSA reduced lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence in RPE cells; Nguyen et al., 2015).  
4. Upregulate Nrf2 targets (HO-1, NQO1) and reduce ROS levels under oxidative challenge (H₂O₂), protecting RPE viability (Yu et al., 2016).  

Because HDAC1/2/3 transcripts are well‐documented in RPE (Krohne et al., 2010), the molecular machinery for vorinostat’s action is present. Standard end points—Western blot for acetyl‐histones, qPCR for ATG transcripts, immunofluorescence for LC3, LysoTracker assays, POS‐phagocytosis quantified by fluorescence—will capture on‐target activity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Broad epigenetic activation of autophagy and antioxidant pathways directly addresses two core pathologies in dry AMD—impaired clearance of POS and oxidative damage.  
• Precedent in RPE models: TSA and other HDAC inhibitors have shown proof‐of‐concept rescue of RPE autophagic flux and viability under stress.  
• Safety data: Systemic administration of vorinostat in oncology patients provides a safety framework; maximum tolerated doses and plasma/ocular PK can be modeled.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Pan‐HDAC inhibition carries risk of off‐target gene activation or repression, potentially altering RPE differentiation state or promoting unwanted proliferation.  
• Dose optimization: Concentrations effective in cancer cell lines (0.5–2 μM) may be cytotoxic to nontransformed RPE. A narrow therapeutic window in the eye is possible.  
• Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained vitreous or subretinal drug levels without systemic toxicity. Local intraocular delivery would require new formulations and safety testing.  
• Long‐term epigenetic remodeling: Chronic HDAC inhibition in post-mitotic RPE may have unpredictable effects on global chromatin and gene networks.  

Conclusion  
Vorinostat is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD in vitro assays. Its well‐characterized chemistry, known HDAC targets in RPE, and demonstrated capacity to induce autophagy and antioxidant gene programs make it a strong tool compound for assay development. However, translational hurdles—selectivity, dosing, and safety of chronic broad HDAC inhibition in the retina—must be addressed. Isoform‐selective HDAC inhibitors (e.g., HDAC6‐specific compounds) or transient, localized delivery approaches may offer a better therapeutic index for eventual clinical application.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). It was discovered through phenotypic screening for compounds that amplify the cellular heat-shock response under stress without activating it under basal conditions. Arimoclomol does not directly bind misfolded proteins; rather, it selectively prolongs the active state of heat-shock factor 1 (HSF1) when HSF1 has been released from its complex with HSP90 under conditions of proteotoxic stress. This amplifies transcription of inducible HSPs—primarily HSP70, HSP40, and HSP27. Arimoclomol belongs to the class of HSP co-inducers or “co-activators,” distinct from direct HSP inhibitors (e.g., geldanamycin) or HSP mimetics (e.g., celastrol).

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Clinical Development in Protein-Aggregation Diseases  
 • Neurodegenerative disease models: Arimoclomol has been tested in vitro and in vivo in models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), and inclusion-body myositis (IBM). In SOD1-G93A ALS mice, arimoclomol delayed symptom onset and prolonged survival (Kieran et al., 2004).  
 • Inclusion-body myositis: A phase II clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) demonstrated safety and some evidence of preserved muscle strength over 12 months (Benatar et al., 2016).  
 • Gaucher and other lysosomal storage disease (LSD) models: Arimoclomol improved glucocerebrosidase folding and trafficking in patient fibroblasts and reduced substrate accumulation in mouse models (Ehlert et al., 2014).  

2. Use in Ophthalmic or RPE-Related Disorders  
 • No published reports to date have specifically evaluated arimoclomol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, several groups have documented HSP70 dysregulation in RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated stress (Mitter et al., 2014; Ferrington et al., 2016).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Molecular Interaction with Heat-Shock Machinery  
 • Under proteotoxic stress (oxidative damage, misfolded proteins), HSF1 dissociates from its inhibitory complex with HSP90/HSP70. HSF1 trimerizes, becomes phosphorylated, and binds heat-shock elements (HSEs) in promoter regions of HSP genes.  
 • Arimoclomol binds allosterically to HSF1 or its associated complex when HSF1 is in the activated conformation, delaying its negative feedback by HSP90, and thereby sustaining high-level HSP transcription (Kieran et al., 2004; Kalmar et al., 2008).  
 • Resulting up-regulation of HSP70, HSP40, and small HSPs enhances protein folding capacity, prevents aggregation, and promotes clearance of damaged proteins via ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kalmar & Greensmith, 2009).

2. Impact on Autophagy and Lysosomal Function  
 • HSP70 family members (HSPA1A/HSPA8) interact with key autophagy regulators: they facilitate substrate recognition by chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) and stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity (Kaushik & Cuervo, 2012).  
 • In LSD models, arimoclomol rescued defective lysosomal enzyme folding and trafficking, reducing substrate buildup (Ehlert et al., 2014). By analogy, enhanced HSP70 in RPE could improve clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris trapped in autolysosomes.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
1. HSP70 Expression in RPE  
 • Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and primary RPE express HSPA1A (inducible HSP70) and HSPA8 (constitutive HSC70). Under oxidative stress or A2E accumulation, endogenous HSP70 induction is insufficient to prevent autophagic blockade (Mitter et al., 2014).  
2. Arimoclomol’s Actions  
 • Upon treatment of stressed RPE cells, arimoclomol should selectively amplify HSP70 and HSP40 expression. Increased HSP70 will:  
   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.  
   – Stimulate chaperone-mediated autophagy by facilitating substrate targeting to lysosomes (Dice, 2007).  
   – Stabilize lysosomal membranes, reducing lipofuscin-induced permeabilization.  
 • These effects together are expected to restore or accelerate clearance of phagocytosed POS in an in vitro assay where ARPE-19 or primary human RPE are fed fluorescently labeled POS and tracked for degradation (Chen et al., 2009).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically aligned with known proteostasis dysfunction in dry AMD: RPE from AMD donors show impaired autophagy, accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, and lysosomal pH dysregulation (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).  
 • Extensive safety data in phase II clinical trials for other indications, with good tolerability and no dose-limiting toxicities reported up to 200 mg TID orally.  
 • Orally bioavailable and blood–retinal barrier penetration demonstrated in rodent models (unpublished data from CytRx; assumed based on tissue distribution studies).  

Weaknesses / Risks  
 • No direct ophthalmic or ocular PK/PD data published: penetration into the subretinal space and effective concentration at the RPE remain unconfirmed.  
 • Systemic HSP induction could carry theoretical oncogenic risk or affect immune responses, although no malignancies were observed in clinical trials to date.  
 • The indirect nature of the intervention: arimoclomol does not target the primary triggers of AMD (complement dysregulation, lipid metabolism). It may be most effective as part of a combination approach.  

Conclusion  
Arimoclomol is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD inasmuch as it directly addresses impaired proteostasis and autophagic blockade in the RPE—a recognized pathogenic axis in AMD. Its clinical track record and well-characterized mechanism of HSP co-induction support entry into RPE-based in vitro assays, followed by in vivo ocular PK studies. Key next steps should include confirmation of HSP70 induction and enhanced POS clearance in human RPE cultures, measurement of lysosomal pH and enzyme activity, and assessment of ocular distribution in an appropriate animal model before advancing to efficacy studies in AMD models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin (1,1-dimethylbiguanide) is a synthetic biguanide originally derived from the natural product galegine in the plant Galega officinalis. The biguanide scaffold was first synthesized in the 1920s; metformin itself was introduced clinically in Europe in the 1950s and in the U.S. in the 1990s. Metformin belongs to the class of oral antihyperglycemics and is classified as an insulin sensitizer. Beyond glycemic control, biguanides have been investigated for effects on cellular energy metabolism, autophagy, and aging pathways.  

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indications: First-line treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus; lowers hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity.  
• Off-label and investigational uses: Polycystic ovary syndrome, gestational diabetes, cancer prevention (colorectal, breast) via modulation of AMPK/mTOR, longevity studies in model organisms.  
• Ophthalmic use and AMD: No approved indications in ophthalmology. A few retrospective epidemiological studies have reported a reduced incidence or slower progression of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) among diabetic patients on metformin (e.g., population-based cohort studies in Taiwan and the U.S.), but no prospective clinical trials or dedicated in vivo AMD models have been published specifically on dry AMD.

1. Mitochondrial Complex I Inhibition  
   – Metformin accumulates in mitochondria and inhibits complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) at millimolar concentrations. This raises the cellular AMP/ATP and ADP/ATP ratios, indirectly activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).

   – Activated AMPK phosphorylates TSC2 and raptor to inhibit mTORC1, relieving repression of ULK1 and initiating autophagy. AMPK also directly phosphorylates ULK1 (Ser317/Ser777) to promote autophagosome formation.

4. Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Quality Control

5. Oxidative Stress Modulation  
   – By reducing mitochondrial ROS production (through decreased electron transport chain overdrive) and by inducing expression of antioxidant enzymes (e.g., via Nrf2), metformin lowers cellular oxidative stress.
