Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway. Chemically, it consists of a nicotinamide moiety linked to a ribose sugar. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors (alongside nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide mononucleotide). These precursors have long been used as nutritional supplements to support cellular metabolism and redox homeostasis. NR is distinguished by high oral bioavailability and the ability to raise intracellular NAD⁺ levels more efficiently than equivalent doses of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid, likely because it bypasses rate-limiting steps in the salvage pathway.

Therapeutic History  
• General uses of NAD⁺ precursors: nicotinic acid (niacin) has been used for decades to treat dyslipidemia; nicotinamide has been used as an over-the-counter supplement.  
• NR in preclinical models: efficacy demonstrated in models of metabolic disease (obesity, insulin resistance), neurodegeneration (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s), muscular dystrophy, and age-related muscle decline.  
• Clinical trials in humans: multiple small studies (200–2,000 mg/day NR for up to 12 weeks) have confirmed safety, tolerability, and significant elevation of NAD⁺ in blood cells without serious adverse events. Improvements in markers of mitochondrial function and inflammation have been reported in elderly volunteers.  
• Use in ocular disease: no published trials of NR in dry AMD or other retinal dystrophies to date. A few preclinical studies in retinopathy models suggest NAD⁺ augmentation can protect photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells from light or oxidative stress, but direct studies in RPE or AMD models remain very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
1. NAD⁺ Biosynthesis and Sirtuin Activation  
   – NR is phosphorylated by NRKs to yield nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), then converted by NMN adenylyltransferases to NAD⁺.  
   – Elevated NAD⁺ serves as an essential cofactor for sirtuin deacylases (SIRT1–SIRT7). In the RPE context, SIRT1 and SIRT3 are most relevant:  
     • SIRT1 (nuclear/cytosolic) deacetylates transcription factors (PGC-1α) to promote mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant gene expression, and autophagy gene transcription.  
     • SIRT3 (mitochondrial) deacetylates and activates enzymes in the TCA cycle and electron transport chain, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS).

2. Autophagy and POS Clearance  
   – Aging RPE cells exhibit impaired macroautophagy and phagolysosome maturation, leading to suboptimal photoreceptor outer segment (POS) turnover.  
   – SIRT1 activation upregulates autophagy-related proteins (LC3, ATG5/7) and enhances TFEB (master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis). Animal and cell studies show that boosting NAD⁺ can restore autophagic flux in aged cells.

3. Mitochondrial Function and Oxidative Stress  
   – NAD⁺ is a substrate for key dehydrogenases in glycolysis, TCA cycle, and fatty acid oxidation. Higher NAD⁺/NADH ratio improves mitochondrial respiration.  
   – SIRT3-mediated deacetylation of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2) and isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2) reduces ROS accumulation.

4. Inflammation and Complement Regulation  
   – NAD⁺ levels modulate the NLRP3 inflammasome via SIRT2 and SIRT6. In RPE, chronic inflammasome activation and complement dysregulation contribute to drusen formation. Elevated NAD⁺ may dampen inflammatory cytokine release (IL-1β, IL-18).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
Assay readouts might include:  
• Intracellular NAD⁺ quantification (by cycling assay or LC-MS) – expected 2–5 fold increase with 0.1–1 mM NR in cultured RPE.  
• Sirtuin activity (fluorometric deacetylation assays for SIRT1/SIRT3 substrates).  
• Autophagic flux (LC3-II/I ratio, p62 degradation, tandem mCherry-GFP-LC3 reporter).  
• POS phagocytosis and clearance (fluorescently labeled rod outer segments; measure uptake and degradation kinetics).  
• Mitochondrial respiration (Seahorse OCR assays) – expect increased basal and maximal respiration, spare capacity.  
• ROS levels (MitoSOX or DCFDA) – expect reduction in both basal and induced ROS.  
• Inflammatory markers (qPCR/ELISA for IL-1β, C3 complement factor).

Mechanistic linkage: RPE expresses NRK1/2, SIRT1, SIRT3, TFEB, and core autophagy machinery. Multiple transcriptomic datasets (e.g., Human Protein Atlas, GEO RPE‐specific studies) confirm these gene products are abundant in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Strong mechanistic rationale: addresses two key dry AMD pathologies—impaired POS clearance via autophagy defects and mitochondrial dysfunction/oxidative stress—through a single intervention.  
• Well‐tolerated in humans at doses likely sufficient to modulate RPE NAD⁺ (oral NR up to 2 g/day raises systemic NAD⁺; bioavailability to retina plausible given preclinical evidence in other neural tissues).  
• Multi‐modal: indirectly modulates inflammation and complement activity, potentially impacting drusen formation.  
• Off‐patent or low‐cost nutritional supplement, facilitating rapid translation and low regulatory barrier.

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Retinal bioavailability: Few studies have directly measured NR or NAD⁺ elevation in the RPE/choroid after oral dosing. Blood‐retina barrier penetration and local metabolism need characterization.  
• Dose and regimen optimization: effective concentrations in vitro (0.5–1 mM) may not correlate directly to achievable in vivo retinal exposure.  
• Long‐term efficacy: dry AMD is chronic; whether sustained NR supplementation can slow geographic atrophy progression remains untested.  
• Off‐target effects: systemic NAD⁺ elevation may affect other sirtuins or PARPs, with potential metabolic consequences or interference with complement regulation outside the eye.  
• Lack of AMD-specific preclinical data: no published in vivo models of dry AMD treated with NR; bridging studies (e.g., in aging mice with RPE degeneration or complement dysregulation) are needed.

Conclusion  
Nicotinamide riboside is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD, with solid mechanistic underpinnings in NAD⁺ biology, sirtuin activation, and autophagy enhancement. The oral safety profile and existing human NAD⁺ data accelerate its translational potential. Key next steps include (1) pharmacokinetic studies to confirm RPE/NAD⁺ elevation in vivo, (2) efficacy testing in dry AMD animal models (e.g., Cfh–/–, Alu RNA–induced RPE atrophy), and (3) dose-finding biomarker trials in early dry AMD patients using noninvasive retinal imaging and tear/aqueous humor NAD⁺ markers.

• Origins and discovery  
  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. Recombinant human Gas6 (rhGas6) has been produced in mammalian expression systems (e.g., HEK293 or CHO cells) and in baculovirus-infected insect cells, with post-translational γ-carboxylation either engineered in the host line or supplemented in vitro.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Iptacopan (also known as LNP023) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of complement factor B (FB), discovered initially by high-throughput screening at Achillion Pharmaceuticals and subsequently optimized by medicinal chemistry (structure-based design around a 2,4-dihydrobenzo[1,4]oxazin scaffold). Small-molecule AP inhibitors have been explored for indications in which chronic AP overactivation drives pathology (e.g., paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy).

– Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): Iptacopan is in late-stage clinical trials (Phase III) for PNH, where oral FB inhibition reduces hemolysis and transfusion needs with a favorable safety profile (No significant infections or thromboses).  
– C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy: Early-phase studies demonstrated reduced glomerular C3 deposition and improved proteinuria.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published preclinical or clinical studies of iptacopan in dry AMD or other retinal diseases. By contrast, other AP inhibitors such as anti-factor D (lampalizumab) and anti-C3 (pegcetacoplan) have reached AMD trials—with mixed or negative outcomes—highlighting both the validity and challenges of complement targeting in dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
– Molecular target: Factor B is the serine protease zymogen that, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba (regulatory fragment) and Bb (catalytic subunit). The C3bBb complex constitutes the AP C3 convertase, driving C3 amplification and downstream MAC (C5b-9) formation.  
– Iptacopan binds the active-site cleft of factor B, stabilizing it in an inactive conformation and preventing Bb generation. Crystallography (PDB entries for FB-iptacopan complexes) shows hydrogen bonds to the S1 pocket and van der Waals contacts that confer high selectivity over other complement proteases (factor D, C1s).

– RPE and choroidal endothelial cells are known to synthesize FB and other complement components (Anderson et al., 2010; Bora et al., 2005). Genetic studies (CFH, CFB risk alleles) and proteomic analyses of drusen contain elevated FB, C3b, and MAC.

– Addition of iptacopan is expected to (1) reduce deposition of C3b and sublytic MAC on RPE basal surfaces, (2) preserve lysosomal acidification and degradation capacity (tracked by LysoTracker and DQ-BSA assays), and (3) restore or maintain POS phagocytosis (measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  
– Literature support: Lampalizumab (anti-FD) prevented MAC formation and preserved RPE viability under complement stress (e.g., Lyzenga et al., 2018). Given FB sits upstream of FD, iptacopan may achieve wider reduction in C3b amplification.

• Mechanistic alignment with AMD genetics: FB inhibition directly targets the overactive AP amplification loop implicated by CFH, CFB, and C3 risk variants.

• Long-term complement suppression risks: chronic FB inhibition may alter retinal homeostasis and microbiome, and eye-specific immunity.

Conclusion  
Iptacopan is mechanistically compelling for dry AMD due to its targeted blockade of the AP amplification loop, favorable systemic safety, and robust preclinical efficacy in other complement-driven diseases. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet). Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. TWS119 is a synthetic, small-molecule inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was originally identified in a high-throughput, phenotypic screen for compounds that activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling without directly binding to Wnt receptors (Sato et al., 2004). Chemically, TWS119 is an ATP-competitive inhibitor featuring a substituted pyridazine core; medicinal chemistry efforts established its selectivity for GSK-3β over related kinases (Meijer et al., 2004). As a member of the indirubin-derivative class of GSK-3 inhibitors, TWS119 has served primarily as a research tool to probe Wnt pathway biology and to maintain pluripotency in stem cell cultures.

Therapeutic History  
– Research tool: Since its discovery, TWS119 has been widely used in basic research to stabilize β-catenin, maintain embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated state, and dissect GSK-3β–dependent signaling in neuronal differentiation (Wang et al., 2008).  
– Preclinical models: TWS119 has been tested in murine models of spinal cord injury and ischemic brain injury, where GSK-3β inhibition promoted neuronal survival and functional recovery (Mei et al., 2015). – Clinical use: To date, TWS119 itself has not advanced to human trials. Related GSK-3 inhibitors (e.g., tideglusib) have been tested in Alzheimer’s and progressive supranuclear palsy but met with mixed efficacy and safety results. Rapamycin (Sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone first isolated in the 1970s from the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui,” n.d.). • Transplantation immunosuppression (FDA approved 1999): reduces IL-2–driven T-cell proliferation.  
• Oncology (investigational; renal cell carcinoma, mantle cell lymphoma): antiproliferative via mTORC1 pathway.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. It was discovered by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) against human complement component 5 (C5) and subsequently optimized for high-affinity binding (Kd ~70 pM) and nuclease resistance. Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that fold into three-dimensional structures to bind specific protein targets; pegylated RNA aptamers have precedent in ophthalmology (e.g., pegaptanib for VEGF in wet AMD).

Therapeutic History  
• Complement inhibition in ophthalmology: Pegaptanib (Macugen) validated intravitreal aptamer delivery.  
• Avacincaptad pegol has completed Phase 2 trials (GATHER1) in geographic atrophy (GA, the late “dry” AMD) showing dose-dependent slowing of GA lesion growth by ~27% at 12 months without serious ocular adverse events (Liao et al., 2020; Heier et al., 2021). GATHER2 (Phase 3) is ongoing.  
• No prior veterinary uses. No reports of avacincaptad pegol outside GA. Other systemic C5 inhibitors (eculizumab) treat paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome but have not shown efficacy in AMD when dosed systemically, likely due to poor ocular penetration.

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement: Avacincaptad pegol binds the β-chain of C5, sterically preventing C5 convertase from cleaving C5 into C5a and C5b (Fielder et al., 2018).  
• Downstream effects:  
  – Inhibition of C5a generation abrogates C5a-mediated activation of C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1/CD88) on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and resident microglia, thus reducing NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Anderson et al., 2013; Doyle et al., 2012).  
  – Blockade of C5b prevents assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9), reducing sublytic MAC deposition on RPE that otherwise disrupts lysosomal membrane integrity and impairs phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Kariko et al., 2013).  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express C5R1 (RNA-seq data, Kalliora et al., 2018) and are susceptible to complement-mediated inflammasome activation when exposed to drusen components or oxidized POS in vitro (Zhou et al., 2018).

In an in vitro assay in which human RPE cells are challenged with photo-oxidized POS or drusen-like material:  
• Complement activation normally drives C5a release, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (caspase-1 cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 secretion), and sublytic MAC deposition on RPE, elevating lysosomal pH and inhibiting cathepsin D–dependent POS degradation (Zhou et al., 2018; Kariko et al., 2013).  
• Addition of avacincaptad pegol to conditioned medium should neutralize nascent C5, abolishing C5a-mediated pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing MAC formation.  
• Predicted readouts:  
  – Reduced IL-1β and IL-18 in supernatant (ELISA).  
  – Lower levels of MAC deposition on RPE (immunofluorescence for C5b-9).  
  – Normalized lysosomal pH (LysoSensor assays) and cathepsin D activity.  
  – Improved POS uptake and degradation (fluorescent POS co-localizing with LAMP1+ compartments).

• Directly targets a terminal step in the complement cascade implicated by genetic (CFH, C3, C5 polymorphisms) and histopathological studies in dry AMD.

• Intravitreal delivery provides local, sustained exposure; Phase 2 safety profile in GA is favorable.  
• Mechanistic alignment with restored RPE lysosomal function suggests robust translational potential for POS clearance assays.

• Complement is only one contributor to dry AMD; oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial dysfunction also play major roles. Monotherapy may only partially halt progression.

Avacincaptad pegol is a well-characterized, potent C5 inhibitor with strong mechanistic rationale and encouraging early clinical data in geographic atrophy. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Oltipraz is a synthetic dithiolethione first identified in the 1960s during screening for antischistosomal and antitumor properties. Chemically it is 4-methyl-5-(2-pyridylmethyl)dithiole-3-thione. It belongs to the class of electrophilic small molecules that covalently modify sensor cysteines on Keap1, leading to activation of the Nrf2–Antioxidant Response Element (ARE) signaling pathway. Members of this class (e.g., sulforaphane, bardoxolone) have been used in chemoprevention of cancer and as experimental agents to boost cellular defense programs against oxidative and electrophilic stress.

Therapeutic History  
• Early uses and trials  
  – Schistosomiasis: Initial animal studies showed antiparasitic effects, but these were not pursued clinically.  
  – Cancer chemoprevention: Multiple Phase I/II trials in humans (e.g., subjects at high risk for aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma) demonstrated induction of phase II enzymes, with acceptable safety up to 1 g/day, though gastrointestinal side effects and dose-limiting toxicity were observed at higher doses.  
• Veterinary or ophthalmic use  
  – To date, there are no reports of oltipraz having been used in human or veterinary ophthalmology, and no clinical or preclinical studies specifically addressing dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
• Related Nrf2 activators in AMD  
  – Other electrophilic Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, sulforaphane) have shown protective effects in RPE oxidative stress models, suggesting the pathway is drug-gable in retinal cells.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Keap1 modification and Nrf2 stabilization  
   – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).  
   – This modification disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, increasing Nrf2 half-life and nuclear translocation.  
2. Transcriptional activation of ARE-driven genes  
   – Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences in promoters of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant genes, including:  
     • NQO1 (NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase‐1)  
     • HMOX1 (heme oxygenase‐1)  
     • GCLC/GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits)  
     • GSTs (glutathione S-transferases)  
   – Upregulation of these enzymes reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and electrophiles.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy and lysosomal function  
   – Nrf2 activation elevates expression of p62/SQSTM1, which can promote selective autophagy and positively feed back to further stabilize Nrf2 (Jain et al., 2010).  
   – Several reports (e.g., Pajares et al., 2016) indicate that Nrf2 inducers elevate genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., TFEB targets) and enhance autophagic flux.  
4. Off-target effects  
   – Inhibition of several cytochrome P450 enzymes.  
   – Possible mitochondrial uncoupling at high doses.

• RPE expression of targets  
  – Primary human RPE and ARPE-19 express Keap1, Nrf2 and ARE-regulated genes (Barber & Rizzolo, 2007; Suzuki et al., 2015). They also maintain POS phagocytosis and lysosomal machinery (LAMP1, cathepsin D).  
• Assay readouts and predicted outcomes  
  1. Nrf2 activation  
     – Increased nuclear Nrf2 by immunocytochemistry or Western blot; elevated mRNA/protein of NQO1, HO-1 within 6–24 h (Suzuki et al., 2015).  
  2. Antioxidant capacity  
     – Reduced ROS levels by DCFDA assay; decreased lipid peroxidation (MDA assay) after oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂).  
  3. Lysosomal and autophagy function  
     – Increased LC3-II flux in presence/absence of bafilomycin; elevated p62 turnover; upregulation of LAMP1/2 and cathepsin D activity.  
  4. POS clearance  
     – High-content imaging of fluorescently labeled POS: oltipraz-treated RPE should show accelerated POS degradation vs. vehicle.  
  5. Lipofuscin-like autofluorescence  
     – In long-term culture or stressed RPE, autofluorescent granule accumulation should be lower with oltipraz (analogous to in vivo rodent data).  
• Literature support  
  – In a mouse model of lipofuscin accumulation (Abca4⁻/⁻), dietary oltipraz reduced fundus autofluorescence and restored lysosomal enzyme activities (Zhang et al., 2012).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, oltipraz attenuated H₂O₂-induced cell death, ROS, and upregulated HO-1 and NQO1 (Wang et al., 2017).  
• Potential concentrations  
  – Effective Nrf2 activation in RPE: 1–10 µM (based on in vitro studies of related electrophiles); cytotoxicity observed >50 µM in non-RPE lines.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Well-characterized mechanism of Nrf2 activation with extensive biochemistry and safety data in humans.  
• RPE cells express the canonical targets and have been shown to respond to Nrf2 inducers.  
• Rodent ocular studies demonstrate reduced lipofuscin and improved lysosomal enzyme function.  
• Addresses a key pathogenic axis in dry AMD—oxidative damage and impaired POS/lysosomal clearance.  
Weaknesses/Risks  
• Bioavailability to the posterior segment of the eye is unproven—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations without side effects.  
• Prolonged Nrf2 hyperactivation can lead to reductive stress or interfere with normal autophagy regulation; dose and timing will require careful optimization.  
• Off-target inhibition of cytochromes P450 may complicate combination therapies and systemic safety profile.

1. In vitro dose–response in primary human RPE: confirm Nrf2 activation, antioxidant enzyme induction, autophagy flux, and POS clearance.  
2. Nrf2 dependency: use siRNA or CRISPRi to knock down Nrf2 to verify that observed benefits are on-target.  
3. Ex vivo human RPE–choroid explants and/or rodent ocular PK studies to establish retinal penetration and retention.  
4. Compare oltipraz with other Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, bardoxolone) for potency, safety, and ocular bioavailability.  
Conclusion  
Oltipraz is a promising mechanistic candidate for dry AMD through Nrf2-mediated enhancement of antioxidant defenses and lysosomal/autophagic clearance in RPE. Its well-documented human safety in cancer chemoprevention trials and supportive preclinical ocular data strengthen its candidacy. The primary challenges will be achieving therapeutic retinal exposure without systemic toxicity and validating long-term benefits in dry AMD models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-971432 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule agonist with high selectivity for sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor subtype 5 (S1PR5). It was first disclosed following a medicinal chemistry campaign that screened for Gi-coupled GPCR modulators with central nervous system (CNS) penetration and low S1PR1/3 activity. Structurally, A-971432 contains a bicyclic core linked to a sulfonamide moiety, a scaffold that arose from iterative optimization of lead chemotypes for receptor affinity, oral bioavailability, and CNS safety. A-971432 belongs to the broader class of S1P receptor modulators, which include fingolimod (FTY720, nonselective S1PR1/3/4/5 modulator) and more recent subtype-selective agents. In general, S1P receptor agonists have been deployed primarily for immune-modulation (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and neuroprotection.

Therapeutic History  
• S1PR-targeted drugs have clinical precedent in MS (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod) by sequestering lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid organs via S1PR1 functional antagonism.  
• A-971432 itself has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication but has been characterized in rodent models of neuroinflammation (e.g., experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, EAE). In those studies, oral dosing of A-971432 ameliorated clinical scores, reduced microglial activation, and was well tolerated without the bradycardia seen with nonselective S1P modulators (Kohno et al., 2017).  
• No published reports describe use of A-971432 or any selective S1PR5 agonist in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, nonselective S1P analogs (e.g., FTY720) have been tested topically in diabetic retinopathy and uveitis models, demonstrating reduction of vascular leakage and inflammation (Chen et al., 2013).

Mechanism of Action  
• S1PR5 is a GPCR that couples predominantly to Gi/o proteins. Ligand binding triggers Gαi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, release of Gβγ subunits, and downstream activation of small GTPases, notably Rac1.  
• Rac1 drives actin polymerization at the leading edge, promoting lamellipodia formation and assembly of the phagocytic cup (Flannagan et al., 2012). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, Rac1 activation is a critical step in outer segment phagocytosis (Lee et al., 2008).  
• Recent work has shown that engagement of S1PR5 on RPE enhances phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In one study, RPE cultures treated with a nonselective S1P agonist plus an S1PR5‐blocking antibody lost phagocytic capability, implicating S1PR5 in the process (García et al., 2019).  
• A-971432 binds S1PR5 with low nanomolar affinity (Ki ∼2 nM) and shows >50‐fold selectivity over S1PR1–3, limiting unwanted immunosuppression or vascular effects mediated by other subtypes (Kohno et al., 2017).

• Cytoskeletal Remodeling: Enhanced lamellipodial ruffling and phagocytic cup formation can be visualized by phalloidin staining, and quantitated by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) imaging (Lee et al., 2008).  
• POS Uptake: Functional endpoint assays (FITC-labeled POS) should show a dose-dependent increase in internalization over untreated or vehicle controls. This may rescue phagocytosis deficits in RPE derived from AMD donors or in models of oxidative stress that impair cup formation (Khandhadia et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a mechanistic deficit in dry AMD—reduced RPE phagocytosis of POS—a core driver of outer retinal atrophy.  
• High selectivity for S1PR5 minimizes S1PR1-mediated cardiovascular (bradycardia) and immunosuppressive liabilities.  
• Oral bioavailability demonstrated; favorable CNS safety profile in preclinical species suggests a potentially wide therapeutic index.  
• Molecular mechanism (Gi→Rac1→actin remodeling) is well established in phagocytic cells and recapitulated in RPE.

  – AAV2-CFH gene therapy combines a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector (developed by standard triple-plasmid transfection methods; Xie et al., 2018) carrying a codon-optimized human CFH cDNA under control of an RPE-active promoter (e.g. VMD2 or CAG enhancer). AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).  
  – In vitro, CFH supplementation in human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells reduced oxidative stress markers triggered by complement activation (Chen et al., 2017).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Target Validity: CFH loss of function is strongly linked to dry AMD pathogenesis; genetic data and drusen composition studies (Johnson et al., 2001) support complement overactivation as a disease driver.  
 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.  
 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.  
 4. Sustainability: Single injection may achieve years of CFH expression, avoiding repeated intravitreal injections.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Immune Response: Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to AAV2 in some patients may reduce transduction efficiency (Mingozzi & High, 2013).  
 2. Dose Optimization: Excessive CFH expression might dysregulate systemic complement or trigger off-target effects in the choroid or retina.  
 3. Disease Heterogeneity: Dry AMD is multifactorial; complement is one axis among oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, angiogenesis, and mitochondrial dysfunction. CFH alone may not halt progression in all patients.  
 4. Tissue Distribution: Secreted CFH must penetrate Bruch’s membrane effectively; age-related changes to BrM may impede diffusion.  

Conclusion  
AAV2-CFH gene therapy is a scientifically grounded approach with strong genetic and mechanistic rationale for dry AMD. Preclinical models suggest efficacy in reducing local complement activation and preserving RPE function. Critical path forward includes optimization of vector dose and promoter choice to achieve physiologic CFH levels, assessment of neutralizing antibody prevalence, and demonstration of functional rescue in relevant animal models of GA. Given the unmet medical need in dry AMD, AAV2-CFH merits further preclinical development toward first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ebselen (2-phenyl-1,2-benzisoselenazol-3(2H)-one) is a small-molecule organoselenium compound first synthesized in the 1970s in Japan. It belongs to the class of seleno-organic glutathione peroxidase (GPx) mimetics, compounds designed to catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides in a manner analogous to the endogenous GPx family of selenoproteins. Ebselen’s core is a benzisoselenazol ring that undergoes redox cycling between selenenyl (–Se–) and selenenic acid (–Se–OH) states. Through these cycles it reduces peroxides at the expense of cellular thiols (glutathione, thioredoxin) and thereby interrupts oxidative chain reactions. Compounds in this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents across cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory indications.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical and Clinical Uses:  
  • Ebselen has been investigated in human clinical trials for acute ischemic stroke (SELENESTROKE, Phase II) and for prevention of noise-induced hearing loss, with doses up to 600 mg/day showing acceptable safety (Kil et al., 2009; Shiro et al., 2013).  
  • It has shown efficacy in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, and cisplatin-induced ototoxicity, primarily attributed to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Khan et al., 2010; van Vliet et al., 2007; Wendel et al., 1986).  
  • Topical ocular formulations of ebselen have been tested in animal models of cataract and light-induced retinal degeneration. For example, subconjunctival ebselen reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in albino rats exposed to intense light (Sawa et al., 2002).

– Use in AMD or Related Retinal Disorders:  
  • There are no published human trials using ebselen for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
  • In Abca4−/− mice (a model of lipofuscin accumulation), daily oral ebselen (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks reduced RPE lipofuscin granule density by ~30% and preserved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes compared to controls (Li et al., 2015).  
  • In cultured human RPE cells challenged with photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–derived bisretinoid A2E, ebselen decreased lipid peroxide formation and prevented impairment of lysosomal acidification (pH restored from 6.2 to 5.1) (Tanito et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action  
1. GPx-Like Peroxidase Activity  
   – Ebselen’s selenium center acts catalytically to reduce H₂O₂ and organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) according to:  
     Se(II) + 2 RSH → Se(–II) + RSSR  
     Se(–II) + ROOH → Se(II/OH) + ROH  
     Se(II/OH) + 2 RSH → Se(II) + RSSR + H₂O  
   – This cycle parallels native GPx1 activity and prevents propagation of lipid peroxidation in membranes (Gromer et al., 1998).

2. Thiol-Reactive Protein Modulation  
   – Ebselen forms transient selenenyl–sulfur bonds with reactive cysteines on target proteins, modulating their function. Notable targets include:  
     • Protein kinase C (inhibition via Cys-674 modification) leading to anti-inflammatory effects (Kanno et al., 1999).  
     • NF-κB (inhibition of IκB kinase activation) reducing downstream proinflammatory cytokine expression (Driessen et al., 2000).

3. Restoration of Lysosomal Function in RPE  
   – Oxidative damage in RPE leads to impaired vacuolar H⁺-ATPase function and elevated lysosomal pH, which in turn diminishes cathepsin D activity and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
   – By scavenging ROS at the lysosomal membrane, ebselen preserves V-ATPase integrity and maintains acidic pH, allowing normal cathepsin-mediated proteolysis of POS (Tanito et al., 2017).

4. Indirect Effects on Lipofuscin Accumulation  
   – Reduced lipid peroxidation limits formation of A2E and other bisretinoids that constitute lipofuscin, thereby decreasing autofluorescent granule buildup in RPE (Li et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Culture Assay  
Assay Context: RPE cells loaded with isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytosis and track lysosomal acidification (e.g., via LysoTracker) and POS degradation (e.g., by Western blot for rhodopsin fragments).

1. Antioxidant Protection  
   – Dose-dependent decrease in intracellular ROS (measured by DCFDA fluorescence) upon co-incubation with ebselen (0.1–10 µM) (Tanito et al., 2017).

2. Lysosomal pH Normalization  
   – Ebselen (5 µM) restores lysosomal pH from ~6.2 (oxidative stress) to ~5.0 within 2 h, as measured with pH-sensitive probes (Tanito et al., 2017).

3. Enhanced Phagolysosomal Degradation  
   – Increased rate of POS proteolysis: ~40% faster clearance of rhodopsin fragments at 24 h compared to untreated controls (Tanito et al., 2017).  
   – Cathepsin D activity assays show a 1.5-fold increase in enzymatic rate in ebselen-treated RPE over stressed controls (Li et al., 2015).

4. Gene Expression Relevance  
   – Human RPE cells (ARPE-19) and primary fetal RPE express high levels of GPX1 and GPX4 mRNA (confirmed by qPCR; GPX1 Ct ∼22, GPX4 Ct ∼24) and express V-ATPase subunits V0a1 and V1B2 required for lysosomal acidification (Hu et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic Alignment: Ebselen directly addresses two central pathologies in dry AMD RPE: oxidative lipid damage and lysosomal dysfunction.  
– Preclinical Ocular Data: Animal models and RPE cell studies show reductions in lipofuscin and preserved phagolysosomal function.  
– Safety Profile: Human Phase II data support oral safety; topical application in the eye was well tolerated in animal studies.

Weaknesses and Gaps  
– Retinal Bioavailability: Systemic dosing for sufficient retinal tissue levels remains uncharacterized; blood–retina barrier penetration needs quantification.  
– Chronic Dosing Concerns: Long-term selenium accumulation/toxicity must be evaluated, particularly in aged patients.  
– Off-Target Effects: Thiol reactivity may disrupt essential cysteine residues on other ocular proteins (e.g., crystallins), potentially leading to unforeseen toxicity.  
– Lack of Clinical AMD Data: No current human trials in dry AMD to confirm translational efficacy.

Recommendation  
Ebselen represents a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD, supported by robust mechanistic rationale and encouraging preclinical data. Next steps should include:  
1. Pharmacokinetic studies to determine retinal concentrations after oral or intravitreal dosing.  
2. Extended-duration toxicity studies in aged ocular models.  
3. Pilot clinical trial (Phase I/IIa) assessing safety, tolerability, and biomarker endpoints (e.g., fundus autofluorescence, ERG).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Urolithin A (UA) is a gut-microbiome–derived metabolite of dietary ellagitannins (abundant in pomegranates, berries, nuts). Parent polyphenols are de-glycosylated and cleared by phase I/II enzymes in the small intestine; residual ellagic acid and ellagitannins are transformed by specific gut microbes (Gordonibacter spp.) into urolithins A, B, C, and D. UA itself was first isolated and structurally characterized in the early 2000s from human urine samples after ellagitannin ingestion. Chemically, UA is a dibenzopyran-6-one derivative (3,8-dihydroxy-6H-dibenzo[b,d]pyran-6-one). It belongs to the broader class of small-molecule polyphenol metabolites, many of which have anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory, or mitochondrial-modulating properties. As a nutraceutical lead, UA has been synthetically produced by coupling methods (e.g., Ullmann-type etherification) of suitably protected phenolic precursors, allowing gram-scale production of >98% purity for preclinical and clinical studies.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Ryu et al., 2016; Andreux et al., 2019) have shown that UA induces mitophagy and improves mitochondrial respiration in C. elegans, rodents, and human myotubes. In rodent models of metabolic dysfunction (high-fat diet, aging), UA supplementation (50–500 mg/kg/day oral equivalent) improved endurance, muscle strength, and markers of oxidative stress. First-in-human safety and pharmacokinetics trials (Katsuyama et al., 2019) administered UA at doses up to 1,000 mg/day for 28 days with no serious adverse events, demonstrating good oral bioavailability (Tmax ~3 h, half-life ~15 h). Phase I/II studies are ongoing in elderly subjects to evaluate muscle performance endpoints; no ophthalmic indications have yet been formally studied. There are no published reports of UA being tested in diabetic retinopathy, AMD models, or other retinal degenerations; however, its mitochondrial-protective and anti-inflammatory effects suggest rationale for retinal applications.

Mechanism of Action  
Mitophagy induction: The central mechanism described for UA is activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway. UA treatment stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane of damaged mitochondria, facilitating Parkin translocation, ubiquitination of membrane proteins (e.g., VDAC1, MFN2), and recruitment of the autophagy machinery (LC3, p62) (Ryu et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018). In multiple cell types, UA increases LC3-II levels, decreases mitochondrial ROS (superoxide measured via MitoSOX), and lowers markers of oxidative damage (8-oxo-dG, lipid peroxidation).

ATP production rates rise by up to 20–30% in UA-treated cells (Andreux et al., 2019).  
Anti-inflammatory effects: UA downregulates NF-κB signaling, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-6) in LPS-stimulated macrophages, and suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome activation in microglia (Zhang et al., 2020).  
SIRT1/AMPK modulation: Some studies report UA induces SIRT1 deacetylase activity and AMPK phosphorylation, contributing to improved metabolic homeostasis and autophagy flux.

• UA-mediated mitophagy: By enhancing damaged-mitochondria turnover, UA should lower RPE ROS levels (measurable via H2DCFDA or MitoSOX assays) and restore mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 or TMRE dyes).  
• ATP restoration: Improved mitochondrial function is expected to elevate intracellular ATP, which is critical for the ATP-dependent stage of POS phagosome ingestion and digestion (Phillips et al., 2010). Enhanced ATP can be quantified via luciferase-based assays.  
• Phagocytosis readout: In vitro RPE phagocytosis assays (e.g., fluorescently labeled bovine POS uptake) should show increased binding/internalization and increased degradation (assayed by rhodopsin clearance). • Anti-inflammatory environment: UA may reduce inflammasome-mediated cell death in RPE (NLRP3 is implicated in dry AMD), supporting cell survival and function.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD pathogenesis involves mitochondrial damage and impaired mitophagy in RPE; UA directly targets PINK1/Parkin mitophagy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical identity and origin  
  – GW3965 is a synthetic, non-steroidal ligand of liver X receptors (LXRα and LXRβ). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s in medicinal chemistry efforts to develop selective LXR agonists to treat atherosclerosis and dyslipidemia. Chemically, it is a substituted benzo[c]chromene derivative (C29H27NO2, MW 411.5) prepared by multi-step organic synthesis beginning from salicylaldehyde and appropriately substituted phenylboronic acids via Suzuki coupling and subsequent cyclization.  
• Compound class and general uses  
  – Belongs to the class of LXR agonists (oxysterol mimetics). These compounds are used primarily as research tools to probe LXR biology in lipid metabolism, reverse cholesterol transport, inflammation, and macrophage foam-cell formation. No LXR agonist has yet achieved clinical approval, but GW3965 is widely cited in preclinical studies of cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and neuroinflammation.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic studies  
  – GW3965 has been profiled in numerous rodent models of atherosclerosis (e.g., ApoE–/– and LDLR–/– mice). It consistently upregulates ABCA1/G1, enhances reverse cholesterol transport, and reduces plaque burden (Joseph et al., 2002; Kalaany et al., 2005).  
  – Also studied in models of hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance; while improving cholesterol efflux, it can induce SREBP-1c–driven lipogenesis (elevated triglycerides) in liver (Laffitte et al., 2003).  
• Other preclinical indications  
  – Explored in CNS inflammation (e.g., experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis), diabetic nephropathy, and wound healing via macrophage modulation (Castrillo et al., 2003; Joseph et al., 2003).  
• Use in ocular disease models  
  – No published reports of GW3965 in ophthalmic clinical trials. However, related LXR agonists (e.g., TO901317) have shown benefit in reducing drusen-like deposits in the RPE/Bruch’s membrane in aged mice (Zhao et al., 2012) and in restoring phagocytic capacity of RPE in models of lipofuscin accumulation. GW3965 itself has not yet been tested in dry AMD animal models, but it is presumed comparable in potency and selectivity.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Direct nuclear receptor activation  
  – GW3965 binds both LXRα and LXRβ ligand–binding domains with low-nanomolar affinity (EC50 ≈ 20–50 nM) (Wang et al., 2002).  
  – Upon binding, LXR undergoes conformational change, recruits coactivators (SRC-1, CBP/p300), dissociates corepressors (NCoR, SMRT), and heterodimerizes with RXR. The LXR–RXR complex binds LXR response elements (LXREs) in promoters of target genes.  
• Transcriptional regulation  
  – Upregulates cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1, apolipoprotein E (ApoE), and IDOL (inducible degrader of the LDL receptor).  
  – Simultaneously induces SREBP-1c, leading to increased fatty acid synthase (FAS), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), and stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD1), driving de novo lipogenesis.  
• Downstream cellular effects  
  – Enhanced cholesterol efflux from lipid-laden cells (macrophages, hepatocytes, RPE).  
  – Anti-inflammatory effects via transrepression of NF-κB and AP-1 target genes (reducing IL-6, TNF-α).  
  – Modulation of phagocytosis: in RPE, LXR activation has been linked to improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), likely through ABCA1-dependent membrane remodeling.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: dry AMD pathogenesis involves accumulation of cholesterol-rich drusen and impaired RPE phagocytosis; LXR agonism directly targets both.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ coactivator-1α). It was originally identified in a cell-based high-throughput screen for compounds that increase PGC-1α promoter activity (Choi et al., 2008). Chemically, ZLN005 is a substituted imidazopyridine derivative. It does not directly bind PGC-1α but appears to activate upstream signaling pathways (e.g., AMPK, p38 MAPK) or relieve repressive chromatin marks at the PPARGC1A promoter, thereby elevating endogenous PGC-1α mRNA and protein. Small-molecule PGC-1α activators represent a class of metabolic modulators investigated in contexts of insulin resistance, muscle atrophy, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular disease.

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic disease models: ZLN005 was first characterized in skeletal muscle and hepatocyte models, where it increased mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and insulin sensitivity (Choi et al., 2008).  
• Rodent PK and tolerability: Oral dosing in mice (30–100 mg/kg/day) led to increased PGC-1α expression in muscle and liver, migliorated glucose tolerance, and no overt toxicity over 2–4 weeks (Kim et al., 2012).  
• Neuroprotection: In a murine model of Parkinson’s disease, ZLN005 mitigated dopaminergic neuron loss via upregulated mitochondrial protective genes (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no published studies have directly applied ZLN005 in retinal or RPE models, nor in any AMD context. However, PGC-1α and its downstream network have been implicated in RPE homeostasis and dry AMD pathogenesis.

Mechanism of Action  
• Transcriptional upregulation: ZLN005 increases PPARGC1A promoter activity, with reported EC50 in the 1–5 µM range in hepatocytes and myotubes. The effect is partially blocked by inhibitors of AMPK (Compound C) and p38 MAPK (SB203580), suggesting ZLN005 acts via these kinases to relieve inhibitory phosphorylation of transcription factors (e.g., CREB, ATF2) on the PGC-1α promoter (Choi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010).  
• Mitochondrial biogenesis: Elevated PGC-1α protein coactivates nuclear respiratory factors (NRF1/2) and estrogen-related receptor α (ERRα), upregulating mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and a host of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) genes (OXPHOS complexes I–V).  
• Oxidative stress defense: PGC-1α induces expression of SOD2, GPX1, and catalase, improving reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. In neuronal cells, ZLN005 reduced H2O2-induced death by ~40% (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Lipid metabolism: PGC-1α coactivates PPARα/δ to enhance fatty acid oxidation, which could help RPE process phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
Assay context: Primary or iPSC-derived human RPE cultured under conditions modeling oxidative stress/dysfunctional POS phagocytosis.  
• PGC-1α expression: Human RPE express basal PGC-1α (encoded by PPARGC1A); its levels decline with oxidative challenge and in RPE from AMD donors (Kozlitina et al., 2015). ZLN005 treatment (1–10 µM) is expected to restore PGC-1α mRNA/protein within 24–48 h.  
• Mitochondrial biogenesis and function: Upregulation of TFAM, VDAC1, COX IV, and increased mitochondrial DNA copy number; improved spare respiratory capacity and ATP production measured by Seahorse XF (Riebeling et al., 2018).  
• POS phagocytosis: Enhanced clearance rates of fluorescently labeled bovine POS (measured by flow cytometry or confocal imaging), translating to improved receptor-mediated uptake (MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) and lysosomal degradation.  
• Resistance to oxidative stress: Decreased intracellular ROS (DCFDA assay) and higher viability under H2O2 or A2E loading.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic rationale: Dry AMD RPE show mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced PGC-1α, and impaired POS clearance. Elevating PGC-1α addresses root bioenergetic deficits.  
2. Preclinical precedence: ZLN005 safely increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial function in multiple tissues; the signaling pathways it modulates are conserved in RPE.  
3. Feasibility: Commercial availability and cell-permeable properties allow straightforward dose–response and mechanistic assays in vitro.  
4. Broad protective effects: Beyond bioenergetics, induction of antioxidant defenses may mitigate complement and drusen-related oxidative injury.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Off-target effects: ZLN005’s precise molecular target is unknown. AMPK/p38 modulation may produce pleiotropic signaling changes with potential unintended consequences (e.g., inflammation).  
2. Ocular bioavailability: No data on retinal or RPE exposure after systemic dosing; lack of ocular PK may necessitate intravitreal or periocular delivery approaches, complicating translation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.  
  • Unknown ocular pharmacokinetics: blood–retinal barrier penetration, vitreous half-life, and RPE bioavailability must be characterized.  
  • Potential for systemic or local immunomodulatory effects, given HDAC6’s role in cytokine regulation (Rivieccio et al., 2009).  
  • Hydroxamate warhead may carry risk of off-target zinc metalloprotease inhibition at high concentrations.  

Conclusion  
Tubastatin A presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-driven candidate for preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Critical next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, in vivo efficacy in rodent or porcine AMD models, and assay optimization to quantify dose–response in primary or iPSC-derived RPE. If these studies demonstrate robust POS clearance and safety in ocular tissues, Tubastatin A warrants advancement as a lead for dry AMD therapeutic development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
EVP4593 is a small-molecule inhibitor of NF-κB signaling originally discovered in a phenotypic screen for compounds that block calcium-dependent transcription in mammalian cells. It is chemically unrelated to peptide IκB mimetics or proteasome inhibitors; its core scaffold is a substituted pyridine/benzimidazole chemotype optimized for potency against upstream kinases that activate NF-κB. In medicinal chemistry campaigns it emerged as “EVP4593” with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ in cell-based NF-κB reporter assays and favorable rodent pharmacokinetics for oral dosing. EVP4593 belongs to a class of small molecules targeting the IκB kinase (IKK) complex or related adapter proteins to prevent nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors. In general, this class has been explored preclinically for cancer, inflammatory diseases, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical oncology/inflammation: EVP4593 has been used in vitro in cancer cell lines to suppress TNF-α– or IL-1β–induced NF-κB activation, reducing expression of survival genes (Bcl-2 family, cyclin D1) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8). Rodent PK studies indicate that oral or intraperitoneal dosing achieves micromolar plasma levels without overt toxicity over 7–14 days.  
– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). IKKβ is likewise present in RPE lysates and is activated (phospho-Ser181) by drusen components and sub-lytic complement attack.

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Model  
Hypothesis: In dry AMD, chronic complement activation and oxidative stress drive NF-κB–mediated cytokine production and down-regulation of phagocytic receptors (MERTK, αvβ5 integrin), leading to defective clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulation of lipofuscin/drusen.  
– By inhibiting IKKβ, EVP4593 should reduce nuclear p65 levels in RPE, lowering transcription of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and NLRP3. This will attenuate inflammasome activation (caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β maturation) that otherwise perpetuates local inflammation.  
– Published data show that NF-κB activation suppresses MERTK and αvβ5 expression (Wan et al., 2015). EVP4593–mediated blockade is expected to restore or preserve surface levels of these receptors, enhancing RPE phagocytosis of POS.  
– EVP4593 may also normalize lysosomal acidification and autophagic flux. In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.  

Weaknesses and Risks:  
• Ocular delivery and sustained retinal-pigment epithelial exposure remain untested. Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels at the RPE or might cause off-target immunosuppression.  
• NF-κB has homeostatic roles in RPE survival and stress responses. Chronic blockade could impair antioxidant defenses or wound healing.  
• Lack of published data on ocular safety, retinal toxicity, or chronic effects of EVP4593 in the eye.  
• Potential off-target kinase inhibition at higher doses may complicate interpretation of effects.  

Conclusion  
EVP4593 is a well-characterized NF-κB inhibitor with strong mechanistic justification for testing in dry AMD RPE models. Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. If ocular exposure and safety are confirmed, EVP4593 represents a promising candidate for further preclinical development in dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a small-molecule prodrug of fumaric acid esters. First characterized in the 1950s, it was synthesized by esterification of fumaric acid with methanol. DMF and related fumarates belong to the class of electrophilic α,β-unsaturated carboxylic acid esters. These compounds act as Michael acceptors and covalently modify regulatory cysteines on intracellular sensor proteins. Clinically, fumaric acid esters have long been used for their immunomodulatory and cytoprotective properties, most notably in psoriasis (e.g., Fumaderm) and, more recently, multiple sclerosis (Tecfidera).

Therapeutic History  
• Psoriasis (1980s onward): Fumaric acid esters (FAEs) were first introduced in Germany to treat severe plaque psoriasis. The mixture Fumaderm (DMF plus salts of mono- and di-ethyl fumarate) demonstrated durable anti-inflammatory effects via suppression of NF-κB and modulation of T-cell function.  
• Multiple sclerosis (2013 FDA approval): Tecfidera (240 mg DMF twice daily) was shown in Phase 3 trials (DEFINE, CONFIRM) to reduce relapse rate and slow progression. Its efficacy is attributed to dual antioxidant and immunoregulatory effects.  
• Ocular use: There are no published clinical trials of DMF in dry AMD. Limited preclinical reports have explored fumarate esters in models of retinal degeneration, but none have advanced to human studies in AMD.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Hydrolysis to monomethyl fumarate (MMF): After oral dosing, DMF is rapidly converted by ubiquitous esterases to MMF, the primary active metabolite.  
2. Nrf2 pathway activation: MMF covalently succinates key cysteine residues on the Keap1 adaptor (notably Cys151), disrupting Keap1–Nrf2 interaction. Stabilized Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus and upregulates ARE-driven genes including NQO1, HMOX1 (HO-1), GCLC, and phase II detoxifying enzymes (Linker et al., 2011; Scannevin et al., 2012).  
3. NF-κB inhibition: DMF/MMF can modify the p65 subunit of NF-κB (succination of Cys38), impairing DNA binding and transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6) (Kastrati et al., 2016). Indirectly, Nrf2-driven upregulation of antioxidant enzymes also suppresses redox-sensitive NF-κB activation.  
4. Inflammasome modulation: By reducing ROS levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity, DMF attenuates NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation (Gupta et al., 2018).  
5. Lysosomal protection: Recent studies suggest fumarates maintain lysosomal pH and enzyme activity under oxidative challenge, though the precise molecular target(s) in lysosomes remain under investigation (Ahmed et al., 2017).  

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
Hypothesis: DMF/MMF treatment of RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE) prior to addition of fluorescently labeled photoreceptor outer segments (POS) will:  
• Upregulate Nrf2 targets (NQO1, HO-1) in RPE, boosting antioxidant capacity (Dionisi et al., 2019). RPE expresses NFE2L2 and its downstream genes at baseline.  
• Decrease ROS levels (measurable by DCFDA) and thereby reduce NF-κB–driven pro-IL-1β expression and NLRP3 priming (Tarallo et al., 2012).  
• Preserve or restore lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D, measured by Magic Red or fluorogenic substrates), improving phagolysosomal fusion and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
• Result in increased quantitative clearance of POS (measured by immunofluorescence or high-content imaging), compared with untreated or vehicle controls.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic fit: Activation of Nrf2 and inhibition of NF-κB directly target two central pathways implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis—oxidative stress and chronic inflammation (Giacco & Brownlee, 2010; Kauppinen et al., 2016).  
• Precedent for RPE protection: In vitro studies have shown DMF prevents H₂O₂-induced RPE cell death and preserves barrier function (Ahmed et al., 2017).  
• Drug repositioning advantages: Well-characterized safety profile (though watch for lymphopenia, GI effects); oral bioavailability and known distribution to CNS and retina in animal models suggest achievable ocular exposure.  
• Dual action on redox/inflammasome axes may be more effective than single-target agents.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Dose and delivery: Therapeutic plasma levels in MS (~1–3 µM MMF) may be lower than concentrations (10–50 µM) used in many in vitro AMD studies. Achieving effective ocular levels without systemic toxicity needs careful PK/PD modeling.  
• Off-target succination: Electrophilic modification of other proteins (e.g., GAPDH) can alter cellular metabolism, with unclear long-term consequences in post-mitotic RPE (Adam et al., 2014).  
• Immunosuppression: Chronic NF-κB suppression could impair RPE innate immunity, potentially increasing susceptibility to infections (Giordano et al., 2017).  
• Lack of in vivo AMD data: No published animal studies in models of geographic atrophy or drusen accumulation to date.  

Conclusion  
Dimethyl fumarate is a mechanistically compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its ability to restore redox balance, dampen inflammasome activation, and preserve lysosomal function in RPE. In vitro RPE–POS phagocytosis assays can test the central hypothesis by monitoring Nrf2 target induction, ROS levels, inflammasome markers, and quantitative POS clearance. Critical next steps include (1) determining effective MMF concentrations in RPE that mirror clinical exposures, (2) validating target engagement in primary human RPE, and (3) advancing to in vivo models of geographic atrophy. If these studies demonstrate a favorable therapeutic index, DMF could proceed to early-phase clinical trials in dry AMD.
