Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Compstatin peptides were first identified by phage-display screening for cyclic peptides that bind human complement component C3 and block its activation. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).  
  – By inhibiting C3b generation, formation of downstream C5 convertase, generation of C5a, and assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) are all suppressed.  
• Downstream cellular and tissue effects  
  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis. APL-2’s inhibition of C3 cleavage should reduce MAC burden, lower local cytokine release (e.g., IL-18, IL-1β), and preserve RPE function.  
  – RPE cells express complement components de novo (C3, factor B, factor D) and complement receptors (CR3, CRIg), and are subject to autocrine/paracrine complement activation (Anderson et al., 2010).  

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assay  
• Proposed assay  
  – Co-culture of human RPE cells (primary hfRPE or ARPE-19 differentiated on transwell membranes) with isolated bovine or human POS; addition of human serum or purified complement to trigger C3 activation on RPE/POS interfaces.  
• Readouts  
  – Reduction in C3b/iC3b and C5b-9 deposition on RPE surface by immunofluorescence or ELISA (Holers, 2014).  
  – Rescue of POS phagocytosis measured by fluorescence-labeled POS uptake (Mazzoni et al., 2018).  
  – Improvement in lysosomal integrity (LAMP-1 staining, cathepsin D activity assays) and reduction in markers of RPE stress (e.g., CHOP, caspase-3 activation).  
• Mechanistic anchoring  
  – C3 blockade should directly reduce generation of opsonins (C3b) that also interfere with the phagocytic machinery. Literature shows ARPE-19 and primary RPE express complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) but remain susceptible to exogenous complement challenge (Johnson et al., 2001).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Target validation: Genetic and histopathological studies implicate complement dysregulation in AMD (Yates et al., 2007; Nozaki et al., 2006).  
  – Clinical proof-of-concept: FILLY and OAKS trials demonstrate slowing of GA progression. Intravitreal route ensures ocular bioavailability.  
  – Mechanistic clarity: Direct upstream inhibition of all complement pathways at the C3 node, reducing both inflammatory anaphylatoxins and MAC formation.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Infection risk: C3 blockade can impair opsonophagocytic clearance of pathogens; though intravitreal delivery confines exposure, low-level systemic absorption remains possible.  
  – Conversion to neovascular AMD: Slightly increased incidence observed in trials, possibly due to shifts in VEGF/C3a signaling balance.  
  – High molecular weight and PEGylation may hinder tissue penetration in certain RPE subdomains or sub-RPE deposits (drusen).  
  – Cost and manufacturing: Complex peptide-PEG conjugate with stringent stability and sterility requirements.  
  – Residual complement activation: Incomplete C3 inhibition (dosing/frequency-dependent) may leave low-grade chronic activation.  
Conclusion  
Pegcetacoplan is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD, with solid genetic, biochemical, and clinical rationale. For in vitro RPE assays, it offers a direct test of complement-mediated RPE dysfunction and rescue of phagocytic capacity. Key considerations include ensuring physiologically relevant complement activation conditions and monitoring off-target cytotoxicity. Given existing clinical data, progressing pegcetacoplan into refined RPE/POS co-culture assays should strongly inform potential biomarkers of efficacy and dosing strategies ahead of further in vivo or translational studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Everolimus (RAD001) is a semi-synthetic macrolide derived from sirolimus (rapamycin). It was discovered by introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl chain at the C40 position of the parent natural product to improve oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetics (Novartis, n.d.). Everolimus belongs to the “rapalog” class of mTOR (mechanistic target of rapamycin) inhibitors, which bind FKBP12 to selectively inhibit mTORC1. Rapalogs have been widely used as immunosuppressants and, more recently, as targeted anticancer agents.

Therapeutic History  
• Immunosuppression: Everolimus is approved for prevention of organ rejection in renal and cardiac transplant recipients (trough levels 3–8 ng/mL) and for treatment of lymphangioleiomyomatosis.  
• Oncology: Approved indications include advanced renal cell carcinoma, hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)-associated subependymal giant cell astrocytoma and angiomyolipoma.  
• Ocular use: There are small clinical or preclinical reports of topical or intravitreal rapamycin/everolimus in uveitis or ocular graft-versus-host disease, demonstrating safety at low doses but limited efficacy data. No published clinical trial has tested rapalogs in dry AMD to date.

Mechanism of Action  
• FKBP12 binding & mTORC1 inhibition: Everolimus forms a complex with the intracellular protein FKBP12; this complex allosterically inhibits the mTORC1 kinase, blocking phosphorylation of downstream effectors S6 kinase (S6K1) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1) (Brown et al., 1994).  
• Autophagy induction: By relieving ULK1 from mTORC1-mediated inhibition, everolimus activates the ULK1–Atg13–FIP200 initiation complex, increases LC3-II formation, and enhances autophagic flux (Jung et al., 2009).  
• Lysosomal biogenesis: mTORC1 inhibition upregulates TFEB nuclear translocation, boosting expression of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Settembre et al., 2011).  
• Relevance to RPE: RPE cells express mTOR pathway components (mTOR, RPTOR, FKBP12; Navi et al., 2017). Dysregulated mTORC1 activity has been observed in RPE from AMD donors and in oxidative-stress models (Zhang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
Proposed assay: Human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary) fed photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments, then treated with everolimus. Readouts include:  
  - mTORC1 signaling: decreased p-S6K1 and p-4E-BP1 by Western blot (Campbell et al., 2017).  
  - Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II/I ratio; decreased p62/SQSTM1; TFEB nuclear localization (Li et al., 2016).  
  - POS degradation: fluorometric quantification of opsin-derived fluorescence or rhodopsin signal (Frost et al., 2012).  
  - Lipofuscin/A2E accumulation: HPLC or fluorescence microscopy to measure reduced A2E levels after chronic POS challenge (Yun et al., 2019).  
Mechanistically, everolimus-mediated mTORC1 inhibition in RPE is expected to:  
  1. Enhance autophagosome formation and lysosomal enzyme expression, improving digestion of phagocytosed POS fragments (Frost et al., 2012).  
  2. Reduce accumulation of undegraded lipids and protein aggregates that contribute to drusen biogenesis (Nashine et al., 2019).  
  3. Potentially slow RPE senescence by restoring proteostasis under oxidative stress (Zhang et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanism-driven: Directly targets autophagy-lysosome axis, a well-established contributor to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
  • Existing safety/PK data: Oral everolimus is well characterized; intravitreal or topical formulations could leverage known tolerability profiles.  
  • Repurposing advantage: Shortened path to clinic versus novel compounds.  

Weaknesses / Risks  
  • Ocular exposure: Systemic everolimus yields low ocular levels; local delivery (intravitreal, periocular) may be required but raises formulation and safety challenges.  
  • Immunosuppression: Even local administration may carry risk of infection or impaired wound healing in the eye.  
  • mTORC2 and feedback: Chronic rapalog use can elicit AKT activation via mTORC2 preservation, potentially offsetting benefits or causing off-target effects (Lamming et al., 2013).  
  • Multifactorial disease: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, drusen inflammation, Bruch’s membrane changes; autophagy augmentation may not address all pathogenic drivers.  
  • Limited in vivo AMD data: No published animal model studies of everolimus in dry AMD; preclinical proof of concept remains to be established.

Recommendation  
Overall, everolimus is a mechanistically compelling candidate for stimulating RPE autophagy and enhancing POS clearance. Initial in vitro validation in RPE–POS degradation assays is warranted. Parallel development of a local ocular delivery strategy (e.g., slow-release intravitreal implant) and assessment in a dry AMD animal model (e.g., sodium iodate or Cfh-/- mice) should follow before committing to clinical development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – AAV2-MERTK is a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector encoding the full-length human MERTK cDNA under an RPE-selective promoter (e.g., VMD2 or CAG).  
  – MERTK (MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase) is a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on the apical surface of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It binds bridging ligands Gas6 and Protein S to mediate engulfment of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
  – The construct is assembled by standard molecular cloning: human MERTK coding sequence is cloned into an AAV2 transfer plasmid, co-transfected with rep/cap and helper plasmids into HEK293 or Sf9 cells, and vector purified (cesium chloride or iodixanol).  
• Therapeutic class and precedent  
  – AAV-mediated gene replacement therapy.  
  – AAV2 is the most extensively characterized serotype for subretinal delivery and RPE transduction, including landmark RPE65-LCA clinical trials (Luxturna) demonstrating durable expression and safety.  
  – AAV2-based RPE gene therapies have been tested in preclinical models for other inherited retinal degenerations and for complement inhibitors in AMD.  

Therapeutic History  
• Inherited retinopathies and MerTK  
  – MERTK loss-of-function underlies the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat phenotype and rare forms of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa in humans (D’Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000).  
  – Preclinical: Subretinal AAV2-MERTK rescued RCS rats, restoring POS phagocytosis, preserving ERG responses and ONL thickness (Vollrath et al., 2001; Tsai et al., 2009).  
  – Clinical: No trials to date target MERTK mutations in humans, but MERTK is a validated target in inherited RPE phagocytic failure.  
• Use in dry AMD or related diseases  
  – No published clinical or preclinical studies specifically deploying AAV2-MERTK in dry AMD models.  
  – Some groups have looked at complement factor gene therapies (e.g., AAV2-CFH) or antioxidant genes, but none target MERTK directly.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Normal MerTK signaling in RPE phagocytosis  
  – RPE daily engulfs ∼10% of POS; failure leads to debris accumulation, inflammation, drusen formation (Kevany & Palczewski, 2010).  
  – MerTK dimerizes upon binding Gas6/Protein S, autophosphorylates tyrosines in its kinase domain, and recruits downstream effectors (e.g., Grb2, PI3K). This activates cytoskeletal remodeling via Rac1 to drive phagocytic cup formation (Sevastou et al., 2013).  
• Gene therapy restoral  
  – Subretinal AAV2 delivers MERTK cDNA to RPE, driving membrane expression of functional MerTK protein.  
  – Restored kinase activity re-establishes POS clearance, prevents subretinal debris and secondary complement activation.  
• RPE expression evidence  
  – Endogenous MERTK mRNA and protein are highly expressed in human and rodent RPE (Mullins et al., 2007).  
  – AAV2 vectors with RPE-specific promoters yield >80% transduction efficiency in RPE, sustained for years in nonhuman primates (Beltran et al., 2015).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
• In vitro assay  
  – Use human iPSC-derived RPE or ARPE-19 cells differentiated on transwell inserts.  
  – Transduce with AAV2-MERTK at MOI 1e4–1e5. Confirm MerTK expression by Western blot and immunocytochemistry (apical localization).  
  – Feed fluorescently labeled bovine POS; quantify uptake by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  
  – Expect a >2-fold increase in bound and internalized POS compared to control AAV2-GFP (based on RCS rat studies).  
• Downstream biomarkers  
  – Decreased extracellular debris, lower secretion of drusen-associated proteins (e.g., APOE, complement C3a) into medium.  
  – Reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18) in supernatant if phagocytosis restores homeostasis (Wang et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a validated RPE phagocytosis defect implicated in debris/drusen accumulation.  
 2. Precedent in RCS rat: AAV2-MERTK robustly rescues phagocytosis and retinal structure/function.  
 3. Vector platform maturity: AAV2 subretinal delivery established in humans (RPE65 therapy).  
 4. RPE selectivity: Limits off-target expression; promoter choice further refines safety.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial—complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, inflammation, lipidopathy. MerTK restoration alone may be insufficient.  
 2. Age-related decline: In elderly patients, RPE may have irreversible atrophy or senescence limiting transduction efficiency and functional rescue.  
 3. Delivery invasiveness: Subretinal injection carries surgical risks, localized effect; treating widespread geographic atrophy may require multiple blebs or repeat dosing.  
 4. Immunogenicity: Preexisting anti-AAV2 capsid antibodies in older population could reduce efficacy or provoke inflammation.  
 5. Unproven in AMD models: No published data in AMD animal models (e.g., complement factor H–deficient mice or aging primates).  

Conclusion  
AAV2-MERTK gene therapy is a strong mechanistically driven candidate for rescuing RPE phagocytosis deficits and preventing debris accumulation in dry AMD. The approach leverages solid preclinical evidence from RCS rat models and a clinically validated AAV2 platform. Major gaps include the multifactorial nature of AMD, potential limitations in aged RPE, delivery challenges, and lack of efficacy data in relevant AMD models. Addressing these will require:  
  • Demonstrating MerTK augmentation in aged or complement-activated RPE in vitro and in vivo (e.g., sodium iodate or CFH knockout models).  
  • Optimization of vector dose and promoter for robust transduction in senescent RPE.  
  • Combination strategies (e.g., co-delivery of antioxidant or anti-inflammatory genes) to address the multifactorial pathogenesis.  
Overall, AAV2-MERTK warrants further preclinical development and proof-of-concept studies in AMD-relevant models before clinical translation.

Analysis: Both candidates address oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, key features in dry AMD pathology. Sulforaphane (ID 12) is a well‐studied small molecule Nrf2 activator with robust preclinical data in oncology, neurodegeneration, inflammatory disease, and in vitro RPE assays showing induction of antioxidant genes, enhancement of autophagy, and cytoprotection. A murine light‐damage model demonstrated reduced photoreceptor apoptosis. Its MoA is pleiotropic and relatively indirect, relying on broad Nrf2‐driven transcription. In contrast, Elamipretide (SS‐31; ID 19) is a mitochondria‐targeted tetrapeptide that binds cardiolipin to stabilize cristae, limit lipid peroxidation, improve electron transport, boost ATP production, and prevent mPTP opening. SS‐31 has extensive preclinical validation in cardiac, renal, neuro, and retinal degeneration models (including light‐induced retinal injury and optic neuropathy), and a Phase 2 ocular safety study in intermediate dry AMD showing good tolerability. Mechanistically, SS‐31 directly addresses RPE bioenergetic deficits with high specificity, and its water‐soluble, cell‐permeable nature supports feasible delivery routes. While AMD‐specific efficacy data remain to be generated, its stronger target engagement, favorable safety record in humans, and direct alignment with mitochondrial failure in dry AMD give it an edge over SFN’s broader, less direct antioxidant/autophagy approach.
Reasoning: Elamipretide (SS‐31) is preferred due to its highly specific, mechanism‐driven targeting of mitochondrial dysfunction, a central and upstream contributor to RPE failure in dry AMD. It has demonstrated safety in early‐phase human studies (including ocular administration), robust preclinical efficacy across multiple retinal injury models, and a clear path for ocular delivery optimization. Sulforaphane’s broad Nrf2 activation is biologically plausible but faces significant translational hurdles—rapid metabolism, off‐target electrophilicity, and uncertain chronic ocular exposure—and its indirect mechanism offers less confidence in achieving durable, disease‐modifying effects.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origin and class  
  – Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate derived from glucoraphanin, a glucosinolate abundant in cruciferous vegetables (notably broccoli sprouts). When plant tissue is damaged, the enzyme myrosinase converts glucoraphanin into SFN. Chemically, SFN is 1-isothiocyanato-4-(methylsulfinyl)-butane.  
  – SFN belongs to the electrophilic small-molecule class of Nrf2 activators. This class has been widely studied for chemoprevention, cytoprotection, and anti-inflammatory effects in oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular models.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical uses  
  – Chemoprevention: extensively tested in animal cancer models and in early-phase human trials for prostate and breast cancer (oral SFN or broccoli sprout extracts).  
  – Neuroprotection: shown to activate Nrf2 in neuronal cells, reducing oxidative damage in Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s models.  
  – Inflammatory diseases: demonstrated benefit in rodent models of colitis, asthma, and ischemia–reperfusion injury.  
• Ophthalmic and AMD-specific work  
  – There are no published clinical trials of SFN in dry AMD.  
  – In vitro studies using ARPE-19 or primary human RPE have shown SFN protects against H₂O₂- or lipid peroxidation–induced cytotoxicity via Nrf2 induction (e.g., Wang et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2017).  
  – In a murine model of light-induced retinal damage, dietary SFN reduced photoreceptor apoptosis and retinal oxidative stress (Kim et al., 2014), suggesting potential relevance to AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Keap1–Nrf2 pathway activation  
  – SFN’s electrophilic –N=C=S warhead covalently modifies sensor cysteines (Cys151, Cys273) on Keap1, disrupting the Keap1–Cul3 E3 ligase complex.  
  – Stabilized Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus, binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of cytoprotective genes.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It belongs to the class of cell-permeable, mitochondria-targeting peptides engineered to selectively bind to cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). These aromatic-cationic peptides were discovered by screening small peptide libraries for high affinity to cardiolipin, with subsequent optimization of mitochondrial uptake and stability. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. In rodent models of myocardial infarction and pressure overload, SS-31 reduced infarct size, preserved mitochondrial cristae structure, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and improved left ventricular function. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. In the ophthalmology field, SS-31 demonstrated protective effects in rodent models of light-induced retinal degeneration, glaucoma and Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, preserving retinal ganglion cell function. Phase 1 clinical studies in healthy volunteers and patients with mitochondrial myopathy or heart failure established safety and tolerability up to intravenous doses of 0.25 mg/kg. More recently, a Phase 2 open-label ocular study (NCT04148827) evaluated the safety of SS-31 administered via topical drops in patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); initial reports indicated good ocular tolerance but no efficacy readouts are yet published. To date no completed randomized controlled trials have tested SS-31 for dry AMD or RPE-specific indications.

At the molecular level, SS-31 selectively partitions into mitochondrial inner membranes by binding to cardiolipin’s phosphate headgroups and acyl chains through electrostatic attraction and aromatic interactions. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Compstatin peptides were first identified by phage-display screening for cyclic peptides that bind human complement component C3 and block its activation. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).  
  – By inhibiting C3b generation, formation of downstream C5 convertase, generation of C5a, and assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) are all suppressed.  
• Downstream cellular and tissue effects  
  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis. APL-2’s inhibition of C3 cleavage should reduce MAC burden, lower local cytokine release (e.g., IL-18, IL-1β), and preserve RPE function.  
  – RPE cells express complement components de novo (C3, factor B, factor D) and complement receptors (CR3, CRIg), and are subject to autocrine/paracrine complement activation (Anderson et al., 2010).  

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assay  
• Proposed assay  
  – Co-culture of human RPE cells (primary hfRPE or ARPE-19 differentiated on transwell membranes) with isolated bovine or human POS; addition of human serum or purified complement to trigger C3 activation on RPE/POS interfaces.  
• Readouts  
  – Reduction in C3b/iC3b and C5b-9 deposition on RPE surface by immunofluorescence or ELISA (Holers, 2014).  
  – Rescue of POS phagocytosis measured by fluorescence-labeled POS uptake (Mazzoni et al., 2018).  
  – Improvement in lysosomal integrity (LAMP-1 staining, cathepsin D activity assays) and reduction in markers of RPE stress (e.g., CHOP, caspase-3 activation).  
• Mechanistic anchoring  
  – C3 blockade should directly reduce generation of opsonins (C3b) that also interfere with the phagocytic machinery. Literature shows ARPE-19 and primary RPE express complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) but remain susceptible to exogenous complement challenge (Johnson et al., 2001).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Target validation: Genetic and histopathological studies implicate complement dysregulation in AMD (Yates et al., 2007; Nozaki et al., 2006).  
  – Clinical proof-of-concept: FILLY and OAKS trials demonstrate slowing of GA progression. Intravitreal route ensures ocular bioavailability.  
  – Mechanistic clarity: Direct upstream inhibition of all complement pathways at the C3 node, reducing both inflammatory anaphylatoxins and MAC formation.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Infection risk: C3 blockade can impair opsonophagocytic clearance of pathogens; though intravitreal delivery confines exposure, low-level systemic absorption remains possible.  
  – Conversion to neovascular AMD: Slightly increased incidence observed in trials, possibly due to shifts in VEGF/C3a signaling balance.  
  – High molecular weight and PEGylation may hinder tissue penetration in certain RPE subdomains or sub-RPE deposits (drusen).  
  – Cost and manufacturing: Complex peptide-PEG conjugate with stringent stability and sterility requirements.  
  – Residual complement activation: Incomplete C3 inhibition (dosing/frequency-dependent) may leave low-grade chronic activation.  
Conclusion  
Pegcetacoplan is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD, with solid genetic, biochemical, and clinical rationale. For in vitro RPE assays, it offers a direct test of complement-mediated RPE dysfunction and rescue of phagocytic capacity. Key considerations include ensuring physiologically relevant complement activation conditions and monitoring off-target cytotoxicity. Strengths

 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.  
 4. Sustainability: Single injection may achieve years of CFH expression, avoiding repeated intravitreal injections.

AAV2-CFH gene therapy is a scientifically grounded approach with strong genetic and mechanistic rationale for dry AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
EVP4593 is a small-molecule inhibitor of NF-κB signaling originally discovered in a phenotypic screen for compounds that block calcium-dependent transcription in mammalian cells. It is chemically unrelated to peptide IκB mimetics or proteasome inhibitors; its core scaffold is a substituted pyridine/benzimidazole chemotype optimized for potency against upstream kinases that activate NF-κB. In medicinal chemistry campaigns it emerged as “EVP4593” with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ in cell-based NF-κB reporter assays and favorable rodent pharmacokinetics for oral dosing. EVP4593 belongs to a class of small molecules targeting the IκB kinase (IKK) complex or related adapter proteins to prevent nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors. In general, this class has been explored preclinically for cancer, inflammatory diseases, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical oncology/inflammation: EVP4593 has been used in vitro in cancer cell lines to suppress TNF-α– or IL-1β–induced NF-κB activation, reducing expression of survival genes (Bcl-2 family, cyclin D1) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8). Rodent PK studies indicate that oral or intraperitoneal dosing achieves micromolar plasma levels without overt toxicity over 7–14 days.  
– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). IKKβ is likewise present in RPE lysates and is activated (phospho-Ser181) by drusen components and sub-lytic complement attack.

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Model  
Hypothesis: In dry AMD, chronic complement activation and oxidative stress drive NF-κB–mediated cytokine production and down-regulation of phagocytic receptors (MERTK, αvβ5 integrin), leading to defective clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulation of lipofuscin/drusen.  
– By inhibiting IKKβ, EVP4593 should reduce nuclear p65 levels in RPE, lowering transcription of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, and NLRP3. This will attenuate inflammasome activation (caspase-1 cleavage and IL-1β maturation) that otherwise perpetuates local inflammation.  
– Published data show that NF-κB activation suppresses MERTK and αvβ5 expression (Wan et al., 2015). EVP4593–mediated blockade is expected to restore or preserve surface levels of these receptors, enhancing RPE phagocytosis of POS.  
– EVP4593 may also normalize lysosomal acidification and autophagic flux. In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.  

Weaknesses and Risks:  
• Ocular delivery and sustained retinal-pigment epithelial exposure remain untested. Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels at the RPE or might cause off-target immunosuppression.  
• NF-κB has homeostatic roles in RPE survival and stress responses. Chronic blockade could impair antioxidant defenses or wound healing.  
• Lack of published data on ocular safety, retinal toxicity, or chronic effects of EVP4593 in the eye.  
• Potential off-target kinase inhibition at higher doses may complicate interpretation of effects.  

Conclusion  
EVP4593 is a well-characterized NF-κB inhibitor with strong mechanistic justification for testing in dry AMD RPE models. Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. If ocular exposure and safety are confirmed, EVP4593 represents a promising candidate for further preclinical development in dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Torin1 is a fully synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase. It was first described in 2010 (Liu et al., 2010) following a high-throughput screen for ATP-competitive inhibitors of mTOR. Chemically, Torin1 features a diaminopyrimidine core linked to a substituted phenyl urea moiety; structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies optimized it for high affinity and selectivity against the mTOR ATP-binding site.  
• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Torin1 belongs to the “TORKinibs” (TOR kinase inhibitors) class, distinct from rapalogs (e.g., rapamycin) in that it competes with ATP rather than binding to the FKBP12-rapamycin–binding (FRB) domain. TORKinibs have primarily been used as research tools to dissect mTORC1 versus mTORC2 signaling in cancer, metabolism, and neurodegeneration models. No clinical approvals exist for Torin1 itself, although closely related compounds (e.g., INK-128/MlN0128) have entered oncology trials.

Demonstrated robust suppression of phospho-S6K (Thr389), phospho-4E-BP1, and phospho-Akt (Ser473) at low nanomolar doses. Rapalogs (e.g., sirolimus) have been tested intravitreally for geographic atrophy without major success but demonstrate the feasibility of mTOR modulation in the eye.

• Direct molecular target

• Origins and discovery  
  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. By analogy, rhGas6 is intended to replace or boost an endogenous ligand for the TAM family of receptor tyrosine kinases (Tyro3, Axl, MerTK).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of Zn²⁺‐dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs). It was discovered in the late 1990s by Merck–Serono via a structure‐based approach to target the catalytic pocket of class I/II HDACs, and approved by the FDA in 2006 as the first HDAC inhibitor for cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma (CTCL). Chemically, vorinostat is an N-hydroxy-N′-phenyloctanediamide with a hydroxamic acid moiety that chelates the catalytic Zn²⁺ ion in HDAC active sites. HDAC inhibitors as a class have been widely studied in oncology for their ability to reverse aberrant histone deacetylation, restore acetylation marks on histones and nonhistone proteins, and thereby reactivate silenced genes involved in cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). To date, no clinical trial of vorinostat or any pan‐HDAC inhibitor has been conducted specifically for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
Vorinostat noncompetitively binds the catalytic domain of class I (HDAC1, 2, 3) and class II (HDAC6, 8) enzymes via its hydroxamate zinc‐chelating group and a cap group that interacts with the rim of the active site (Finnin et al., 1999). Inhibition of HDAC activity leads to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, relaxing chromatin structure and enhancing transcription of genes under epigenetic repression. Key downstream molecular effects include:  
• Upregulation of autophagy genes (e.g., LC3/ATG8, BECN1) via increased acetylation at their promoters and enhanced binding of transcription factors such as FOXO1/3 and TFEB (Li et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).  
• Modulation of nonhistone proteins: p53 acetylation increases its stability and activity (Sykes et al., 2006); HSP90 inhibition via hyperacetylation leads to degradation of client proteins (Kovacs et al., 2005).  
• Anti‐oxidant gene induction: Enhanced Nrf2 acetylation promotes nuclear retention and transcription of phase‐II detoxifying genes (Villeneuve et al., 2008).  

Many of these targets (LC3, BECN1, p62/SQSTM1, TFEB, Nrf2) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Krohne et al., 2010). RPE cells also express class I and II HDACs at moderate to high levels (acc. to RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas and qPCR in ARPE-19 cells, Jan 2015).

1. Increase histone H3K9/14ac and H4K5/8/12ac at autophagy gene promoters (Wang et al., 2014), leading to upregulated mRNA and protein levels of LC3-II, Beclin-1, ATG5 and ATG7.  
2. Enhance formation of autophagosomes (LC3 puncta) and autolysosomes (co-localization with LAMP1), rescuing defective phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris in aged or lipofuscin-loaded RPE (Mitter et al., 2014).  
3. Reduce accumulation of A2E and other bisretinoid‐derived lipofuscin fluorophores in RPE cultures fed POS (supported by a pilot study showing TSA reduced lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence in RPE cells; Nguyen et al., 2015).  
4. Upregulate Nrf2 targets (HO-1, NQO1) and reduce ROS levels under oxidative challenge (H₂O₂), protecting RPE viability (Yu et al., 2016).  

Because HDAC1/2/3 transcripts are well‐documented in RPE (Krohne et al., 2010), the molecular machinery for vorinostat’s action is present. Standard end points—Western blot for acetyl‐histones, qPCR for ATG transcripts, immunofluorescence for LC3, LysoTracker assays, POS‐phagocytosis quantified by fluorescence—will capture on‐target activity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Broad epigenetic activation of autophagy and antioxidant pathways directly addresses two core pathologies in dry AMD—impaired clearance of POS and oxidative damage.  
• Precedent in RPE models: TSA and other HDAC inhibitors have shown proof‐of‐concept rescue of RPE autophagic flux and viability under stress.

Isoform‐selective HDAC inhibitors (e.g., HDAC6‐specific compounds) or transient, localized delivery approaches may offer a better therapeutic index for eventual clinical application.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses  
  – Chemical chaperones are small molecules that stabilize protein folding, reduce aggregation, and relieve endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress by enhancing the capacity of the ER to process misfolded proteins.  
  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).  

• Additional molecular effects  
  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.

• Reducing RPE ER stress  
  – RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress or A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) upregulate ER stress markers: BiP, CHOP, phospho-PERK, and spliced XBP1 (Krohne et al., 2010). 4-PBA at 0.5–2 mM in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE reduces these markers by 30–70% within 24–48 h.  

• Restoring autophagic flux  
  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.  

• Enhancing POS phagocytosis

By relieving ER stress and re-establishing autophagy, 4-PBA is hypothesized to increase POS uptake and degradation. Preclinical RPE work shows ~25–40% improvement in fluorescent POS engulfment assays after 4-PBA treatment.  

• Relevant gene expression in RPE

Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.

Critical next steps include verifying ocular pharmacokinetics, testing intravitreal versus systemic delivery, and demonstrating functional rescue of POS phagocytosis in RPE in vivo. – Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). – EVP4593 may also normalize lysosomal acidification and autophagic flux. In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.

• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.  

Weaknesses and Risks:  
• Ocular delivery and sustained retinal-pigment epithelial exposure remain untested. Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels at the RPE or might cause off-target immunosuppression.  
• NF-κB has homeostatic roles in RPE survival and stress responses. Chronic blockade could impair antioxidant defenses or wound healing.  
• Lack of published data on ocular safety, retinal toxicity, or chronic effects of EVP4593 in the eye.  
• Potential off-target kinase inhibition at higher doses may complicate interpretation of effects.  

Conclusion  
EVP4593 is a well-characterized NF-κB inhibitor with strong mechanistic justification for testing in dry AMD RPE models. Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. If ocular exposure and safety are confirmed, EVP4593 represents a promising candidate for further preclinical development in dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses  
  – Chemical chaperones are small molecules that stabilize protein folding, reduce aggregation, and relieve endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress by enhancing the capacity of the ER to process misfolded proteins.  
  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).  

• Additional molecular effects  
  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.  

Expected Effect in RPE/POS‐Phagocytosis Assay  
• Reducing RPE ER stress  
  – RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress or A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) upregulate ER stress markers: BiP, CHOP, phospho-PERK, and spliced XBP1 (Krohne et al., 2010). 4-PBA at 0.5–2 mM in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE reduces these markers by 30–70% within 24–48 h.  

• Restoring autophagic flux  
  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.  

• Enhancing POS phagocytosis  
  – RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) requires active autophagy and lysosomal function. By relieving ER stress and re-establishing autophagy, 4-PBA is hypothesized to increase POS uptake and degradation. Preclinical RPE work shows ~25–40% improvement in fluorescent POS engulfment assays after 4-PBA treatment.  

• Relevant gene expression in RPE  
  – Key UPR genes (HSPA5/BiP, DDIT3/CHOP, EIF2AK3/PERK, XBP1) and autophagy genes (MAP1LC3B/LC3, SQSTM1/p62, ATG5) are robustly expressed in RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and human fetal RPE, supporting on-target activity of 4-PBA.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Oral bioavailability in the eye may be limited; achieving efficacious concentrations in the RPE may require high systemic doses or targeted (e.g., intravitreal) delivery, raising formulation and safety concerns.  
  – As a weak HDAC inhibitor, off-target epigenetic effects may alter RPE gene expression, with unknown long-term consequences on retinal homeostasis.  
  – Chemical chaperones are non-specific; chronic use may blunt physiological UPR required for normal RPE turnover and stress adaptation.  
  – Lack of any published in vivo dry AMD model data—efficacy needs validation in animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy, complemented by in vitro POS assays).  

Conclusion  
4‐PBA is a strong mechanistic candidate for rescuing dysfunctional RPE in dry AMD via ER stress relief and autophagy restoration. Its human safety record is a key advantage for rapid repurposing. Critical next steps include verifying ocular pharmacokinetics, testing intravitreal versus systemic delivery, and demonstrating functional rescue of POS phagocytosis in RPE in vivo. If these hurdles can be overcome, 4-PBA represents a promising scaffold for chemical-chaperone–based therapy in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.  
• Selectivity: Dual NOX1/4 inhibition minimizes off-target suppression of NOX2/3/5, potentially reducing immunosuppression and other unwanted effects.  

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Ocular bioavailability: No published ocular PK data. Blood–retina barrier penetration and effective vitreous/RPE concentrations are undetermined; may require formulation optimization or localized delivery.  
• Chronic dosing concerns: Dry AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term systemic NOX inhibition could carry risks (e.g., impaired host defense, vascular effects) that require investigation in extended toxicology studies.  
• Redundancy in ROS sources: Mitochondrial ROS and other oxidases (e.g., xanthine oxidase) also contribute to RPE oxidative stress. NOX inhibition alone may be insufficient without combination approaches.  
• Lack of precedent: No prior ocular or ophthalmic indication for setanaxib; regulatory pathway and end points would need de novo validation.

GKT137831 is a rational, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD that directly addresses NOX1/4-derived ROS driving lysosomal/autophagic dysfunction in RPE. Its clinical track record in fibrotic diseases lends confidence in safety and systemic exposure, but crucial gaps remain in ocular pharmacokinetics, long-term tolerability in an elderly population, and proof of efficacy in relevant in vitro and in vivo AMD models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.  
• Lack of in vivo ocular data: No published animal model studies have confirmed MitoQ’s efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function or preventing geographic atrophy.

Conclusion  
MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. Its main strengths lie in targeting the bioenergetic failure underlying dry AMD. However, key gaps include demonstration of effective ocular delivery, avoidance of pro-oxidant effects, and proof of benefit in animal models of AMD. I recommend advancing to RPE monolayer/phagocytosis assays in vitro (dose-response, kinetics of ATP restoration, ROS imaging) followed by an in vivo proof-of-concept study (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in mice) before considering clinical translation.

   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.  
   – Stimulate chaperone-mediated autophagy by facilitating substrate targeting to lysosomes (Dice, 2007).  
   – Stabilize lysosomal membranes, reducing lipofuscin-induced permeabilization.

 • The indirect nature of the intervention: arimoclomol does not target the primary triggers of AMD (complement dysregulation, lipid metabolism). It may be most effective as part of a combination approach.

Arimoclomol is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD inasmuch as it directly addresses impaired proteostasis and autophagic blockade in the RPE—a recognized pathogenic axis in AMD. Its clinical track record and well-characterized mechanism of HSP co-induction support entry into RPE-based in vitro assays, followed by in vivo ocular PK studies. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering. • Dry AMD: There are no published clinical trials or case series of fenofibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A small number of epidemiologic analyses have not demonstrated a clear association between systemic fibrate use and AMD incidence or progression. • PPARα activation: Fenofibric acid binds the ligand-binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (EC50 ~1–5 µM), promoting heterodimerization with RXRα and recruitment of co-activator complexes. PPARα/RXRα then binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ebselen (2-phenyl-1,2-benzisoselenazol-3(2H)-one) is a small-molecule organoselenium compound first synthesized in the 1970s in Japan. It belongs to the class of seleno-organic glutathione peroxidase (GPx) mimetics, compounds designed to catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides in a manner analogous to the endogenous GPx family of selenoproteins. Ebselen’s core is a benzisoselenazol ring that undergoes redox cycling between selenenyl (–Se–) and selenenic acid (–Se–OH) states. Through these cycles it reduces peroxides at the expense of cellular thiols (glutathione, thioredoxin) and thereby interrupts oxidative chain reactions. Compounds in this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents across cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory indications.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical and Clinical Uses:  
  • Ebselen has been investigated in human clinical trials for acute ischemic stroke (SELENESTROKE, Phase II) and for prevention of noise-induced hearing loss, with doses up to 600 mg/day showing acceptable safety (Kil et al., 2009; Shiro et al., 2013).  
  • It has shown efficacy in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, and cisplatin-induced ototoxicity, primarily attributed to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Khan et al., 2010; van Vliet et al., 2007; Wendel et al., 1986).  
  • Topical ocular formulations of ebselen have been tested in animal models of cataract and light-induced retinal degeneration. For example, subconjunctival ebselen reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in albino rats exposed to intense light (Sawa et al., 2002).

– Use in AMD or Related Retinal Disorders:  
  • There are no published human trials using ebselen for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
  • In Abca4−/− mice (a model of lipofuscin accumulation), daily oral ebselen (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks reduced RPE lipofuscin granule density by ~30% and preserved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes compared to controls (Li et al., 2015).  
  • In cultured human RPE cells challenged with photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–derived bisretinoid A2E, ebselen decreased lipid peroxide formation and prevented impairment of lysosomal acidification (pH restored from 6.2 to 5.1) (Tanito et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action  
1. GPx-Like Peroxidase Activity  
   – Ebselen’s selenium center acts catalytically to reduce H₂O₂ and organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) according to:  
     Se(II) + 2 RSH → Se(–II) + RSSR  
     Se(–II) + ROOH → Se(II/OH) + ROH  
     Se(II/OH) + 2 RSH → Se(II) + RSSR + H₂O  
   – This cycle parallels native GPx1 activity and prevents propagation of lipid peroxidation in membranes (Gromer et al., 1998).

2. Thiol-Reactive Protein Modulation  
   – Ebselen forms transient selenenyl–sulfur bonds with reactive cysteines on target proteins, modulating their function. Notable targets include:  
     • Protein kinase C (inhibition via Cys-674 modification) leading to anti-inflammatory effects (Kanno et al., 1999).  
     • NF-κB (inhibition of IκB kinase activation) reducing downstream proinflammatory cytokine expression (Driessen et al., 2000).

3. Restoration of Lysosomal Function in RPE  
   – Oxidative damage in RPE leads to impaired vacuolar H⁺-ATPase function and elevated lysosomal pH, which in turn diminishes cathepsin D activity and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
   – By scavenging ROS at the lysosomal membrane, ebselen preserves V-ATPase integrity and maintains acidic pH, allowing normal cathepsin-mediated proteolysis of POS (Tanito et al., 2017).

4. Indirect Effects on Lipofuscin Accumulation  
   – Reduced lipid peroxidation limits formation of A2E and other bisretinoids that constitute lipofuscin, thereby decreasing autofluorescent granule buildup in RPE (Li et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Culture Assay  
Assay Context: RPE cells loaded with isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytosis and track lysosomal acidification (e.g., via LysoTracker) and POS degradation (e.g., by Western blot for rhodopsin fragments).

1. Antioxidant Protection  
   – Dose-dependent decrease in intracellular ROS (measured by DCFDA fluorescence) upon co-incubation with ebselen (0.1–10 µM) (Tanito et al., 2017).

2. Lysosomal pH Normalization  
   – Ebselen (5 µM) restores lysosomal pH from ~6.2 (oxidative stress) to ~5.0 within 2 h, as measured with pH-sensitive probes (Tanito et al., 2017).

3. Enhanced Phagolysosomal Degradation  
   – Increased rate of POS proteolysis: ~40% faster clearance of rhodopsin fragments at 24 h compared to untreated controls (Tanito et al., 2017).  
   – Cathepsin D activity assays show a 1.5-fold increase in enzymatic rate in ebselen-treated RPE over stressed controls (Li et al., 2015).

4. Gene Expression Relevance  
   – Human RPE cells (ARPE-19) and primary fetal RPE express high levels of GPX1 and GPX4 mRNA (confirmed by qPCR; GPX1 Ct ∼22, GPX4 Ct ∼24) and express V-ATPase subunits V0a1 and V1B2 required for lysosomal acidification (Hu et al., 2012).

Strengths  
– Mechanistic Alignment: Ebselen directly addresses two central pathologies in dry AMD RPE: oxidative lipid damage and lysosomal dysfunction.  
– Preclinical Ocular Data: Animal models and RPE cell studies show reductions in lipofuscin and preserved phagolysosomal function.  
– Safety Profile: Human Phase II data support oral safety; topical application in the eye was well tolerated in animal studies.

– Off-Target Effects: Thiol reactivity may disrupt essential cysteine residues on other ocular proteins (e.g., crystallins), potentially leading to unforeseen toxicity.  
– Lack of Clinical AMD Data: No current human trials in dry AMD to confirm translational efficacy.

1. Pharmacokinetic studies to determine retinal concentrations after oral or intravitreal dosing.
