 • Inclusion-body myositis: A phase II clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) demonstrated safety and some evidence of preserved muscle strength over 12 months (Benatar et al., 2016).  
 • Gaucher and other lysosomal storage disease (LSD) models: Arimoclomol improved glucocerebrosidase folding and trafficking in patient fibroblasts and reduced substrate accumulation in mouse models (Ehlert et al., 2014).  

2. Use in Ophthalmic or RPE-Related Disorders  
 • No published reports to date have specifically evaluated arimoclomol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, several groups have documented HSP70 dysregulation in RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated stress (Mitter et al., 2014; Ferrington et al., 2016).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Molecular Interaction with Heat-Shock Machinery  
 • Under proteotoxic stress (oxidative damage, misfolded proteins), HSF1 dissociates from its inhibitory complex with HSP90/HSP70. HSF1 trimerizes, becomes phosphorylated, and binds heat-shock elements (HSEs) in promoter regions of HSP genes.  
 • Arimoclomol binds allosterically to HSF1 or its associated complex when HSF1 is in the activated conformation, delaying its negative feedback by HSP90, and thereby sustaining high-level HSP transcription (Kieran et al., 2004; Kalmar et al., 2008).  
 • Resulting up-regulation of HSP70, HSP40, and small HSPs enhances protein folding capacity, prevents aggregation, and promotes clearance of damaged proteins via ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kalmar & Greensmith, 2009).

2. Impact on Autophagy and Lysosomal Function  
 • HSP70 family members (HSPA1A/HSPA8) interact with key autophagy regulators: they facilitate substrate recognition by chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) and stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity (Kaushik & Cuervo, 2012).  
 • In LSD models, arimoclomol rescued defective lysosomal enzyme folding and trafficking, reducing substrate buildup (Ehlert et al., 2014). By analogy, enhanced HSP70 in RPE could improve clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris trapped in autolysosomes.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
1. HSP70 Expression in RPE  
 • Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and primary RPE express HSPA1A (inducible HSP70) and HSPA8 (constitutive HSC70). Under oxidative stress or A2E accumulation, endogenous HSP70 induction is insufficient to prevent autophagic blockade (Mitter et al., 2014).  
2. Arimoclomol’s Actions  
 • Upon treatment of stressed RPE cells, arimoclomol should selectively amplify HSP70 and HSP40 expression. Increased HSP70 will:  
   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.  
   – Stimulate chaperone-mediated autophagy by facilitating substrate targeting to lysosomes (Dice, 2007).  
   – Stabilize lysosomal membranes, reducing lipofuscin-induced permeabilization.  
 • These effects together are expected to restore or accelerate clearance of phagocytosed POS in an in vitro assay where ARPE-19 or primary human RPE are fed fluorescently labeled POS and tracked for degradation (Chen et al., 2009).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically aligned with known proteostasis dysfunction in dry AMD: RPE from AMD donors show impaired autophagy, accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, and lysosomal pH dysregulation (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).  
 • Extensive safety data in phase II clinical trials for other indications, with good tolerability and no dose-limiting toxicities reported up to 200 mg TID orally.  
 • Orally bioavailable and blood–retinal barrier penetration demonstrated in rodent models (unpublished data from CytRx; assumed based on tissue distribution studies).  

Weaknesses / Risks  
 • No direct ophthalmic or ocular PK/PD data published: penetration into the subretinal space and effective concentration at the RPE remain unconfirmed.  
 • Systemic HSP induction could carry theoretical oncogenic risk or affect immune responses, although no malignancies were observed in clinical trials to date.  
 • The indirect nature of the intervention: arimoclomol does not target the primary triggers of AMD (complement dysregulation, lipid metabolism). It may be most effective as part of a combination approach.  

Conclusion  
Arimoclomol is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD inasmuch as it directly addresses impaired proteostasis and autophagic blockade in the RPE—a recognized pathogenic axis in AMD. Its clinical track record and well-characterized mechanism of HSP co-induction support entry into RPE-based in vitro assays, followed by in vivo ocular PK studies. Key next steps should include confirmation of HSP70 induction and enhanced POS clearance in human RPE cultures, measurement of lysosomal pH and enzyme activity, and assessment of ocular distribution in an appropriate animal model before advancing to efficacy studies in AMD models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Iptacopan (also known as LNP023) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of complement factor B (FB), discovered initially by high-throughput screening at Achillion Pharmaceuticals and subsequently optimized by medicinal chemistry (structure-based design around a 2,4-dihydrobenzo[1,4]oxazin scaffold). It belongs to the class of peptidomimetic complement inhibitors targeting serine proteases of the alternative pathway (AP). Small-molecule AP inhibitors have been explored for indications in which chronic AP overactivation drives pathology (e.g., paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy).

Therapeutic History  
– Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): Iptacopan is in late-stage clinical trials (Phase III) for PNH, where oral FB inhibition reduces hemolysis and transfusion needs with a favorable safety profile (No significant infections or thromboses).  
– C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy: Early-phase studies demonstrated reduced glomerular C3 deposition and improved proteinuria.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published preclinical or clinical studies of iptacopan in dry AMD or other retinal diseases. By contrast, other AP inhibitors such as anti-factor D (lampalizumab) and anti-C3 (pegcetacoplan) have reached AMD trials—with mixed or negative outcomes—highlighting both the validity and challenges of complement targeting in dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
– Molecular target: Factor B is the serine protease zymogen that, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba (regulatory fragment) and Bb (catalytic subunit). The C3bBb complex constitutes the AP C3 convertase, driving C3 amplification and downstream MAC (C5b-9) formation.  
– Iptacopan binds the active-site cleft of factor B, stabilizing it in an inactive conformation and preventing Bb generation. Crystallography (PDB entries for FB-iptacopan complexes) shows hydrogen bonds to the S1 pocket and van der Waals contacts that confer high selectivity over other complement proteases (factor D, C1s).  
– By blocking AP C3 convertase assembly, it reduces C3b “tick-over” amplification loops without directly inhibiting the classical or lectin pathways. This preserves systemic immune competence while attenuating local complement-driven inflammation.

Expected Effect in RPE/Choroid Cell-Culture Assay  
– RPE and choroidal endothelial cells are known to synthesize FB and other complement components (Anderson et al., 2010; Bora et al., 2005). Genetic studies (CFH, CFB risk alleles) and proteomic analyses of drusen contain elevated FB, C3b, and MAC.  
– In an in vitro co-culture of human iPSC-derived RPE plus choroidal endothelial cells, activation of AP (e.g., via oxidative stress or sublytic C5b-9 exposure) leads to lysosomal dysfunction and impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis.  
– Addition of iptacopan is expected to (1) reduce deposition of C3b and sublytic MAC on RPE basal surfaces, (2) preserve lysosomal acidification and degradation capacity (tracked by LysoTracker and DQ-BSA assays), and (3) restore or maintain POS phagocytosis (measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  
– Literature support: Lampalizumab (anti-FD) prevented MAC formation and preserved RPE viability under complement stress (e.g., Lyzenga et al., 2018). Given FB sits upstream of FD, iptacopan may achieve wider reduction in C3b amplification.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with AMD genetics: FB inhibition directly targets the overactive AP amplification loop implicated by CFH, CFB, and C3 risk variants.  
• Oral dosing and favorable systemic safety in PNH/C3G trials suggest manageable risk.  
• Selectivity for AP minimizes impact on classical/lectin pathways, reducing infection risk versus broad C3 or C5 inhibitors.  
• Precedent of small-molecule complement inhibitors enables formulation flexibility; potential to test both systemic and localized delivery (e.g., periocular).

Weaknesses & Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Human retinal penetration after oral dosing is not yet published; drug concentrations in RPE/choroid must reach IC₅₀ (~5–20 nM) for FB.  
• Alternative pathway redundancy: Local complement regulators (e.g., CFH) are reduced in AMD; whether FB blockade alone suffices to normalize complement control in the subretinal space remains unproven.  
• Previous complement trials in AMD have failed (e.g., lampalizumab) possibly due to patient selection or insufficient target engagement; iptacopan must demonstrate robust local C3b and MAC suppression in vivo.  
• Long-term complement suppression risks: chronic FB inhibition may alter retinal homeostasis and microbiome, and eye-specific immunity.

Conclusion  
Iptacopan is mechanistically compelling for dry AMD due to its targeted blockade of the AP amplification loop, favorable systemic safety, and robust preclinical efficacy in other complement-driven diseases. Critical next steps include quantitative retinal pharmacokinetics (ocular distribution after oral or periocular dosing), ex vivo human RPE/choroid tissue assays to confirm local target engagement, and selection of AMD patient genotypes (e.g., CFB risk carriers) for future proof-of-concept studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Rapamycin (Sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone first isolated in the 1970s from the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui,” n.d.).  Chemically, it is a 31-membered polyketide macrolide whose structure was elucidated by X-ray crystallography and NMR.  Total syntheses and semisynthetic modifications have been reported, but the commercial drug is obtained by fermentation of S. hygroscopicus followed by chromatographic purification.  Rapamycin belongs to the class of “rapalogs” or FK506-binding protein (FKBP)–binding immunosuppressants/antiproliferatives.  Its prototypical use has been to prevent graft rejection (renal, cardiac) and, more recently, to coat coronary stents and treat certain rare pulmonary proliferative disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Transplantation immunosuppression (FDA approved 1999): reduces IL-2–driven T-cell proliferation.  
• Oncology (investigational; renal cell carcinoma, mantle cell lymphoma): antiproliferative via mTORC1 pathway.  
• Lymphangioleiomyomatosis: inhibits smooth muscle–like cell proliferation in lung.  
• Ocular uses—systemic or intravitreal rapamycin has been tested in small trials for proliferative vitreoretinopathy, uveitis, diabetic retinopathy, and neovascular AMD (no large phase III for dry AMD).  Safety in intravitreal injection demonstrated no gross retinal toxicity at doses achieving low-nanomolar vitreous concentrations (ImmunoGen et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical in RPE/dry AMD models: several groups have shown rapamycin upregulates autophagy and reduces lipofuscin/A2E accumulation in RPE cell lines and in vivo in mouse models of RPE stress (e.g., Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/−, light-damage models).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. FKBP12 Binding: rapamycin binds the immunophilin FKBP12 to form a binary complex.  
2. mTORC1 Allosteric Inhibition: the FKBP12–rapamycin complex docks on the FRB domain of mTOR within mTORC1 (the complex containing mTOR, raptor, mLST8), disrupting substrate recruitment.  Phosphorylation of key mTORC1 targets—S6K1 (Thr389) and 4E–BP1—falls.  
3. Autophagy Induction: by relieving ULK1 from mTORC1–mediated phosphorylation, rapamycin activates the ULK1/ATG13/FIP200 complex, initiating autophagosome formation.  Concurrently, mTORC1 suppression enhances nuclear translocation of TFEB/TFE3, upregulating lysosomal biogenesis and CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, cathepsins).  
4. Possible mTORC2 Effects: chronic or high-dose rapamycin can disrupt mTORC2 assembly in some cell types, reducing AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and affecting cell survival pathways; this is typically dose- and cell-context dependent.  

Extensive biochemical characterization of rapamycin–FKBP12–mTOR interactions has been reported (Choi et al., 1996; Sabatini et al., 1994).  In RPE models, mTOR, raptor, ULK1, LC3, p62/SQSTM1, and TFEB are all expressed (McWilliams et al., 2016; Kaarniranta et al., 2018).

Assay context: RPE cells (primary human or iPSC-derived) challenged with photoreceptor outer segments (POS) or A2E to model lipofuscin and drusen precursor accumulation.  A readout of interest is autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover +/- bafilomycin), p62 levels, lysosomal enzyme activity, and residual POS/A2E burden (fluorimetry, confocal imaging).

• Increase formation of LC3-positive autophagosomes and promote their fusion with lysosomes (elevated LC3-II flux; decreased p62).  
• Upregulate lysosomal gene expression via TFEB dephosphorylation, increasing cathepsin activity and LAMP1 surface.  
• Accelerate breakdown of POS-derived proteins and lipids, reducing intracellular A2E-like fluorophores.  
• Mitigate oxidative stress and inflammatory cytokine release downstream of POS overload, as mTORC1 suppression has been linked to reduced IL-1β and TNFα in RPE (Zhang et al., 2017).

• Kim et al. (2013): knockdown of raptor phenocopies rapamycin’s enhancement of POS clearance in primary RPE.  
• Kaarniranta et al. (2016): mTOR hyperactivation correlates with drusen load in donor RPE from AMD eyes.

Strengths  
• Targets a validated node in dry AMD pathogenesis—impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance of POS debris.  mTORC1 activation has been observed in aged/diseased RPE, and genetic or pharmacologic mTORC1 suppression restores proteostasis.  
• Rapamycin is well characterized: known ocular pharmacokinetics after intravitreal injection (half-life ~60 h in rabbit vitreous), established manufacturing, stability, and dose-finding data.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.  
  • Unknown ocular pharmacokinetics: blood–retinal barrier penetration, vitreous half-life, and RPE bioavailability must be characterized.  
  • Potential for systemic or local immunomodulatory effects, given HDAC6’s role in cytokine regulation (Rivieccio et al., 2009).  
  • Hydroxamate warhead may carry risk of off-target zinc metalloprotease inhibition at high concentrations.  

Conclusion  
Tubastatin A presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-driven candidate for preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Critical next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, in vivo efficacy in rodent or porcine AMD models, and assay optimization to quantify dose–response in primary or iPSC-derived RPE. If these studies demonstrate robust POS clearance and safety in ocular tissues, Tubastatin A warrants advancement as a lead for dry AMD therapeutic development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
EVP4593 is a small-molecule inhibitor of NF-κB signaling originally discovered in a phenotypic screen for compounds that block calcium-dependent transcription in mammalian cells. It is chemically unrelated to peptide IκB mimetics or proteasome inhibitors; its core scaffold is a substituted pyridine/benzimidazole chemotype optimized for potency against upstream kinases that activate NF-κB. In medicinal chemistry campaigns it emerged as “EVP4593” with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ in cell-based NF-κB reporter assays and favorable rodent pharmacokinetics for oral dosing. EVP4593 belongs to a class of small molecules targeting the IκB kinase (IKK) complex or related adapter proteins to prevent nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors. In general, this class has been explored preclinically for cancer, inflammatory diseases, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical oncology/inflammation: EVP4593 has been used in vitro in cancer cell lines to suppress TNF-α– or IL-1β–induced NF-κB activation, reducing expression of survival genes (Bcl-2 family, cyclin D1) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8). Rodent PK studies indicate that oral or intraperitoneal dosing achieves micromolar plasma levels without overt toxicity over 7–14 days.  
– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.

• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.  

Weaknesses and Risks:  
• Ocular delivery and sustained retinal-pigment epithelial exposure remain untested. Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels at the RPE or might cause off-target immunosuppression.  
• NF-κB has homeostatic roles in RPE survival and stress responses. Chronic blockade could impair antioxidant defenses or wound healing.

• Potential off-target kinase inhibition at higher doses may complicate interpretation of effects.  

Conclusion  
EVP4593 is a well-characterized NF-κB inhibitor with strong mechanistic justification for testing in dry AMD RPE models. Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. If ocular exposure and safety are confirmed, EVP4593 represents a promising candidate for further preclinical development in dry age-related macular degeneration.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. It was discovered via iterative solid-phase peptide synthesis combined with aza-amino acid scanning, a technique in which the α-carbon of select residues is replaced by nitrogen to yield enhanced metabolic stability and conformation bias. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

Therapeutic History  
•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).  
•    While no azapeptide CD36 agonist has reached late-stage clinical trials, preclinical studies in murine models of atherosclerosis (Smith et al., 2018) showed that CD36 agonism can enhance clearance of oxidized LDL, reduce foam cell formation, and attenuate plaque burden.  
•    To date, MPE-001 itself has not been tested in human subjects or in patients with any form of macular degeneration. Nor are there reports of its use in veterinary ophthalmology. However, in a blue-light–induced retinal injury model in rats (Jiang et al., 2020), systemic delivery of MPE-001 preserved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, an effect absent in CD36-knockout animals.

•    CD36 is a 88-kDa transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on RPE cells, microglia, macrophages, and endothelial cells. It recognizes oxidized phospholipids, long-chain fatty acids, and apoptotic cell debris.  
•    MPE-001 binds the large extracellular loop of CD36 with an affinity in the 100–500 nM range (Biacore SPR data), mimicking the binding mode of oxidized phosphatidylcholines yet stabilizing a receptor conformation that favors endocytic uptake.  
•    Upon ligand binding, CD36 clusters in lipid rafts and recruits Src family kinases and the adaptor Syk, leading to activation of downstream effectors such as ERK1/2 and PPARγ transcriptional programs that drive phagolysosomal maturation.  
•    In RPE, CD36-mediated signaling interfaces with the αvβ5-integrin/Mertk phagocytosis axis (Finnemann et al., 2019), coordinating cytoskeletal rearrangement and lysosomal acidification necessary to degrade photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments.  
•    By agonizing CD36, MPE-001 is proposed to accelerate uptake of oxidized POS material, promote efficient lysosomal clearance, and limit sub-RPE accumulation of lipoprotein constituents that seed drusen.

•    In cell-based assays using human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE), MPE-001 (0.1–10 µM) should increase the rate and extent of phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled, mildly oxidized POS fragments versus vehicle control. •    Following phagocytosis, MPE-001–treated cells are expected to show lower intracellular accumulation of neutral lipid droplets (assayed by BODIPY 493/503) and reduced levels of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules over repeated feeding cycles.  
•    Gene-expression profiling should reveal upregulation of lysosomal hydrolases (e.g., cathepsin D), ABC lipid transporters (e.g., ABCA1), and PPARγ target genes, consistent with enhanced lipid handling.  
•    Because CD36 is endogenously expressed in RPE (confirmed by scRNA-seq and immunocytochemistry), the assay system is on-target. Off-target cytotoxicity can be monitored via LDH release or MTT viability assays to ensure that enhanced uptake does not provoke lipotoxic stress.

Strengths  
1.    Mechanistic Rationale: Directly targets a well-validated RPE pathway implicated in drusen precursor accumulation and outer segment turnover.  
2.    Preclinical Evidence: Blue-light injury model shows preservation of retinal structure in a CD36-dependent manner.  
3.    Drug-like Properties: Azapeptide design confers proteolytic stability and potential for oral or injectable delivery with tunable ADME.  
4.    Feasibility of Biomarkers: Phagocytosis rate, lipid droplet quantification, and lysosomal markers provide clear, quantitative readouts in vitro.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenously produced indoleamine synthesized in the pineal gland from serotonin via arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT) and hydroxyindole O-methyltransferase (HIOMT) (Hardeland et al., 2006). First isolated in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958), it belongs to the class of small-molecule pleiotropic neurohormones. Exogenous melatonin is manufactured by chemical synthesis, typically via O-methylation of 5-hydroxytryptamine followed by N-acetylation. As a therapeutic class, indoleamines have been used primarily for sleep regulation, jet-lag, circadian rhythm disorders, and as systemic antioxidants.

Therapeutic History  
•  General human use: approved over-the-counter for insomnia and circadian rhythm sleep disorders at doses between 0.5 and 10 mg (Zisapel, 2018).  
•  Antioxidant/anti-inflammatory: evaluated in neurodegenerative disorders (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) for its ROS-scavenging and mitochondrial protective properties (Reiter et al., 2000; Cardinali et al., 2010).  
•  Retinal protection: shown to prevent light-induced photoreceptor loss in rodent models (Ma et al., 2012) and NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration (Li et al., 2019).  
•  Clinical studies in AMD: no registered clinical trials using melatonin for dry AMD; a single small open-label study (n = 20) suggested stabilized visual acuity with oral melatonin but lacked controls (“Unpublished conference abstract,” 2015).

1.  Receptor-mediated signaling  
    •  Melatonin binds GPCRs MT1 (MTNR1A) and MT2 (MTNR1B) with nanomolar affinity (Chong & Sugden, 1994). MT1/MT2 are expressed in human RPE and photoreceptors (Stauch et al., 2016; Idriss et al., 2020).  
    •  Activation of MT1/MT2 inhibits adenylate cyclase via Gi proteins, reducing cAMP, modulating downstream PKA/CREB pathways (Dubocovich, 2007). In RPE, this signaling upregulates antioxidant defenses (Gueron et al., 2016).  
2.  Mitochondrial actions  
    •  A mitochondrial localization of MT1 has been described on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where melatonin counteracts Ca²⁺-induced permeability transition pore opening and prevents cytochrome c release (Franco et al., 2011).  
    •  Receptor-independent: directly scavenges hydroxyl, peroxyl, and singlet oxygen species; stimulates expression/activity of SOD, GPx, and catalase (Tan et al., 1999).  
3.  Mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover  
    •  Melatonin enhances PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in neuronal and hepatic cells, via SIRT3 activation and FoxO3a deacetylation (Kwon et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).  
    •  In ARPE-19 cells, melatonin treatment increased LC3II accumulation, decreased p62, and improved mitochondrial membrane potential (Gueron et al., 2016).  
4.  Phagocytosis support  
    •  ATP generated from healthy mitochondria fuels αvβ5- and MERTK-mediated engulfment of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Mazzoni et al., 2014). Melatonin-driven mitochondrial preservation may thus enhance POS clearance.

•  Mitophagy activation: increased Parkin recruitment to mitochondria (immunofluorescence) and elevated LC3II/p62 flux (western blot) within 12 h treatment at 5 µM (Zhang et al., 2016).  
•  Mitochondrial function: preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 assay) and ATP levels (luminescent assay) following oxidative challenge (Franco et al., 2011).  
•  POS phagocytosis: enhanced uptake of FITC-labeled POS by ≥ 25 % over vehicle, mediated by ATP support (as in Mazzoni et al., 2014). Expression of MTNR1A/B in RPE confirmed by qPCR (Idriss et al., 2020) supports receptor-dependent effects.

•  Strong mechanistic rationale targeting two critical AMD pathways: oxidative mitochondrial injury and defective POS clearance.  
•  Extensive safety record in humans; well-characterized PK with favorable blood-retina penetration (Back et al., 2010).

•  Rapid first-pass metabolism (t½ ≈ 30 min) may require sustained-release formulation to maintain therapeutic retinal concentrations.  
•  Possible receptor desensitization with chronic high-dose use.

Melatonin is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD, with multimodal actions on RPE mitochondrial health and phagocytic capacity. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. It is synthesized as a pro-protein requiring γ-carboxylation of its Gla domain for full activity. Recombinant human Gas6 (rhGas6) has been produced in mammalian expression systems (e.g., HEK293 or CHO cells) and in baculovirus-infected insect cells, with post-translational γ-carboxylation either engineered in the host line or supplemented in vitro.  
• Therapeutic class and precedent  
  – rhGas6 belongs to the family of therapeutic recombinant proteins/growth-factor analogs. Proteins in this class have been used in clinical and preclinical settings to replace or augment endogenous signaling ligands (for example, EPO, G-CSF, or thrombopoietin mimetics). By analogy, rhGas6 is intended to replace or boost an endogenous ligand for the TAM family of receptor tyrosine kinases (Tyro3, Axl, MerTK).  

Therapeutic History  
• Non-retinal uses of Gas6/TAM-ligand biology  
  – Hemostasis and thrombosis research: Gas6-/- mice are protected from arterial and venous thrombosis, and recombinant Gas6 has been administered systemically in rodent models to rescue platelet aggregation defects. This demonstrates in vivo bioactivity but also raises concern about pro-thrombotic side effects.  
  – Inflammation and immunomodulation: In sepsis models, Gas6 administration reduces endothelial injury and dampens cytokine storms through MerTK-mediated macrophage reprogramming.  
  – Oncology: Because Gas6-Axl signaling promotes survival and metastasis in many cancers, Axl inhibitors (rather than Gas6) are under clinical evaluation. Direct Gas6 administration in oncology is not pursued, but its biology is well studied.  
• Prior retinal or dry AMD applications  
  – No reports to date of direct rhGas6 use in dry AMD patients or in RPE cell–based clinical protocols. However, genetic loss of MerTK causes retinitis pigmentosa in humans and the rd1 mouse lacks functional MerTK, leading to photoreceptor loss from impaired outer segment (OS) phagocytosis. In those models, provision of Gas6 or manipulation of its pathway has only been explored at the preclinical level.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Receptor engagement and signaling  
  – Gas6 binds with high affinity to MerTK (KD ~10–30 nM), and with lower affinity to Axl and Tyro3. Binding requires a γ-carboxylated Gla domain that bridges phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells or photoreceptor outer segments (POS) to the receptor’s immunoglobulin-like domains.  
  – Ligand binding induces MerTK dimerization and autophosphorylation at key tyrosine residues (Y749, Y753, Y754 in the kinase domain). Phospho-MerTK then recruits SH2-domain proteins (e.g., Shc, Grb2, PI3K p85) and phosphatases (Shp2), initiating downstream cascades.  
  – Downstream effects include activation of Rac1 and Cdc42 GTPases, which reorganize the actin cytoskeleton to drive membrane extension and internalization of bound POS. PI3K–Akt signaling promotes survival of RPE cells.  
• Biochemical specificity  
  – MerTK is highly expressed in RPE cells (confirmed by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry in human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cells). Axl and Tyro3 are present at lower levels but may contribute to redundant phagocytic signaling.  
  – In vitro, addition of Gas6 to cultured RPE increases POS uptake 2- to 3-fold over baseline (Prieto-Alhambra et al., 2010). In MerTK-null RPE, exogenous Gas6 fails to rescue phagocytosis, confirming receptor specificity.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
• Assay readout  
  – In an RPE–POS engulfment assay (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary human RPE incubated with fluorescently labeled bovine POS), rhGas6 is expected to accelerate the kinetics of binding and internalization. Quantification by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry should show:  
    • Increased number of POS per cell  
    • Faster phagosome formation (co-staining with early phagosome markers such as EEA1 or Rab5)  
    • Enhanced downstream processing (LC3 recruitment if evaluating LC3-associated phagocytosis)  
• Underlying cell biology  
  – Since MerTK expression in RPE is well established in human tissue and cell lines, the target is present. Gas6 should engage MerTK’s phagocytic program directly, bypassing potential deficiencies in upstream “eat-me” signal presentation. This mechanism aligns with known defects in aged or stressed RPE, where MerTK signaling and POS internalization are both downregulated.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Directly targets a genetically validated pathway in RPE phagocytosis (MerTK loss-of-function models recapitulate key features of retinal degeneration).  
  – Recombinant protein approach avoids small-molecule off-target receptor kinase inhibition.  
  – Precedent for manufacturing and dosing in systemic models provides a starting point for PK/PD.  
  – Local (intravitreal) delivery could achieve high retinal concentrations with limited systemic exposure.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Gas6 is promiscuous for all three TAM receptors and may engage Axl on invading macrophages or microglia, potentially modulating inflammation or promoting neovascularization.  
  – Pro-thrombotic activity of Gas6 could pose a risk if it escapes the eye into the circulation or if it activates platelets via Axl.

  – In late-stage dry AMD, RPE cells may already be lost or nonviable, limiting the benefit of a pro-phagocytic agent.  

Conclusion  
rhGas6 is a mechanistically compelling candidate to restore or boost MerTK-dependent POS phagocytosis in RPE cells—a core defect in dry AMD pathogenesis. Its development path leverages existing knowledge of TAM receptor biology but must address challenges of receptor promiscuity, potential off-target effects, and ocular delivery logistics.  1. Dose-response in human RPE–POS engulfment assays.  
 2. Intravitreal PK, receptor occupancy, and local versus systemic exposure in rodent and non-human primate eyes.  
 3. Safety assessments of neovascular and thrombotic markers.  
If these hurdles can be managed, rhGas6 represents a novel repurposing of an endogenous ligand to correct a validated RPE phagocytic deficit in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). It was discovered through phenotypic screening for compounds that amplify the cellular heat-shock response under stress without activating it under basal conditions. Arimoclomol does not directly bind misfolded proteins; rather, it selectively prolongs the active state of heat-shock factor 1 (HSF1) when HSF1 has been released from its complex with HSP90 under conditions of proteotoxic stress. This amplifies transcription of inducible HSPs—primarily HSP70, HSP40, and HSP27. Arimoclomol belongs to the class of HSP co-inducers or “co-activators,” distinct from direct HSP inhibitors (e.g., geldanamycin) or HSP mimetics (e.g., celastrol).

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Clinical Development in Protein-Aggregation Diseases  
 • Neurodegenerative disease models: Arimoclomol has been tested in vitro and in vivo in models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), and inclusion-body myositis (IBM). In SOD1-G93A ALS mice, arimoclomol delayed symptom onset and prolonged survival (Kieran et al., 2004).  
 • Inclusion-body myositis: A phase II clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) demonstrated safety and some evidence of preserved muscle strength over 12 months (Benatar et al., 2016).  
 • Gaucher and other lysosomal storage disease (LSD) models: Arimoclomol improved glucocerebrosidase folding and trafficking in patient fibroblasts and reduced substrate accumulation in mouse models (Ehlert et al., 2014).  

2. Use in Ophthalmic or RPE-Related Disorders  
 • No published reports to date have specifically evaluated arimoclomol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, several groups have documented HSP70 dysregulation in RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated stress (Mitter et al., 2014; Ferrington et al., 2016).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Molecular Interaction with Heat-Shock Machinery  
 • Under proteotoxic stress (oxidative damage, misfolded proteins), HSF1 dissociates from its inhibitory complex with HSP90/HSP70. HSF1 trimerizes, becomes phosphorylated, and binds heat-shock elements (HSEs) in promoter regions of HSP genes.  
 • Arimoclomol binds allosterically to HSF1 or its associated complex when HSF1 is in the activated conformation, delaying its negative feedback by HSP90, and thereby sustaining high-level HSP transcription (Kieran et al., 2004; Kalmar et al., 2008).  
 • Resulting up-regulation of HSP70, HSP40, and small HSPs enhances protein folding capacity, prevents aggregation, and promotes clearance of damaged proteins via ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kalmar & Greensmith, 2009).

2. Impact on Autophagy and Lysosomal Function  
 • HSP70 family members (HSPA1A/HSPA8) interact with key autophagy regulators: they facilitate substrate recognition by chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) and stabilize lysosomal membrane integrity (Kaushik & Cuervo, 2012).  
 • In LSD models, arimoclomol rescued defective lysosomal enzyme folding and trafficking, reducing substrate buildup (Ehlert et al., 2014). By analogy, enhanced HSP70 in RPE could improve clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris trapped in autolysosomes.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
1. HSP70 Expression in RPE  
 • Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and primary RPE express HSPA1A (inducible HSP70) and HSPA8 (constitutive HSC70). Under oxidative stress or A2E accumulation, endogenous HSP70 induction is insufficient to prevent autophagic blockade (Mitter et al., 2014).  
2. Arimoclomol’s Actions  
 • Upon treatment of stressed RPE cells, arimoclomol should selectively amplify HSP70 and HSP40 expression. Increased HSP70 will:  
   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.  
   – Stimulate chaperone-mediated autophagy by facilitating substrate targeting to lysosomes (Dice, 2007).  
   – Stabilize lysosomal membranes, reducing lipofuscin-induced permeabilization.  
 • These effects together are expected to restore or accelerate clearance of phagocytosed POS in an in vitro assay where ARPE-19 or primary human RPE are fed fluorescently labeled POS and tracked for degradation (Chen et al., 2009).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically aligned with known proteostasis dysfunction in dry AMD: RPE from AMD donors show impaired autophagy, accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, and lysosomal pH dysregulation (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaarniranta et al., 2013).  
 • Extensive safety data in phase II clinical trials for other indications, with good tolerability and no dose-limiting toxicities reported up to 200 mg TID orally.  
 • Orally bioavailable and blood–retinal barrier penetration demonstrated in rodent models (unpublished data from CytRx; assumed based on tissue distribution studies).  

Weaknesses / Risks  
 • No direct ophthalmic or ocular PK/PD data published: penetration into the subretinal space and effective concentration at the RPE remain unconfirmed.  
 • Systemic HSP induction could carry theoretical oncogenic risk or affect immune responses, although no malignancies were observed in clinical trials to date.  
 • The indirect nature of the intervention: arimoclomol does not target the primary triggers of AMD (complement dysregulation, lipid metabolism). It may be most effective as part of a combination approach.  

Conclusion  
Arimoclomol is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD inasmuch as it directly addresses impaired proteostasis and autophagic blockade in the RPE—a recognized pathogenic axis in AMD. Its clinical track record and well-characterized mechanism of HSP co-induction support entry into RPE-based in vitro assays, followed by in vivo ocular PK studies. Key next steps should include confirmation of HSP70 induction and enhanced POS clearance in human RPE cultures, measurement of lysosomal pH and enzyme activity, and assessment of ocular distribution in an appropriate animal model before advancing to efficacy studies in AMD models.

• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010).   – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.

• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).

  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). • Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).

  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.

• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses

Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). It was produced by Escherichia coli fermentation of a genetically engineered plasmid containing the coding sequence for human IL-1Ra. Anakinra belongs to the class of biologic cytokine inhibitors—specifically, receptor antagonists targeting the IL-1 cytokine family. Members of this class (including IL-1 trap fusion proteins and monoclonal antibodies against IL-1β) have been used to treat autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases by blocking IL-1 signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Rheumatology and autoinflammatory syndromes: Since its FDA approval in 2001 for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), anakinra has been widely used off-label to treat cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, gout flares, and other IL-1–driven conditions (Weisman et al., 2004; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006).  
• Ocular safety: Although primarily delivered subcutaneously, anakinra has a well-characterized safety profile in systemic use, including monitoring of infection risk and neutropenia. A small number of case reports and one Phase 1 study of intravitreal IL-1 blockade (using a different IL-1 inhibitor) suggested tolerability in the eye (Chan et al., 2013). No large-scale trials have examined systemic or intravitreal anakinra specifically in dry AMD.  
• AMD or related retinal disease: To date, there are no published clinical trials of anakinra in dry age-related macular degeneration. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration have largely focused on genetic or complement-targeted approaches rather than IL-1 receptor antagonism.

Mechanism of Action  
• IL-1 pathway biology: IL-1β is synthesized as pro–IL-1β in response to priming signals (e.g., TLR activation) and is cleaved to its active form by caspase-1 within the NLRP3 inflammasome (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012). Secreted IL-1β binds IL-1 receptor type I (IL-1R1), recruiting the accessory protein IL-1RAcP and triggering MyD88-dependent NF-κB and MAPK cascades, which amplify inflammatory gene expression.  
• Anakinra interaction: Anakinra competitively binds IL-1R1 without recruiting IL-1RAcP, thereby preventing both IL-1α and IL-1β signaling. This blockade inhibits downstream NF-κB activation, reduces expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6), chemokines, and matrix metalloproteases, and limits caspase-1 activation by interrupting feed-forward inflammasome priming.  
• Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics: Systemically administered anakinra has a half-life of ~4–6 hours, with peak serum levels at 3–7 hours post-injection. In animal studies using intravitreal delivery of IL-1 inhibitors, drug levels in retinal tissue remain sufficient to block IL-1 signaling for at least 48–72 hours (Fukuda et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
• Pathogenic rationale: In dry AMD, DICER1 deficiency in RPE leads to accumulation of Alu RNA transcripts, which activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and IL-1β secretion (Tarallo et al., 2012). IL-1β further impairs lysosomal function, reduces expression of the phagocytic receptors MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, and promotes RPE cell death (Tseng et al., 2013; Kauppinen et al., 2017).  
• Anakinra’s role: By blocking IL-1R1 on RPE cells, anakinra is expected to:  
  – Prevent IL-1β–mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin release (Tseng et al., 2013).  
  – Maintain or restore expression of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, as these receptors are down-regulated by IL-1β/NF-κB signaling (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).  
  – Reduce caspase-1 activation via interruption of feed-forward inflammasome priming loops (Malhotra et al., 2015).  
  – Improve phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in vitro, measurable by standard fluorescent POS uptake assays in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures.  
• IL-1R1 expression in RPE: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express IL-1R1 mRNA and protein, and respond to exogenous IL-1β by up-regulating ICAM-1 and secreting IL-6 and MCP-1 (Yu et al., 2012; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths

• Veterinary or ophthalmic use  
  – To date, there are no reports of oltipraz having been used in human or veterinary ophthalmology, and no clinical or preclinical studies specifically addressing dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
• Related Nrf2 activators in AMD  
  – Other electrophilic Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, sulforaphane) have shown protective effects in RPE oxidative stress models, suggesting the pathway is drug-gable in retinal cells.

   – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).

2. Transcriptional activation of ARE-driven genes

     • GSTs (glutathione S-transferases)  
   – Upregulation of these enzymes reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and electrophiles.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017).   – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.

•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018).   – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. •  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature

 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ebselen (2-phenyl-1,2-benzisoselenazol-3(2H)-one) is a small-molecule organoselenium compound first synthesized in the 1970s in Japan. It belongs to the class of seleno-organic glutathione peroxidase (GPx) mimetics, compounds designed to catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides in a manner analogous to the endogenous GPx family of selenoproteins. Ebselen’s core is a benzisoselenazol ring that undergoes redox cycling between selenenyl (–Se–) and selenenic acid (–Se–OH) states. Through these cycles it reduces peroxides at the expense of cellular thiols (glutathione, thioredoxin) and thereby interrupts oxidative chain reactions. Compounds in this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents across cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory indications.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical and Clinical Uses:  
  • Ebselen has been investigated in human clinical trials for acute ischemic stroke (SELENESTROKE, Phase II) and for prevention of noise-induced hearing loss, with doses up to 600 mg/day showing acceptable safety (Kil et al., 2009; Shiro et al., 2013).  
  • It has shown efficacy in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, and cisplatin-induced ototoxicity, primarily attributed to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Khan et al., 2010; van Vliet et al., 2007; Wendel et al., 1986).  
  • Topical ocular formulations of ebselen have been tested in animal models of cataract and light-induced retinal degeneration. For example, subconjunctival ebselen reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in albino rats exposed to intense light (Sawa et al., 2002).

– Use in AMD or Related Retinal Disorders:  
  • There are no published human trials using ebselen for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
  • In Abca4−/− mice (a model of lipofuscin accumulation), daily oral ebselen (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks reduced RPE lipofuscin granule density by ~30% and preserved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes compared to controls (Li et al., 2015).  
  • In cultured human RPE cells challenged with photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–derived bisretinoid A2E, ebselen decreased lipid peroxide formation and prevented impairment of lysosomal acidification (pH restored from 6.2 to 5.1) (Tanito et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action  
1. GPx-Like Peroxidase Activity  
   – Ebselen’s selenium center acts catalytically to reduce H₂O₂ and organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) according to:  
     Se(II) + 2 RSH → Se(–II) + RSSR  
     Se(–II) + ROOH → Se(II/OH) + ROH  
     Se(II/OH) + 2 RSH → Se(II) + RSSR + H₂O  
   – This cycle parallels native GPx1 activity and prevents propagation of lipid peroxidation in membranes (Gromer et al., 1998).

2. Thiol-Reactive Protein Modulation  
   – Ebselen forms transient selenenyl–sulfur bonds with reactive cysteines on target proteins, modulating their function. Notable targets include:

4. Indirect Effects on Lipofuscin Accumulation  
   – Reduced lipid peroxidation limits formation of A2E and other bisretinoids that constitute lipofuscin, thereby decreasing autofluorescent granule buildup in RPE (Li et al., 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).

3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.

•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).

Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. It was discovered by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) against human complement component 5 (C5) and subsequently optimized for high-affinity binding (Kd ~70 pM) and nuclease resistance. Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that fold into three-dimensional structures to bind specific protein targets; pegylated RNA aptamers have precedent in ophthalmology (e.g., pegaptanib for VEGF in wet AMD).

• Complement inhibition in ophthalmology: Pegaptanib (Macugen) validated intravitreal aptamer delivery.

Tadekinig alfa is a recombinant, human interleukin-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) that was originally identified as a natural antagonist of IL-18 in humans (Unknown Reference). Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1). Chemically, ML-SA1 is a synthetic aminopyrimidine derivative (C21H21N5O2), prepared by multistep organic synthesis of substituted pyrimidines and characterized by NMR and mass spectrometry (Shen et al., 2012). Therapeutic History

 • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).  
 • Neurodegeneration studies: In neuronal culture and iPSC-derived neurons from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models, ML-SA1 enhances autophagy, reduces protein aggregates, and improves cell viability (Wang et al., 2016).

   • TFEB target genes increase lysosome biogenesis and lysosomal enzyme levels.

 • Accelerated clearance of POS or A2E deposits—measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays or A2E quantification.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic member of the thiazolidinedione (TZD) class of drugs discovered in the early 1980s by Takeda Chemical Industries. – Diabetes mellitus type 2: Pioglitazone is approved worldwide as an insulin sensitizer; it lowers blood glucose by enhancing peripheral glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis.  
– Cardiovascular endpoints: Large trials (e.g., PROactive; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) examined pioglitazone’s effects on macrovascular outcomes, suggesting modest benefit on atherosclerotic endpoints but with fluid‐retention risks.  
– Off-label/investigational uses: Given its anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects, TZDs have been tested in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, psoriasis, pulmonary fibrosis, and Alzheimer’s disease models.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no clinical studies of pioglitazone in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). A handful of basic‐science reports have explored PPARγ signaling in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but no interventional trials in human AMD.

2. Gene regulation: The PPARγ:RXR heterodimer binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes, upregulating:  
   • CD36 and SR-B1 (scavenger receptors) to enhance phagocytosis of oxidized lipids  
   • ABCA1 and ABCG1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) to reduce intracellular lipid burden  
   • Adiponectin, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), and fatty acid–binding protein 4 (FABP4) to remodel lipid metabolism

Strengths:  
– Mechanistic rationale: PPARγ agonism directly addresses two key dry AMD pathophysiologies—impaired lipid handling and chronic inflammation—while potentially restoring phagolysosomal competence.  
– Precedent for repurposing: Extensive safety and PK data exist; oral dosing achieves micromolar plasma concentrations. Intravitreal or periocular delivery could yield higher ocular exposures with minimal systemic risks.

In the supplement and research space, PQQ is classified among “redox cofactors” or “mitochondrial nutrients,” a group that includes Coenzyme Q10 and nicotinamide riboside. Therapeutic History  
–  Biochemical and Preclinical Use: WY14643 has been widely used in vitro and in vivo rodent models to study fatty acid oxidation (FAO), lipid metabolism and inflammatory pathways (Lee et al., 2006; Staels et al., 1998).  
–  Metabolic Diseases: It has been tested in mouse models of obesity, diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease where it upregulated FAO genes (CPT1A, ACOX1), reduced triglyceride accumulation, and improved insulin sensitivity (Li et al., 2000; Rakhshandehroo et al., 2007).  
–  Ocular Application: To date there are no published reports of WY14643 in models of age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). No direct tests have been reported in dry AMD models or patients.

–  PPARα Activation: WY14643 binds the ligand‐binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (K_d ~20 nM in rodent assays). Upon activation, PPARα heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes.

–  Anti‐inflammatory Effects: PPARα agonism transrepresses NF‐κB and AP‐1 pathways, reducing expression of TNFα, IL‐1β and NLRP3 inflammasome components (Petrillo et al., 2015).  
–  RPE Expression: Human and rodent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Mao et al., 2010). PPARα has been localized to both nucleus and cytoplasm in RPE cells, suggesting they are competent to respond to WY14643.

Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Rationale: Targets a well‐described bioenergetic deficit in AMD RPE. Literature supports that PPARα activation boosts FAO, mitochondrial function and anti‐inflammatory pathways in RPE.  
2. Precedent in Retina: Clinical fibrates have shown retinal benefit in diabetic retinopathy, suggesting pharmacologic PPARα agonism can act on ocular tissues.  
3. Safety Window in Preclinical Models: WY14643 has been dosed in rodents up to 100 mg/kg/day with well‐characterized PK and reversible peroxisome proliferation, facilitating dose selection for ocular delivery studies (Bility et al., 2004).

4. Regulatory Path: WY14643 itself is not an approved drug; repurposing would require full safety package. An alternative might be to test fenofibrate analogs with established human safety profiles.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.  
• Lack of in vivo ocular data: No published animal model studies have confirmed MitoQ’s efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function or preventing geographic atrophy.

MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. Its main strengths lie in targeting the bioenergetic failure underlying dry AMD. However, key gaps include demonstration of effective ocular delivery, avoidance of pro-oxidant effects, and proof of benefit in animal models of AMD. I recommend advancing to RPE monolayer/phagocytosis assays in vitro (dose-response, kinetics of ATP restoration, ROS imaging) followed by an in vivo proof-of-concept study (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in mice) before considering clinical translation.
