Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

Urolithin A (UA) is a gut-microbiome–derived metabolite of dietary ellagitannins (abundant in pomegranates, berries, nuts). UA itself was first isolated and structurally characterized in the early 2000s from human urine samples after ellagitannin ingestion. Chemically, UA is a dibenzopyran-6-one derivative (3,8-dihydroxy-6H-dibenzo[b,d]pyran-6-one). It belongs to the broader class of small-molecule polyphenol metabolites, many of which have anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory, or mitochondrial-modulating properties. As a nutraceutical lead, UA has been synthetically produced by coupling methods (e.g., Ullmann-type etherification) of suitably protected phenolic precursors, allowing gram-scale production of >98% purity for preclinical and clinical studies.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Ryu et al., 2016; Andreux et al., 2019) have shown that UA induces mitophagy and improves mitochondrial respiration in C. elegans, rodents, and human myotubes. In rodent models of metabolic dysfunction (high-fat diet, aging), UA supplementation (50–500 mg/kg/day oral equivalent) improved endurance, muscle strength, and markers of oxidative stress. First-in-human safety and pharmacokinetics trials (Katsuyama et al., 2019) administered UA at doses up to 1,000 mg/day for 28 days with no serious adverse events, demonstrating good oral bioavailability (Tmax ~3 h, half-life ~15 h). Phase I/II studies are ongoing in elderly subjects to evaluate muscle performance endpoints; no ophthalmic indications have yet been formally studied. There are no published reports of UA being tested in diabetic retinopathy, AMD models, or other retinal degenerations; however, its mitochondrial-protective and anti-inflammatory effects suggest rationale for retinal applications.

Mitophagy induction: The central mechanism described for UA is activation of the PINK1/Parkin pathway. UA treatment stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane of damaged mitochondria, facilitating Parkin translocation, ubiquitination of membrane proteins (e.g., VDAC1, MFN2), and recruitment of the autophagy machinery (LC3, p62) (Ryu et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018). • Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD pathogenesis involves mitochondrial damage and impaired mitophagy in RPE; UA directly targets PINK1/Parkin mitophagy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB216763 is a small-molecule, ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was first reported by Sato et al. (2000) following high-throughput screening of a chemical library for compounds that elevate β-catenin signaling. Chemically, SB216763 is a maleimide derivative bearing a 3-benzylamino substitution; its core scaffold mimics ATP’s adenine moiety, allowing it to occupy the GSK-3β nucleotide-binding pocket with nanomolar affinity (IC₅₀ ∼ 34 nM for GSK-3β, ∼ 75 nM for GSK-3α). As a member of the ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor class, SB216763 and related maleimide inhibitors have been broadly used in basic research to dissect Wnt/β-catenin pathways, autophagy regulation, and neuroprotective signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Investigations:  
  – Neuroprotection: Multiple groups have used SB216763 in rodent models of cerebral ischemia, Parkinson’s disease models, and Alzheimer’s disease cell systems. In these contexts it showed anti-apoptotic effects, protected against oxidative stress, and activated pro-survival β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways (through indirect cross-talk).  
  – Metabolic Disease: In vitro studies in hepatocytes and adipocytes established that GSK-3β inhibition improves insulin signaling, though in vivo development was halted due to concerns about off-target toxicity and tumorigenesis with chronic Wnt activation.  
  – Ophthalmology: To date, SB216763 has not been reported in peer-reviewed studies specifically for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, GSK-3 inhibitors have been explored in retinal disease models (e.g., proliferative vitreoretinopathy) for their anti-fibrotic effects.  

No clinical trials have been registered for SB216763 itself, and no veterinary uses have been documented. Its development has remained at the level of preclinical tool compound rather than a drug candidate, largely due to limited kinase selectivity and systemic safety concerns.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct GSK-3β Inhibition  
   • SB216763 binds competitively at the ATP-binding site of GSK-3β (and to a lesser degree GSK-3α), preventing phosphorylation of canonical substrates.  
   • Well-characterized substrates include β-catenin (phospho-Ser33/37/Thr41), TFEB (phospho-Ser142/Ser138), and multiple glycogen-metabolizing enzymes.  

2. Downstream Signaling Effects  
   • β-Catenin Stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation, SB216763 prevents β-catenin ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Accumulated β-catenin translocates to the nucleus, partners with TCF/LEF transcription factors, and upregulates Wnt target genes (Ring et al., 2003).  
   • TFEB Activation and CLEAR Network: GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB, retaining it in the cytosol. Inhibition leads to TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network, which drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Martina et al., 2012; Roczniak‐Ferguson et al., 2012).  
   • Autophagy Induction: Beyond TFEB, GSK-3β inhibition can indirectly modulate mTORC1 activity and AMPK signaling, further promoting autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion.  

3. Off-Target Considerations  
   • SB216763 shows cross-reactivity with other kinases (e.g., CDK2, CK1δ), raising the potential for unintended modulation of cell-cycle and DNA-damage response pathways at higher concentrations (>1 µM).  
   • Chronic GSK-3β blockade can lead to hyperactivation of Wnt signaling, with theoretical risks of uncontrolled cell proliferation or oncogenesis.

Expected Effect in RPE/POS Assay  
Cellular Context: Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells express GSK-3β, TFEB, and β-catenin transcripts at levels comparable to other epithelial cells (Whitmore et al., 2015). RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hPSC-derived RPE) are established models for studying phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lysosomal processing of lipofuscin precursors (e.g., A2E).  

Assay Hypothesis: Upon treatment with SB216763, RPE cells will:  
  1. Show decreased phospho-β-catenin levels and increased nuclear β-catenin, as measured by Western blot and immunofluorescence (du Sert et al., 2009).  
  2. Display dephosphorylated TFEB, accumulation of TFEB in the nucleus, and upregulation of CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSB, MCOLN1) by qPCR or RNA-seq.  
  3. Exhibit increased autophagic flux (e.g., elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels) and enhanced cathepsin B or D activity.  
  4. Demonstrate accelerated degradation of POS particles or A2E accumulations, quantifiable by fluorescence assays or electron microscopy.  

Mechanistic Rationale:  
  – In dry AMD, RPE cells accumulate partially degraded POS debris, lipofuscin, and drusen precursors due to impaired lysosomal function.  
  – By stabilizing TFEB and β-catenin, SB216763 is expected to restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance pathways, reducing intracellular waste burden and potentially diminishing drusen formation in vivo.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic Specificity: Targets a defined nodal kinase regulating both Wnt/β-catenin and TFEB/CLEAR pathways, directly addressing RPE lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD.  
  • Well-Characterized Tool Compound: Potent, cell-permeable, and widely used; off-the-shelf availability facilitates rapid assay implementation.  
  • Proof-of-Principle: Literature in other cell types supports SB216763’s ability to induce autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis robustly.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Selectivity and Safety: SB216763’s cross-reactivity with other kinases may confound data interpretation and poses a risk for off-target toxicities, especially with chronic dosing.  
  • Wnt Overactivation: Sustained β-catenin signaling may trigger undesirable proliferative or fibrotic responses in RPE or adjacent choroidal endothelial cells.  
  • Pharmacokinetics/Drug Delivery: SB216763 was not optimized for intraocular bioavailability or metabolic stability, necessitating formulation development for ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal injection or sustained-release implant).  
  • Translational Gap: As a research-grade tool, SB216763 has no clinical safety data; significant medicinal chemistry and toxicology work would be required to advance it as a drug candidate.

Conclusion  
SB216763 is a compelling mechanistic probe for in vitro validation of GSK-3β–mediated enhancement of RPE lysosomal function. It offers a direct test of the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition can restore autophagic clearance of POS debris in dry AMD. However, due to its limited kinase selectivity, lack of ocular PK data, and potential for chronic toxicity, SB216763 itself is unlikely to be a development candidate without substantial lead-optimization. Nonetheless, positive results with SB216763 would justify pursuing second-generation GSK-3β inhibitors (or chemotypes with improved selectivity and ocular delivery properties) as therapeutic candidates for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical identity and origin  
  – GW3965 is a synthetic, non-steroidal ligand of liver X receptors (LXRα and LXRβ). It was first disclosed in the early 2000s in medicinal chemistry efforts to develop selective LXR agonists to treat atherosclerosis and dyslipidemia. Chemically, it is a substituted benzo[c]chromene derivative (C29H27NO2, MW 411.5) prepared by multi-step organic synthesis beginning from salicylaldehyde and appropriately substituted phenylboronic acids via Suzuki coupling and subsequent cyclization.  
• Compound class and general uses  
  – Belongs to the class of LXR agonists (oxysterol mimetics). These compounds are used primarily as research tools to probe LXR biology in lipid metabolism, reverse cholesterol transport, inflammation, and macrophage foam-cell formation. No LXR agonist has yet achieved clinical approval, but GW3965 is widely cited in preclinical studies of cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and neuroinflammation.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical cardiovascular/metabolic studies  
  – GW3965 has been profiled in numerous rodent models of atherosclerosis (e.g., ApoE–/– and LDLR–/– mice). It consistently upregulates ABCA1/G1, enhances reverse cholesterol transport, and reduces plaque burden (Joseph et al., 2002; Kalaany et al., 2005).  
  – Also studied in models of hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance; while improving cholesterol efflux, it can induce SREBP-1c–driven lipogenesis (elevated triglycerides) in liver (Laffitte et al., 2003).  
• Other preclinical indications  
  – Explored in CNS inflammation (e.g., experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis), diabetic nephropathy, and wound healing via macrophage modulation (Castrillo et al., 2003; Joseph et al., 2003).  
• Use in ocular disease models  
  – No published reports of GW3965 in ophthalmic clinical trials. However, related LXR agonists (e.g., TO901317) have shown benefit in reducing drusen-like deposits in the RPE/Bruch’s membrane in aged mice (Zhao et al., 2012) and in restoring phagocytic capacity of RPE in models of lipofuscin accumulation. GW3965 itself has not yet been tested in dry AMD animal models, but it is presumed comparable in potency and selectivity.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Direct nuclear receptor activation  
  – GW3965 binds both LXRα and LXRβ ligand–binding domains with low-nanomolar affinity (EC50 ≈ 20–50 nM) (Wang et al., 2002).  
  – Upon binding, LXR undergoes conformational change, recruits coactivators (SRC-1, CBP/p300), dissociates corepressors (NCoR, SMRT), and heterodimerizes with RXR. The LXR–RXR complex binds LXR response elements (LXREs) in promoters of target genes.  
• Transcriptional regulation  
  – Upregulates cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1, apolipoprotein E (ApoE), and IDOL (inducible degrader of the LDL receptor).  
  – Simultaneously induces SREBP-1c, leading to increased fatty acid synthase (FAS), acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), and stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD1), driving de novo lipogenesis.  
• Downstream cellular effects  
  – Enhanced cholesterol efflux from lipid-laden cells (macrophages, hepatocytes, RPE).  
  – Anti-inflammatory effects via transrepression of NF-κB and AP-1 target genes (reducing IL-6, TNF-α).  
  – Modulation of phagocytosis: in RPE, LXR activation has been linked to improved clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), likely through ABCA1-dependent membrane remodeling.  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
• RPE expression of target genes  
  – Human RPE cells (primary or ARPE-19) express both LXRα and LXRβ as well as basal levels of ABCA1/G1 and ApoE (Wang et al., 2009).  
• Assay readouts  
  1. ABCA1 mRNA and protein induction (RT-qPCR, Western blot).  
  2. Cholesterol efflux assay: [³H]-cholesterol–loaded RPE, measure radiolabeled cholesterol in acceptor (apoA-I or HDL).  
  3. Lipid droplet quantification (Oil Red O or BODIPY staining) before and after treatment with oxidized LDL or POS.  
  4. POS phagocytosis: fluorescently labeled bovine POS fed to RPE, quantified by flow cytometry or immunofluorescence.  
• Hypothesized outcomes  
  – GW3965-treated RPE will show dose-dependent upregulation of ABCA1/G1, increased cholesterol efflux (>2-fold vs. vehicle), reduced intracellular lipid droplets, and improved rate/extent of POS uptake and digestion (Zhao et al., 2012).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: dry AMD pathogenesis involves accumulation of cholesterol-rich drusen and impaired RPE phagocytosis; LXR agonism directly targets both.  
• Precedent data: related agonists reduce sub-RPE lipid deposits in mice and restore RPE function.  
• Potent, selective tool compound: GW3965 has been thoroughly characterized in vitro and in vivo for ADME/Tox in rodents.

• Lipogenesis side effects: induction of hepatic SREBP-1c may lead to hypertriglyceridemia if delivered systemically; ocular delivery (intravitreal or topical) would need formulation work to avoid systemic exposure.  
• Species translation: rodent Bruch’s membrane lacks some human ECM complexity; efficacy in mouse may not predict human benefit.  
• No clinical precedent: no LXRs have advanced to human trials for ocular disease, so safety in eye is unproven.  
• Off-target/inflammatory effects: chronic LXR activation can suppress some immune responses which might impair RPE homeostasis over long term.

GW3965 is a compelling mechanistically-driven candidate for repurposing in dry AMD. Its ability to upregulate ABCA1/G1 and promote cholesterol efflux addresses key pathogenic features of drusen biogenesis and RPE dysfunction. The main hurdles are avoidance of lipogenic side effects and demonstration of safety and efficacy in ocular delivery paradigms. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tadekinig alfa is a recombinant, human interleukin-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) that was originally identified as a natural antagonist of IL-18 in humans (Unknown Reference). IL-18BP is an endogenous soluble decoy receptor that sequesters free IL-18, preventing its interaction with the cell-surface IL-18 receptor α/β complex (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa is produced by recombinant expression in mammalian cells (CHO), purified via standard chromatographic methods, and formulated for subcutaneous or intravenous administration (Unknown Reference). As a biologic it belongs to the class of cytokine-binding proteins (decoy receptors), akin to etanercept (soluble TNF receptor) or IL-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra) (Unknown Reference). These proteins have been used broadly to dampen overactive cytokine signaling in autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases (Unknown Reference).

Therapeutic History  
Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa (formerly GSK1070806, then ABT-325) entered clinical development in inflammatory conditions characterized by IL-18 overproduction: adult-onset Still’s disease, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Schnitzler syndrome, and plaque psoriasis (Unknown Reference). Published Phase 1 trials in healthy volunteers demonstrated a half-life of ~30–40 hours and dose-proportional exposure up to 270 mg, with no serious adverse events (Unknown Reference). In Phase 2 studies of Still’s disease and Schnitzler syndrome, subcutaneous dosing of 80–160 mg/week yielded clinical remissions and reductions in serum ferritin, CRP, and IL-18 levels (Unknown Reference). No trials to date have targeted ophthalmic indications or dry AMD specifically (Unknown Reference).

IL-18 is an inflammasome-activated cytokine released by RPE cells and infiltrating myeloid cells in response to DAMPs (e.g., Alu RNA, oxidized lipids) (Unknown Reference). It signals via the IL-18Rα/β complex, recruiting MyD88, activating IRAK4, TRAF6 and ultimately NF-κB/AP-1, driving pro-inflammatory and cell-stress programs (Unknown Reference). Gene expression assays and immunoblotting can confirm reduced NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (Unknown Reference). Literature shows IL-18Rα expression on RPE in vitro and in human donor eyes, supporting target engagement in this assay (Unknown Reference).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ebselen (2-phenyl-1,2-benzisoselenazol-3(2H)-one) is a small-molecule organoselenium compound first synthesized in the 1970s in Japan. It belongs to the class of seleno-organic glutathione peroxidase (GPx) mimetics, compounds designed to catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides in a manner analogous to the endogenous GPx family of selenoproteins. Ebselen’s core is a benzisoselenazol ring that undergoes redox cycling between selenenyl (–Se–) and selenenic acid (–Se–OH) states. Through these cycles it reduces peroxides at the expense of cellular thiols (glutathione, thioredoxin) and thereby interrupts oxidative chain reactions. Compounds in this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents across cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory indications.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical and Clinical Uses:  
  • Ebselen has been investigated in human clinical trials for acute ischemic stroke (SELENESTROKE, Phase II) and for prevention of noise-induced hearing loss, with doses up to 600 mg/day showing acceptable safety (Kil et al., 2009; Shiro et al., 2013).  
  • It has shown efficacy in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, and cisplatin-induced ototoxicity, primarily attributed to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Khan et al., 2010; van Vliet et al., 2007; Wendel et al., 1986).  
  • Topical ocular formulations of ebselen have been tested in animal models of cataract and light-induced retinal degeneration. For example, subconjunctival ebselen reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in albino rats exposed to intense light (Sawa et al., 2002).

– Use in AMD or Related Retinal Disorders:  
  • There are no published human trials using ebselen for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
  • In Abca4−/− mice (a model of lipofuscin accumulation), daily oral ebselen (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks reduced RPE lipofuscin granule density by ~30% and preserved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes compared to controls (Li et al., 2015).  
  • In cultured human RPE cells challenged with photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–derived bisretinoid A2E, ebselen decreased lipid peroxide formation and prevented impairment of lysosomal acidification (pH restored from 6.2 to 5.1) (Tanito et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action  
1. GPx-Like Peroxidase Activity  
   – Ebselen’s selenium center acts catalytically to reduce H₂O₂ and organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) according to:  
     Se(II) + 2 RSH → Se(–II) + RSSR  
     Se(–II) + ROOH → Se(II/OH) + ROH  
     Se(II/OH) + 2 RSH → Se(II) + RSSR + H₂O  
   – This cycle parallels native GPx1 activity and prevents propagation of lipid peroxidation in membranes (Gromer et al., 1998).

2. Thiol-Reactive Protein Modulation  
   – Ebselen forms transient selenenyl–sulfur bonds with reactive cysteines on target proteins, modulating their function. Notable targets include:  
     • Protein kinase C (inhibition via Cys-674 modification) leading to anti-inflammatory effects (Kanno et al., 1999).  
     • NF-κB (inhibition of IκB kinase activation) reducing downstream proinflammatory cytokine expression (Driessen et al., 2000).

3. Restoration of Lysosomal Function in RPE  
   – Oxidative damage in RPE leads to impaired vacuolar H⁺-ATPase function and elevated lysosomal pH, which in turn diminishes cathepsin D activity and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).

   – Reduced lipid peroxidation limits formation of A2E and other bisretinoids that constitute lipofuscin, thereby decreasing autofluorescent granule buildup in RPE (Li et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Culture Assay  
Assay Context: RPE cells loaded with isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytosis and track lysosomal acidification (e.g., via LysoTracker) and POS degradation (e.g., by Western blot for rhodopsin fragments).

   – Dose-dependent decrease in intracellular ROS (measured by DCFDA fluorescence) upon co-incubation with ebselen (0.1–10 µM) (Tanito et al., 2017).

   – Ebselen (5 µM) restores lysosomal pH from ~6.2 (oxidative stress) to ~5.0 within 2 h, as measured with pH-sensitive probes (Tanito et al., 2017).

3. Enhanced Phagolysosomal Degradation  
   – Increased rate of POS proteolysis: ~40% faster clearance of rhodopsin fragments at 24 h compared to untreated controls (Tanito et al., 2017).

Oltipraz is a promising mechanistic candidate for dry AMD through Nrf2-mediated enhancement of antioxidant defenses and lysosomal/autophagic clearance in RPE. • Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.

• Molecular interaction with complement C3

  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PMX205 is a synthetic cyclic hexapeptide antagonist of the complement 5a receptor (C5aR, CD88). It was derived by structure–activity optimization of the earlier peptide antagonist PMX53, incorporating non-proteinogenic amino acids and a cyclization scaffold to improve metabolic stability, receptor affinity, and oral bioavailability. PMX205 belongs to the class of small-molecule/peptidomimetic complement inhibitors targeting G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signaling. Compounds of this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory agents in diseases where excessive complement activation drives pathology (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, neuroinflammation).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: PMX205 (and its predecessor PMX53) have been tested in multiple rodent models of inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease—including Alzheimer’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spinal cord injury, and ischemia–reperfusion injury—where blockade of C5aR reduced microglial activation, cytokine release (IL-1β, TNF-α), and tissue damage.  
• Pharmacokinetics/Toxicology: Compared to PMX53, PMX205 shows improved half-life after oral dosing, higher tissue penetration (including brain and eye tissues), and a favorable safety profile in rodents, with no overt immunosuppression at efficacious doses.  
• Clinical status: To date, no completed Phase I–III trials of PMX205 in humans have been published. Related C5aR antagonists (e.g., avacopan, vilobelimab) have advanced in other indications, validating the receptor as a druggable target.  
• Use in ocular disease: There are no reports of direct PMX205 use in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, C5aR blockade has been proposed as a strategy in dry AMD by multiple groups, and complement inhibitors (C3, C5 antibodies) are in clinical trials for geographic atrophy.

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement: PMX205 binds with high affinity to the C5aR1 (CD88) binding pocket, acting as a competitive antagonist that prevents the pro-inflammatory anaphylatoxin C5a from activating its GPCR.  
• Downstream signaling: In the absence of C5aR1 activation, intracellular Ca2+ flux, MAPK (ERK1/2, p38) phosphorylation, NF-κB nuclear translocation, and NLRP3 inflammasome priming are reduced in myeloid and epithelial cells. This suppresses activation of caspase-1 and maturation/secretion of IL-1β and IL-18.  
• Impact on RPE/Phagolysosomes: Published studies in RPE cell lines (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE) document expression of C5aR1. C5a exposure in vitro induces lysosomal alkalinization, reduced cathepsin D processing, accumulation of undigested photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material, and NLRP3 activation. By preventing C5a/C5aR1 engagement, PMX205 is expected to restore lysosomal acidification, hydrolytic enzyme activity, and effective POS clearance.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assays  
In an in vitro RPE assay combining oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2 or blue-light exposure), complement activation (addition of recombinant human C5a or serum with activated complement), and POS feeding:  
• PMX205 should dose-dependently inhibit C5a-mediated Ca2+ influx (IC50 in low nM range).  
• It should reduce expression of NLRP3, pro-IL-1β, cleavage of caspase-1 (p20 fragment), and secretion of mature IL-1β/IL-18 (reportable by ELISA).  
• Restoration of lysosomal pH can be assayed with LysoTracker or pH-sensitive probes, and cathepsin D activity monitored with fluorogenic substrates.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: C5a/C5aR1–driven inflammasome activation and lysosomal dysfunction are well documented in dry AMD pathogenesis. Targeting this axis addresses both inflammation and RPE clearance impairment.  
• Preclinical Validation: Robust data exist for PMX205 (and analogs) in inflammatory/neurodegenerative models, including ocular tissue penetration.

• Origins and discovery  
  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. Recombinant human Gas6 (rhGas6) has been produced in mammalian expression systems (e.g., HEK293 or CHO cells) and in baculovirus-infected insect cells, with post-translational γ-carboxylation either engineered in the host line or supplemented in vitro.  
• Therapeutic class and precedent

Proteins in this class have been used in clinical and preclinical settings to replace or augment endogenous signaling ligands (for example, EPO, G-CSF, or thrombopoietin mimetics). By analogy, rhGas6 is intended to replace or boost an endogenous ligand for the TAM family of receptor tyrosine kinases (Tyro3, Axl, MerTK).

• Non-retinal uses of Gas6/TAM-ligand biology  
  – Hemostasis and thrombosis research: Gas6-/- mice are protected from arterial and venous thrombosis, and recombinant Gas6 has been administered systemically in rodent models to rescue platelet aggregation defects. This demonstrates in vivo bioactivity but also raises concern about pro-thrombotic side effects.

  – Oncology: Because Gas6-Axl signaling promotes survival and metastasis in many cancers, Axl inhibitors (rather than Gas6) are under clinical evaluation. Direct Gas6 administration in oncology is not pursued, but its biology is well studied.

However, genetic loss of MerTK causes retinitis pigmentosa in humans and the rd1 mouse lacks functional MerTK, leading to photoreceptor loss from impaired outer segment (OS) phagocytosis. In those models, provision of Gas6 or manipulation of its pathway has only been explored at the preclinical level.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Receptor engagement and signaling  
  – Gas6 binds with high affinity to MerTK (KD ~10–30 nM), and with lower affinity to Axl and Tyro3. Binding requires a γ-carboxylated Gla domain that bridges phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cells or photoreceptor outer segments (POS) to the receptor’s immunoglobulin-like domains.

• Biochemical specificity  
  – MerTK is highly expressed in RPE cells (confirmed by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry in human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cells). Axl and Tyro3 are present at lower levels but may contribute to redundant phagocytic signaling.

• Underlying cell biology  
  – Since MerTK expression in RPE is well established in human tissue and cell lines, the target is present. Gas6 should engage MerTK’s phagocytic program directly, bypassing potential deficiencies in upstream “eat-me” signal presentation. This mechanism aligns with known defects in aged or stressed RPE, where MerTK signaling and POS internalization are both downregulated.

Strengths  
  – Directly targets a genetically validated pathway in RPE phagocytosis (MerTK loss-of-function models recapitulate key features of retinal degeneration).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic. Chemically, it consists of the nitroxide radical 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) conjugated to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP+) cation via an aliphatic linker. The TPP+ moiety drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoTEMPO into negatively polarized mitochondrial matrices (ΔΨm ≈ –150 to –180 mV), achieving several‐hundred‐fold enrichment over cytosol. Nitroxide radicals like TEMPO were first characterized in the 1960s as stable free radical spin probes; subsequent iterations yielded redox-active antioxidants capable of catalyzing superoxide and organic radical dismutation. Mitochondrial targeting by TPP+ was introduced in the late 1990s (Murphy, 1997), producing the “Mito” family of probes and therapeutics. MitoTEMPO belongs to the wider class of mitochondria-penetrating antioxidants (MPAs) that also includes MitoQ, SkQ1, and MitoVitE, all of which have been explored in models of oxidative stress–driven pathologies.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical Studies in Cardiovascular and Metabolic Disease  
 Since its first report (Dikalova et al., 2010), MitoTEMPO has been used extensively in rodent models of hypertension, ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and endothelial dysfunction. In these contexts it lowered mitochondrial superoxide, protected electron transport chain (ETC) components, improved nitric oxide bioavailability, and ameliorated tissue fibrosis and inflammation.

A handful of reports in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models demonstrated decreased lesion size and oxidative markers. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.  
• Selectivity: Dual NOX1/4 inhibition minimizes off-target suppression of NOX2/3/5, potentially reducing immunosuppression and other unwanted effects.  

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Ocular bioavailability: No published ocular PK data. Blood–retina barrier penetration and effective vitreous/RPE concentrations are undetermined; may require formulation optimization or localized delivery.  
• Chronic dosing concerns: Dry AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term systemic NOX inhibition could carry risks (e.g., impaired host defense, vascular effects) that require investigation in extended toxicology studies.  
• Redundancy in ROS sources: Mitochondrial ROS and other oxidases (e.g., xanthine oxidase) also contribute to RPE oxidative stress. NOX inhibition alone may be insufficient without combination approaches.  
• Lack of precedent: No prior ocular or ophthalmic indication for setanaxib; regulatory pathway and end points would need de novo validation.  

Conclusion  
GKT137831 is a rational, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD that directly addresses NOX1/4-derived ROS driving lysosomal/autophagic dysfunction in RPE. Its clinical track record in fibrotic diseases lends confidence in safety and systemic exposure, but crucial gaps remain in ocular pharmacokinetics, long-term tolerability in an elderly population, and proof of efficacy in relevant in vitro and in vivo AMD models. A focused program of RPE cell–based assays, ocular PK studies in rodents or rabbits, and evaluation in dry AMD animal models (e.g., NaIO3-induced RPE atrophy, Abca4−/−Rdh8−/− phototoxicity) would be the next logical steps to determine viability for clinical repurposing.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.  
  – AAV2-CFH gene therapy combines a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector (developed by standard triple-plasmid transfection methods; Xie et al., 2018) carrying a codon-optimized human CFH cDNA under control of an RPE-active promoter (e.g. VMD2 or CAG enhancer). AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).  
  – In vitro, CFH supplementation in human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells reduced oxidative stress markers triggered by complement activation (Chen et al., 2017).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Target Validity: CFH loss of function is strongly linked to dry AMD pathogenesis; genetic data and drusen composition studies (Johnson et al., 2001) support complement overactivation as a disease driver.  
 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.  
 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.  
 4. Sustainability: Single injection may achieve years of CFH expression, avoiding repeated intravitreal injections.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Immune Response: Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to AAV2 in some patients may reduce transduction efficiency (Mingozzi & High, 2013).  
 2. Dose Optimization: Excessive CFH expression might dysregulate systemic complement or trigger off-target effects in the choroid or retina.  
 3. Disease Heterogeneity: Dry AMD is multifactorial; complement is one axis among oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, angiogenesis, and mitochondrial dysfunction. CFH alone may not halt progression in all patients.  
 4. Tissue Distribution: Secreted CFH must penetrate Bruch’s membrane effectively; age-related changes to BrM may impede diffusion.

AAV2-CFH gene therapy is a scientifically grounded approach with strong genetic and mechanistic rationale for dry AMD. Preclinical models suggest efficacy in reducing local complement activation and preserving RPE function. Critical path forward includes optimization of vector dose and promoter choice to achieve physiologic CFH levels, assessment of neutralizing antibody prevalence, and demonstration of functional rescue in relevant animal models of GA. Given the unmet medical need in dry AMD, AAV2-CFH merits further preclinical development toward first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.  
• Lack of in vivo ocular data: No published animal model studies have confirmed MitoQ’s efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function or preventing geographic atrophy.

Conclusion  
MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. Its main strengths lie in targeting the bioenergetic failure underlying dry AMD. However, key gaps include demonstration of effective ocular delivery, avoidance of pro-oxidant effects, and proof of benefit in animal models of AMD. I recommend advancing to RPE monolayer/phagocytosis assays in vitro (dose-response, kinetics of ATP restoration, ROS imaging) followed by an in vivo proof-of-concept study (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in mice) before considering clinical translation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Torin1 is a fully synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase. It was first described in 2010 (Liu et al., 2010) following a high-throughput screen for ATP-competitive inhibitors of mTOR. Chemically, Torin1 features a diaminopyrimidine core linked to a substituted phenyl urea moiety; structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies optimized it for high affinity and selectivity against the mTOR ATP-binding site.  
• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Torin1 belongs to the “TORKinibs” (TOR kinase inhibitors) class, distinct from rapalogs (e.g., rapamycin) in that it competes with ATP rather than binding to the FKBP12-rapamycin–binding (FRB) domain. TORKinibs have primarily been used as research tools to dissect mTORC1 versus mTORC2 signaling in cancer, metabolism, and neurodegeneration models. No clinical approvals exist for Torin1 itself, although closely related compounds (e.g., INK-128/MlN0128) have entered oncology trials.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical/biochemical uses  
  – Widely employed in cell-based and animal studies to achieve near-complete, dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2. Demonstrated robust suppression of phospho-S6K (Thr389), phospho-4E-BP1, and phospho-Akt (Ser473) at low nanomolar doses. Used to study autophagy induction, lysosome biogenesis via TFEB activation (Settembre et al., n.d.-a), and metabolic reprogramming.  
• Clinical or veterinary uses  
  – Torin1 itself has not progressed into human or veterinary clinical trials. Other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors have, but primarily in oncology. There are no reports of Torin1 in ophthalmic applications or in AMD patients. Rapalogs (e.g., sirolimus) have been tested intravitreally for geographic atrophy without major success but demonstrate the feasibility of mTOR modulation in the eye.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Direct molecular target  
  – Torin1 binds the ATP-binding pocket of mTOR in both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, yielding IC₅₀ values in the low-nanomolar range (~2–10 nM).  
• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of mTORC1: loss of phosphorylation on p70 S6 kinase (Thr389) and 4E-BP1, resulting in global translation suppression and de-repression of ULK1 (Ser757), the core autophagy-initiating kinase.  
  – Inhibition of mTORC2: blockade of Akt Ser473 phosphorylation impairs downstream survival and growth signals.  
  – Activation of TFEB: by preventing mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB at Ser142/Ser211, Torin1 promotes nuclear translocation of TFEB, upregulating CLEAR network genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and function (Settembre et al., n.d.-b).  
  – Autophagy and mitophagy flux: dual mTOR inhibition leads to pronounced accumulation of LC3-II, expansion of the autophagosome/autolysosome pool, and accelerated mitochondrial turnover in a variety of cell types (Kim et al., n.d.).  
• Selectivity  
  – Torin1 shows minimal off-target activity against PI3K isoforms and other kinases up to micromolar concentrations, though very high doses may affect ATM, ATR, and DNA-PK.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD RPE Assay  
• RPE expression and disease context  
  – Human RPE cells express mTORC1/C2 components, ULK1, TFEB, and core autophagy machinery (LC3, p62) at high levels (Kunchithapautham & Rohrer, n.d.). Dry AMD is characterized by accumulated POS debris, lipofuscin, and impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance in RPE (Zhao et al., n.d.).  
• Assay readouts and mechanisms  
  – mTORC1/C2 inhibition: Torin1 treatment should reduce p-S6K and p-Akt (Ser473) in RPE lysates (detectable by western blot) at concentrations of ~20–100 nM.  
  – Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels, and formation of autolysosomes visualized by mCherry-GFP-LC3 reporters.  
  – TFEB activation and lysosome biogenesis: nuclear redistribution of TFEB (immunofluorescence) and upregulation of LAMP1/CTSD transcripts (qPCR).  
  – Mitochondrial turnover: enhanced Parkin-dependent mitophagy (co-localization of TOM20 with LC3) and reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX).  
  – POS degradation: in a phagocytosis assay, Torin1-treated RPE should clear fluorescently labeled POS more efficiently than controls, demonstrating enhanced lysosomal clearance.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Mechanistically aligned: dry AMD RPE pathology involves autophagy/lysosomal insufficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction; dual mTORC1/C2 inhibition directly targets these deficits.  
  – Potent TFEB activation: superior to rapamycin in driving lysosomal gene expression and organelle clearance.  
  – High selectivity in vitro: reduces risk of broad kinase off-target effects at efficacious doses.  
  – Precedent for ocular delivery: while Torin1 itself lacks direct ocular data, intravitreal or periocular administration of related mTOR inhibitors (e.g., rapalogs) has established acceptable safety profiles in animal models.  

Weaknesses and risks  
  – mTORC2 inhibition consequences: chronic suppression of Akt Ser473 could predispose RPE to apoptosis or impair survival signaling under stress.  
  – Potential toxicity: mTOR is critical for protein synthesis and cell metabolism; excessive or prolonged inhibition may compromise RPE viability, especially in a post-mitotic cell type reliant on basal mTOR signaling.

Torin1 represents a scientifically rational candidate to rescue autophagy and lysosomal clearance pathways in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD pathology. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic. Chemically, it consists of the nitroxide radical 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) conjugated to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP+) cation via an aliphatic linker. The TPP+ moiety drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoTEMPO into negatively polarized mitochondrial matrices (ΔΨm ≈ –150 to –180 mV), achieving several‐hundred‐fold enrichment over cytosol. Nitroxide radicals like TEMPO were first characterized in the 1960s as stable free radical spin probes; subsequent iterations yielded redox-active antioxidants capable of catalyzing superoxide and organic radical dismutation. Mitochondrial targeting by TPP+ was introduced in the late 1990s (Murphy, 1997), producing the “Mito” family of probes and therapeutics. MitoTEMPO belongs to the wider class of mitochondria-penetrating antioxidants (MPAs) that also includes MitoQ, SkQ1, and MitoVitE, all of which have been explored in models of oxidative stress–driven pathologies.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical Studies in Cardiovascular and Metabolic Disease  
 Since its first report (Dikalova et al., 2010), MitoTEMPO has been used extensively in rodent models of hypertension, ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and endothelial dysfunction. In these contexts it lowered mitochondrial superoxide, protected electron transport chain (ETC) components, improved nitric oxide bioavailability, and ameliorated tissue fibrosis and inflammation.  
Neurological and Neurodegenerative Models  
 MitoTEMPO has shown benefit in models of Parkinson’s disease (by rescuing complex I activity and reducing α-synuclein aggregation), Alzheimer’s disease (by attenuating Aβ-induced ROS), and traumatic brain injury (by limiting secondary oxidative damage).  
Ocular and Retinal Applications  
 While MitoQ and other MPAs have been tested in retinal degeneration or diabetic retinopathy models, direct studies of MitoTEMPO in the eye are fewer. A handful of reports in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models demonstrated decreased lesion size and oxidative markers. To date, no published study has evaluated MitoTEMPO in dry AMD animal models or advanced RPE cultures, though its successful retinal distribution in rodents (intra-vitreal injection and systemic dosing) and favorable ocular safety profile have been noted (Smith et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action  
ROS Scavenging at the Mitochondrial Inner Membrane  
 MitoTEMPO’s TEMPO moiety undergoes redox cycling between nitroxide and hydroxylamine forms. In the presence of superoxide (O2•–), it catalyzes dismutation to H2O2 and O2, mimicking endogenous SOD2, but with targeting to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

 By removing O2•– proximal to complexes I and III, MitoTEMPO prevents oxidative inactivation of iron–sulfur clusters and cardiolipin peroxidation. Studies (Dikalova et al., 2012) show restored complex I–driven respiration, higher membrane potential (ΔΨm), and reduced cytochrome c release.  
Modulation of Downstream Redox Signaling  
 Lowering mitochondrial ROS blunts activation of redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., JNK, p38 MAPK) and transcription factors (e.g., NF-κB), thereby reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression (TNF-α, IL-1β) and NLRP3 inflammasome activation. In RPE, mitochondrial ROS have been linked to drusen component upregulation (complement factors) and NLRP3 priming.

 Some evidence suggests that by normalizing redox state, MitoTEMPO can promote PGC-1α–mediated mitochondrial biogenesis and improve Parkin/PINK1-dependent mitophagy (Chen et al., 2018), restoring a healthy mitochondrial network in aged or stressed cells.
