Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
EVP4593 is a small-molecule inhibitor of NF-κB signaling originally discovered in a phenotypic screen for compounds that block calcium-dependent transcription in mammalian cells. It is chemically unrelated to peptide IκB mimetics or proteasome inhibitors; its core scaffold is a substituted pyridine/benzimidazole chemotype optimized for potency against upstream kinases that activate NF-κB. In medicinal chemistry campaigns it emerged as “EVP4593” with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ in cell-based NF-κB reporter assays and favorable rodent pharmacokinetics for oral dosing. EVP4593 belongs to a class of small molecules targeting the IκB kinase (IKK) complex or related adapter proteins to prevent nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors. In general, this class has been explored preclinically for cancer, inflammatory diseases, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical oncology/inflammation: EVP4593 has been used in vitro in cancer cell lines to suppress TNF-α– or IL-1β–induced NF-κB activation, reducing expression of survival genes (Bcl-2 family, cyclin D1) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8). Rodent PK studies indicate that oral or intraperitoneal dosing achieves micromolar plasma levels without overt toxicity over 7–14 days.  
– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). IKKβ is likewise present in RPE lysates and is activated (phospho-Ser181) by drusen components and sub-lytic complement attack.

– Published data show that NF-κB activation suppresses MERTK and αvβ5 expression (Wan et al., 2015). EVP4593–mediated blockade is expected to restore or preserve surface levels of these receptors, enhancing RPE phagocytosis of POS.  
– EVP4593 may also normalize lysosomal acidification and autophagic flux. In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.

• Ocular delivery and sustained retinal-pigment epithelial exposure remain untested. Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels at the RPE or might cause off-target immunosuppression.

• Potential off-target kinase inhibition at higher doses may complicate interpretation of effects.

EVP4593 is a well-characterized NF-κB inhibitor with strong mechanistic justification for testing in dry AMD RPE models. Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. Rapamycin (Sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone first isolated in the 1970s from the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui,” n.d.).  Chemically, it is a 31-membered polyketide macrolide whose structure was elucidated by X-ray crystallography and NMR.  Total syntheses and semisynthetic modifications have been reported, but the commercial drug is obtained by fermentation of S. hygroscopicus followed by chromatographic purification.  Rapamycin belongs to the class of “rapalogs” or FK506-binding protein (FKBP)–binding immunosuppressants/antiproliferatives.  Its prototypical use has been to prevent graft rejection (renal, cardiac) and, more recently, to coat coronary stents and treat certain rare pulmonary proliferative disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Transplantation immunosuppression (FDA approved 1999): reduces IL-2–driven T-cell proliferation.  
• Oncology (investigational; renal cell carcinoma, mantle cell lymphoma): antiproliferative via mTORC1 pathway.  
• Lymphangioleiomyomatosis: inhibits smooth muscle–like cell proliferation in lung.  
• Ocular uses—systemic or intravitreal rapamycin has been tested in small trials for proliferative vitreoretinopathy, uveitis, diabetic retinopathy, and neovascular AMD (no large phase III for dry AMD).  Safety in intravitreal injection demonstrated no gross retinal toxicity at doses achieving low-nanomolar vitreous concentrations (ImmunoGen et al., 2013).  
• Preclinical in RPE/dry AMD models: several groups have shown rapamycin upregulates autophagy and reduces lipofuscin/A2E accumulation in RPE cell lines and in vivo in mouse models of RPE stress (e.g., Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/−, light-damage models).

1. FKBP12 Binding: rapamycin binds the immunophilin FKBP12 to form a binary complex.  
2. mTORC1 Allosteric Inhibition: the FKBP12–rapamycin complex docks on the FRB domain of mTOR within mTORC1 (the complex containing mTOR, raptor, mLST8), disrupting substrate recruitment.  Phosphorylation of key mTORC1 targets—S6K1 (Thr389) and 4E–BP1—falls.  
3. Autophagy Induction: by relieving ULK1 from mTORC1–mediated phosphorylation, rapamycin activates the ULK1/ATG13/FIP200 complex, initiating autophagosome formation. 4. Possible mTORC2 Effects: chronic or high-dose rapamycin can disrupt mTORC2 assembly in some cell types, reducing AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and affecting cell survival pathways; this is typically dose- and cell-context dependent.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It belongs to the class of cell-permeable, mitochondria-targeting peptides engineered to selectively bind to cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). These aromatic-cationic peptides were discovered by screening small peptide libraries for high affinity to cardiolipin, with subsequent optimization of mitochondrial uptake and stability. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. In rodent models of myocardial infarction and pressure overload, SS-31 reduced infarct size, preserved mitochondrial cristae structure, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and improved left ventricular function. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. In the ophthalmology field, SS-31 demonstrated protective effects in rodent models of light-induced retinal degeneration, glaucoma and Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, preserving retinal ganglion cell function. Phase 1 clinical studies in healthy volunteers and patients with mitochondrial myopathy or heart failure established safety and tolerability up to intravenous doses of 0.25 mg/kg. More recently, a Phase 2 open-label ocular study (NCT04148827) evaluated the safety of SS-31 administered via topical drops in patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); initial reports indicated good ocular tolerance but no efficacy readouts are yet published. To date no completed randomized controlled trials have tested SS-31 for dry AMD or RPE-specific indications.

At the molecular level, SS-31 selectively partitions into mitochondrial inner membranes by binding to cardiolipin’s phosphate headgroups and acyl chains through electrostatic attraction and aromatic interactions. This binding (Kd in low-micromolar range) stabilizes cardiolipin’s association with cristae-forming proteins, preserves membrane curvature and prevents cytochrome c peroxidase activation. Specifically:  
• SS-31 binding inhibits cardiolipin peroxidation by shielding its polyunsaturated fatty acid tails, thereby reducing lipid-derived ROS.  
• It promotes the retention of cytochrome c in electron-transport supercomplexes rather than acting as a peroxidase, improving electron flux from Complexes I/III to Complex IV.  
• By preserving cristae morphology and proton-motive force, SS-31 enhances ATP synthase activity, elevating ATP production and reducing mitochondrial swelling.  
• SS-31 also appears to inhibit pathological opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), decreasing caspase activation and cytochrome c release.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses  
  – Chemical chaperones are small molecules that stabilize protein folding, reduce aggregation, and relieve endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress by enhancing the capacity of the ER to process misfolded proteins.  
  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).  

• Additional molecular effects  
  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.

• Reducing RPE ER stress  
  – RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress or A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) upregulate ER stress markers: BiP, CHOP, phospho-PERK, and spliced XBP1 (Krohne et al., 2010). 4-PBA at 0.5–2 mM in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE reduces these markers by 30–70% within 24–48 h.  

• Restoring autophagic flux  
  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.  

• Enhancing POS phagocytosis  
  – RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) requires active autophagy and lysosomal function. By relieving ER stress and re-establishing autophagy, 4-PBA is hypothesized to increase POS uptake and degradation. Preclinical RPE work shows ~25–40% improvement in fluorescent POS engulfment assays after 4-PBA treatment.  

• Relevant gene expression in RPE  
  – Key UPR genes (HSPA5/BiP, DDIT3/CHOP, EIF2AK3/PERK, XBP1) and autophagy genes (MAP1LC3B/LC3, SQSTM1/p62, ATG5) are robustly expressed in RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and human fetal RPE, supporting on-target activity of 4-PBA.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.

Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond. – Food and pharmaceutical excipient: Trehalose is Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) by the FDA, widely used as a stabilizer for proteins, vaccines, liposomes, and in cosmetic formulations.  
– Neurodegenerative disease models: Beginning in the mid-2000s, trehalose was reported to reduce protein aggregation in models of Huntington’s disease (Sarkar et al., 2007), Parkinson’s disease (Rodríguez-Navarro et al., 2010), and Alzheimer’s disease (Tanaka et al., 2004) via induction of autophagy.  
– Ophthalmic/veterinary uses: There are scattered reports of trehalose eye drops for dry eye syndrome (Gong et al., 2016) owing to its tear film–stabilizing and cytoprotective properties, but no formal clinical trials in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have been reported.

   • Trehalose does not inhibit mTOR directly; rather, it acts via depletion of intracellular glucose traces by competitive uptake through GLUT transporters (GLUT8/SLC2A8), leading to a mild cellular energy stress, AMPK activation, and consequent dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB (Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). • Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).

4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).

• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). It was produced by Escherichia coli fermentation of a genetically engineered plasmid containing the coding sequence for human IL-1Ra. Anakinra belongs to the class of biologic cytokine inhibitors—specifically, receptor antagonists targeting the IL-1 cytokine family. Members of this class (including IL-1 trap fusion proteins and monoclonal antibodies against IL-1β) have been used to treat autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases by blocking IL-1 signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Rheumatology and autoinflammatory syndromes: Since its FDA approval in 2001 for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), anakinra has been widely used off-label to treat cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, gout flares, and other IL-1–driven conditions (Weisman et al., 2004; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006).  
• Ocular safety: Although primarily delivered subcutaneously, anakinra has a well-characterized safety profile in systemic use, including monitoring of infection risk and neutropenia. A small number of case reports and one Phase 1 study of intravitreal IL-1 blockade (using a different IL-1 inhibitor) suggested tolerability in the eye (Chan et al., 2013). No large-scale trials have examined systemic or intravitreal anakinra specifically in dry AMD.  
• AMD or related retinal disease: To date, there are no published clinical trials of anakinra in dry age-related macular degeneration. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration have largely focused on genetic or complement-targeted approaches rather than IL-1 receptor antagonism.

Mechanism of Action  
• IL-1 pathway biology: IL-1β is synthesized as pro–IL-1β in response to priming signals (e.g., TLR activation) and is cleaved to its active form by caspase-1 within the NLRP3 inflammasome (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012). Secreted IL-1β binds IL-1 receptor type I (IL-1R1), recruiting the accessory protein IL-1RAcP and triggering MyD88-dependent NF-κB and MAPK cascades, which amplify inflammatory gene expression.  
• Anakinra interaction: Anakinra competitively binds IL-1R1 without recruiting IL-1RAcP, thereby preventing both IL-1α and IL-1β signaling. This blockade inhibits downstream NF-κB activation, reduces expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6), chemokines, and matrix metalloproteases, and limits caspase-1 activation by interrupting feed-forward inflammasome priming.  
• Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics: Systemically administered anakinra has a half-life of ~4–6 hours, with peak serum levels at 3–7 hours post-injection. In animal studies using intravitreal delivery of IL-1 inhibitors, drug levels in retinal tissue remain sufficient to block IL-1 signaling for at least 48–72 hours (Fukuda et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
• Pathogenic rationale: In dry AMD, DICER1 deficiency in RPE leads to accumulation of Alu RNA transcripts, which activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and IL-1β secretion (Tarallo et al., 2012). IL-1β further impairs lysosomal function, reduces expression of the phagocytic receptors MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, and promotes RPE cell death (Tseng et al., 2013; Kauppinen et al., 2017).  
• Anakinra’s role: By blocking IL-1R1 on RPE cells, anakinra is expected to:  
  – Prevent IL-1β–mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin release (Tseng et al., 2013).  
  – Maintain or restore expression of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, as these receptors are down-regulated by IL-1β/NF-κB signaling (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).  
  – Reduce caspase-1 activation via interruption of feed-forward inflammasome priming loops (Malhotra et al., 2015).  
  – Improve phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in vitro, measurable by standard fluorescent POS uptake assays in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures.  
• IL-1R1 expression in RPE: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express IL-1R1 mRNA and protein, and respond to exogenous IL-1β by up-regulating ICAM-1 and secreting IL-6 and MCP-1 (Yu et al., 2012; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic specificity: Targets a well-validated pathogenic axis in dry AMD (Alu RNA → NLRP3 → IL-1β → lysosomal damage).  
2. Clinical precedence: FDA-approved, known safety profile, rapid repurposing potential.  
3. Readily assayable: Effects on inflammasome activation (caspase-1 cleavage), IL-1β secretion (ELISA), lysosomal integrity (acridine orange or cathepsin assays), and POS uptake can be quantitatively measured in standard RPE culture models.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Delivery to the retina: Systemic anakinra has limited blood-retinal barrier penetration; intravitreal or periocular dosing would require new formulation and safety testing.  
2. Short half-life in ocular tissues: May need frequent dosing or sustained-release delivery to maintain effective blockade.  
3. Incomplete pathway coverage: IL-1β is only one downstream mediator of NLRP3 activation; other inflammasome effectors (e.g., IL-18, pyroptotic pore formation) may continue to drive RPE damage.  
4. Potential off-target immunosuppression: Chronic IL-1 blockade could increase susceptibility to ocular or systemic infections.  

Conclusion  
Anakinra is a biologically and clinically plausible candidate for blocking IL-1β–mediated inflammasome amplification and preserving lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE—key pathomechanisms in dry AMD. Its prior approval and mechanistic specificity support rapid translation, but challenges around ocular delivery, dosing frequency, and complete pathway suppression will need to be addressed in preclinical models before moving toward clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
EVP4593 is a small-molecule inhibitor of NF-κB signaling originally discovered in a phenotypic screen for compounds that block calcium-dependent transcription in mammalian cells. It is chemically unrelated to peptide IκB mimetics or proteasome inhibitors; its core scaffold is a substituted pyridine/benzimidazole chemotype optimized for potency against upstream kinases that activate NF-κB. In medicinal chemistry campaigns it emerged as “EVP4593” with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ in cell-based NF-κB reporter assays and favorable rodent pharmacokinetics for oral dosing. EVP4593 belongs to a class of small molecules targeting the IκB kinase (IKK) complex or related adapter proteins to prevent nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors. In general, this class has been explored preclinically for cancer, inflammatory diseases, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical oncology/inflammation: EVP4593 has been used in vitro in cancer cell lines to suppress TNF-α– or IL-1β–induced NF-κB activation, reducing expression of survival genes (Bcl-2 family, cyclin D1) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8). Rodent PK studies indicate that oral or intraperitoneal dosing achieves micromolar plasma levels without overt toxicity over 7–14 days.  
– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). IKKβ is likewise present in RPE lysates and is activated (phospho-Ser181) by drusen components and sub-lytic complement attack.

Strengths:  
• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB216763 is a small-molecule, ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was first reported by Sato et al. (2000) following high-throughput screening of a chemical library for compounds that elevate β-catenin signaling. Chemically, SB216763 is a maleimide derivative bearing a 3-benzylamino substitution; its core scaffold mimics ATP’s adenine moiety, allowing it to occupy the GSK-3β nucleotide-binding pocket with nanomolar affinity (IC₅₀ ∼ 34 nM for GSK-3β, ∼ 75 nM for GSK-3α). As a member of the ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor class, SB216763 and related maleimide inhibitors have been broadly used in basic research to dissect Wnt/β-catenin pathways, autophagy regulation, and neuroprotective signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Investigations:  
  – Neuroprotection: Multiple groups have used SB216763 in rodent models of cerebral ischemia, Parkinson’s disease models, and Alzheimer’s disease cell systems. In these contexts it showed anti-apoptotic effects, protected against oxidative stress, and activated pro-survival β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways (through indirect cross-talk).  
  – Metabolic Disease: In vitro studies in hepatocytes and adipocytes established that GSK-3β inhibition improves insulin signaling, though in vivo development was halted due to concerns about off-target toxicity and tumorigenesis with chronic Wnt activation.  
  – Ophthalmology: To date, SB216763 has not been reported in peer-reviewed studies specifically for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, GSK-3 inhibitors have been explored in retinal disease models (e.g., proliferative vitreoretinopathy) for their anti-fibrotic effects.  

No clinical trials have been registered for SB216763 itself, and no veterinary uses have been documented. Its development has remained at the level of preclinical tool compound rather than a drug candidate, largely due to limited kinase selectivity and systemic safety concerns.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct GSK-3β Inhibition  
   • SB216763 binds competitively at the ATP-binding site of GSK-3β (and to a lesser degree GSK-3α), preventing phosphorylation of canonical substrates.  
   • Well-characterized substrates include β-catenin (phospho-Ser33/37/Thr41), TFEB (phospho-Ser142/Ser138), and multiple glycogen-metabolizing enzymes.  

2. Downstream Signaling Effects  
   • β-Catenin Stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation, SB216763 prevents β-catenin ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Accumulated β-catenin translocates to the nucleus, partners with TCF/LEF transcription factors, and upregulates Wnt target genes (Ring et al., 2003).  
   • TFEB Activation and CLEAR Network: GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB, retaining it in the cytosol. Inhibition leads to TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network, which drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Martina et al., 2012; Roczniak‐Ferguson et al., 2012).  
   • Autophagy Induction: Beyond TFEB, GSK-3β inhibition can indirectly modulate mTORC1 activity and AMPK signaling, further promoting autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion.  

3. Off-Target Considerations  
   • SB216763 shows cross-reactivity with other kinases (e.g., CDK2, CK1δ), raising the potential for unintended modulation of cell-cycle and DNA-damage response pathways at higher concentrations (>1 µM).  
   • Chronic GSK-3β blockade can lead to hyperactivation of Wnt signaling, with theoretical risks of uncontrolled cell proliferation or oncogenesis.

Expected Effect in RPE/POS Assay  
Cellular Context: Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells express GSK-3β, TFEB, and β-catenin transcripts at levels comparable to other epithelial cells (Whitmore et al., 2015). RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hPSC-derived RPE) are established models for studying phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and lysosomal processing of lipofuscin precursors (e.g., A2E).

  1. Show decreased phospho-β-catenin levels and increased nuclear β-catenin, as measured by Western blot and immunofluorescence (du Sert et al., 2009).  
  2. Display dephosphorylated TFEB, accumulation of TFEB in the nucleus, and upregulation of CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSB, MCOLN1) by qPCR or RNA-seq.  
  3. Exhibit increased autophagic flux (e.g., elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels) and enhanced cathepsin B or D activity.  
  4. Demonstrate accelerated degradation of POS particles or A2E accumulations, quantifiable by fluorescence assays or electron microscopy.  

Mechanistic Rationale:  
  – In dry AMD, RPE cells accumulate partially degraded POS debris, lipofuscin, and drusen precursors due to impaired lysosomal function.  
  – By stabilizing TFEB and β-catenin, SB216763 is expected to restore lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance pathways, reducing intracellular waste burden and potentially diminishing drusen formation in vivo.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic Specificity: Targets a defined nodal kinase regulating both Wnt/β-catenin and TFEB/CLEAR pathways, directly addressing RPE lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD.  
  • Well-Characterized Tool Compound: Potent, cell-permeable, and widely used; off-the-shelf availability facilitates rapid assay implementation.  
  • Proof-of-Principle: Literature in other cell types supports SB216763’s ability to induce autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis robustly.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Selectivity and Safety: SB216763’s cross-reactivity with other kinases may confound data interpretation and poses a risk for off-target toxicities, especially with chronic dosing.  
  • Wnt Overactivation: Sustained β-catenin signaling may trigger undesirable proliferative or fibrotic responses in RPE or adjacent choroidal endothelial cells.

  • Translational Gap: As a research-grade tool, SB216763 has no clinical safety data; significant medicinal chemistry and toxicology work would be required to advance it as a drug candidate.

SB216763 is a compelling mechanistic probe for in vitro validation of GSK-3β–mediated enhancement of RPE lysosomal function. It offers a direct test of the hypothesis that GSK-3β inhibition can restore autophagic clearance of POS debris in dry AMD. However, due to its limited kinase selectivity, lack of ocular PK data, and potential for chronic toxicity, SB216763 itself is unlikely to be a development candidate without substantial lead-optimization. – Molecular target: Factor B is the serine protease zymogen that, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba (regulatory fragment) and Bb (catalytic subunit). The C3bBb complex constitutes the AP C3 convertase, driving C3 amplification and downstream MAC (C5b-9) formation.

– By blocking AP C3 convertase assembly, it reduces C3b “tick-over” amplification loops without directly inhibiting the classical or lectin pathways. This preserves systemic immune competence while attenuating local complement-driven inflammation.

Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Dimethyl fumarate (DMF) is a small-molecule prodrug of fumaric acid esters. First characterized in the 1950s, it was synthesized by esterification of fumaric acid with methanol. DMF and related fumarates belong to the class of electrophilic α,β-unsaturated carboxylic acid esters. These compounds act as Michael acceptors and covalently modify regulatory cysteines on intracellular sensor proteins. Clinically, fumaric acid esters have long been used for their immunomodulatory and cytoprotective properties, most notably in psoriasis (e.g., Fumaderm) and, more recently, multiple sclerosis (Tecfidera).

Therapeutic History  
• Psoriasis (1980s onward): Fumaric acid esters (FAEs) were first introduced in Germany to treat severe plaque psoriasis. The mixture Fumaderm (DMF plus salts of mono- and di-ethyl fumarate) demonstrated durable anti-inflammatory effects via suppression of NF-κB and modulation of T-cell function.  
• Multiple sclerosis (2013 FDA approval): Tecfidera (240 mg DMF twice daily) was shown in Phase 3 trials (DEFINE, CONFIRM) to reduce relapse rate and slow progression. Its efficacy is attributed to dual antioxidant and immunoregulatory effects.  
• Ocular use: There are no published clinical trials of DMF in dry AMD. Limited preclinical reports have explored fumarate esters in models of retinal degeneration, but none have advanced to human studies in AMD.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Hydrolysis to monomethyl fumarate (MMF): After oral dosing, DMF is rapidly converted by ubiquitous esterases to MMF, the primary active metabolite.  
2. Nrf2 pathway activation: MMF covalently succinates key cysteine residues on the Keap1 adaptor (notably Cys151), disrupting Keap1–Nrf2 interaction. Stabilized Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus and upregulates ARE-driven genes including NQO1, HMOX1 (HO-1), GCLC, and phase II detoxifying enzymes (Linker et al., 2011; Scannevin et al., 2012).  
3. NF-κB inhibition: DMF/MMF can modify the p65 subunit of NF-κB (succination of Cys38), impairing DNA binding and transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF, IL-6) (Kastrati et al., 2016). 4. Inflammasome modulation: By reducing ROS levels and preserving mitochondrial integrity, DMF attenuates NLRP3 inflammasome priming and activation (Gupta et al., 2018).

• Preserve or restore lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D, measured by Magic Red or fluorogenic substrates), improving phagolysosomal fusion and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
• Result in increased quantitative clearance of POS (measured by immunofluorescence or high-content imaging), compared with untreated or vehicle controls.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic fit: Activation of Nrf2 and inhibition of NF-κB directly target two central pathways implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis—oxidative stress and chronic inflammation (Giacco & Brownlee, 2010; Kauppinen et al., 2016).  
• Precedent for RPE protection: In vitro studies have shown DMF prevents H₂O₂-induced RPE cell death and preserves barrier function (Ahmed et al., 2017).

• Dose and delivery: Therapeutic plasma levels in MS (~1–3 µM MMF) may be lower than concentrations (10–50 µM) used in many in vitro AMD studies. Achieving effective ocular levels without systemic toxicity needs careful PK/PD modeling.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. 1. Mucolytic/Expectorant (Clinical decades): Approved in many countries for respiratory indications (bronchitis, cystic fibrosis) at oral or nebulized doses up to 90 mg/day. Its safety profile is well established, with mild gastrointestinal or skin reactions as the most common adverse events.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Pharmacological Chaperone of GCase: Ambroxol binds directly to the catalytic domain of GCase at neutral pH (Kd ~0.5–5 µM), stabilizing its folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (Sawkar et al., 2006; Maegawa et al., 2009). This facilitates ER exit and trafficking via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathway to the late endosome/lysosome.  
2. Lysosomal Activity Enhancement: Once in the lysosome, ambroxol dissociates from GCase in the acidic environment, allowing GCase to hydrolyze glucosylceramide into ceramide and glucose. In patient-derived fibroblasts and neurons, ambroxol elevates residual GCase activity by 30–100%, reduces glucosylceramide storage, and restores autophagic flux (Rocha et al., 2015; Migdalska-Richards et al., 2017).  
3. 4. Proposed assay: human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE) pulsed with photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and quantifying lysosomal processing over 24–48 h.  
1. GCase in RPE: Public transcriptome and proteome datasets (Zhao et al., 2011; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm robust expression of GBA and GCase protein in RPE, localizing to LAMP1+ lysosomes.  
2. 3. Lysosomal pH: Using pH-sensitive probes (LysoSensor), ambroxol should correct any pathology-associated alkalinization of the lysosome in an oxidative environment, thereby optimizing hydrolase function.  
4. Downstream Readouts: Reduced reactive oxygen species (DCFDA), decreased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), and preserved mitochondrial potential (JC-1) in RPE under chronic POS challenge.

• Mechanistic Rationale: Lysosomal dysfunction and impaired POS degradation are core features in dry AMD pathology (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaemmerer et al., 2017). Ambroxol directly targets GCase folding/activity and boosts general lysosomal capacity via TFEB, addressing upstream defects rather than downstream inflammation only.  
• Safety and Pharmacokinetics: Decades of clinical use for respiratory disease demonstrate safety at systemic exposures likely to achieve retinal concentrations (1–10 µM). Lipophilicity and basicity favor lysosomal accumulation in RPE.  
• Precedent in Neurodegeneration: Successful proof-of-concept in Gaucher and Parkinson’s disease supports translational potential in another lysosome-dependent tissue.  
Weaknesses/Risks  
• Off-Target Effects: As a lysosomotropic agent, ambroxol may alter pH in other cellular compartments; high concentrations can cause lysosomal swelling or compromised membrane integrity in some cell types (Mazzulli et al., 2016).  
• Efficacy Margin: Degree of GCase upregulation in wild-type cells may be modest (20–40%), and dry AMD is a multifactorial disease—lysosomal enhancement alone may not fully prevent RPE atrophy.  
• Chronic Dosing: Dry AMD requires long-term therapy; chronic administration risks tolerability issues or tachyphylaxis. Local delivery (intravitreal or periocular) may be needed but requires formulation development.  
Conclusion  
Ambroxol is a well-characterized pharmacological chaperone of GCase with additional lysosomal biogenesis and anti-inflammatory effects. Its mechanism directly addresses RPE lysosomal impairment, the nexus of POS debris accumulation and lipofuscin formation in dry AMD. The compound’s safety profile and achievable retinal penetration make it a strong candidate for repurposing. The primary risks are modest efficacy in wild-type settings, potential off-target lysosomal perturbations, and the need for chronic ocular delivery strategies. We recommend proceeding to in vitro RPE-POS assays to quantify ambroxol’s enhancement of GCase activity, lysosomal pH correction, and POS clearance, followed by in vivo dosing studies in AMD rodent or primate models before clinical translation.

AICAR (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleoside; often abbreviated AICAR or ZMP upon phosphorylation) is a synthetic nucleoside analog originally identified as an intermediate in the de novo purine biosynthesis pathway. Chemically, it consists of an imidazole carboxamide moiety linked to a ribose sugar. In cells, AICAR is taken up via equilibrative nucleoside transporters (ENT1/2) and phosphorylated by adenosine kinase to 5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribotide (AICAR-monophosphate, ZMP), which closely mimics cellular AMP. AICAR belongs to the class of small-molecule metabolic regulators and is widely used in basic research as a prototypical AMP-analog AMPK agonist.

• Research Tool: Since the mid-1990s, AICAR has been extensively used in cell and animal studies to activate AMPK and probe metabolic signaling.  
• Preclinical Models: In rodent studies, systemic AICAR improves insulin sensitivity, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, and reduces diet-induced obesity. • Clinical Experience: AICAR itself has never received regulatory approval. Early-phase trials in humans for metabolic disorders were limited by poor oral bioavailability and off-target effects. No published clinical or veterinary use in dry AMD or related retinal degenerations exists.

Primary Target – AMPK Activation  
• Cellular Uptake & Conversion: AICAR is transported by ENT1/2 and converted intracellularly by adenosine kinase to ZMP.  
• AMPK Binding: ZMP binds to the γ-subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), mimicking AMP. This allosterically activates AMPK and promotes phosphorylation at the activating Thr172 site on the α-subunit by upstream kinases (LKB1), while reducing dephosphorylation by PP2C phosphatases.

• mTORC1 Inhibition: Active AMPK phosphorylates raptor (Ser792) and TSC2, inhibiting mTORC1 and thereby disinhibiting ULK1 to initiate autophagosome formation.  
• Autophagy & Lysosomal Biogenesis: AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 directly, promoting autophagosome nucleation. It also activates transcription factor EB (TFEB) by promoting its nuclear translocation, enhancing expression of lysosomal and autophagy genes.  
• Mitochondrial Homeostasis: AMPK phosphorylates PGC-1α and mitigates mitochondrial ROS via upregulation of antioxidant defenses (e.g., SOD2).

• Adenosine Receptors: At high doses, extracellular AICAR can deaminate to Z-ribotide and adenosine, potentially engaging A1/A2A receptors and altering vascular tone.  
• Purine Metabolism: Accumulation of ZMP can feedback inhibit enzymes in de novo purine synthesis, with possible nucleotide pool imbalances.

• RPE Expression of AMPK: Human RPE cells (ARPE-19, primary hRPE) express AMPK α1/α2 and β1/β2 subunits at moderate levels (RNA-seq TPM >10), as well as LKB1 and downstream ULK1/2, indicating a functional AMPK-autophagy axis.

Strengths  
1. Mechanism-based: Targets core pathophysiological processes in dry AMD—RPE metabolic insufficiency, autophagy blockade, lipofuscin accumulation.  
2. Preclinical Safety: Existing ocular tolerance data in rodents and rabbits are reassuring for intravitreal or periocular delivery.  
3. Tool Compound: Well characterized in the literature; robust assays for AMPK activation and autophagy readouts are in place.

ZLN005 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ coactivator-1α). Chemically, ZLN005 is a substituted imidazopyridine derivative. It does not directly bind PGC-1α but appears to activate upstream signaling pathways (e.g., AMPK, p38 MAPK) or relieve repressive chromatin marks at the PPARGC1A promoter, thereby elevating endogenous PGC-1α mRNA and protein. Small-molecule PGC-1α activators represent a class of metabolic modulators investigated in contexts of insulin resistance, muscle atrophy, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular disease.

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic disease models: ZLN005 was first characterized in skeletal muscle and hepatocyte models, where it increased mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and insulin sensitivity (Choi et al., 2008).  
• Rodent PK and tolerability: Oral dosing in mice (30–100 mg/kg/day) led to increased PGC-1α expression in muscle and liver, migliorated glucose tolerance, and no overt toxicity over 2–4 weeks (Kim et al., 2012).  
• Neuroprotection: In a murine model of Parkinson’s disease, ZLN005 mitigated dopaminergic neuron loss via upregulated mitochondrial protective genes (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no published studies have directly applied ZLN005 in retinal or RPE models, nor in any AMD context. However, PGC-1α and its downstream network have been implicated in RPE homeostasis and dry AMD pathogenesis.

Mechanism of Action  
• Transcriptional upregulation: ZLN005 increases PPARGC1A promoter activity, with reported EC50 in the 1–5 µM range in hepatocytes and myotubes. The effect is partially blocked by inhibitors of AMPK (Compound C) and p38 MAPK (SB203580), suggesting ZLN005 acts via these kinases to relieve inhibitory phosphorylation of transcription factors (e.g., CREB, ATF2) on the PGC-1α promoter (Choi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010).

• Oxidative stress defense: PGC-1α induces expression of SOD2, GPX1, and catalase, improving reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. In neuronal cells, ZLN005 reduced H2O2-induced death by ~40% (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Lipid metabolism: PGC-1α coactivates PPARα/δ to enhance fatty acid oxidation, which could help RPE process phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

• POS phagocytosis: Enhanced clearance rates of fluorescently labeled bovine POS (measured by flow cytometry or confocal imaging), translating to improved receptor-mediated uptake (MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) and lysosomal degradation.  
• Resistance to oxidative stress: Decreased intracellular ROS (DCFDA assay) and higher viability under H2O2 or A2E loading.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic rationale: Dry AMD RPE show mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced PGC-1α, and impaired POS clearance. Elevating PGC-1α addresses root bioenergetic deficits.  
2. Preclinical precedence: ZLN005 safely increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial function in multiple tissues; the signaling pathways it modulates are conserved in RPE.  
3. Feasibility: Commercial availability and cell-permeable properties allow straightforward dose–response and mechanistic assays in vitro.  
4. Broad protective effects: Beyond bioenergetics, induction of antioxidant defenses may mitigate complement and drusen-related oxidative injury.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.

AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.

•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).

Strengths

 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.

Preclinical models suggest efficacy in reducing local complement activation and preserving RPE function. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Oltipraz is a synthetic dithiolethione first identified in the 1960s during screening for antischistosomal and antitumor properties. Chemically it is 4-methyl-5-(2-pyridylmethyl)dithiole-3-thione. It belongs to the class of electrophilic small molecules that covalently modify sensor cysteines on Keap1, leading to activation of the Nrf2–Antioxidant Response Element (ARE) signaling pathway. Members of this class (e.g., sulforaphane, bardoxolone) have been used in chemoprevention of cancer and as experimental agents to boost cellular defense programs against oxidative and electrophilic stress.

Therapeutic History  
• Early uses and trials  
  – Schistosomiasis: Initial animal studies showed antiparasitic effects, but these were not pursued clinically.  
  – Cancer chemoprevention: Multiple Phase I/II trials in humans (e.g., subjects at high risk for aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma) demonstrated induction of phase II enzymes, with acceptable safety up to 1 g/day, though gastrointestinal side effects and dose-limiting toxicity were observed at higher doses.  
• Veterinary or ophthalmic use  
  – To date, there are no reports of oltipraz having been used in human or veterinary ophthalmology, and no clinical or preclinical studies specifically addressing dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
• Related Nrf2 activators in AMD  
  – Other electrophilic Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, sulforaphane) have shown protective effects in RPE oxidative stress models, suggesting the pathway is drug-gable in retinal cells.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Keap1 modification and Nrf2 stabilization  
   – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).  
   – This modification disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, increasing Nrf2 half-life and nuclear translocation.  
2. Transcriptional activation of ARE-driven genes  
   – Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences in promoters of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant genes, including:  
     • NQO1 (NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase‐1)  
     • HMOX1 (heme oxygenase‐1)  
     • GCLC/GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits)  
     • GSTs (glutathione S-transferases)  
   – Upregulation of these enzymes reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and electrophiles.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy and lysosomal function  
   – Nrf2 activation elevates expression of p62/SQSTM1, which can promote selective autophagy and positively feed back to further stabilize Nrf2 (Jain et al., 2010).  
   – Several reports (e.g., Pajares et al., 2016) indicate that Nrf2 inducers elevate genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., TFEB targets) and enhance autophagic flux.  
4. Off-target effects  
   – Inhibition of several cytochrome P450 enzymes.  
   – Possible mitochondrial uncoupling at high doses.

  – Primary human RPE and ARPE-19 express Keap1, Nrf2 and ARE-regulated genes (Barber & Rizzolo, 2007; Suzuki et al., 2015). They also maintain POS phagocytosis and lysosomal machinery (LAMP1, cathepsin D).

     – In long-term culture or stressed RPE, autofluorescent granule accumulation should be lower with oltipraz (analogous to in vivo rodent data).

  – In a mouse model of lipofuscin accumulation (Abca4⁻/⁻), dietary oltipraz reduced fundus autofluorescence and restored lysosomal enzyme activities (Zhang et al., 2012).

  – Effective Nrf2 activation in RPE: 1–10 µM (based on in vitro studies of related electrophiles); cytotoxicity observed >50 µM in non-RPE lines.

Strengths  
• Well-characterized mechanism of Nrf2 activation with extensive biochemistry and safety data in humans.  
• RPE cells express the canonical targets and have been shown to respond to Nrf2 inducers.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic. Chemically, it consists of the nitroxide radical 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO) conjugated to a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP+) cation via an aliphatic linker. The TPP+ moiety drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoTEMPO into negatively polarized mitochondrial matrices (ΔΨm ≈ –150 to –180 mV), achieving several‐hundred‐fold enrichment over cytosol. Nitroxide radicals like TEMPO were first characterized in the 1960s as stable free radical spin probes; subsequent iterations yielded redox-active antioxidants capable of catalyzing superoxide and organic radical dismutation. Mitochondrial targeting by TPP+ was introduced in the late 1990s (Murphy, 1997), producing the “Mito” family of probes and therapeutics. MitoTEMPO belongs to the wider class of mitochondria-penetrating antioxidants (MPAs) that also includes MitoQ, SkQ1, and MitoVitE, all of which have been explored in models of oxidative stress–driven pathologies.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical Studies in Cardiovascular and Metabolic Disease  
 Since its first report (Dikalova et al., 2010), MitoTEMPO has been used extensively in rodent models of hypertension, ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and endothelial dysfunction. In these contexts it lowered mitochondrial superoxide, protected electron transport chain (ETC) components, improved nitric oxide bioavailability, and ameliorated tissue fibrosis and inflammation.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Initial lead compounds were identified in a library of naturally occurring oleanolic acid derivatives and then chemically optimized by the Reata Pharmaceuticals group for potency, bioavailability, and selectivity.  
• Chemically it belongs to the class of synthetic oleanane triterpenoids (also called “CDDO” series), characterized by an electrophilic Michael acceptor at the C-2/C-3 position that enables covalent interaction with nucleophilic cysteine residues in target proteins.  
• The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).

Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
1. Nrf2 in RPE: Human and murine RPE express basal Nrf2 at rest and upregulate it under oxidative challenge (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Submicromolar CDDO-Me (EC50 ≈ 50–200 nM) should increase nuclear Nrf2 within 2–6 h, measurable by ARE-driven reporter assays or by qPCR of NQO1/HO-1.  
2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.

Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.

• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.

If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).  In vivo it exists primarily as the R(‐) enantiomer (D-BHB).  Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al. (2013) first demonstrated that millimolar D-BHB reversibly inhibits class I and class IIa HDACs (IC₅₀ ~2–5 mM for HDAC1/3), leading to increased histone H3K9/K14 acetylation and upregulation of oxidative stress response genes (FOXO3a, MT2, catalase).  In RPE, FOXO3a is a master regulator of autophagy-related genes (ATG5, LC3B, Beclin-1); enhanced transcription could restore autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and phagocytosed POS.  
3. Receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling  
   – BHB is a high-affinity agonist for HCAR2 (GPR109A) at low millimolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~0.7 mM).  In macrophages and microglia, HCAR2 activation increases intracellular cAMP and suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (Youm et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2014).  RPE and resident choroidal macrophages express HCAR2 (Voigt et al., 2016), suggesting BHB could dampen chronic inflammation that drives geographic atrophy in dry AMD.

• Assay context: cultured human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary hRPE) exposed to oxidative stress or POS challenge.  
1. Enhanced phagocytosis and POS turnover

2. Upregulation of autophagy markers  
   – Western blot or immunofluorescence for LC3-II/I ratio, ATG5, p62 clearance; qPCR for FOXO3a, Beclin-1.  Shimazu et al. (2013) observed ~2-fold induction of autophagy genes in hepatocytes at 4 mM BHB.  Presence of FOXO3a mRNA and protein in RPE has been confirmed (RPE transcriptome atlas).

   – In cytokine-primed RPE (e.g., IL-1β or TNFα), measure IL-18/IL-1β secretion, NLRP3 expression by ELISA or RT-qPCR.  Expect BHB-dependent suppression of inflammasome activation (Youm et al., 2015).  
4. Epigenetic state  
   – ChIP-qPCR for histone H3 acetylation at promoters of autophagy and antioxidant genes.  Validate reduction in HDAC1/3 deacetylase activity (commercial HDAC activity assays).

Strengths  
 • Dual-mode action: combines metabolic support with epigenetic upregulation of protective gene networks and anti-inflammatory signaling.

 • Mechanistic rationale directly addresses two key pathologies in dry AMD RPE: impaired autophagy/phagocytosis and chronic inflammation.  
 • Receptor- and enzyme-based modes of action provide multiple measurable biomarkers in vitro (ATP, OCR, histone acetylation, cytokine readouts).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.
