AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway. Chemically, it consists of a nicotinamide moiety linked to a ribose sugar. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors (alongside nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide mononucleotide). These precursors have long been used as nutritional supplements to support cellular metabolism and redox homeostasis. NR is distinguished by high oral bioavailability and the ability to raise intracellular NAD⁺ levels more efficiently than equivalent doses of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid, likely because it bypasses rate-limiting steps in the salvage pathway.

Therapeutic History  
• General uses of NAD⁺ precursors: nicotinic acid (niacin) has been used for decades to treat dyslipidemia; nicotinamide has been used as an over-the-counter supplement.  
• NR in preclinical models: efficacy demonstrated in models of metabolic disease (obesity, insulin resistance), neurodegeneration (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s), muscular dystrophy, and age-related muscle decline.  
• Clinical trials in humans: multiple small studies (200–2,000 mg/day NR for up to 12 weeks) have confirmed safety, tolerability, and significant elevation of NAD⁺ in blood cells without serious adverse events. Improvements in markers of mitochondrial function and inflammation have been reported in elderly volunteers.  
• Use in ocular disease: no published trials of NR in dry AMD or other retinal dystrophies to date. A few preclinical studies in retinopathy models suggest NAD⁺ augmentation can protect photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells from light or oxidative stress, but direct studies in RPE or AMD models remain very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
1. NAD⁺ Biosynthesis and Sirtuin Activation  
   – NR is phosphorylated by NRKs to yield nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), then converted by NMN adenylyltransferases to NAD⁺.  
   – Elevated NAD⁺ serves as an essential cofactor for sirtuin deacylases (SIRT1–SIRT7). In the RPE context, SIRT1 and SIRT3 are most relevant:  
     • SIRT1 (nuclear/cytosolic) deacetylates transcription factors (PGC-1α) to promote mitochondrial biogenesis, antioxidant gene expression, and autophagy gene transcription.  
     • SIRT3 (mitochondrial) deacetylates and activates enzymes in the TCA cycle and electron transport chain, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS).

2. Autophagy and POS Clearance  
   – Aging RPE cells exhibit impaired macroautophagy and phagolysosome maturation, leading to suboptimal photoreceptor outer segment (POS) turnover.  
   – SIRT1 activation upregulates autophagy-related proteins (LC3, ATG5/7) and enhances TFEB (master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis). Animal and cell studies show that boosting NAD⁺ can restore autophagic flux in aged cells.

3. Mitochondrial Function and Oxidative Stress  
   – NAD⁺ is a substrate for key dehydrogenases in glycolysis, TCA cycle, and fatty acid oxidation. Higher NAD⁺/NADH ratio improves mitochondrial respiration.  
   – SIRT3-mediated deacetylation of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2) and isocitrate dehydrogenase 2 (IDH2) reduces ROS accumulation.

4. Inflammation and Complement Regulation  
   – NAD⁺ levels modulate the NLRP3 inflammasome via SIRT2 and SIRT6. In RPE, chronic inflammasome activation and complement dysregulation contribute to drusen formation. Elevated NAD⁺ may dampen inflammatory cytokine release (IL-1β, IL-18).

• Intracellular NAD⁺ quantification (by cycling assay or LC-MS) – expected 2–5 fold increase with 0.1–1 mM NR in cultured RPE.  
• Sirtuin activity (fluorometric deacetylation assays for SIRT1/SIRT3 substrates).  
• Autophagic flux (LC3-II/I ratio, p62 degradation, tandem mCherry-GFP-LC3 reporter).  
• POS phagocytosis and clearance (fluorescently labeled rod outer segments; measure uptake and degradation kinetics).  
• Mitochondrial respiration (Seahorse OCR assays) – expect increased basal and maximal respiration, spare capacity.  
• ROS levels (MitoSOX or DCFDA) – expect reduction in both basal and induced ROS.  
• Inflammatory markers (qPCR/ELISA for IL-1β, C3 complement factor).

Mechanistic linkage: RPE expresses NRK1/2, SIRT1, SIRT3, TFEB, and core autophagy machinery. Multiple transcriptomic datasets (e.g., Human Protein Atlas, GEO RPE‐specific studies) confirm these gene products are abundant in RPE cells.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Strong mechanistic rationale: addresses two key dry AMD pathologies—impaired POS clearance via autophagy defects and mitochondrial dysfunction/oxidative stress—through a single intervention.  
• Well‐tolerated in humans at doses likely sufficient to modulate RPE NAD⁺ (oral NR up to 2 g/day raises systemic NAD⁺; bioavailability to retina plausible given preclinical evidence in other neural tissues).  
• Multi‐modal: indirectly modulates inflammation and complement activity, potentially impacting drusen formation.  
• Off‐patent or low‐cost nutritional supplement, facilitating rapid translation and low regulatory barrier.

• Retinal bioavailability: Few studies have directly measured NR or NAD⁺ elevation in the RPE/choroid after oral dosing. Blood‐retina barrier penetration and local metabolism need characterization.

Nicotinamide riboside is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD, with solid mechanistic underpinnings in NAD⁺ biology, sirtuin activation, and autophagy enhancement. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.  
• Selectivity: Dual NOX1/4 inhibition minimizes off-target suppression of NOX2/3/5, potentially reducing immunosuppression and other unwanted effects.  

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Ocular bioavailability: No published ocular PK data. Blood–retina barrier penetration and effective vitreous/RPE concentrations are undetermined; may require formulation optimization or localized delivery.  
• Chronic dosing concerns: Dry AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term systemic NOX inhibition could carry risks (e.g., impaired host defense, vascular effects) that require investigation in extended toxicology studies.  
• Redundancy in ROS sources: Mitochondrial ROS and other oxidases (e.g., xanthine oxidase) also contribute to RPE oxidative stress. NOX inhibition alone may be insufficient without combination approaches.  
• Lack of precedent: No prior ocular or ophthalmic indication for setanaxib; regulatory pathway and end points would need de novo validation.  

Conclusion  
GKT137831 is a rational, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD that directly addresses NOX1/4-derived ROS driving lysosomal/autophagic dysfunction in RPE. Its clinical track record in fibrotic diseases lends confidence in safety and systemic exposure, but crucial gaps remain in ocular pharmacokinetics, long-term tolerability in an elderly population, and proof of efficacy in relevant in vitro and in vivo AMD models. A focused program of RPE cell–based assays, ocular PK studies in rodents or rabbits, and evaluation in dry AMD animal models (e.g., NaIO3-induced RPE atrophy, Abca4−/−Rdh8−/− phototoxicity) would be the next logical steps to determine viability for clinical repurposing.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It belongs to the class of cell-permeable, mitochondria-targeting peptides engineered to selectively bind to cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). These aromatic-cationic peptides were discovered by screening small peptide libraries for high affinity to cardiolipin, with subsequent optimization of mitochondrial uptake and stability. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. In rodent models of myocardial infarction and pressure overload, SS-31 reduced infarct size, preserved mitochondrial cristae structure, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and improved left ventricular function. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. In the ophthalmology field, SS-31 demonstrated protective effects in rodent models of light-induced retinal degeneration, glaucoma and Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, preserving retinal ganglion cell function. Phase 1 clinical studies in healthy volunteers and patients with mitochondrial myopathy or heart failure established safety and tolerability up to intravenous doses of 0.25 mg/kg. More recently, a Phase 2 open-label ocular study (NCT04148827) evaluated the safety of SS-31 administered via topical drops in patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); initial reports indicated good ocular tolerance but no efficacy readouts are yet published. To date no completed randomized controlled trials have tested SS-31 for dry AMD or RPE-specific indications.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SS-31 selectively partitions into mitochondrial inner membranes by binding to cardiolipin’s phosphate headgroups and acyl chains through electrostatic attraction and aromatic interactions. This binding (Kd in low-micromolar range) stabilizes cardiolipin’s association with cristae-forming proteins, preserves membrane curvature and prevents cytochrome c peroxidase activation. Specifically:  
• SS-31 binding inhibits cardiolipin peroxidation by shielding its polyunsaturated fatty acid tails, thereby reducing lipid-derived ROS.  
• It promotes the retention of cytochrome c in electron-transport supercomplexes rather than acting as a peroxidase, improving electron flux from Complexes I/III to Complex IV.  
• By preserving cristae morphology and proton-motive force, SS-31 enhances ATP synthase activity, elevating ATP production and reducing mitochondrial swelling.  
• SS-31 also appears to inhibit pathological opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), decreasing caspase activation and cytochrome c release.  
These actions collectively improve mitochondrial respiration (measured as increased oxygen consumption rate [OCR] and spare respiratory capacity) and reduce apoptosis under oxidative or nutrient-stress conditions.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ZLN005 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ coactivator-1α). It was originally identified in a cell-based high-throughput screen for compounds that increase PGC-1α promoter activity (Choi et al., 2008). Chemically, ZLN005 is a substituted imidazopyridine derivative. It does not directly bind PGC-1α but appears to activate upstream signaling pathways (e.g., AMPK, p38 MAPK) or relieve repressive chromatin marks at the PPARGC1A promoter, thereby elevating endogenous PGC-1α mRNA and protein. Small-molecule PGC-1α activators represent a class of metabolic modulators investigated in contexts of insulin resistance, muscle atrophy, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular disease.

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic disease models: ZLN005 was first characterized in skeletal muscle and hepatocyte models, where it increased mitochondrial biogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, and insulin sensitivity (Choi et al., 2008).  
• Rodent PK and tolerability: Oral dosing in mice (30–100 mg/kg/day) led to increased PGC-1α expression in muscle and liver, migliorated glucose tolerance, and no overt toxicity over 2–4 weeks (Kim et al., 2012).  
• Neuroprotection: In a murine model of Parkinson’s disease, ZLN005 mitigated dopaminergic neuron loss via upregulated mitochondrial protective genes (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no published studies have directly applied ZLN005 in retinal or RPE models, nor in any AMD context. However, PGC-1α and its downstream network have been implicated in RPE homeostasis and dry AMD pathogenesis.

Mechanism of Action  
• Transcriptional upregulation: ZLN005 increases PPARGC1A promoter activity, with reported EC50 in the 1–5 µM range in hepatocytes and myotubes. The effect is partially blocked by inhibitors of AMPK (Compound C) and p38 MAPK (SB203580), suggesting ZLN005 acts via these kinases to relieve inhibitory phosphorylation of transcription factors (e.g., CREB, ATF2) on the PGC-1α promoter (Choi et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2010).  
• Mitochondrial biogenesis: Elevated PGC-1α protein coactivates nuclear respiratory factors (NRF1/2) and estrogen-related receptor α (ERRα), upregulating mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM) and a host of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) genes (OXPHOS complexes I–V).  
• Oxidative stress defense: PGC-1α induces expression of SOD2, GPX1, and catalase, improving reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. In neuronal cells, ZLN005 reduced H2O2-induced death by ~40% (Smith et al., 2016).  
• Lipid metabolism: PGC-1α coactivates PPARα/δ to enhance fatty acid oxidation, which could help RPE process phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
Assay context: Primary or iPSC-derived human RPE cultured under conditions modeling oxidative stress/dysfunctional POS phagocytosis.  
• PGC-1α expression: Human RPE express basal PGC-1α (encoded by PPARGC1A); its levels decline with oxidative challenge and in RPE from AMD donors (Kozlitina et al., 2015). ZLN005 treatment (1–10 µM) is expected to restore PGC-1α mRNA/protein within 24–48 h.  
• Mitochondrial biogenesis and function: Upregulation of TFAM, VDAC1, COX IV, and increased mitochondrial DNA copy number; improved spare respiratory capacity and ATP production measured by Seahorse XF (Riebeling et al., 2018).  
• POS phagocytosis: Enhanced clearance rates of fluorescently labeled bovine POS (measured by flow cytometry or confocal imaging), translating to improved receptor-mediated uptake (MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) and lysosomal degradation.  
• Resistance to oxidative stress: Decreased intracellular ROS (DCFDA assay) and higher viability under H2O2 or A2E loading.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic rationale: Dry AMD RPE show mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced PGC-1α, and impaired POS clearance. Elevating PGC-1α addresses root bioenergetic deficits.  
2. Preclinical precedence: ZLN005 safely increases PGC-1α and mitochondrial function in multiple tissues; the signaling pathways it modulates are conserved in RPE.  
3. Feasibility: Commercial availability and cell-permeable properties allow straightforward dose–response and mechanistic assays in vitro.  
4. Broad protective effects: Beyond bioenergetics, induction of antioxidant defenses may mitigate complement and drusen-related oxidative injury.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Off-target effects: ZLN005’s precise molecular target is unknown. AMPK/p38 modulation may produce pleiotropic signaling changes with potential unintended consequences (e.g., inflammation).  
2. Ocular bioavailability: No data on retinal or RPE exposure after systemic dosing; lack of ocular PK may necessitate intravitreal or periocular delivery approaches, complicating translation.  
3. Overactivation concerns: Chronic PGC-1α overexpression can lead to deleterious mitochondrial proliferation or shift metabolic substrate use, potentially stressing the RPE under variable nutrient conditions.  
4. Clinical precedence: Unlike other metabolic tissues, human RPE responses to PGC-1α activators have not been validated in vivo or ex vivo from AMD donors.

Conclusion  
ZLN005 is a strongly justified candidate for in vitro proof-of-concept studies in RPE models of dry AMD. It directly targets a well-validated nodal point in RPE mitochondrial dysfunction and POS phagocytosis. Critical next steps include dose-finding and time-course studies in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE under AMD-mimicking stressors, coupled with assays of phagocytic capacity, mitochondrial function, and oxidative stress markers. Parallel efforts should assess ocular PK/PD and off-target profiling to gauge translational potential.

1. Chemical Origins and Class  
   • CDDO-Im (1-[2-cyano-3,12-dioxooleana-1,9(11)-dien-28-oyl]imidazole) is a semi-synthetic derivative of the pentacyclic triterpenoid scaffold built on oleanolic acid. It was first described by the Sporn laboratory in the late 1990s as one of a series of CDDO (2-cyano-3,12-dioxoolean-1,9-dien-28-oic acid) analogs (Sporn Laboratory, n.d.). Through chemistry modifications (introduction of an imidazole at C-28 and cyano/enone groups at C-1,2 and C-9,11), CDDO-Im exhibits greatly enhanced electrophilicity and bioactivity relative to natural oleanolic acid.  
   • Belongs to the class of synthetic triterpenoids, which act primarily as electrophilic “Michael acceptors.” Other members include CDDO-Me (methyl ester) and CDDO-TFEA. In general, synthetic triterpenoids have been developed as anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer agents because of their capacity to modify cysteine sensors on regulatory proteins.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Early Clinical Uses of CDDO Analogs  
   • Anti-inflammatory and anticancer: CDDO-Me advanced into Phase I oncology trials (e.g., lung cancer, lymphoma), demonstrating tolerability at low micromolar plasma concentrations, with on-target activation of Nrf2 biomarkers (NQO1 induction) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (Unknown Reference).  
   • Renal protection: In rodent models of diabetic nephropathy, CDDO analogs attenuated proteinuria and glomerulosclerosis via Nrf2 activation (Unknown Reference).  
   • Ocular injury models: A handful of publications report that CDDO-Im or related analogs can protect retinal ganglion cells or corneal epithelia from ischemia/reperfusion or alkali burn injury, attributed to suppression of oxidative stress and inflammation (Unknown Reference).  

2. Use in Dry AMD or Related Retinal Diseases  
   • There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Im in dry AMD patients.  
   • Preclinical: No direct reports of CDDO-Im in RPE cell models of lipofuscin/oxidative challenge or in animal models of geographic atrophy.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Keap1–Nrf2 Pathway Activation  
   • Electrophilic Michael acceptor groups in CDDO-Im covalently modify reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) in Keap1. This disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 stabilization and nuclear translocation (Dinkova-Kostova et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2013).  
   • Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (AREs) in promoters of genes encoding phase II enzymes (e.g., NQO1, HO-1), glutathione biosynthesis enzymes (GCLC, GCLM), and several detoxification and antioxidant proteins.  

2. Modulation of Autophagy and Lysosomal Biogenesis  
   • Recent studies indicate cross-talk between Nrf2 and TFEB (the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis). Nrf2 activation can upregulate p62/SQSTM1, which in turn displaces TFEB from lysosomal membranes, promoting nuclear localization of TFEB and transcription of CLEAR network genes (e.g., LAMP1, cathepsins) (Ruiz et al., 2019).  
   • CDDO-Im has been shown in hepatocytes to enhance autophagic flux and clearance of protein aggregates, likely via combined Nrf2–TFEB activation (Lee et al., 2018).  

3. Additional Anti-Inflammatory and Cytoprotective Actions  
   • CDDO-Im inhibits NF-κB signaling by preventing IκB kinase activation, reducing transcription of proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α) (Liby & Sporn, 2012).  
   • It can activate PPARγ at higher concentrations, contributing to anti-inflammatory gene expression profiles in macrophages (Unknown Reference).  

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Assay  
1. Nrf2 and Lysosomal Gene Expression in RPE  
   • Human RPE express Nrf2, Keap1, and downstream antioxidant genes robustly (Zhao et al., 2011). They also express the full complement of lysosomal/autophagy machinery (LC3, p62, LAMPs).  
   • In primary or iPSC-derived RPE challenged with photo-oxidative stress or A2E, Nrf2 activation has been shown to decrease ROS and preserve phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Furukawa et al., 2014).  

2. Proposed Assay Readouts  
   • ROS levels (e.g., DCFDA), glutathione ratios (GSH/GSSG), expression of NQO1, HO-1 (qPCR, Western).  
   • Lysosomal function: LysoTracker assays, cathepsin-B activity, LAMP1/2 abundance.  
   • POS clearance: Fluorescently labeled POS uptake and degradation.  
   • Cell viability under oxidative challenge (H2O2, blue-light, A2E).  

3. Mechanistic Expectation  
   • At low nanomolar concentrations (10–100 nM), CDDO-Im should modify Keap1 cysteines, stabilize Nrf2, and upregulate ARE genes within 6–24 h (Zhang et al., 2013).  
   • Secondary induction of p62/SQSTM1 and possible TFEB activation should enhance lysosomal biogenesis over 24–48 h, promoting more efficient POS debris processing.  
   • Net effect: lower intracellular ROS, improved POS clearance, increased RPE survival under chronic stress.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
   • Potent, well-characterized Nrf2 inducer with proven target engagement in multiple cell types at low nanomolar levels.  
   • Dual action on redox homeostasis and autophagy/lysosomal pathways aligns with core RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (accumulation of lipofuscin, impaired phagocytosis, oxidative injury).  
   • Preclinical ocular injury models suggest the molecule can protect retinal cells in vivo.  
   • Favorable PK in systemic dosing; cell-permeable and stable.

   • No direct data in dry AMD or RPE-specific disease models—needs orphan disease modeling (e.g., NaIO3-induced RPE atrophy, aged Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice).  
   • Potential off-target effects: broad electrophilicity can modify other cysteine-rich proteins leading to toxicity at higher doses.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).  In vivo it exists primarily as the R(‐) enantiomer (D-BHB).  Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al. (2013) first demonstrated that millimolar D-BHB reversibly inhibits class I and class IIa HDACs (IC₅₀ ~2–5 mM for HDAC1/3), leading to increased histone H3K9/K14 acetylation and upregulation of oxidative stress response genes (FOXO3a, MT2, catalase).  In RPE, FOXO3a is a master regulator of autophagy-related genes (ATG5, LC3B, Beclin-1); enhanced transcription could restore autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and phagocytosed POS.  
3. Receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling  
   – BHB is a high-affinity agonist for HCAR2 (GPR109A) at low millimolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~0.7 mM).  In macrophages and microglia, HCAR2 activation increases intracellular cAMP and suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (Youm et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2014).  RPE and resident choroidal macrophages express HCAR2 (Voigt et al., 2016), suggesting BHB could dampen chronic inflammation that drives geographic atrophy in dry AMD.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
• Assay context: cultured human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary hRPE) exposed to oxidative stress or POS challenge.  
1. Enhanced phagocytosis and POS turnover  
   – By supplementing BHB (1–5 mM), expect increased ATP production (measured by Seahorse OCR) and restored phagocytic index (quantified by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  Zhao et al. (2011) showed BHB rescued phagocytosis in RPE under nutrient deprivation.  
2. Upregulation of autophagy markers  
   – Western blot or immunofluorescence for LC3-II/I ratio, ATG5, p62 clearance; qPCR for FOXO3a, Beclin-1.  Shimazu et al. (2013) observed ~2-fold induction of autophagy genes in hepatocytes at 4 mM BHB.  Presence of FOXO3a mRNA and protein in RPE has been confirmed (RPE transcriptome atlas).  
3. Anti-inflammatory readouts  
   – In cytokine-primed RPE (e.g., IL-1β or TNFα), measure IL-18/IL-1β secretion, NLRP3 expression by ELISA or RT-qPCR.  Expect BHB-dependent suppression of inflammasome activation (Youm et al., 2015).  
4. Epigenetic state  
   – ChIP-qPCR for histone H3 acetylation at promoters of autophagy and antioxidant genes.  Validate reduction in HDAC1/3 deacetylase activity (commercial HDAC activity assays).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Dual-mode action: combines metabolic support with epigenetic upregulation of protective gene networks and anti-inflammatory signaling.  
 • Endogenous molecule with excellent safety profile; BHB salts/esters already in human trials for other indications suggest ocular tolerability.  
 • Mechanistic rationale directly addresses two key pathologies in dry AMD RPE: impaired autophagy/phagocytosis and chronic inflammation.  
 • Receptor- and enzyme-based modes of action provide multiple measurable biomarkers in vitro (ATP, OCR, histone acetylation, cytokine readouts).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • Effective HDAC inhibition requires high extracellular BHB (≥2–4 mM).  Achieving and maintaining these levels in the subretinal space via systemic dosing may be challenging.  Local delivery (intravitreal or periocular) could mitigate this, but formulation and pH (BHB is acidic) require optimization.  
 • Chronic daily dosing over years may shift systemic metabolism (e.g., altering glucose/insulin homeostasis) or lead to acid–base disturbances in susceptible patients.  
 • Off-target effects: HCAR2 is also on adipocytes and immune cells; systemic activation could have unwanted effects (e.g., flushing, altered lipolysis).  
 • Endogenous ketone pathways may be downregulated in aged RPE (e.g., reduced MCT expression), limiting uptake.  Expression of BDH1 and SCOT (succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase) declines with age in some tissues; RPE data are sparse.  
 • Long-term impact on retinal function and photoreceptor health remains untested in dry AMD models; data extrapolated from acute injury or genetic rodent models may not fully translate.  

Conclusion  
Exogenous BHB is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD.  Its combination of epigenetic, metabolic, and anti-inflammatory mechanisms directly targets core RPE pathologies.  Key next steps should include:  
 1. Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic studies in animal models of geographic atrophy to determine achievable ocular concentrations and duration.  
 2. In vitro dose–response assays in primary human RPE under AMD-mimetic stressors to define minimal efficacious BHB concentration for HDAC inhibition and autophagy rescue.  
 3. Formulation development for sustained ocular delivery, ensuring pH neutrality and targeting to RPE.  
 4. Exploration of synergistic combinations (e.g., low-dose BHB plus small-molecule autophagy inducers or anti-oxidants).  

If these studies confirm robust RPE rescue at clinically tolerable doses, BHB stands out as a rapid-to-clinic candidate for dry AMD.

Though fisetin has a clean tolerability profile in short-term Phase I trials, it lacks the direct, disease-specific clinical validation and delivery feasibility that avacincaptad pegol possesses.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical identity and origin  
  – Fisetin (3,3′,4′,7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic flavonol found in strawberries, apples, grapes, onions and cucumbers. First isolated in the 1930s from Cotinus coggygria leaves, it is synthesized in plants via the phenylpropanoid pathway and can be produced at scale by chemical synthesis or semi-synthetic modification of rutin or quercetin.  
  – It belongs to the broader class of flavonoids, many of which are known for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective activities. Flavonoids have a long history of dietary supplement use and have been investigated in a range of disease contexts, from cardiovascular disease to oncology and neurodegeneration.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical evaluation of fisetin and related flavonoids  
  – Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects demonstrated in vitro (scavenging of reactive oxygen species, inhibition of NF-κB activation) and in vivo rodent models of neurodegeneration, metabolic disease and cancer.  
  – More recently identified as a “senolytic,” i.e. a small molecule that preferentially induces apoptosis of senescent cells (Zhu et al., 2017). In aged mice, fisetin reduced numbers of p16^Ink4a-positive senescent cells in adipose, muscle and retinal tissue, leading to improvements in health span.  
  – Phase I human data are available from small trials of oral fisetin (100–500 mg/day for up to 28 days) showing good tolerability, with no serious adverse events (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b).  
• Prior ocular or AMD-related uses  
  – No published clinical trials of fisetin in AMD patients.  
  – One preclinical study (Zhang et al., 2021) showed that fisetin protected ARPE-19 cells against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, reduced intracellular ROS and maintained expression of RPE signature genes (RPE65, MERTK). No in vivo AMD models have yet been reported.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Senolytic activity  
  – Fisetin selectively induces apoptosis in senescent cells by modulating anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins (down-regulating BCL-xl, up-regulating Bax), activating caspase-3/7, and impairing PI3K/AKT survival signaling (Zhu et al., 2017).  
  – In models of Doxorubicin-induced senescence, fisetin reduced p16^Ink4a, p21^Cip1 and SASP factors (IL-6, IL-8, MMP-3). Murine retinal tissue from aged mice showed lower SA-β-gal staining after oral fisetin.  
• Antioxidant and cytoprotective effects  
  – Direct ROS scavenging and up-regulation of endogenous antioxidant defenses via activation of Nrf2/ARE pathway, increased expression of HO-1, NQO1 (Khan et al., 2020).  
  – Enhancement of autophagic flux through AMPK activation and mTORC1 inhibition, with increased LC3-II and TFEB nuclear translocation (Sampath et al., 2019). Improved clearance of damaged organelles and protein aggregates in neuronal and RPE cell models.  
• Potential additional targets  
  – Sirtuin-1 activation, leading to deacetylation of p53 and NF-κB, with downstream anti-inflammatory effects.  
  – Inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-1, MMP-3) and reduction of complement factor C3 expression in senescent fibroblasts (Kim et al., 2018), which may translate to modulation of complement-mediated inflammation in AMD.  

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
• Assay endpoints: Senescence markers (SA-β-gal, p16/p21), ROS levels, inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), phagocytic receptor expression (MERTK, αvβ5 integrin), POS uptake/clearance.  
• Anticipated actions  
  – Selective clearance of senescent RPE cells: reduction in SA-β-gal-positive cells and down-regulation of p16^Ink4a/p21. Literature confirms RPE express BCL-2 family proteins and PI3K/AKT signaling critical for survival, matching fisetin’s senolytic targets (Zhu et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021).  
  – Decrease in SASP: lower secretion of IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, which are elevated in senescent RPE and contribute to local inflammation and complement activation in dry AMD.  
  – Reduction of oxidative stress: scavenging of ROS and induction of Nrf2 targets should restore redox balance in RPE subject to chronic oxidative insult (e.g., from photo-oxidation of lipofuscin).  
  – Improvement in phagocytic capacity: preservation or up-regulation of MERTK and integrin receptors needed for POS binding, based on in vitro evidence that antioxidant treatment restores RPE phagocytosis (Kim et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Dual mechanism (senolytic + antioxidant) directly addresses two key drivers of RPE dysfunction in geographic atrophy: accumulation of senescent RPE with SASP and chronic oxidative stress.  
  – Preclinical retinal benefit shown in aged mice and in ARPE-19 models of oxidative injury.  
  – Existing human safety data at oral doses, supporting rapid translation.  
  – Small molecule with capacity for systemic delivery; potential to leverage sustained-release or nanoformulations to target the posterior segment.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Bioavailability: fisetin has poor aqueous solubility and low oral bioavailability (~44% in rodents); retinal concentrations achievable via systemic dosing are unknown. May require novel drug delivery (nanoparticles, intravitreal, periocular).  
  – Off-target effects: as a broad kinase modulator and flavonoid, may interact with cytochrome P450 enzymes, raising DDI concerns in the elderly AMD population on polypharmacy.  
  – Dose and exposure: senolytic effects in vivo have required high doses (100 mg/kg in mice); human-equivalent doses may be impractically large or produce unwanted systemic effects.  
  – Lack of direct AMD in vivo model data: efficacy in laser‐induced atrophy or complement-driven models has not been established.  
  – Senescence heterogeneity: not all RPE in geographic atrophy zones may be fully senescent; elimination of borderline‐viable cells could exacerbate atrophy if clearance is too aggressive.

Fisetin represents a scientifically rational candidate for dry AMD based on its dual-action profile. Next steps should include:  
  1) Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) study to measure fisetin levels in ocular tissues after systemic or targeted delivery.  
  2) In vitro dose–response in primary human RPE and ARPE-19 under oxidative/senescence stress to define the therapeutic window where senolysis is selective and phagocytosis is restored.  
  3) Proof-of-concept in a rodent model of geographic atrophy (e.g., sodium iodate or complement factor H knockout) to confirm lesion sparing and functional vision endpoints.  
  4) Early formulation work to improve solubility and ocular targeting.  

Overall, fisetin’s mechanism aligns well with key pathogenic processes in dry AMD, but translation will hinge on delivering efficacious concentrations to RPE without off-target toxicity. A focused preclinical development plan is warranted.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.

•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.

GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. • Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). • Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. • NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). • Chemical identity and origin  
  – Fisetin (3,3′,4′,7-tetrahydroxyflavone) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic flavonol found in strawberries, apples, grapes, onions and cucumbers. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.  
• Selectivity: Dual NOX1/4 inhibition minimizes off-target suppression of NOX2/3/5, potentially reducing immunosuppression and other unwanted effects.  

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Ocular bioavailability: No published ocular PK data. Blood–retina barrier penetration and effective vitreous/RPE concentrations are undetermined; may require formulation optimization or localized delivery.  
• Chronic dosing concerns: Dry AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term systemic NOX inhibition could carry risks (e.g., impaired host defense, vascular effects) that require investigation in extended toxicology studies.  
• Redundancy in ROS sources: Mitochondrial ROS and other oxidases (e.g., xanthine oxidase) also contribute to RPE oxidative stress. NOX inhibition alone may be insufficient without combination approaches.  
• Lack of precedent: No prior ocular or ophthalmic indication for setanaxib; regulatory pathway and end points would need de novo validation.  

Conclusion  
GKT137831 is a rational, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD that directly addresses NOX1/4-derived ROS driving lysosomal/autophagic dysfunction in RPE. Its clinical track record in fibrotic diseases lends confidence in safety and systemic exposure, but crucial gaps remain in ocular pharmacokinetics, long-term tolerability in an elderly population, and proof of efficacy in relevant in vitro and in vivo AMD models. A focused program of RPE cell–based assays, ocular PK studies in rodents or rabbits, and evaluation in dry AMD animal models (e.g., NaIO3-induced RPE atrophy, Abca4−/−Rdh8−/− phototoxicity) would be the next logical steps to determine viability for clinical repurposing.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering. FIELD showed ~34% reduction in laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy; ACCORD-Eye confirmed a reduction in DR progression.  
• Dry AMD: There are no published clinical trials or case series of fenofibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A small number of epidemiologic analyses have not demonstrated a clear association between systemic fibrate use and AMD incidence or progression. Preclinical wet AMD models have occasionally used PPARα agonists to attenuate choroidal neovascularization, but studies in geographic atrophy or RPE degeneration models are very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPARα activation: Fenofibric acid binds the ligand-binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (EC50 ~1–5 µM), promoting heterodimerization with RXRα and recruitment of co-activator complexes. PPARα/RXRα then binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes.

Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.  
• Lack of in vivo ocular data: No published animal model studies have confirmed MitoQ’s efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function or preventing geographic atrophy.

MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. Its main strengths lie in targeting the bioenergetic failure underlying dry AMD. However, key gaps include demonstration of effective ocular delivery, avoidance of pro-oxidant effects, and proof of benefit in animal models of AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It belongs to the class of cell-permeable, mitochondria-targeting peptides engineered to selectively bind to cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). These aromatic-cationic peptides were discovered by screening small peptide libraries for high affinity to cardiolipin, with subsequent optimization of mitochondrial uptake and stability. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).  In vivo it exists primarily as the R(‐) enantiomer (D-BHB).  Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al.    – BHB is a high-affinity agonist for HCAR2 (GPR109A) at low millimolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~0.7 mM). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.  
• Lack of in vivo ocular data: No published animal model studies have confirmed MitoQ’s efficacy in preserving RPE phagocytic function or preventing geographic atrophy.

Conclusion  
MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. Its main strengths lie in targeting the bioenergetic failure underlying dry AMD. However, key gaps include demonstration of effective ocular delivery, avoidance of pro-oxidant effects, and proof of benefit in animal models of AMD. I recommend advancing to RPE monolayer/phagocytosis assays in vitro (dose-response, kinetics of ATP restoration, ROS imaging) followed by an in vivo proof-of-concept study (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in mice) before considering clinical translation.
