Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.  
  • Unknown ocular pharmacokinetics: blood–retinal barrier penetration, vitreous half-life, and RPE bioavailability must be characterized.  
  • Potential for systemic or local immunomodulatory effects, given HDAC6’s role in cytokine regulation (Rivieccio et al., 2009).  
  • Hydroxamate warhead may carry risk of off-target zinc metalloprotease inhibition at high concentrations.  

Conclusion  
Tubastatin A presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-driven candidate for preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Critical next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, in vivo efficacy in rodent or porcine AMD models, and assay optimization to quantify dose–response in primary or iPSC-derived RPE. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of Zn²⁺‐dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs). Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). – C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy: Early-phase studies demonstrated reduced glomerular C3 deposition and improved proteinuria.

Mechanism of Action  
– Molecular target: Factor B is the serine protease zymogen that, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba (regulatory fragment) and Bb (catalytic subunit). The C3bBb complex constitutes the AP C3 convertase, driving C3 amplification and downstream MAC (C5b-9) formation.

• Mechanistic alignment with AMD genetics: FB inhibition directly targets the overactive AP amplification loop implicated by CFH, CFB, and C3 risk variants.

Iptacopan is mechanistically compelling for dry AMD due to its targeted blockade of the AP amplification loop, favorable systemic safety, and robust preclinical efficacy in other complement-driven diseases. Ambroxol (trans-4-[(2-amino-3,5-dibromobenzyl)amino]cyclohexanol) is a small-molecule mucolytic originally synthesized in the 1970s as an active metabolite of bromhexine. Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al. (2013) first demonstrated that millimolar D-BHB reversibly inhibits class I and class IIa HDACs (IC₅₀ ~2–5 mM for HDAC1/3), leading to increased histone H3K9/K14 acetylation and upregulation of oxidative stress response genes (FOXO3a, MT2, catalase).  In RPE, FOXO3a is a master regulator of autophagy-related genes (ATG5, LC3B, Beclin-1); enhanced transcription could restore autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and phagocytosed POS.  
3. Receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling  
   – BHB is a high-affinity agonist for HCAR2 (GPR109A) at low millimolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~0.7 mM).  In macrophages and microglia, HCAR2 activation increases intracellular cAMP and suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (Youm et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2014).  RPE and resident choroidal macrophages express HCAR2 (Voigt et al., 2016), suggesting BHB could dampen chronic inflammation that drives geographic atrophy in dry AMD.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant Assay  
• Assay context: cultured human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary hRPE) exposed to oxidative stress or POS challenge.  
1. Enhanced phagocytosis and POS turnover  
   – By supplementing BHB (1–5 mM), expect increased ATP production (measured by Seahorse OCR) and restored phagocytic index (quantified by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  Zhao et al. (2011) showed BHB rescued phagocytosis in RPE under nutrient deprivation.  
2. Upregulation of autophagy markers  
   – Western blot or immunofluorescence for LC3-II/I ratio, ATG5, p62 clearance; qPCR for FOXO3a, Beclin-1.  Shimazu et al. (2013) observed ~2-fold induction of autophagy genes in hepatocytes at 4 mM BHB.  Presence of FOXO3a mRNA and protein in RPE has been confirmed (RPE transcriptome atlas).  
3. Anti-inflammatory readouts  
   – In cytokine-primed RPE (e.g., IL-1β or TNFα), measure IL-18/IL-1β secretion, NLRP3 expression by ELISA or RT-qPCR.  Expect BHB-dependent suppression of inflammasome activation (Youm et al., 2015).  
4. Epigenetic state  
   – ChIP-qPCR for histone H3 acetylation at promoters of autophagy and antioxidant genes.  Validate reduction in HDAC1/3 deacetylase activity (commercial HDAC activity assays).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Dual-mode action: combines metabolic support with epigenetic upregulation of protective gene networks and anti-inflammatory signaling.  
 • Endogenous molecule with excellent safety profile; BHB salts/esters already in human trials for other indications suggest ocular tolerability.  
 • Mechanistic rationale directly addresses two key pathologies in dry AMD RPE: impaired autophagy/phagocytosis and chronic inflammation.  
 • Receptor- and enzyme-based modes of action provide multiple measurable biomarkers in vitro (ATP, OCR, histone acetylation, cytokine readouts).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • Effective HDAC inhibition requires high extracellular BHB (≥2–4 mM).  Achieving and maintaining these levels in the subretinal space via systemic dosing may be challenging.  Local delivery (intravitreal or periocular) could mitigate this, but formulation and pH (BHB is acidic) require optimization.  
 • Chronic daily dosing over years may shift systemic metabolism (e.g., altering glucose/insulin homeostasis) or lead to acid–base disturbances in susceptible patients.  
 • Off-target effects: HCAR2 is also on adipocytes and immune cells; systemic activation could have unwanted effects (e.g., flushing, altered lipolysis).  
 • Endogenous ketone pathways may be downregulated in aged RPE (e.g., reduced MCT expression), limiting uptake.  Expression of BDH1 and SCOT (succinyl-CoA:3-oxoacid CoA transferase) declines with age in some tissues; RPE data are sparse.  
 • Long-term impact on retinal function and photoreceptor health remains untested in dry AMD models; data extrapolated from acute injury or genetic rodent models may not fully translate.  

Conclusion  
Exogenous BHB is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD.  Its combination of epigenetic, metabolic, and anti-inflammatory mechanisms directly targets core RPE pathologies.  Key next steps should include:  
 1. Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic studies in animal models of geographic atrophy to determine achievable ocular concentrations and duration.  
 2. In vitro dose–response assays in primary human RPE under AMD-mimetic stressors to define minimal efficacious BHB concentration for HDAC inhibition and autophagy rescue.  
 3. Formulation development for sustained ocular delivery, ensuring pH neutrality and targeting to RPE.  
 4. Exploration of synergistic combinations (e.g., low-dose BHB plus small-molecule autophagy inducers or anti-oxidants).  

If these studies confirm robust RPE rescue at clinically tolerable doses, BHB stands out as a rapid-to-clinic candidate for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.  
  • Unknown ocular pharmacokinetics: blood–retinal barrier penetration, vitreous half-life, and RPE bioavailability must be characterized.  
  • Potential for systemic or local immunomodulatory effects, given HDAC6’s role in cytokine regulation (Rivieccio et al., 2009).  
  • Hydroxamate warhead may carry risk of off-target zinc metalloprotease inhibition at high concentrations.  

Conclusion  
Tubastatin A presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-driven candidate for preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Critical next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, in vivo efficacy in rodent or porcine AMD models, and assay optimization to quantify dose–response in primary or iPSC-derived RPE. If these studies demonstrate robust POS clearance and safety in ocular tissues, Tubastatin A warrants advancement as a lead for dry AMD therapeutic development.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ambroxol (trans-4-[(2-amino-3,5-dibromobenzyl)amino]cyclohexanol) is a small-molecule mucolytic originally synthesized in the 1970s as an active metabolite of bromhexine. Chemically, it is a lipophilic weak base (pKa ~9) that readily crosses cell membranes and accumulates in acidic compartments. Ambroxol belongs to the class of pharmacological chaperones for lysosomal enzymes: small compounds that bind and stabilize mutant or labile enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum, promoting proper folding and trafficking to the lysosome. Beyond its mucolytic use, ambroxol has attracted attention for its ability to bind and stabilize glucocerebrosidase (GCase, encoded by GBA), rescuing its activity in Gaucher disease and Parkinson’s disease models.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Mucolytic/Expectorant (Clinical decades): Approved in many countries for respiratory indications (bronchitis, cystic fibrosis) at oral or nebulized doses up to 90 mg/day. Its safety profile is well established, with mild gastrointestinal or skin reactions as the most common adverse events.  
2. Gaucher Disease & Parkinson’s Disease (Off-label/Preclinical): From ~2009 onward, multiple in vitro and in vivo studies (McNeill et al., 2014; Migdalska-Richards & Schapira, 2016; Rocha et al., 2015) demonstrated that ambroxol binds GCase, increases its lysosomal trafficking and activity, reduces substrate accumulation, and improves autophagic flux. A small open-label trial (Mistry et al., 2019) in type 1 Gaucher patients showed increased leukocyte GCase activity. Early Parkinson’s trials are ongoing.  
3. Use in Ophthalmology: No published studies to date have tested ambroxol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or any primary retinal disease. However, tissue distribution models and animal PK studies indicate that systemically administered ambroxol reaches the retina and vitreous at pharmacologically relevant concentrations (≤1–10 µM), warranting exploration in retinal degenerations characterized by lysosomal dysfunction.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Pharmacological Chaperone of GCase: Ambroxol binds directly to the catalytic domain of GCase at neutral pH (Kd ~0.5–5 µM), stabilizing its folding in the endoplasmic reticulum (Sawkar et al., 2006; Maegawa et al., 2009). This facilitates ER exit and trafficking via the mannose-6-phosphate receptor pathway to the late endosome/lysosome.  
2. Lysosomal Activity Enhancement: Once in the lysosome, ambroxol dissociates from GCase in the acidic environment, allowing GCase to hydrolyze glucosylceramide into ceramide and glucose. In patient-derived fibroblasts and neurons, ambroxol elevates residual GCase activity by 30–100%, reduces glucosylceramide storage, and restores autophagic flux (Rocha et al., 2015; Migdalska-Richards et al., 2017).  
3. Lysosomal Biogenesis and Acidification: Several studies (Song et al., 2013; Parenti et al., 2014) report that ambroxol upregulates TFEB (transcription factor EB), the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, leading to increased expression of lysosomal proteins (e.g., LAMP1, cathepsin D) and enhanced lysosomal acidification.  
4. Anti-Inflammatory and Anti-Oxidative Effects: In respiratory models ambroxol suppresses NF-κB activation and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α), scavenges ROS, and stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential—effects that may be relevant in the RPE under chronic oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2012).

1. GCase in RPE: Public transcriptome and proteome datasets (Zhao et al., 2011; Whitmore et al., 2015) confirm robust expression of GBA and GCase protein in RPE, localizing to LAMP1+ lysosomes.  
2. Hypothesis Testing: Ambroxol (1–10 µM) pretreatment should increase GCase activity (measured by 4-MUG substrate assay) and enhance co-localization of POS markers (rhodopsin) with lysosomal markers (LAMP1/CTSD) at early time points (2–6 h), reduce accumulation of POS-derived autofluorescent lipofuscin bisretinoids (A2E) at 48 h, and increase cathepsin D and LC3-II turnover as readouts of improved autophagic flux.  
3. Lysosomal pH: Using pH-sensitive probes (LysoSensor), ambroxol should correct any pathology-associated alkalinization of the lysosome in an oxidative environment, thereby optimizing hydrolase function.  
4. Downstream Readouts: Reduced reactive oxygen species (DCFDA), decreased secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8), and preserved mitochondrial potential (JC-1) in RPE under chronic POS challenge.

• Mechanistic Rationale: Lysosomal dysfunction and impaired POS degradation are core features in dry AMD pathology (Mitter et al., 2014; Kaemmerer et al., 2017). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. It was discovered by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) against human complement component 5 (C5) and subsequently optimized for high-affinity binding (Kd ~70 pM) and nuclease resistance. Aptamers are single-stranded oligonucleotides that fold into three-dimensional structures to bind specific protein targets; pegylated RNA aptamers have precedent in ophthalmology (e.g., pegaptanib for VEGF in wet AMD).

Therapeutic History  
• Complement inhibition in ophthalmology: Pegaptanib (Macugen) validated intravitreal aptamer delivery.  
• Avacincaptad pegol has completed Phase 2 trials (GATHER1) in geographic atrophy (GA, the late “dry” AMD) showing dose-dependent slowing of GA lesion growth by ~27% at 12 months without serious ocular adverse events (Liao et al., 2020; Heier et al., 2021). GATHER2 (Phase 3) is ongoing.  
• No prior veterinary uses. No reports of avacincaptad pegol outside GA. Other systemic C5 inhibitors (eculizumab) treat paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome but have not shown efficacy in AMD when dosed systemically, likely due to poor ocular penetration.

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement: Avacincaptad pegol binds the β-chain of C5, sterically preventing C5 convertase from cleaving C5 into C5a and C5b (Fielder et al., 2018).  
• Downstream effects:  
  – Inhibition of C5a generation abrogates C5a-mediated activation of C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1/CD88) on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells and resident microglia, thus reducing NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Anderson et al., 2013; Doyle et al., 2012).  
  – Blockade of C5b prevents assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9), reducing sublytic MAC deposition on RPE that otherwise disrupts lysosomal membrane integrity and impairs phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Kariko et al., 2013).  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express C5R1 (RNA-seq data, Kalliora et al., 2018) and are susceptible to complement-mediated inflammasome activation when exposed to drusen components or oxidized POS in vitro (Zhou et al., 2018).

Expected Effect in RPE/POS Phagocytosis Assay  
In an in vitro assay in which human RPE cells are challenged with photo-oxidized POS or drusen-like material:  
• Complement activation normally drives C5a release, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (caspase-1 cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 secretion), and sublytic MAC deposition on RPE, elevating lysosomal pH and inhibiting cathepsin D–dependent POS degradation (Zhou et al., 2018; Kariko et al., 2013).  
• Addition of avacincaptad pegol to conditioned medium should neutralize nascent C5, abolishing C5a-mediated pro-inflammatory signaling and preventing MAC formation.  
• Predicted readouts:  
  – Reduced IL-1β and IL-18 in supernatant (ELISA).  
  – Lower levels of MAC deposition on RPE (immunofluorescence for C5b-9).  
  – Normalized lysosomal pH (LysoSensor assays) and cathepsin D activity.  
  – Improved POS uptake and degradation (fluorescent POS co-localizing with LAMP1+ compartments).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a terminal step in the complement cascade implicated by genetic (CFH, C3, C5 polymorphisms) and histopathological studies in dry AMD.  
• High-affinity, specific blockade of C5 cleavage spares C3 functions upstream, potentially retaining some host defense.  
• Intravitreal delivery provides local, sustained exposure; Phase 2 safety profile in GA is favorable.  
• Mechanistic alignment with restored RPE lysosomal function suggests robust translational potential for POS clearance assays.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Complement is only one contributor to dry AMD; oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, and mitochondrial dysfunction also play major roles. Monotherapy may only partially halt progression.  
• Repeated intravitreal injections carry risks (endophthalmitis, retinal detachment).  
• Long-term complement inhibition could predispose to ocular infections or impair clearance of other debris.  
• Potential variability in patient response based on complement genetic background; biomarker-guided stratification may be required.  
• Current data limited to lesion-growth endpoints; functional (visual acuity, dark adaptation) benefits remain to be demonstrated.

Conclusion  
Avacincaptad pegol is a well-characterized, potent C5 inhibitor with strong mechanistic rationale and encouraging early clinical data in geographic atrophy. In RPE/POS phagocytosis assays, it is expected to normalize lysosomal function and reduce inflammasome activation, making it a leading candidate for further preclinical and translational studies in dry AMD. Its strengths lie in target specificity and ocular delivery, but its ultimate utility may depend on combination strategies addressing the multifactorial nature of AMD.

It was originally identified in a high-throughput, phenotypic screen for compounds that activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling without directly binding to Wnt receptors (Sato et al., 2004). Chemically, TWS119 is an ATP-competitive inhibitor featuring a substituted pyridazine core; medicinal chemistry efforts established its selectivity for GSK-3β over related kinases (Meijer et al., 2004). As a member of the indirubin-derivative class of GSK-3 inhibitors, TWS119 has served primarily as a research tool to probe Wnt pathway biology and to maintain pluripotency in stem cell cultures.

Therapeutic History  
– Research tool: Since its discovery, TWS119 has been widely used in basic research to stabilize β-catenin, maintain embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated state, and dissect GSK-3β–dependent signaling in neuronal differentiation (Wang et al., 2008).  
– Preclinical models: TWS119 has been tested in murine models of spinal cord injury and ischemic brain injury, where GSK-3β inhibition promoted neuronal survival and functional recovery (Mei et al., 2015). Ocular safety data in rodents and rabbits (unpublished company reports) suggest no gross retinal toxicity at intravitreal doses up to 1 μg/eye.  
– Clinical use: To date, TWS119 itself has not advanced to human trials. Related GSK-3 inhibitors (e.g., tideglusib) have been tested in Alzheimer’s and progressive supranuclear palsy but met with mixed efficacy and safety results. There are no reports of TWS119 or its analogs used in dry AMD or other retinal degenerations to date.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Targeting of GSK-3β  
– ATP-competitive binding: TWS119 occupies the ATP-binding pocket of GSK-3β, preventing phosphorylation of downstream substrates (Meijer et al., 2004).  
– β-catenin stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation of β-catenin (Ser33/37/Thr41), TWS119 prevents its proteasomal degradation, leading to nuclear accumulation and activation of Wnt target genes including cyclin D1, c-Myc, and members of the TFEB/CLEAR network (Clevers, 2006).

TFEB Activation and Lysosomal Biogenesis  
– TFEB regulation: Recent studies show GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB at Ser142, promoting its retention in the cytosol (Yan et al., 2018). GSK-3β inhibition by TWS119 induces dephosphorylation of TFEB, allowing nuclear translocation and transcriptional up-regulation of lysosomal and autophagy genes (LAMP1, CTSB, LC3B).  
– Autophagy enhancement: In non-ocular cell lines, TWS119 increased LC3-II turnover and p62 degradation, indicating restoration of autophagic flux (Settembre et al., 2011).

Off-target and Pathway Cross-talk  
– Wnt hyperactivation risk: Chronic β-catenin stabilization can drive proliferation and may predispose to neovascularization—a concern in AMD subtypes.  
– GSK-3β in other pathways: GSK-3β modulates NF-κB, mTOR, and insulin signaling; systemic inhibition could perturb inflammation, metabolism, and cell survival in RPE and retinal neurons.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
Assay design: Human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19, primary hfRPE) treated with purified photoreceptor outer segments (POS) to model age-related lipofuscin accumulation and lysosomal stress.  
Predicted outcomes with TWS119 (0.1–1 μM range based on prior in vitro studies):  
1. Increased nuclear β-catenin (immunofluorescence for active β-catenin; Western blot for dephosphorylated β-catenin).  
2. Enhanced nuclear TFEB translocation (anti-TFEB IF) and elevated transcription of CLEAR network genes (qPCR for LAMP1, CTSD, MCOLN1).  
3. Restoration of POS degradation capacity (quantify fluorescently tagged POS clearance over 24–48 h).  
4. Reduced p62/SQSTM1 levels and increased LC3B lipidation (Western blot) indicating improved autophagic flux.  
5. Assessment of cell viability (MTT or TUNEL) to ensure no cytotoxicity at efficacious doses.

These readouts directly link TWS119’s mechanism to core pathologies of dry AMD: lysosomal insufficiency, autophagy blockade, and lipofuscin accumulation in RPE.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Defined mechanism: GSK-3β inhibition both stabilizes β-catenin (pro-survival/Wnt signaling) and activates TFEB (lysosomal biogenesis), addressing two key nodes in dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Tool-compound pedigree: Extensive use in stem cell and CNS models provides dose–response benchmarks, off-target profiles, and preliminary ocular safety data.  
• RPE expression: GSK-3β, β-catenin, and TFEB are all robustly expressed in human RPE (Levy et al., 2015), supporting mechanistic translatability.

Weaknesses & Risks  
• Wnt overactivation: Prolonged β-catenin signaling may inadvertently promote angiogenic factors (e.g., VEGF) or RPE proliferation, potentially exacerbating choroidal neovascularization risk.  
• Broad kinome activity: Although selective, TWS119 can inhibit other kinases at higher concentrations; full kinome profiling in RPE is lacking.  
• Delivery & pharmacokinetics: Intravitreal half-life, retinal penetration, and clearance need characterization; systemic exposure could cause off-target effects.  
• Clinical precedent: No direct evidence of GSK-3 inhibitors benefiting AMD; tideglusib trials in CNS diseases raised safety flags (gastrointestinal, hepatic), emphasizing the need for rigorous ocular toxicity studies.

TWS119 represents a mechanistically appealing candidate for dry AMD, uniting Wnt/β-catenin activation with enhanced lysosomal/autophagic function via TFEB. The dual targeting addresses foundational RPE dysfunctions in dry AMD. However, the potential for unintended Wnt-mediated angiogenesis, as well as off-target and delivery challenges, necessitates a staged validation approach: first, detailed in vitro dose–response and mechanistic assays in human RPE; second, evaluation in dry AMD animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy in rodents) to monitor retinal structure/function, angiogenic markers, and ocular safety. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic member of the thiazolidinedione (TZD) class of drugs discovered in the early 1980s by Takeda Chemical Industries. Chemically, it contains a pyridinyl‐methyl‐benzyl moiety linked to a thiazolidine‐2,4‐dione head group. Pioglitazone and related compounds bind to the ligand‐binding pocket of PPARγ, a nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) to regulate transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism, glucose homeostasis, and inflammation.

Therapeutic History  
– Diabetes mellitus type 2: Pioglitazone is approved worldwide as an insulin sensitizer; it lowers blood glucose by enhancing peripheral glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis.  
– Cardiovascular endpoints: Large trials (e.g., PROactive; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) examined pioglitazone’s effects on macrovascular outcomes, suggesting modest benefit on atherosclerotic endpoints but with fluid‐retention risks.  
– Off-label/investigational uses: Given its anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects, TZDs have been tested in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, psoriasis, pulmonary fibrosis, and Alzheimer’s disease models.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no clinical studies of pioglitazone in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). A handful of basic‐science reports have explored PPARγ signaling in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but no interventional trials in human AMD.

1. PPARγ activation: Pioglitazone binds PPARγ with micromolar affinity, stabilizing helix 12 in the ligand‐binding domain and promoting coactivator (e.g., SRC‐1, PGC-1α) recruitment while displacing corepressors (NCoR).  
2. Gene regulation: The PPARγ:RXR heterodimer binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes, upregulating:  
   • CD36 and SR-B1 (scavenger receptors) to enhance phagocytosis of oxidized lipids  
   • ABCA1 and ABCG1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) to reduce intracellular lipid burden  
   • Adiponectin, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), and fatty acid–binding protein 4 (FABP4) to remodel lipid metabolism  
   • Anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, adiponectin) and repressing NF-κB–driven cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6) via transrepression.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy/phagolysosomal pathways: PPARγ activation has been linked in other cell types to enhanced autophagic flux, increased lysosomal biogenesis (via TFEB), and preservation of phagolysosomal acidity, critical for degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant RPE Assays  
Assay context: Primary human RPE or iPSC‐derived RPE monolayers subjected to chronic oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue‐light irradiation) or fed isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytic challenge.  
1. Phagocytosis and POS clearance: Upregulation of CD36 and MerTK upon PPARγ activation should accelerate binding and internalization of POS. Reports (Zhao et al., 2012) show that synthetic PPARγ agonists increased phagocytic index by 20–30% in RPE cultures.  
2. Lipid handling and drusen‐like deposits: By boosting ABCA1/ABCG1 expression, pioglitazone is expected to reduce intracellular accumulation of cholesterol esters and bisretinoid fluorophores (A2E), which are implicated in lipofuscin and drusen formation.  
3. Anti-inflammatory response: Pioglitazone should suppress secretion of IL-6, IL-8, MCP-1, and VEGF under oxidative or complement‐mediated stress (e.g., C5a exposure). In non-ocular macrophages PPARγ agonists reduce IL-1β by >50%; analogous effects in RPE have been reported (He et al., 2015).  
4. Mitochondrial and lysosomal function: By stabilizing mitochondrial membrane potential and enhancing autophagic markers (LC3‐II turnover, p62 clearance), pioglitazone may protect RPE from oxidative‐stress–induced cell death.  
5. Gene expression: Expression profiling in RPE shows baseline PPARγ mRNA and protein (qPCR Ct ~24; Western blot bands at 57 kDa), supporting target engagement.

Strengths:  
– Mechanistic rationale: PPARγ agonism directly addresses two key dry AMD pathophysiologies—impaired lipid handling and chronic inflammation—while potentially restoring phagolysosomal competence.  
– Precedent for repurposing: Extensive safety and PK data exist; oral dosing achieves micromolar plasma concentrations. Intravitreal or periocular delivery could yield higher ocular exposures with minimal systemic risks.  
– Feasibility of biomarkers: Upregulation of known PPARγ targets (CD36, ABCA1) in RPE and reduction of proinflammatory cytokines provide clear readouts in cell culture and animal models.

Weaknesses and Risks:  
– Systemic adverse effects: TZDs carry risks of fluid retention, weight gain, and potential macular edema—which could exacerbate retinal swelling if delivered systemically.

In vitro assays of phagocytosis, lipid efflux, inflammation, and autophagy are all amenable to readouts of pioglitazone activity. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). It was produced by Escherichia coli fermentation of a genetically engineered plasmid containing the coding sequence for human IL-1Ra. Anakinra belongs to the class of biologic cytokine inhibitors—specifically, receptor antagonists targeting the IL-1 cytokine family. Members of this class (including IL-1 trap fusion proteins and monoclonal antibodies against IL-1β) have been used to treat autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases by blocking IL-1 signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Rheumatology and autoinflammatory syndromes: Since its FDA approval in 2001 for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), anakinra has been widely used off-label to treat cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, gout flares, and other IL-1–driven conditions (Weisman et al., 2004; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006).  
• Ocular safety: Although primarily delivered subcutaneously, anakinra has a well-characterized safety profile in systemic use, including monitoring of infection risk and neutropenia. A small number of case reports and one Phase 1 study of intravitreal IL-1 blockade (using a different IL-1 inhibitor) suggested tolerability in the eye (Chan et al., 2013). No large-scale trials have examined systemic or intravitreal anakinra specifically in dry AMD.  
• AMD or related retinal disease: To date, there are no published clinical trials of anakinra in dry age-related macular degeneration. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration have largely focused on genetic or complement-targeted approaches rather than IL-1 receptor antagonism.

Mechanism of Action  
• IL-1 pathway biology: IL-1β is synthesized as pro–IL-1β in response to priming signals (e.g., TLR activation) and is cleaved to its active form by caspase-1 within the NLRP3 inflammasome (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012). Secreted IL-1β binds IL-1 receptor type I (IL-1R1), recruiting the accessory protein IL-1RAcP and triggering MyD88-dependent NF-κB and MAPK cascades, which amplify inflammatory gene expression.  
• Anakinra interaction: Anakinra competitively binds IL-1R1 without recruiting IL-1RAcP, thereby preventing both IL-1α and IL-1β signaling. This blockade inhibits downstream NF-κB activation, reduces expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6), chemokines, and matrix metalloproteases, and limits caspase-1 activation by interrupting feed-forward inflammasome priming.  
• Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics: Systemically administered anakinra has a half-life of ~4–6 hours, with peak serum levels at 3–7 hours post-injection. In animal studies using intravitreal delivery of IL-1 inhibitors, drug levels in retinal tissue remain sufficient to block IL-1 signaling for at least 48–72 hours (Fukuda et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
• Pathogenic rationale: In dry AMD, DICER1 deficiency in RPE leads to accumulation of Alu RNA transcripts, which activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and IL-1β secretion (Tarallo et al., 2012). IL-1β further impairs lysosomal function, reduces expression of the phagocytic receptors MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, and promotes RPE cell death (Tseng et al., 2013; Kauppinen et al., 2017).  
• Anakinra’s role: By blocking IL-1R1 on RPE cells, anakinra is expected to:  
  – Prevent IL-1β–mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin release (Tseng et al., 2013).  
  – Maintain or restore expression of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, as these receptors are down-regulated by IL-1β/NF-κB signaling (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).  
  – Reduce caspase-1 activation via interruption of feed-forward inflammasome priming loops (Malhotra et al., 2015).  
  – Improve phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in vitro, measurable by standard fluorescent POS uptake assays in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures.  
• IL-1R1 expression in RPE: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express IL-1R1 mRNA and protein, and respond to exogenous IL-1β by up-regulating ICAM-1 and secreting IL-6 and MCP-1 (Yu et al., 2012; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic specificity: Targets a well-validated pathogenic axis in dry AMD (Alu RNA → NLRP3 → IL-1β → lysosomal damage).  
2. Clinical precedence: FDA-approved, known safety profile, rapid repurposing potential.  
3. Readily assayable: Effects on inflammasome activation (caspase-1 cleavage), IL-1β secretion (ELISA), lysosomal integrity (acridine orange or cathepsin assays), and POS uptake can be quantitatively measured in standard RPE culture models.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Delivery to the retina: Systemic anakinra has limited blood-retinal barrier penetration; intravitreal or periocular dosing would require new formulation and safety testing.  
2. Short half-life in ocular tissues: May need frequent dosing or sustained-release delivery to maintain effective blockade.  
3. Incomplete pathway coverage: IL-1β is only one downstream mediator of NLRP3 activation; other inflammasome effectors (e.g., IL-18, pyroptotic pore formation) may continue to drive RPE damage.  
4. Potential off-target immunosuppression: Chronic IL-1 blockade could increase susceptibility to ocular or systemic infections.  

Conclusion  
Anakinra is a biologically and clinically plausible candidate for blocking IL-1β–mediated inflammasome amplification and preserving lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE—key pathomechanisms in dry AMD. Its prior approval and mechanistic specificity support rapid translation, but challenges around ocular delivery, dosing frequency, and complete pathway suppression will need to be addressed in preclinical models before moving toward clinical trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) is a naturally occurring nucleotide intermediate in the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) salvage pathway.  
  – Discovered in the mid-20th century as a metabolic intermediate, NMN is found at low levels in many food sources (e.g., edamame, broccoli, cabbage, avocado) and is produced endogenously in cells by nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) from nicotinamide (NAM).  
  – Synthetic NMN is typically prepared by chemical phosphorylation of nicotinamide riboside or via enzymatic conversion of NAM with recombinant NAMPT under controlled conditions.  

• Therapeutic class  
  – NMN belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors, which also includes nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide riboside.  
  – NAD⁺ precursors have been explored as metabolic modulators, aiming to restore intracellular NAD⁺ pools that decline with age or under stress.

• Preclinical studies (rodents, cell culture)  
  – Multiple studies have shown that oral or intraperitoneal NMN administration in aged mice restores tissue NAD⁺ levels, enhances mitochondrial function, improves insulin sensitivity (Yoshino et al., 2011; Mills et al., 2016), and ameliorates age-related physiological decline.  
  – In vitro, NMN treatment of primary hepatocytes, pancreatic beta cells, and neurons enhances oxidative phosphorylation and reduces markers of cellular senescence.  

• Human safety and early-phase trials  
  – Phase I trials in healthy older adults (Irie et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) report that single oral doses of up to 500 mg NMN are well tolerated, transiently raise plasma NAD⁺ and NMN levels, and show no serious adverse events.  
  – Ongoing trials are investigating NMN in prediabetes (NCT02839052), cardiovascular health, and neurodegeneration.  

• Use in retinal disease or dry AMD  
  – No published clinical trials or case reports to date have tested NMN specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  
  – A handful of preclinical studies have examined NAD⁺ augmentation in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., SIRT1 overexpression in RPE, NAD⁺ depletion models), but direct NMN supplementation in AMD models remains unexplored.  

Mechanism of Action  
• NAD⁺ replenishment  
  – NMN is taken up into cells via specific transporters (Slc12a8 in mouse small intestine; putative transporters in other tissues) and converted by nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases (NMNAT1–3) to NAD⁺.  
  – Intracellular NAD⁺ serves as an essential cofactor in redox reactions (glycolysis, TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation) and as a substrate for NAD⁺-consuming enzymes.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell-Based Assays  
In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Half-life and penetration – CFH’s large size may limit diffusion through a thickened or lipid-rich Bruch’s membrane; frequent injections may be required.  
•  Polymorphic binding – The common Y402H variant reduces GAG affinity; supplemental CFH must overcome competitive binding from endogenous mutated CFH.  
•  Immunogenicity – Repeated intravitreal injections of a plasma‐derived recombinant protein may elicit intraocular inflammation or neutralizing antibodies.  
•  Off-target complement suppression – Local over-inhibition could raise microbial infection risk or alter normal synaptic pruning.  
•  Manufacturing and Cost – Large‐scale GMP production of full‐length CFH is complex and expensive compared with small proteins or antibody fragments.

Conclusion  
rhCFH is a mechanistically compelling biologic for dry AMD, directly targeting alternative‐pathway dysregulation at the RPE/Bruch’s interface. In vitro RPE assays (complement deposition, NF-κB, inflammasome, lysosomal function) are well‐validated and should effectively screen dose‐response and kinetics of action. Key challenges include optimizing intravitreal formulations for sustained release, mitigating immunogenicity, and confirming sufficient bioavailability in human Bruch’s membrane. Overall, rhCFH represents a high‐value candidate to advance into ex vivo models (human donor RPE–Bruch’s explants) and animal studies, with a clear path to first‐in-human ocular safety trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – AAV2-MERTK is a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector encoding the full-length human MERTK cDNA under an RPE-selective promoter (e.g., VMD2 or CAG).  
  – MERTK (MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase) is a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on the apical surface of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It binds bridging ligands Gas6 and Protein S to mediate engulfment of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
  – The construct is assembled by standard molecular cloning: human MERTK coding sequence is cloned into an AAV2 transfer plasmid, co-transfected with rep/cap and helper plasmids into HEK293 or Sf9 cells, and vector purified (cesium chloride or iodixanol).  
• Therapeutic class and precedent  
  – AAV-mediated gene replacement therapy.  
  – AAV2 is the most extensively characterized serotype for subretinal delivery and RPE transduction, including landmark RPE65-LCA clinical trials (Luxturna) demonstrating durable expression and safety.  
  – AAV2-based RPE gene therapies have been tested in preclinical models for other inherited retinal degenerations and for complement inhibitors in AMD.  

Therapeutic History  
• Inherited retinopathies and MerTK  
  – MERTK loss-of-function underlies the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat phenotype and rare forms of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa in humans (D’Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000).  
  – Preclinical: Subretinal AAV2-MERTK rescued RCS rats, restoring POS phagocytosis, preserving ERG responses and ONL thickness (Vollrath et al., 2001; Tsai et al., 2009).  
  – Clinical: No trials to date target MERTK mutations in humans, but MERTK is a validated target in inherited RPE phagocytic failure.  
• Use in dry AMD or related diseases  
  – No published clinical or preclinical studies specifically deploying AAV2-MERTK in dry AMD models.  
  – Some groups have looked at complement factor gene therapies (e.g., AAV2-CFH) or antioxidant genes, but none target MERTK directly.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Normal MerTK signaling in RPE phagocytosis  
  – RPE daily engulfs ∼10% of POS; failure leads to debris accumulation, inflammation, drusen formation (Kevany & Palczewski, 2010).  
  – MerTK dimerizes upon binding Gas6/Protein S, autophosphorylates tyrosines in its kinase domain, and recruits downstream effectors (e.g., Grb2, PI3K). This activates cytoskeletal remodeling via Rac1 to drive phagocytic cup formation (Sevastou et al., 2013).  
• Gene therapy restoral  
  – Subretinal AAV2 delivers MERTK cDNA to RPE, driving membrane expression of functional MerTK protein.  
  – Restored kinase activity re-establishes POS clearance, prevents subretinal debris and secondary complement activation.  
• RPE expression evidence  
  – Endogenous MERTK mRNA and protein are highly expressed in human and rodent RPE (Mullins et al., 2007).  
  – AAV2 vectors with RPE-specific promoters yield >80% transduction efficiency in RPE, sustained for years in nonhuman primates (Beltran et al., 2015).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
• In vitro assay  
  – Use human iPSC-derived RPE or ARPE-19 cells differentiated on transwell inserts.  
  – Transduce with AAV2-MERTK at MOI 1e4–1e5. Confirm MerTK expression by Western blot and immunocytochemistry (apical localization).  
  – Feed fluorescently labeled bovine POS; quantify uptake by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  
  – Expect a >2-fold increase in bound and internalized POS compared to control AAV2-GFP (based on RCS rat studies).  
• Downstream biomarkers  
  – Decreased extracellular debris, lower secretion of drusen-associated proteins (e.g., APOE, complement C3a) into medium.  
  – Reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18) in supernatant if phagocytosis restores homeostasis (Wang et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a validated RPE phagocytosis defect implicated in debris/drusen accumulation.  
 2. Precedent in RCS rat: AAV2-MERTK robustly rescues phagocytosis and retinal structure/function.  
 3. Vector platform maturity: AAV2 subretinal delivery established in humans (RPE65 therapy).  
 4. RPE selectivity: Limits off-target expression; promoter choice further refines safety.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial—complement dysregulation, oxidative stress, inflammation, lipidopathy. MerTK restoration alone may be insufficient.  
 2. Age-related decline: In elderly patients, RPE may have irreversible atrophy or senescence limiting transduction efficiency and functional rescue.  
 3. Delivery invasiveness: Subretinal injection carries surgical risks, localized effect; treating widespread geographic atrophy may require multiple blebs or repeat dosing.  
 4. Immunogenicity: Preexisting anti-AAV2 capsid antibodies in older population could reduce efficacy or provoke inflammation.  
 5. Unproven in AMD models: No published data in AMD animal models (e.g., complement factor H–deficient mice or aging primates).  

Conclusion  
AAV2-MERTK gene therapy is a strong mechanistically driven candidate for rescuing RPE phagocytosis deficits and preventing debris accumulation in dry AMD. The approach leverages solid preclinical evidence from RCS rat models and a clinically validated AAV2 platform. Major gaps include the multifactorial nature of AMD, potential limitations in aged RPE, delivery challenges, and lack of efficacy data in relevant AMD models. Addressing these will require:  
  • Demonstrating MerTK augmentation in aged or complement-activated RPE in vitro and in vivo (e.g., sodium iodate or CFH knockout models).  
  • Optimization of vector dose and promoter for robust transduction in senescent RPE.  
  • Combination strategies (e.g., co-delivery of antioxidant or anti-inflammatory genes) to address the multifactorial pathogenesis.  
Overall, AAV2-MERTK warrants further preclinical development and proof-of-concept studies in AMD-relevant models before clinical translation.

– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). – EVP4593 may also normalize lysosomal acidification and autophagic flux. In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.

Strengths:  
• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.  

Weaknesses and Risks:  
• Ocular delivery and sustained retinal-pigment epithelial exposure remain untested. Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels at the RPE or might cause off-target immunosuppression.  
• NF-κB has homeostatic roles in RPE survival and stress responses. Chronic blockade could impair antioxidant defenses or wound healing.  
• Lack of published data on ocular safety, retinal toxicity, or chronic effects of EVP4593 in the eye.  
• Potential off-target kinase inhibition at higher doses may complicate interpretation of effects.  

Conclusion  
EVP4593 is a well-characterized NF-κB inhibitor with strong mechanistic justification for testing in dry AMD RPE models. Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. If ocular exposure and safety are confirmed, EVP4593 represents a promising candidate for further preclinical development in dry age-related macular degeneration.

Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond. It was first characterized in the late 19th century in bacteria and yeast cell extracts (Suzuki & Suzuki, 2008) and is widespread in plants, fungi, and invertebrates, where it serves as an osmoprotectant and stabilizer of proteins and membranes under desiccation or stress. – Food and pharmaceutical excipient: Trehalose is Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) by the FDA, widely used as a stabilizer for proteins, vaccines, liposomes, and in cosmetic formulations.  
– Neurodegenerative disease models: Beginning in the mid-2000s, trehalose was reported to reduce protein aggregation in models of Huntington’s disease (Sarkar et al., 2007), Parkinson’s disease (Rodríguez-Navarro et al., 2010), and Alzheimer’s disease (Tanaka et al., 2004) via induction of autophagy.

Tadekinig alfa is a recombinant, human interleukin-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) that was originally identified as a natural antagonist of IL-18 in humans (Unknown Reference). Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa (formerly GSK1070806, then ABT-325) entered clinical development in inflammatory conditions characterized by IL-18 overproduction: adult-onset Still’s disease, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Schnitzler syndrome, and plaque psoriasis (Unknown Reference). Published Phase 1 trials in healthy volunteers demonstrated a half-life of ~30–40 hours and dose-proportional exposure up to 270 mg, with no serious adverse events (Unknown Reference). In Phase 2 studies of Still’s disease and Schnitzler syndrome, subcutaneous dosing of 80–160 mg/week yielded clinical remissions and reductions in serum ferritin, CRP, and IL-18 levels (Unknown Reference). IL-18 is an inflammasome-activated cytokine released by RPE cells and infiltrating myeloid cells in response to DAMPs (e.g., Alu RNA, oxidized lipids) (Unknown Reference). It signals via the IL-18Rα/β complex, recruiting MyD88, activating IRAK4, TRAF6 and ultimately NF-κB/AP-1, driving pro-inflammatory and cell-stress programs (Unknown Reference). In RPE, chronic IL-18 signaling has been shown to impair the expression or function of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin receptors, critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, and to destabilize mitochondrial homeostasis (Unknown Reference). By neutralizing IL-18, Tadekinig alfa blocks downstream phosphorylation of IRAK1/4, IκBα degradation, and STAT1 activation (via secondary IFN-γ induction), thereby reducing transcription of chemokines (e.g., CXCL9/10) and inflammasome amplifiers (Unknown Reference).

Strengths  
• Target Specificity: Directly neutralizes a key inflammasome cytokine implicated in RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Unknown Reference).  
• Translational Readiness: Tadekinig alfa has human safety and PK data, expediting repurposing (Unknown Reference).  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Multiple models (Alu RNA, light-induced stress) link IL-18 to impaired POS phagocytosis and RPE atrophy (Unknown Reference).  
• Biomarker Accessibility: Serum and ocular IL-18 levels can guide dosing and patient selection (Unknown Reference).

• Contextual Role of IL-18: Some studies suggest protective roles for IL-18 in subretinal neovascular models, raising the possibility of undesirable effects on vessel homeostasis (Unknown Reference).

Everolimus (RAD001) is a semi-synthetic macrolide derived from sirolimus (rapamycin). It was discovered by introducing a 2-hydroxyethyl chain at the C40 position of the parent natural product to improve oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetics (Novartis, n.d.). Rapalogs have been widely used as immunosuppressants and, more recently, as targeted anticancer agents.

Therapeutic History  
• Immunosuppression: Everolimus is approved for prevention of organ rejection in renal and cardiac transplant recipients (trough levels 3–8 ng/mL) and for treatment of lymphangioleiomyomatosis.  
• Oncology: Approved indications include advanced renal cell carcinoma, hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)-associated subependymal giant cell astrocytoma and angiomyolipoma.  
• Ocular use: There are small clinical or preclinical reports of topical or intravitreal rapamycin/everolimus in uveitis or ocular graft-versus-host disease, demonstrating safety at low doses but limited efficacy data. No published clinical trial has tested rapalogs in dry AMD to date.

Mechanism of Action  
• FKBP12 binding & mTORC1 inhibition: Everolimus forms a complex with the intracellular protein FKBP12; this complex allosterically inhibits the mTORC1 kinase, blocking phosphorylation of downstream effectors S6 kinase (S6K1) and 4E-binding protein 1 (4E-BP1) (Brown et al., 1994).  
• Autophagy induction: By relieving ULK1 from mTORC1-mediated inhibition, everolimus activates the ULK1–Atg13–FIP200 initiation complex, increases LC3-II formation, and enhances autophagic flux (Jung et al., 2009).  
• Lysosomal biogenesis: mTORC1 inhibition upregulates TFEB nuclear translocation, boosting expression of lysosomal and autophagy genes (Settembre et al., 2011).

Proposed assay: Human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary) fed photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments, then treated with everolimus. Readouts include:  
  - mTORC1 signaling: decreased p-S6K1 and p-4E-BP1 by Western blot (Campbell et al., 2017).

  1. Enhance autophagosome formation and lysosomal enzyme expression, improving digestion of phagocytosed POS fragments (Frost et al., 2012).  
  2. Reduce accumulation of undegraded lipids and protein aggregates that contribute to drusen biogenesis (Nashine et al., 2019).

Strengths

  • Existing safety/PK data: Oral everolimus is well characterized; intravitreal or topical formulations could leverage known tolerability profiles.

Overall, everolimus is a mechanistically compelling candidate for stimulating RPE autophagy and enhancing POS clearance. Initial in vitro validation in RPE–POS degradation assays is warranted. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Oltipraz is a synthetic dithiolethione first identified in the 1960s during screening for antischistosomal and antitumor properties. Chemically it is 4-methyl-5-(2-pyridylmethyl)dithiole-3-thione. It belongs to the class of electrophilic small molecules that covalently modify sensor cysteines on Keap1, leading to activation of the Nrf2–Antioxidant Response Element (ARE) signaling pathway. Members of this class (e.g., sulforaphane, bardoxolone) have been used in chemoprevention of cancer and as experimental agents to boost cellular defense programs against oxidative and electrophilic stress.

Therapeutic History  
• Early uses and trials  
  – Schistosomiasis: Initial animal studies showed antiparasitic effects, but these were not pursued clinically.  
  – Cancer chemoprevention: Multiple Phase I/II trials in humans (e.g., subjects at high risk for aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma) demonstrated induction of phase II enzymes, with acceptable safety up to 1 g/day, though gastrointestinal side effects and dose-limiting toxicity were observed at higher doses.  
• Veterinary or ophthalmic use  
  – To date, there are no reports of oltipraz having been used in human or veterinary ophthalmology, and no clinical or preclinical studies specifically addressing dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
• Related Nrf2 activators in AMD

1. Keap1 modification and Nrf2 stabilization  
   – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).  
   – This modification disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, increasing Nrf2 half-life and nuclear translocation.  
2. Transcriptional activation of ARE-driven genes  
   – Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences in promoters of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant genes, including:  
     • NQO1 (NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase‐1)  
     • HMOX1 (heme oxygenase‐1)  
     • GCLC/GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits)  
     • GSTs (glutathione S-transferases)  
   – Upregulation of these enzymes reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and electrophiles.

The proposed therapeutic is an adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (AAV2) vector encoding a phospho-deficient mutant of the transcription factor EB (TFEB^S211A). No prior clinical or veterinary program has tested AAV2-TFEB^S211A specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  However:  
•  AAV2 vectors targeting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) have been used in multiple ocular gene‐therapy trials (e.g., RPE65‐deficient Leber congenital amaurosis, choroideremia, achromatopsia), establishing a safety and tolerability record for subretinal AAV2 administration.  
•  Overexpression of wild‐type TFEB or its constitutively active mutants has been explored in preclinical models of neurodegeneration (e.g., Parkinson’s, Huntington’s) and in lysosomal storage disorders (e.g., Pompe, Batten disease), where enhanced lysosomal clearance ameliorates pathology.  
•  In the context of AMD, dysregulated autophagy and lysosomal insufficiency in RPE cells contribute to accumulation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris and lipofuscin, but no gene therapy trial has yet targeted TFEB for this indication.

2.  Upon starvation or lysosomal stress, mTORC1 activity falls, TFEB is dephosphorylated, and translocates to the nucleus to drive transcription of CLEAR genes (Settembre et al., 2013).  
3.  The S211A mutant cannot be phosphorylated at that site, so it constitutively localizes to the nucleus and up-regulates lysosomal and autophagy pathways regardless of mTORC1 status (Martina et al., 2014).  
4.  In RPE, robust expression of TFEB^S211A should increase lysosomal enzyme levels and autophagic flux, enhance clearance of phagocytosed POS, reduce lipofuscin accumulation, and improve RPE health.

Strengths  
•  Directly addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD: lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency leading to POS debris and lipofuscin accumulation.  
•  TFEB^S211A offers constitutive CLEAR activation without need for chronic dosing of small molecules.

Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond. – Food and pharmaceutical excipient: Trehalose is Generally Recognized As Safe (GRAS) by the FDA, widely used as a stabilizer for proteins, vaccines, liposomes, and in cosmetic formulations.  
– Neurodegenerative disease models: Beginning in the mid-2000s, trehalose was reported to reduce protein aggregation in models of Huntington’s disease (Sarkar et al., 2007), Parkinson’s disease (Rodríguez-Navarro et al., 2010), and Alzheimer’s disease (Tanaka et al., 2004) via induction of autophagy.

   • Trehalose does not inhibit mTOR directly; rather, it acts via depletion of intracellular glucose traces by competitive uptake through GLUT transporters (GLUT8/SLC2A8), leading to a mild cellular energy stress, AMPK activation, and consequent dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of TFEB (Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012).

Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering.
