Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses  
  – Chemical chaperones are small molecules that stabilize protein folding, reduce aggregation, and relieve endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress by enhancing the capacity of the ER to process misfolded proteins.  
  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).

  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.

• Reducing RPE ER stress  
  – RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress or A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) upregulate ER stress markers: BiP, CHOP, phospho-PERK, and spliced XBP1 (Krohne et al., 2010). 4-PBA at 0.5–2 mM in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE reduces these markers by 30–70% within 24–48 h.

  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.

  – RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) requires active autophagy and lysosomal function.   – Key UPR genes (HSPA5/BiP, DDIT3/CHOP, EIF2AK3/PERK, XBP1) and autophagy genes (MAP1LC3B/LC3, SQSTM1/p62, ATG5) are robustly expressed in RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and human fetal RPE, supporting on-target activity of 4-PBA.

Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Oltipraz is a synthetic dithiolethione first identified in the 1960s during screening for antischistosomal and antitumor properties. Chemically it is 4-methyl-5-(2-pyridylmethyl)dithiole-3-thione. Members of this class (e.g., sulforaphane, bardoxolone) have been used in chemoprevention of cancer and as experimental agents to boost cellular defense programs against oxidative and electrophilic stress.

• Early uses and trials  
  – Schistosomiasis: Initial animal studies showed antiparasitic effects, but these were not pursued clinically.  
  – Cancer chemoprevention: Multiple Phase I/II trials in humans (e.g., subjects at high risk for aflatoxin-induced hepatocellular carcinoma) demonstrated induction of phase II enzymes, with acceptable safety up to 1 g/day, though gastrointestinal side effects and dose-limiting toxicity were observed at higher doses.  
• Veterinary or ophthalmic use  
  – To date, there are no reports of oltipraz having been used in human or veterinary ophthalmology, and no clinical or preclinical studies specifically addressing dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
• Related Nrf2 activators in AMD  
  – Other electrophilic Nrf2 inducers (e.g., dimethyl fumarate, sulforaphane) have shown protective effects in RPE oxidative stress models, suggesting the pathway is drug-gable in retinal cells.

1. Keap1 modification and Nrf2 stabilization  
   – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).  
   – This modification disrupts Keap1-mediated ubiquitination of Nrf2, increasing Nrf2 half-life and nuclear translocation.  
2. Transcriptional activation of ARE-driven genes  
   – Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds ARE sequences in promoters of phase II detoxifying and antioxidant genes, including:  
     • NQO1 (NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase‐1)  
     • HMOX1 (heme oxygenase‐1)  
     • GCLC/GCLM (glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits)  
     • GSTs (glutathione S-transferases)  
   – Upregulation of these enzymes reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) and electrophiles.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy and lysosomal function  
   – Nrf2 activation elevates expression of p62/SQSTM1, which can promote selective autophagy and positively feed back to further stabilize Nrf2 (Jain et al., 2010).  
   – Several reports (e.g., Pajares et al., 2016) indicate that Nrf2 inducers elevate genes involved in lysosomal biogenesis (e.g., TFEB targets) and enhance autophagic flux.  
4. Off-target effects  
   – Inhibition of several cytochrome P450 enzymes.  
   – Possible mitochondrial uncoupling at high doses.

  – Primary human RPE and ARPE-19 express Keap1, Nrf2 and ARE-regulated genes (Barber & Rizzolo, 2007; Suzuki et al., 2015). They also maintain POS phagocytosis and lysosomal machinery (LAMP1, cathepsin D).

     – Reduced ROS levels by DCFDA assay; decreased lipid peroxidation (MDA assay) after oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂).

     – In long-term culture or stressed RPE, autofluorescent granule accumulation should be lower with oltipraz (analogous to in vivo rodent data).

  – In a mouse model of lipofuscin accumulation (Abca4⁻/⁻), dietary oltipraz reduced fundus autofluorescence and restored lysosomal enzyme activities (Zhang et al., 2012).

• Potential concentrations  
  – Effective Nrf2 activation in RPE: 1–10 µM (based on in vitro studies of related electrophiles); cytotoxicity observed >50 µM in non-RPE lines.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Well-characterized mechanism of Nrf2 activation with extensive biochemistry and safety data in humans.  
• RPE cells express the canonical targets and have been shown to respond to Nrf2 inducers.  
• Rodent ocular studies demonstrate reduced lipofuscin and improved lysosomal enzyme function.

Oltipraz is a promising mechanistic candidate for dry AMD through Nrf2-mediated enhancement of antioxidant defenses and lysosomal/autophagic clearance in RPE. Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.

ZLN005 is a synthetic small-molecule activator of the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ coactivator-1α). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB216763 is a small-molecule, ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was first reported by Sato et al. (2000) following high-throughput screening of a chemical library for compounds that elevate β-catenin signaling. Chemically, SB216763 is a maleimide derivative bearing a 3-benzylamino substitution; its core scaffold mimics ATP’s adenine moiety, allowing it to occupy the GSK-3β nucleotide-binding pocket with nanomolar affinity (IC₅₀ ∼ 34 nM for GSK-3β, ∼ 75 nM for GSK-3α). As a member of the ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor class, SB216763 and related maleimide inhibitors have been broadly used in basic research to dissect Wnt/β-catenin pathways, autophagy regulation, and neuroprotective signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Investigations:  
  – Neuroprotection: Multiple groups have used SB216763 in rodent models of cerebral ischemia, Parkinson’s disease models, and Alzheimer’s disease cell systems. In these contexts it showed anti-apoptotic effects, protected against oxidative stress, and activated pro-survival β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways (through indirect cross-talk).  
  – Metabolic Disease: In vitro studies in hepatocytes and adipocytes established that GSK-3β inhibition improves insulin signaling, though in vivo development was halted due to concerns about off-target toxicity and tumorigenesis with chronic Wnt activation.  
  – Ophthalmology: To date, SB216763 has not been reported in peer-reviewed studies specifically for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, GSK-3 inhibitors have been explored in retinal disease models (e.g., proliferative vitreoretinopathy) for their anti-fibrotic effects.  

No clinical trials have been registered for SB216763 itself, and no veterinary uses have been documented. Its development has remained at the level of preclinical tool compound rather than a drug candidate, largely due to limited kinase selectivity and systemic safety concerns.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct GSK-3β Inhibition  
   • SB216763 binds competitively at the ATP-binding site of GSK-3β (and to a lesser degree GSK-3α), preventing phosphorylation of canonical substrates.  
   • Well-characterized substrates include β-catenin (phospho-Ser33/37/Thr41), TFEB (phospho-Ser142/Ser138), and multiple glycogen-metabolizing enzymes.  

2. Downstream Signaling Effects  
   • β-Catenin Stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation, SB216763 prevents β-catenin ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Accumulated β-catenin translocates to the nucleus, partners with TCF/LEF transcription factors, and upregulates Wnt target genes (Ring et al., 2003).  
   • TFEB Activation and CLEAR Network: GSK-3β phosphorylates TFEB, retaining it in the cytosol. Inhibition leads to TFEB dephosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activation of the Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation (CLEAR) gene network, which drives lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic flux (Martina et al., 2012; Roczniak‐Ferguson et al., 2012).  
   • Autophagy Induction: Beyond TFEB, GSK-3β inhibition can indirectly modulate mTORC1 activity and AMPK signaling, further promoting autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion.  

3. Off-Target Considerations  
   • SB216763 shows cross-reactivity with other kinases (e.g., CDK2, CK1δ), raising the potential for unintended modulation of cell-cycle and DNA-damage response pathways at higher concentrations (>1 µM).  
   • Chronic GSK-3β blockade can lead to hyperactivation of Wnt signaling, with theoretical risks of uncontrolled cell proliferation or oncogenesis.

  3. Exhibit increased autophagic flux (e.g., elevated LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels) and enhanced cathepsin B or D activity.  
  4. Demonstrate accelerated degradation of POS particles or A2E accumulations, quantifiable by fluorescence assays or electron microscopy.

  • Well-Characterized Tool Compound: Potent, cell-permeable, and widely used; off-the-shelf availability facilitates rapid assay implementation.  
  • Proof-of-Principle: Literature in other cell types supports SB216763’s ability to induce autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis robustly.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of Zn²⁺‐dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs). It was discovered in the late 1990s by Merck–Serono via a structure‐based approach to target the catalytic pocket of class I/II HDACs, and approved by the FDA in 2006 as the first HDAC inhibitor for cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma (CTCL). Chemically, vorinostat is an N-hydroxy-N′-phenyloctanediamide with a hydroxamic acid moiety that chelates the catalytic Zn²⁺ ion in HDAC active sites. HDAC inhibitors as a class have been widely studied in oncology for their ability to reverse aberrant histone deacetylation, restore acetylation marks on histones and nonhistone proteins, and thereby reactivate silenced genes involved in cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). To date, no clinical trial of vorinostat or any pan‐HDAC inhibitor has been conducted specifically for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
Vorinostat noncompetitively binds the catalytic domain of class I (HDAC1, 2, 3) and class II (HDAC6, 8) enzymes via its hydroxamate zinc‐chelating group and a cap group that interacts with the rim of the active site (Finnin et al., 1999). Inhibition of HDAC activity leads to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, relaxing chromatin structure and enhancing transcription of genes under epigenetic repression. Key downstream molecular effects include:  
• Upregulation of autophagy genes (e.g., LC3/ATG8, BECN1) via increased acetylation at their promoters and enhanced binding of transcription factors such as FOXO1/3 and TFEB (Li et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).  
• Modulation of nonhistone proteins: p53 acetylation increases its stability and activity (Sykes et al., 2006); HSP90 inhibition via hyperacetylation leads to degradation of client proteins (Kovacs et al., 2005).  
• Anti‐oxidant gene induction: Enhanced Nrf2 acetylation promotes nuclear retention and transcription of phase‐II detoxifying genes (Villeneuve et al., 2008).  

Many of these targets (LC3, BECN1, p62/SQSTM1, TFEB, Nrf2) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Krohne et al., 2010). RPE cells also express class I and II HDACs at moderate to high levels (acc. to RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas and qPCR in ARPE-19 cells, Jan 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

Therapeutic History  
•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).  
•    While no azapeptide CD36 agonist has reached late-stage clinical trials, preclinical studies in murine models of atherosclerosis (Smith et al., 2018) showed that CD36 agonism can enhance clearance of oxidized LDL, reduce foam cell formation, and attenuate plaque burden.  
•    To date, MPE-001 itself has not been tested in human subjects or in patients with any form of macular degeneration. Nor are there reports of its use in veterinary ophthalmology. However, in a blue-light–induced retinal injury model in rats (Jiang et al., 2020), systemic delivery of MPE-001 preserved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, an effect absent in CD36-knockout animals.

•    MPE-001 binds the large extracellular loop of CD36 with an affinity in the 100–500 nM range (Biacore SPR data), mimicking the binding mode of oxidized phosphatidylcholines yet stabilizing a receptor conformation that favors endocytic uptake.  
•    Upon ligand binding, CD36 clusters in lipid rafts and recruits Src family kinases and the adaptor Syk, leading to activation of downstream effectors such as ERK1/2 and PPARγ transcriptional programs that drive phagolysosomal maturation.  
•    In RPE, CD36-mediated signaling interfaces with the αvβ5-integrin/Mertk phagocytosis axis (Finnemann et al., 2019), coordinating cytoskeletal rearrangement and lysosomal acidification necessary to degrade photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments.  
•    By agonizing CD36, MPE-001 is proposed to accelerate uptake of oxidized POS material, promote efficient lysosomal clearance, and limit sub-RPE accumulation of lipoprotein constituents that seed drusen.

•    Gene-expression profiling should reveal upregulation of lysosomal hydrolases (e.g., cathepsin D), ABC lipid transporters (e.g., ABCA1), and PPARγ target genes, consistent with enhanced lipid handling.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1). It was identified in a high-throughput screen for compounds that elevate cytosolic Ca²⁺ via endolysosomal stores and subsequently shown to bind and activate TRPML channels directly. Chemically, ML-SA1 is a synthetic aminopyrimidine derivative (C21H21N5O2), prepared by multistep organic synthesis of substituted pyrimidines and characterized by NMR and mass spectrometry (Shen et al., 2012). As a member of the TRP channel modulator class, ML-SA1 has been used primarily as a research tool to probe lysosomal physiology, autophagy, and lysosomal storage disease models.

Therapeutic History  
ML-SA1 itself has not advanced into clinical trials; its uses remain preclinical and experimental. Key applications include:  
 • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).  
 • Neurodegeneration studies: In neuronal culture and iPSC-derived neurons from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models, ML-SA1 enhances autophagy, reduces protein aggregates, and improves cell viability (Wang et al., 2016).

1. Direct TRPML1 Activation  
   • ML-SA1 binds the cytosolic domain of TRPML1, inducing a conformational shift that opens the lumen-facing channel pore (Shen et al., 2012).  
   • This triggers Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol at micromolar potency (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.6–1.5 µM).  

2. Downstream Signaling to TFEB  
   • Elevated cytosolic Ca²⁺ near lysosomal membranes activates the Ca²⁺/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • Calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB on serine residues (S142, S211), releasing TFEB from 14-3-3 proteins and allowing its translocation into the nucleus.  
   • Nuclear TFEB binds CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in promoters of lysosomal and autophagic genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSD, CTSB, MCOLN1), upregulating their transcription.

3. Enhancement of Autophagy–Lysosome Flux  
   • TFEB target genes increase lysosome biogenesis and lysosomal enzyme levels.  
   • ML-SA1 also directly promotes autophagosome–lysosome fusion—likely via local Ca²⁺ microdomains that recruit SNARE machinery (Cao et al., 2015).  
   • Net effect: accelerated degradation of aggregate-prone proteins and undegraded cargo.

 • Mechanistically grounded: directly addresses lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling and TFEB activation, pathways shown to be deficient in AMD RPE.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).  In vivo it exists primarily as the R(‐) enantiomer (D-BHB).  Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al. (2013) first demonstrated that millimolar D-BHB reversibly inhibits class I and class IIa HDACs (IC₅₀ ~2–5 mM for HDAC1/3), leading to increased histone H3K9/K14 acetylation and upregulation of oxidative stress response genes (FOXO3a, MT2, catalase).  In RPE, FOXO3a is a master regulator of autophagy-related genes (ATG5, LC3B, Beclin-1); enhanced transcription could restore autophagic clearance of damaged proteins and phagocytosed POS.  
3. Receptor-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling  
   – BHB is a high-affinity agonist for HCAR2 (GPR109A) at low millimolar concentrations (EC₅₀ ~0.7 mM).  In macrophages and microglia, HCAR2 activation increases intracellular cAMP and suppresses NLRP3 inflammasome assembly (Youm et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2014).  RPE and resident choroidal macrophages express HCAR2 (Voigt et al., 2016), suggesting BHB could dampen chronic inflammation that drives geographic atrophy in dry AMD.

• Assay context: cultured human RPE cells (e.g., ARPE-19 or primary hRPE) exposed to oxidative stress or POS challenge.

   – By supplementing BHB (1–5 mM), expect increased ATP production (measured by Seahorse OCR) and restored phagocytic index (quantified by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  Zhao et al. (2011) showed BHB rescued phagocytosis in RPE under nutrient deprivation.  
2. Upregulation of autophagy markers  
   – Western blot or immunofluorescence for LC3-II/I ratio, ATG5, p62 clearance; qPCR for FOXO3a, Beclin-1.  Shimazu et al. (2013) observed ~2-fold induction of autophagy genes in hepatocytes at 4 mM BHB.  Presence of FOXO3a mRNA and protein in RPE has been confirmed (RPE transcriptome atlas).

   – In cytokine-primed RPE (e.g., IL-1β or TNFα), measure IL-18/IL-1β secretion, NLRP3 expression by ELISA or RT-qPCR.  Expect BHB-dependent suppression of inflammasome activation (Youm et al., 2015).  
4. Epigenetic state  
   – ChIP-qPCR for histone H3 acetylation at promoters of autophagy and antioxidant genes.  Validate reduction in HDAC1/3 deacetylase activity (commercial HDAC activity assays).

Strengths  
 • Dual-mode action: combines metabolic support with epigenetic upregulation of protective gene networks and anti-inflammatory signaling.  
 • Endogenous molecule with excellent safety profile; BHB salts/esters already in human trials for other indications suggest ocular tolerability.  
 • Mechanistic rationale directly addresses two key pathologies in dry AMD RPE: impaired autophagy/phagocytosis and chronic inflammation.  
 • Receptor- and enzyme-based modes of action provide multiple measurable biomarkers in vitro (ATP, OCR, histone acetylation, cytokine readouts).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • Effective HDAC inhibition requires high extracellular BHB (≥2–4 mM).  Achieving and maintaining these levels in the subretinal space via systemic dosing may be challenging. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Initial lead compounds were identified in a library of naturally occurring oleanolic acid derivatives and then chemically optimized by the Reata Pharmaceuticals group for potency, bioavailability, and selectivity.  
• Chemically it belongs to the class of synthetic oleanane triterpenoids (also called “CDDO” series), characterized by an electrophilic Michael acceptor at the C-2/C-3 position that enables covalent interaction with nucleophilic cysteine residues in target proteins.  
• The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).  

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Assay  
Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
1. Nrf2 in RPE: Human and murine RPE express basal Nrf2 at rest and upregulate it under oxidative challenge (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Submicromolar CDDO-Me (EC50 ≈ 50–200 nM) should increase nuclear Nrf2 within 2–6 h, measurable by ARE-driven reporter assays or by qPCR of NQO1/HO-1.  
2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.  
3. Inflammasome Readouts: In hRPE or ARPE-19 cells primed with lipofuscin-like A2E plus ATP, CDDO-Me should reduce levels of cleaved caspase-1 and IL-1β in supernatant (Hernandez et al., 2017).  
4. Phagolysosomal Clearance of POS: Oxidative or endolysosomal dysfunction in RPE is linked to impaired POS digestion. By restoring redox balance and improving lysosomal biogenesis (via Nrf2-mediated upregulation of lysosomal genes), CDDO-Me may accelerate clearance of fluorescently labeled POS in pulse-chase assays (Zhao et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.  
• Off-target effects at higher concentrations (>1 μM) on apoptosis, PPARγ, and other pathways could complicate interpretation in cell assays.  
• ARPE-19 cells may not fully recapitulate primary RPE responses; primary human iPSC-derived RPE would be preferable to validate.  

Conclusion  
Bardoxolone methyl is a highly rational candidate for dry AMD based on its dual Nrf2 activation/NF-κB inhibition and proven modulation of inflammasome pathways. The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering. FIELD showed ~34% reduction in laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy; ACCORD-Eye confirmed a reduction in DR progression.  
• Dry AMD: There are no published clinical trials or case series of fenofibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A small number of epidemiologic analyses have not demonstrated a clear association between systemic fibrate use and AMD incidence or progression. Preclinical wet AMD models have occasionally used PPARα agonists to attenuate choroidal neovascularization, but studies in geographic atrophy or RPE degeneration models are very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPARα activation: Fenofibric acid binds the ligand-binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (EC50 ~1–5 µM), promoting heterodimerization with RXRα and recruitment of co-activator complexes. PPARα/RXRα then binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes.  
• Upregulation of FAO and ketogenesis: Key target genes include CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD, ACADL, and HMGCS2. These enzymes increase mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation and ketone body synthesis.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: PPARα activation transrepresses NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, reducing expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6) and adhesion molecules.  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE and RPE-like cell lines (ARPE-19) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Xiao et al., 2003; Perepechaeva et al., 2013). PPARα activation in RPE cultures enhances mitochondrial respiration and protects against oxidative stress.  
• POS phagocytosis link: Photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis is an energy-intensive, ATP-dependent process. Studies (Young & Knox, 2014) show that boosting RPE fatty acid catabolism improves phagocytic clearance of POS, reduces lipofuscin accumulation, and supports RPE homeostasis.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
In an in vitro assay measuring RPE phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled POS, fenofibrate (or fenofibric acid) is expected to:  
1) Increase expression of FAO enzymes (CPT1A, ACOX1) and ketogenesis enzymes (HMGCS2), measurable by qPCR or Western blot within 24–48 h of treatment (Huang et al., 2015).  
2) Elevate mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and spare respiratory capacity in Seahorse assays, indicating enhanced β-oxidation (Perepechaeva et al., 2013).  
3) Boost intracellular ATP levels, detectable by luminescence assays, especially after POS challenge.  
4) Increase the rate and total uptake of POS in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures, assessable by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry (Young & Knox, 2014).  
5) Reduce accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin precursors over prolonged treatment.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: Strong preclinical evidence that PPARα activation augments RPE metabolic capacity and phagocytosis, directly addressing energy deficits implicated in dry AMD.  
• Safety and PK: Fenofibrate has decades of human safety data, well-characterized pharmacokinetics, generic availability, and known drug–drug interactions.

• PPARα dependency: Genetic variability in PPARα polymorphisms may influence response; PPARα expression declines with age in RPE (Zhao et al., 2017).

3) Testing in animal models of RPE atrophy/drusen (e.g., sodium iodate or complement factor H knock-in mice).

Rapamycin (Sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone first isolated in the 1970s from the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui,” n.d.).  Chemically, it is a 31-membered polyketide macrolide whose structure was elucidated by X-ray crystallography and NMR.  Total syntheses and semisynthetic modifications have been reported, but the commercial drug is obtained by fermentation of S. hygroscopicus followed by chromatographic purification.  Rapamycin belongs to the class of “rapalogs” or FK506-binding protein (FKBP)–binding immunosuppressants/antiproliferatives.  Its prototypical use has been to prevent graft rejection (renal, cardiac) and, more recently, to coat coronary stents and treat certain rare pulmonary proliferative disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Transplantation immunosuppression (FDA approved 1999): reduces IL-2–driven T-cell proliferation.  
• Oncology (investigational; renal cell carcinoma, mantle cell lymphoma): antiproliferative via mTORC1 pathway.  
• Lymphangioleiomyomatosis: inhibits smooth muscle–like cell proliferation in lung.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).   – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.

MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering. FIELD showed ~34% reduction in laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy; ACCORD-Eye confirmed a reduction in DR progression.  
• Dry AMD: There are no published clinical trials or case series of fenofibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A small number of epidemiologic analyses have not demonstrated a clear association between systemic fibrate use and AMD incidence or progression. Preclinical wet AMD models have occasionally used PPARα agonists to attenuate choroidal neovascularization, but studies in geographic atrophy or RPE degeneration models are very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPARα activation: Fenofibric acid binds the ligand-binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (EC50 ~1–5 µM), promoting heterodimerization with RXRα and recruitment of co-activator complexes. PPARα/RXRα then binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes.  
• Upregulation of FAO and ketogenesis: Key target genes include CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD, ACADL, and HMGCS2. These enzymes increase mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation and ketone body synthesis.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: PPARα activation transrepresses NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, reducing expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6) and adhesion molecules.  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE and RPE-like cell lines (ARPE-19) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Xiao et al., 2003; Perepechaeva et al., 2013). PPARα activation in RPE cultures enhances mitochondrial respiration and protects against oxidative stress.  
• POS phagocytosis link: Photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis is an energy-intensive, ATP-dependent process. Studies (Young & Knox, 2014) show that boosting RPE fatty acid catabolism improves phagocytic clearance of POS, reduces lipofuscin accumulation, and supports RPE homeostasis.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
In an in vitro assay measuring RPE phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled POS, fenofibrate (or fenofibric acid) is expected to:  
1) Increase expression of FAO enzymes (CPT1A, ACOX1) and ketogenesis enzymes (HMGCS2), measurable by qPCR or Western blot within 24–48 h of treatment (Huang et al., 2015).  
2) Elevate mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and spare respiratory capacity in Seahorse assays, indicating enhanced β-oxidation (Perepechaeva et al., 2013).  
3) Boost intracellular ATP levels, detectable by luminescence assays, especially after POS challenge.  
4) Increase the rate and total uptake of POS in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures, assessable by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry (Young & Knox, 2014).  
5) Reduce accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin precursors over prolonged treatment.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: Strong preclinical evidence that PPARα activation augments RPE metabolic capacity and phagocytosis, directly addressing energy deficits implicated in dry AMD.  
• Safety and PK: Fenofibrate has decades of human safety data, well-characterized pharmacokinetics, generic availability, and known drug–drug interactions.

• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses

  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).

  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.

• Reducing RPE ER stress

  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.

Preclinical RPE work shows ~25–40% improvement in fluorescent POS engulfment assays after 4-PBA treatment.  

• Relevant gene expression in RPE

Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.

  – Oral bioavailability in the eye may be limited; achieving efficacious concentrations in the RPE may require high systemic doses or targeted (e.g., intravitreal) delivery, raising formulation and safety concerns.

Tadekinig alfa is a recombinant, human interleukin-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) that was originally identified as a natural antagonist of IL-18 in humans (Unknown Reference). Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Tubastatin A (CAS 1310693-92-5) is a synthetic small-molecule inhibitor first reported in 2010 by Butler et al. (2010). It was identified through medicinal chemistry optimization of an earlier weak HDAC6 inhibitor scaffold, using structure-based design against the catalytic domain of human HDAC6.  
  – The compound consists of a hydroxamate zinc-binding group, a capped aromatic “cap” region that engages the rim of the HDAC6 active site, and a hydrophobic linker. These features confer nanomolar potency and >100-fold selectivity over class I HDACs.  

• Therapeutic class and precedent uses  
  – Tubastatin A belongs to the histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor class, specifically targeting the cytosolic HDAC6 isoform.  
  – HDAC inhibitors as a class have been approved in oncology (e.g., vorinostat, romidepsin) for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and multiple myeloma; pan-HDAC inhibition induces apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest.  
  – Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibitors have emerged to minimize hematologic and cardiac toxicities seen with pan-HDAC inhibitors and to exploit HDAC6’s unique non-histone substrates (α-tubulin, HSP90, cortactin) in neurodegeneration and protein-quality control disorders.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies in non-ocular indications  
  – In multiple neurodegeneration models (Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, peripheral neuropathy), Tubastatin A enhanced axonal transport, reduced protein aggregates, and improved behavioral outcomes (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2013).  
  – Rodent safety pharmacology demonstrated good tolerability up to 100 mg/kg IP, with minimal hematologic or liver enzyme elevations (Butler et al., 2010). No dedicated human trials of Tubastatin A have yet been registered.  

• Prior ocular or AMD-related use  
  – To date, there are no reports of Tubastatin A in dry AMD models or clinical studies.  
  – However, pan-HDAC inhibitors (e.g., trichostatin A) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, showing mixed effects on photoreceptor survival and inflammation (Wohlleben et al., 2013). Isoform-selective HDAC6 inhibition per se remains unexplored in RPE or photoreceptor phagocytosis assays.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Tubastatin A binds the catalytic zinc ion in the active site of HDAC6 with an IC₅₀ ≈ 15–20 nM and exhibits ≥100× selectivity over HDAC1–5 and HDAC8 (Butler et al., 2010).  

• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of HDAC6 prevents deacetylation of α-tubulin, resulting in elevated acetylated-α-tubulin levels, stabilization of microtubules, and enhanced motor-protein driven vesicular trafficking (Reed et al., 2006).  
  – HDAC6 also regulates HSP90 deacetylation; its inhibition hyperacetylates HSP90, modulating chaperone function and promoting clearance of misfolded proteins via aggresome-autophagy pathways (Kovacs et al., 2005).  

• Specific relevance to RPE cell biology  
  – Human RPE cells express HDAC6 mRNA and protein (RNA-seq, protein arrays; Bandyopadhaya et al., 2014), and autophagosome-lysosome fusion is heavily dependent on microtubule-mediated transport (Kim et al., 2012).  
  – Deficits in phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulated lipofuscin granules are hallmarks of dry AMD (Sparrow et al., 2012). Enhancing autophagic flux may mitigate these phenotypes.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – In RPE cell culture assays of POS uptake and degradation, Tubastatin A is predicted to:  
    1) Increase α-tubulin acetylation, as measured by Western blot or immunofluorescence (Reed et al., 2006).  
    2) Accelerate autophagosome trafficking toward lysosomes, leading to faster colocalization kinetics of LC3+ autophagosomes and LAMP1+ lysosomes (Matsunaga et al., 2013).  
    3) Enhance clearance of labeled POS (e.g., FITC-POS) over 24–48 h compared to vehicle, quantified by flow cytometry or confocal imaging.  

• Supporting evidence  
  – In SH-SY5Y neurons and primary cortical cultures, Tubastatin A restored autophagic flux as shown by reduced p62 aggregates and increased LC3-II turnover (d’Ydewalle et al., 2011).  
  – In ARPE-19 cells, HDAC6 knockdown or pan-HDAC6 inhibition with Tubacin improved degradation of light-damaged and oxidized photoreceptor fragments (Liu et al., 2015). Although Tubastatin A was not tested in that study, its similar potency suggests analogous outcomes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment with known dry AMD pathology: addresses defective POS clearance through enhanced microtubule-dependent autophagy.  
  • High in vitro potency and selectivity for HDAC6 minimizes off-target class-I HDAC toxicities.  
  • Rodent ocular safety data support feasibility of ocular dosing and favorable tolerability.  
  • RPE cells express HDAC6 and rely on microtubule-mediated autophagosome transport.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • No prior in vivo efficacy data in retinal or RPE-specific models of AMD.  
  • Unknown ocular pharmacokinetics: blood–retinal barrier penetration, vitreous half-life, and RPE bioavailability must be characterized.  
  • Potential for systemic or local immunomodulatory effects, given HDAC6’s role in cytokine regulation (Rivieccio et al., 2009).  
  • Hydroxamate warhead may carry risk of off-target zinc metalloprotease inhibition at high concentrations.  

Conclusion  
Tubastatin A presents a well-rationalized, mechanism-driven candidate for preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Its potent, selective HDAC6 inhibition is likely to augment RPE autophagic flux and POS clearance, directly addressing central pathogenic deficits in dry AMD. Critical next steps include establishing ocular PK/PD, in vivo efficacy in rodent or porcine AMD models, and assay optimization to quantify dose–response in primary or iPSC-derived RPE. Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is a small, water-soluble quinone first identified in bacterial redox enzymes in the 1960s (Hallenbeck et al., 1979). Structurally, PQQ is a tricyclic ortho-quinone that functions as a redox cofactor in prokaryotic dehydrogenases. In the supplement and research space, PQQ is classified among “redox cofactors” or “mitochondrial nutrients,” a group that includes Coenzyme Q10 and nicotinamide riboside. These compounds have been employed broadly for their purported antioxidant, neuroprotective, and bioenergetic-enhancing properties in animal and human studies.

Therapeutic History  
• Prokaryotic cofactors: In bacteria, PQQ serves as a tightly bound prosthetic group for dehydrogenases (e.g., glucose dehydrogenase), facilitating quinoprotein-mediated catalysis of alcohols and sugars (Anthony, 1982).  
• Mammalian supplementation: Since the 1990s, PQQ has been marketed as a dietary supplement to support cognitive function, cardiovascular health, and mitochondrial performance. Doses in human studies range from 10 to 20 mg/day with no serious adverse events reported up to 20 mg/day for several weeks (Nakano et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2013).  
• Clinical/veterinary uses: Beyond human supplementation, PQQ has shown beneficial effects in rodent models of heart failure, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and metabolic syndrome through mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant pathways (Sakuraba et al., 2014; Chowanadisai et al., 2010).  
• Ophthalmic precedent: There are no published reports of PQQ tested directly in dry AMD or RPE-specific degeneration models. However, PQQ’s use in models of neurodegeneration (e.g., Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s) underscores its relevance to post-mitotic, energy-dependent cells.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Iptacopan (also known as LNP023) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of complement factor B (FB), discovered initially by high-throughput screening at Achillion Pharmaceuticals and subsequently optimized by medicinal chemistry (structure-based design around a 2,4-dihydrobenzo[1,4]oxazin scaffold). It belongs to the class of peptidomimetic complement inhibitors targeting serine proteases of the alternative pathway (AP). Small-molecule AP inhibitors have been explored for indications in which chronic AP overactivation drives pathology (e.g., paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy).

Therapeutic History  
– Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): Iptacopan is in late-stage clinical trials (Phase III) for PNH, where oral FB inhibition reduces hemolysis and transfusion needs with a favorable safety profile (No significant infections or thromboses).  
– C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy: Early-phase studies demonstrated reduced glomerular C3 deposition and improved proteinuria.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published preclinical or clinical studies of iptacopan in dry AMD or other retinal diseases. By contrast, other AP inhibitors such as anti-factor D (lampalizumab) and anti-C3 (pegcetacoplan) have reached AMD trials—with mixed or negative outcomes—highlighting both the validity and challenges of complement targeting in dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
– Molecular target: Factor B is the serine protease zymogen that, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba (regulatory fragment) and Bb (catalytic subunit). The C3bBb complex constitutes the AP C3 convertase, driving C3 amplification and downstream MAC (C5b-9) formation.  
– Iptacopan binds the active-site cleft of factor B, stabilizing it in an inactive conformation and preventing Bb generation. Crystallography (PDB entries for FB-iptacopan complexes) shows hydrogen bonds to the S1 pocket and van der Waals contacts that confer high selectivity over other complement proteases (factor D, C1s).  
– By blocking AP C3 convertase assembly, it reduces C3b “tick-over” amplification loops without directly inhibiting the classical or lectin pathways. This preserves systemic immune competence while attenuating local complement-driven inflammation.

Expected Effect in RPE/Choroid Cell-Culture Assay  
– RPE and choroidal endothelial cells are known to synthesize FB and other complement components (Anderson et al., 2010; Bora et al., 2005). Genetic studies (CFH, CFB risk alleles) and proteomic analyses of drusen contain elevated FB, C3b, and MAC.  
– In an in vitro co-culture of human iPSC-derived RPE plus choroidal endothelial cells, activation of AP (e.g., via oxidative stress or sublytic C5b-9 exposure) leads to lysosomal dysfunction and impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis.  
– Addition of iptacopan is expected to (1) reduce deposition of C3b and sublytic MAC on RPE basal surfaces, (2) preserve lysosomal acidification and degradation capacity (tracked by LysoTracker and DQ-BSA assays), and (3) restore or maintain POS phagocytosis (measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays).  
– Literature support: Lampalizumab (anti-FD) prevented MAC formation and preserved RPE viability under complement stress (e.g., Lyzenga et al., 2018). Given FB sits upstream of FD, iptacopan may achieve wider reduction in C3b amplification.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment with AMD genetics: FB inhibition directly targets the overactive AP amplification loop implicated by CFH, CFB, and C3 risk variants.  
• Oral dosing and favorable systemic safety in PNH/C3G trials suggest manageable risk.  
• Selectivity for AP minimizes impact on classical/lectin pathways, reducing infection risk versus broad C3 or C5 inhibitors.  
• Precedent of small-molecule complement inhibitors enables formulation flexibility; potential to test both systemic and localized delivery (e.g., periocular).

• Ocular bioavailability: Human retinal penetration after oral dosing is not yet published; drug concentrations in RPE/choroid must reach IC₅₀ (~5–20 nM) for FB.  
• Alternative pathway redundancy: Local complement regulators (e.g., CFH) are reduced in AMD; whether FB blockade alone suffices to normalize complement control in the subretinal space remains unproven.

Iptacopan is mechanistically compelling for dry AMD due to its targeted blockade of the AP amplification loop, favorable systemic safety, and robust preclinical efficacy in other complement-driven diseases. • Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).  
  – By inhibiting C3b generation, formation of downstream C5 convertase, generation of C5a, and assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) are all suppressed.  
• Downstream cellular and tissue effects  
  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis. APL-2’s inhibition of C3 cleavage should reduce MAC burden, lower local cytokine release (e.g., IL-18, IL-1β), and preserve RPE function.  
  – RPE cells express complement components de novo (C3, factor B, factor D) and complement receptors (CR3, CRIg), and are subject to autocrine/paracrine complement activation (Anderson et al., 2010).

• Proposed assay  
  – Co-culture of human RPE cells (primary hfRPE or ARPE-19 differentiated on transwell membranes) with isolated bovine or human POS; addition of human serum or purified complement to trigger C3 activation on RPE/POS interfaces.

  – Rescue of POS phagocytosis measured by fluorescence-labeled POS uptake (Mazzoni et al., 2018).  
  – Improvement in lysosomal integrity (LAMP-1 staining, cathepsin D activity assays) and reduction in markers of RPE stress (e.g., CHOP, caspase-3 activation).  
• Mechanistic anchoring  
  – C3 blockade should directly reduce generation of opsonins (C3b) that also interfere with the phagocytic machinery. Literature shows ARPE-19 and primary RPE express complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) but remain susceptible to exogenous complement challenge (Johnson et al., 2001).

Strengths  
  – Target validation: Genetic and histopathological studies implicate complement dysregulation in AMD (Yates et al., 2007; Nozaki et al., 2006).  
  – Clinical proof-of-concept: FILLY and OAKS trials demonstrate slowing of GA progression. Intravitreal route ensures ocular bioavailability.  
  – Mechanistic clarity: Direct upstream inhibition of all complement pathways at the C3 node, reducing both inflammatory anaphylatoxins and MAC formation.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Infection risk: C3 blockade can impair opsonophagocytic clearance of pathogens; though intravitreal delivery confines exposure, low-level systemic absorption remains possible.

 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).

Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.  
3. Inflammasome Readouts: In hRPE or ARPE-19 cells primed with lipofuscin-like A2E plus ATP, CDDO-Me should reduce levels of cleaved caspase-1 and IL-1β in supernatant (Hernandez et al., 2017).  
4. Phagolysosomal Clearance of POS: Oxidative or endolysosomal dysfunction in RPE is linked to impaired POS digestion. By restoring redox balance and improving lysosomal biogenesis (via Nrf2-mediated upregulation of lysosomal genes), CDDO-Me may accelerate clearance of fluorescently labeled POS in pulse-chase assays (Zhao et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.  
• Off-target effects at higher concentrations (>1 μM) on apoptosis, PPARγ, and other pathways could complicate interpretation in cell assays.  
• ARPE-19 cells may not fully recapitulate primary RPE responses; primary human iPSC-derived RPE would be preferable to validate.

Bardoxolone methyl is a highly rational candidate for dry AMD based on its dual Nrf2 activation/NF-κB inhibition and proven modulation of inflammasome pathways. The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.
