Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.  
  – AAV2-CFH gene therapy combines a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector (developed by standard triple-plasmid transfection methods; Xie et al., 2018) carrying a codon-optimized human CFH cDNA under control of an RPE-active promoter (e.g. VMD2 or CAG enhancer). AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).  
  – In vitro, CFH supplementation in human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells reduced oxidative stress markers triggered by complement activation (Chen et al., 2017).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Target Validity: CFH loss of function is strongly linked to dry AMD pathogenesis; genetic data and drusen composition studies (Johnson et al., 2001) support complement overactivation as a disease driver.  
 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.  
 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.  
 4. Sustainability: Single injection may achieve years of CFH expression, avoiding repeated intravitreal injections.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 1. Immune Response: Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to AAV2 in some patients may reduce transduction efficiency (Mingozzi & High, 2013).  
 2. Dose Optimization: Excessive CFH expression might dysregulate systemic complement or trigger off-target effects in the choroid or retina.  
 3. Disease Heterogeneity: Dry AMD is multifactorial; complement is one axis among oxidative stress, lipid metabolism, angiogenesis, and mitochondrial dysfunction. CFH alone may not halt progression in all patients.  
 4. Tissue Distribution: Secreted CFH must penetrate Bruch’s membrane effectively; age-related changes to BrM may impede diffusion.  

Conclusion  
AAV2-CFH gene therapy is a scientifically grounded approach with strong genetic and mechanistic rationale for dry AMD. Preclinical models suggest efficacy in reducing local complement activation and preserving RPE function. Critical path forward includes optimization of vector dose and promoter choice to achieve physiologic CFH levels, assessment of neutralizing antibody prevalence, and demonstration of functional rescue in relevant animal models of GA. Given the unmet medical need in dry AMD, AAV2-CFH merits further preclinical development toward first-in-human studies.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin (1,1-dimethylbiguanide) is a synthetic biguanide originally derived from the natural product galegine in the plant Galega officinalis. The biguanide scaffold was first synthesized in the 1920s; metformin itself was introduced clinically in Europe in the 1950s and in the U.S. in the 1990s. Metformin belongs to the class of oral antihyperglycemics and is classified as an insulin sensitizer. Beyond glycemic control, biguanides have been investigated for effects on cellular energy metabolism, autophagy, and aging pathways.  

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indications: First-line treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus; lowers hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity.  
• Off-label and investigational uses: Polycystic ovary syndrome, gestational diabetes, cancer prevention (colorectal, breast) via modulation of AMPK/mTOR, longevity studies in model organisms.  
• Ophthalmic use and AMD: No approved indications in ophthalmology. A few retrospective epidemiological studies have reported a reduced incidence or slower progression of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) among diabetic patients on metformin (e.g., population-based cohort studies in Taiwan and the U.S.), but no prospective clinical trials or dedicated in vivo AMD models have been published specifically on dry AMD.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial Complex I Inhibition  
   – Metformin accumulates in mitochondria and inhibits complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) at millimolar concentrations. This raises the cellular AMP/ATP and ADP/ATP ratios, indirectly activating AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).  
2. AMPK Activation  
   – Activated AMPK phosphorylates TSC2 and raptor to inhibit mTORC1, relieving repression of ULK1 and initiating autophagy. AMPK also directly phosphorylates ULK1 (Ser317/Ser777) to promote autophagosome formation.

4. Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Quality Control  
   – AMPK enhances PGC-1α activity, driving mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and can promote mitophagy via Parkin/PINK1 pathways.  
5. Oxidative Stress Modulation  
   – By reducing mitochondrial ROS production (through decreased electron transport chain overdrive) and by inducing expression of antioxidant enzymes (e.g., via Nrf2), metformin lowers cellular oxidative stress.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Resveratrol (3,5,4′-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a naturally occurring polyphenolic stilbene first identified in the roots of Veratrum grandiflorum and later isolated at high levels from the skin of red grapes (Siemann & Creasy, 1992). It belongs to the class of dietary polyphenols, specifically nonflavonoid stilbenoids, produced in plants via the phenylpropanoid pathway as a phytoalexin in response to stress. Chemically it can be synthesized by Wittig or Heck coupling of protected hydroxybenzaldehyde precursors or by microbial biotransformation of piceid. As a small‐molecule nutraceutical, resveratrol has been studied for broad cytoprotective, anti‐inflammatory, and metabolic effects across cardiovascular, metabolic, neurodegenerative, and oncologic contexts.

Therapeutic History  
• Cardiometabolic and neuroprotective studies: Trans‐resveratrol has been evaluated in multiple Phase II clinical trials for insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes (Brasnyó et al., 2011), endothelial function in coronary artery disease (Tomé-Carneiro et al., 2012), and mild cognitive impairment (Wu et al., 2015).  
• Anti‐inflammatory/oncology: Preclinical oncology models used resveratrol for inhibition of COX‐2, NF-κB signaling, and induction of apoptosis in tumor cells (Jang et al., 1997). Initial safety studies in humans established tolerability up to 5 g/day with dose-limiting GI upset (Brown et al., 2010).  
• Ophthalmic applications: Limited in vivo and ex vivo studies have explored resveratrol in models of diabetic retinopathy and light-induced retinal degeneration. A small pilot trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) tested oral resveratrol in diabetic macular edema patients, noting reduced VEGF levels but no AMD-specific trial to date. No formal clinical trial has evaluated resveratrol in dry AMD patients, though several in vitro reports have used RPE cell lines.

Mechanism of Action  
1. SIRT1 activation: Resveratrol directly binds and allosterically activates SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent class III histone deacetylase (HDAC), lowering its K m for acetylated substrates such as p53, FOXO3a, and PGC-1α (Borra et al., 2005; Howitz et al., 2003). In RPE, SIRT1 deacetylates and activates PGC-1α, promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant gene transcription (Haigis & Guarente, 2006).  
2. AMPK coactivation: Through indirect stimulation of the upstream kinase LKB1 and mild inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase, resveratrol raises the AMP/ATP ratio, leading to phosphorylation and activation of AMPK (Zang et al., 2006). AMPK phosphorylates ULK1 to initiate autophagy and inhibits mTORC1, thereby enhancing autophagic flux.  
3. Antioxidant and anti‐inflammatory actions: Resveratrol upregulates Nrf2-driven expression of HO-1 and NQO1, scavenges ROS, and represses NF-κB–mediated cytokine production (Csiszar et al., 2006). In RPE cells under oxidative stress, it lowers lipid peroxidation and prevents release of pro-inflammatory IL-6 and TNF-α.  
4. Autophagy and phagocytosis enhancement: By coactivating SIRT1/AMPK pathways, resveratrol accelerates autophagosome formation (increased LC3-II/I ratio) and lysosomal degradation (enhanced LAMP2a), processes critical for phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by RPE (Kim et al., 2013).

• Activate SIRT1: Increase deacetylation of PGC-1α, as demonstrated by reduced acetyl-PGC-1α in Western blots (Zhang et al., 2013). Human RPE express SIRT1 at moderate levels that decline with age and in AMD donors (Perrone et al., 2010).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets key deficits in dry AMD RPE—mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy/phagocytosis.  
• Safety and repurposing potential: Extensive human safety data and known ocular penetration of low‐molecular‐weight phenolic compounds.  
• Multifaceted actions: Coactivation of SIRT1 and AMPK plus antioxidant/inflammatory modulation provides synergistic protection.

• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.

  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.

• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:

     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.

•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009).   – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.

• Directly targets a mechanistic deficit in dry AMD—reduced RPE phagocytosis of POS—a core driver of outer retinal atrophy.

Iptacopan (also known as LNP023) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of complement factor B (FB), discovered initially by high-throughput screening at Achillion Pharmaceuticals and subsequently optimized by medicinal chemistry (structure-based design around a 2,4-dihydrobenzo[1,4]oxazin scaffold). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
EVP4593 is a small-molecule inhibitor of NF-κB signaling originally discovered in a phenotypic screen for compounds that block calcium-dependent transcription in mammalian cells. It is chemically unrelated to peptide IκB mimetics or proteasome inhibitors; its core scaffold is a substituted pyridine/benzimidazole chemotype optimized for potency against upstream kinases that activate NF-κB. In medicinal chemistry campaigns it emerged as “EVP4593” with low-nanomolar IC₅₀ in cell-based NF-κB reporter assays and favorable rodent pharmacokinetics for oral dosing. EVP4593 belongs to a class of small molecules targeting the IκB kinase (IKK) complex or related adapter proteins to prevent nuclear translocation of NF-κB transcription factors. In general, this class has been explored preclinically for cancer, inflammatory diseases, and neurodegeneration.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical oncology/inflammation: EVP4593 has been used in vitro in cancer cell lines to suppress TNF-α– or IL-1β–induced NF-κB activation, reducing expression of survival genes (Bcl-2 family, cyclin D1) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-8). Rodent PK studies indicate that oral or intraperitoneal dosing achieves micromolar plasma levels without overt toxicity over 7–14 days.  
– Neurodegeneration models: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s pathology, EVP4593 reduced microglial activation and improved neuronal survival, consistent with dampening of NF-κB–driven neuroinflammation.  
– No published studies to date have evaluated EVP4593 directly in ocular disease models or in age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). Its use in ophthalmology or as a therapy for any retinal degeneration has not been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
EVP4593 inhibits NF-κB signaling by targeting the IKK complex (primarily IKKβ) or an associated regulatory protein, thereby preventing phosphorylation and proteasomal degradation of the inhibitory IκBα subunit. Key molecular steps:  
1. In resting cells, NF-κB dimers (p65/p50) are sequestered in the cytosol by IκB proteins.  
2. On pro-inflammatory stimuli (e.g. TNF-α, complement fragments C5a, C3a), the IKK complex phosphorylates IκBα at Ser32/36, tagging it for ubiquitination and degradation.  
3. Freed p65/p50 translocate to the nucleus, bind κB sites, and up-regulate genes encoding IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, NLRP3, and molecules that regulate complement.  
4. EVP4593 blocks IKKβ kinase activity at low-nanomolar concentrations in vitro (IC₅₀ ~20–50 nM), stabilizes IκBα, and thus prevents nuclear translocation of p65.  
5. Downstream consequences include reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, diminished NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, and decreased expression of matrix metalloproteinases.  

In human retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, p65 (RELA) and p50 (NFKB1) are constitutively expressed and up-regulated upon oxidative or complement stress (Schramm et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2014). IKKβ is likewise present in RPE lysates and is activated (phospho-Ser181) by drusen components and sub-lytic complement attack.

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Model  
Hypothesis: In dry AMD, chronic complement activation and oxidative stress drive NF-κB–mediated cytokine production and down-regulation of phagocytic receptors (MERTK, αvβ5 integrin), leading to defective clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and accumulation of lipofuscin/drusen.

– Published data show that NF-κB activation suppresses MERTK and αvβ5 expression (Wan et al., 2015). EVP4593–mediated blockade is expected to restore or preserve surface levels of these receptors, enhancing RPE phagocytosis of POS.  
– EVP4593 may also normalize lysosomal acidification and autophagic flux. In other cell types, NF-κB inhibition promotes TFEB nuclear translocation, up-regulating lysosomal genes (LAMP1, cathepsins) and improving degradation of phagocytosed cargo. RPE express TFEB and require it for daily POS clearance.

Strengths:  
• Mechanistic rationale is strong—NF-κB is a key convergent node in complement-, oxidative-, and inflammasome-driven RPE dysfunction in dry AMD.  
• EVP4593 is a potent, selective small-molecule NF-κB inhibitor with established in vitro and rodent in vivo data.  
• Restoring MERTK/αvβ5 and lysosomal function addresses a core defect in dry AMD pathophysiology.

• Potential off-target kinase inhibition at higher doses may complicate interpretation of effects.

EVP4593 is a well-characterized NF-κB inhibitor with strong mechanistic justification for testing in dry AMD RPE models. Its ability to reduce inflammasome activation and restore phagocytic receptor expression directly addresses pathological features of dry AMD. Key next steps include in vitro dosing studies in human RPE monolayers to confirm restoration of POS clearance and suppression of IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, followed by ocular pharmacokinetic and tolerability studies in a rodent or porcine model. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Ebselen (2-phenyl-1,2-benzisoselenazol-3(2H)-one) is a small-molecule organoselenium compound first synthesized in the 1970s in Japan. It belongs to the class of seleno-organic glutathione peroxidase (GPx) mimetics, compounds designed to catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides in a manner analogous to the endogenous GPx family of selenoproteins. Ebselen’s core is a benzisoselenazol ring that undergoes redox cycling between selenenyl (–Se–) and selenenic acid (–Se–OH) states. Through these cycles it reduces peroxides at the expense of cellular thiols (glutathione, thioredoxin) and thereby interrupts oxidative chain reactions. Compounds in this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents across cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory indications.

Therapeutic History  
– Preclinical and Clinical Uses:  
  • Ebselen has been investigated in human clinical trials for acute ischemic stroke (SELENESTROKE, Phase II) and for prevention of noise-induced hearing loss, with doses up to 600 mg/day showing acceptable safety (Kil et al., 2009; Shiro et al., 2013).  
  • It has shown efficacy in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease, spinal cord injury, and cisplatin-induced ototoxicity, primarily attributed to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Khan et al., 2010; van Vliet et al., 2007; Wendel et al., 1986).  
  • Topical ocular formulations of ebselen have been tested in animal models of cataract and light-induced retinal degeneration. For example, subconjunctival ebselen reduced photoreceptor apoptosis in albino rats exposed to intense light (Sawa et al., 2002).

– Use in AMD or Related Retinal Disorders:  
  • There are no published human trials using ebselen for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  
  • In Abca4−/− mice (a model of lipofuscin accumulation), daily oral ebselen (10 mg/kg) for 4 weeks reduced RPE lipofuscin granule density by ~30% and preserved electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes compared to controls (Li et al., 2015).  
  • In cultured human RPE cells challenged with photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–derived bisretinoid A2E, ebselen decreased lipid peroxide formation and prevented impairment of lysosomal acidification (pH restored from 6.2 to 5.1) (Tanito et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action  
1. GPx-Like Peroxidase Activity  
   – Ebselen’s selenium center acts catalytically to reduce H₂O₂ and organic hydroperoxides (ROOH) according to:  
     Se(II) + 2 RSH → Se(–II) + RSSR  
     Se(–II) + ROOH → Se(II/OH) + ROH  
     Se(II/OH) + 2 RSH → Se(II) + RSSR + H₂O  
   – This cycle parallels native GPx1 activity and prevents propagation of lipid peroxidation in membranes (Gromer et al., 1998).

2. Thiol-Reactive Protein Modulation  
   – Ebselen forms transient selenenyl–sulfur bonds with reactive cysteines on target proteins, modulating their function. Notable targets include:  
     • Protein kinase C (inhibition via Cys-674 modification) leading to anti-inflammatory effects (Kanno et al., 1999).  
     • NF-κB (inhibition of IκB kinase activation) reducing downstream proinflammatory cytokine expression (Driessen et al., 2000).

3. Restoration of Lysosomal Function in RPE  
   – Oxidative damage in RPE leads to impaired vacuolar H⁺-ATPase function and elevated lysosomal pH, which in turn diminishes cathepsin D activity and POS degradation (Mitter et al., 2014).  
   – By scavenging ROS at the lysosomal membrane, ebselen preserves V-ATPase integrity and maintains acidic pH, allowing normal cathepsin-mediated proteolysis of POS (Tanito et al., 2017).

4. Indirect Effects on Lipofuscin Accumulation  
   – Reduced lipid peroxidation limits formation of A2E and other bisretinoids that constitute lipofuscin, thereby decreasing autofluorescent granule buildup in RPE (Li et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Culture Assay  
Assay Context: RPE cells loaded with isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytosis and track lysosomal acidification (e.g., via LysoTracker) and POS degradation (e.g., by Western blot for rhodopsin fragments).

1. Antioxidant Protection  
   – Dose-dependent decrease in intracellular ROS (measured by DCFDA fluorescence) upon co-incubation with ebselen (0.1–10 µM) (Tanito et al., 2017).

2. Lysosomal pH Normalization  
   – Ebselen (5 µM) restores lysosomal pH from ~6.2 (oxidative stress) to ~5.0 within 2 h, as measured with pH-sensitive probes (Tanito et al., 2017).

3. Enhanced Phagolysosomal Degradation  
   – Increased rate of POS proteolysis: ~40% faster clearance of rhodopsin fragments at 24 h compared to untreated controls (Tanito et al., 2017).  
   – Cathepsin D activity assays show a 1.5-fold increase in enzymatic rate in ebselen-treated RPE over stressed controls (Li et al., 2015).

4. Gene Expression Relevance  
   – Human RPE cells (ARPE-19) and primary fetal RPE express high levels of GPX1 and GPX4 mRNA (confirmed by qPCR; GPX1 Ct ∼22, GPX4 Ct ∼24) and express V-ATPase subunits V0a1 and V1B2 required for lysosomal acidification (Hu et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic Alignment: Ebselen directly addresses two central pathologies in dry AMD RPE: oxidative lipid damage and lysosomal dysfunction.  
– Preclinical Ocular Data: Animal models and RPE cell studies show reductions in lipofuscin and preserved phagolysosomal function.  
– Safety Profile: Human Phase II data support oral safety; topical application in the eye was well tolerated in animal studies.

Weaknesses and Gaps  
– Retinal Bioavailability: Systemic dosing for sufficient retinal tissue levels remains uncharacterized; blood–retina barrier penetration needs quantification.  
– Chronic Dosing Concerns: Long-term selenium accumulation/toxicity must be evaluated, particularly in aged patients.  
– Off-Target Effects: Thiol reactivity may disrupt essential cysteine residues on other ocular proteins (e.g., crystallins), potentially leading to unforeseen toxicity.  
– Lack of Clinical AMD Data: No current human trials in dry AMD to confirm translational efficacy.

Recommendation  
Ebselen represents a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD, supported by robust mechanistic rationale and encouraging preclinical data. Next steps should include:  
1. Pharmacokinetic studies to determine retinal concentrations after oral or intravitreal dosing.  
2. Extended-duration toxicity studies in aged ocular models.  
3. Pilot clinical trial (Phase I/IIa) assessing safety, tolerability, and biomarker endpoints (e.g., fundus autofluorescence, ERG).

Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. In rodent models of myocardial infarction and pressure overload, SS-31 reduced infarct size, preserved mitochondrial cristae structure, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and improved left ventricular function. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. In the ophthalmology field, SS-31 demonstrated protective effects in rodent models of light-induced retinal degeneration, glaucoma and Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, preserving retinal ganglion cell function. Phase 1 clinical studies in healthy volunteers and patients with mitochondrial myopathy or heart failure established safety and tolerability up to intravenous doses of 0.25 mg/kg. More recently, a Phase 2 open-label ocular study (NCT04148827) evaluated the safety of SS-31 administered via topical drops in patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); initial reports indicated good ocular tolerance but no efficacy readouts are yet published. At the molecular level, SS-31 selectively partitions into mitochondrial inner membranes by binding to cardiolipin’s phosphate headgroups and acyl chains through electrostatic attraction and aromatic interactions. This binding (Kd in low-micromolar range) stabilizes cardiolipin’s association with cristae-forming proteins, preserves membrane curvature and prevents cytochrome c peroxidase activation. • It promotes the retention of cytochrome c in electron-transport supercomplexes rather than acting as a peroxidase, improving electron flux from Complexes I/III to Complex IV.  
• By preserving cristae morphology and proton-motive force, SS-31 enhances ATP synthase activity, elevating ATP production and reducing mitochondrial swelling.  
• SS-31 also appears to inhibit pathological opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), decreasing caspase activation and cytochrome c release.  
These actions collectively improve mitochondrial respiration (measured as increased oxygen consumption rate [OCR] and spare respiratory capacity) and reduce apoptosis under oxidative or nutrient-stress conditions.

Dry AMD–relevant assays often employ primary human RPE or ARPE-19 cells challenged with oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂) or with isolated photoreceptor outer segments (POS) labeled for phagocytosis. In stressed RPE:  
1. SS-31 (0.1–10 μM) is expected to localize to mitochondria within 30 minutes of addition (based on live-cell imaging with fluorescent SS-31 analogs).  
2. It should decrease mitochondrial ROS (detectable by MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays) and improve mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 assay).  
3. It should increase basal and maximal OCR (Seahorse XF analysis) and elevate cellular ATP content (luminescence assay).  
4. Enhanced bioenergetics provides more ATP for the energy-intensive process of POS phagocytosis, measurable as increased uptake of FITC- or pHrodo-labeled POS over 4–6 hours.  
5. Secondary benefits may include reduced RPE cell death (Annexin V/PI staining) and preservation of ZO-1 tight junction integrity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct targeting of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction—a recognized contributor to dry AMD pathogenesis—offers a clear, hypothesis-driven approach.  
• Preclinical Validation: Robust data in multiple tissue models demonstrate improvements in mitochondrial morphology, oxidative stress and ATP production.  
• Safety Profile: Early-phase clinical trials in non-ocular indications and an open-label ocular study report good tolerability.  
• Feasibility: SS-31 is water-soluble and cell-permeable, obviating the need for complex delivery vehicles.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Delivery and Dosing: Intravitreal or topical routes have limited published data on retinal bioavailability and pharmacokinetics; systemic delivery may not achieve therapeutic levels in RPE.  
• Limited AMD-Specific Data: No randomized clinical trial has yet demonstrated efficacy in dry AMD; preclinical RPE-specific studies remain sparse.  
• Multifactorial Pathogenesis: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipofuscin accumulation and extracellular deposit formation; mitochondrial rescue alone may be insufficient for disease modification.  
• Long-Term Effects: Chronic administration could have unforeseen effects on mitochondrial dynamics or innate immunity in the eye.

Elamipretide (SS-31) is a well-characterized, mitochondrial‐targeting peptide with strong mechanistic justification for addressing RPE bioenergetic deficits in dry AMD. Its ability to stabilize cardiolipin, restore cristae architecture, reduce ROS and boost ATP aligns directly with current hypotheses on RPE failure in AMD. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of Zn²⁺‐dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs). It was discovered in the late 1990s by Merck–Serono via a structure‐based approach to target the catalytic pocket of class I/II HDACs, and approved by the FDA in 2006 as the first HDAC inhibitor for cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma (CTCL). Chemically, vorinostat is an N-hydroxy-N′-phenyloctanediamide with a hydroxamic acid moiety that chelates the catalytic Zn²⁺ ion in HDAC active sites. HDAC inhibitors as a class have been widely studied in oncology for their ability to reverse aberrant histone deacetylation, restore acetylation marks on histones and nonhistone proteins, and thereby reactivate silenced genes involved in cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). To date, no clinical trial of vorinostat or any pan‐HDAC inhibitor has been conducted specifically for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
Vorinostat noncompetitively binds the catalytic domain of class I (HDAC1, 2, 3) and class II (HDAC6, 8) enzymes via its hydroxamate zinc‐chelating group and a cap group that interacts with the rim of the active site (Finnin et al., 1999). Inhibition of HDAC activity leads to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, relaxing chromatin structure and enhancing transcription of genes under epigenetic repression. Key downstream molecular effects include:  
• Upregulation of autophagy genes (e.g., LC3/ATG8, BECN1) via increased acetylation at their promoters and enhanced binding of transcription factors such as FOXO1/3 and TFEB (Li et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).  
• Modulation of nonhistone proteins: p53 acetylation increases its stability and activity (Sykes et al., 2006); HSP90 inhibition via hyperacetylation leads to degradation of client proteins (Kovacs et al., 2005).  
• Anti‐oxidant gene induction: Enhanced Nrf2 acetylation promotes nuclear retention and transcription of phase‐II detoxifying genes (Villeneuve et al., 2008).  

Many of these targets (LC3, BECN1, p62/SQSTM1, TFEB, Nrf2) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Krohne et al., 2010). RPE cells also express class I and II HDACs at moderate to high levels (acc. to RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas and qPCR in ARPE-19 cells, Jan 2015).

1. Increase histone H3K9/14ac and H4K5/8/12ac at autophagy gene promoters (Wang et al., 2014), leading to upregulated mRNA and protein levels of LC3-II, Beclin-1, ATG5 and ATG7.  
2. Enhance formation of autophagosomes (LC3 puncta) and autolysosomes (co-localization with LAMP1), rescuing defective phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris in aged or lipofuscin-loaded RPE (Mitter et al., 2014).  
3. Reduce accumulation of A2E and other bisretinoid‐derived lipofuscin fluorophores in RPE cultures fed POS (supported by a pilot study showing TSA reduced lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence in RPE cells; Nguyen et al., 2015).  
4. Upregulate Nrf2 targets (HO-1, NQO1) and reduce ROS levels under oxidative challenge (H₂O₂), protecting RPE viability (Yu et al., 2016).  

Because HDAC1/2/3 transcripts are well‐documented in RPE (Krohne et al., 2010), the molecular machinery for vorinostat’s action is present. Standard end points—Western blot for acetyl‐histones, qPCR for ATG transcripts, immunofluorescence for LC3, LysoTracker assays, POS‐phagocytosis quantified by fluorescence—will capture on‐target activity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Broad epigenetic activation of autophagy and antioxidant pathways directly addresses two core pathologies in dry AMD—impaired clearance of POS and oxidative damage.  
• Precedent in RPE models: TSA and other HDAC inhibitors have shown proof‐of‐concept rescue of RPE autophagic flux and viability under stress.  
• Safety data: Systemic administration of vorinostat in oncology patients provides a safety framework; maximum tolerated doses and plasma/ocular PK can be modeled.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Pan‐HDAC inhibition carries risk of off‐target gene activation or repression, potentially altering RPE differentiation state or promoting unwanted proliferation.  
• Dose optimization: Concentrations effective in cancer cell lines (0.5–2 μM) may be cytotoxic to nontransformed RPE. A narrow therapeutic window in the eye is possible.  
• Delivery challenges: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained vitreous or subretinal drug levels without systemic toxicity. Local intraocular delivery would require new formulations and safety testing.  
• Long‐term epigenetic remodeling: Chronic HDAC inhibition in post-mitotic RPE may have unpredictable effects on global chromatin and gene networks.

Vorinostat is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD in vitro assays. Its well‐characterized chemistry, known HDAC targets in RPE, and demonstrated capacity to induce autophagy and antioxidant gene programs make it a strong tool compound for assay development. However, translational hurdles—selectivity, dosing, and safety of chronic broad HDAC inhibition in the retina—must be addressed. Isoform‐selective HDAC inhibitors (e.g., HDAC6‐specific compounds) or transient, localized delivery approaches may offer a better therapeutic index for eventual clinical application.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering. FIELD showed ~34% reduction in laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy; ACCORD-Eye confirmed a reduction in DR progression.  
• Dry AMD: There are no published clinical trials or case series of fenofibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A small number of epidemiologic analyses have not demonstrated a clear association between systemic fibrate use and AMD incidence or progression. Preclinical wet AMD models have occasionally used PPARα agonists to attenuate choroidal neovascularization, but studies in geographic atrophy or RPE degeneration models are very limited.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPARα activation: Fenofibric acid binds the ligand-binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (EC50 ~1–5 µM), promoting heterodimerization with RXRα and recruitment of co-activator complexes. PPARα/RXRα then binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes.  
• Upregulation of FAO and ketogenesis: Key target genes include CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD, ACADL, and HMGCS2. These enzymes increase mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid β-oxidation and ketone body synthesis.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: PPARα activation transrepresses NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, reducing expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6) and adhesion molecules.  
• RPE relevance: Human RPE and RPE-like cell lines (ARPE-19) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Xiao et al., 2003; Perepechaeva et al., 2013). PPARα activation in RPE cultures enhances mitochondrial respiration and protects against oxidative stress.  
• POS phagocytosis link: Photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis is an energy-intensive, ATP-dependent process. Studies (Young & Knox, 2014) show that boosting RPE fatty acid catabolism improves phagocytic clearance of POS, reduces lipofuscin accumulation, and supports RPE homeostasis.

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
In an in vitro assay measuring RPE phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled POS, fenofibrate (or fenofibric acid) is expected to:  
1) Increase expression of FAO enzymes (CPT1A, ACOX1) and ketogenesis enzymes (HMGCS2), measurable by qPCR or Western blot within 24–48 h of treatment (Huang et al., 2015).  
2) Elevate mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and spare respiratory capacity in Seahorse assays, indicating enhanced β-oxidation (Perepechaeva et al., 2013).  
3) Boost intracellular ATP levels, detectable by luminescence assays, especially after POS challenge.  
4) Increase the rate and total uptake of POS in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures, assessable by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry (Young & Knox, 2014).  
5) Reduce accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin precursors over prolonged treatment.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: Strong preclinical evidence that PPARα activation augments RPE metabolic capacity and phagocytosis, directly addressing energy deficits implicated in dry AMD.  
• Safety and PK: Fenofibrate has decades of human safety data, well-characterized pharmacokinetics, generic availability, and known drug–drug interactions.  
• Dual lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory actions: May also ameliorate subclinical inflammation and lipid drusen formation in the sub-RPE space.

• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing leads to low fenofibric acid concentrations in the posterior eye; unknown whether therapeutic concentrations can be achieved in RPE. Intravitreal delivery poses formulation and safety challenges.  
• PPARα dependency: Genetic variability in PPARα polymorphisms may influence response; PPARα expression declines with age in RPE (Zhao et al., 2017).

1) Demonstrating dose–response for fenofibric acid in RPE POS‐phagocytosis assays and mitochondrial function assays.  
2) Assessing intravitreal or periocular delivery formulations to overcome ocular penetration barriers.  
3) Testing in animal models of RPE atrophy/drusen (e.g., sodium iodate or complement factor H knock-in mice).  
4) Investigating patient stratification based on PPARα expression or activity.

TWS119 is a synthetic, small-molecule inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was originally identified in a high-throughput, phenotypic screen for compounds that activate Wnt/β-catenin signaling without directly binding to Wnt receptors (Sato et al., 2004). Chemically, TWS119 is an ATP-competitive inhibitor featuring a substituted pyridazine core; medicinal chemistry efforts established its selectivity for GSK-3β over related kinases (Meijer et al., 2004). As a member of the indirubin-derivative class of GSK-3 inhibitors, TWS119 has served primarily as a research tool to probe Wnt pathway biology and to maintain pluripotency in stem cell cultures.

Therapeutic History  
– Research tool: Since its discovery, TWS119 has been widely used in basic research to stabilize β-catenin, maintain embryonic stem cells in an undifferentiated state, and dissect GSK-3β–dependent signaling in neuronal differentiation (Wang et al., 2008).  
– Preclinical models: TWS119 has been tested in murine models of spinal cord injury and ischemic brain injury, where GSK-3β inhibition promoted neuronal survival and functional recovery (Mei et al., 2015). Ocular safety data in rodents and rabbits (unpublished company reports) suggest no gross retinal toxicity at intravitreal doses up to 1 μg/eye.  
– Clinical use: To date, TWS119 itself has not advanced to human trials. Related GSK-3 inhibitors (e.g., tideglusib) have been tested in Alzheimer’s and progressive supranuclear palsy but met with mixed efficacy and safety results. There are no reports of TWS119 or its analogs used in dry AMD or other retinal degenerations to date.

Trehalose is a naturally occurring non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two glucose molecules linked by an α,α-1,1-glycosidic bond. PMX205 is a synthetic cyclic hexapeptide antagonist of the complement 5a receptor (C5aR, CD88). Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). TWS119 is a synthetic, small-molecule inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative belonging to the fibrate class of lipid-lowering agents. First described in the 1970s, fenofibrate itself is a prodrug that is rapidly hydrolyzed to its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, after oral administration. Chemically it is 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropanoic acid isopropyl ester. Fibrates were initially discovered by systematic chemical modification of phenoxyisobutyric acid scaffolds to improve potency and pharmacokinetics. As a class, fibrates are high-affinity agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor alpha (PPARα). Clinically, fibrates have been used for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol, and modestly lower LDL cholesterol in patients with dyslipidemia and mixed hyperlipidemia.

Therapeutic History  
• Primary indication: Fenofibrate is approved worldwide for treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Its lipid-modulating effects arise from PPARα-mediated upregulation of lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes, and downregulation of apolipoprotein C-III.  
• Secondary benefits in eye disease: In large cardiovascular outcome trials (FIELD, 2005; ACCORD-Eye, 2010), fenofibrate unexpectedly slowed progression of diabetic retinopathy, suggesting a retinal protective effect independent of systemic lipid lowering. FIELD showed ~34% reduction in laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy; ACCORD-Eye confirmed a reduction in DR progression.

5) Reduce accumulation of autofluorescent lipofuscin precursors over prolonged treatment.

3) Testing in animal models of RPE atrophy/drusen (e.g., sodium iodate or complement factor H knock-in mice).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Arimoclomol (chemical name: N-[(2S)-2-[(dimethylamino)methyl]-1-hydroxyethyl]-5-methylisoxazole-4-carboxamide) is a small-molecule co-inducer of heat-shock proteins (HSPs). It was discovered through phenotypic screening for compounds that amplify the cellular heat-shock response under stress without activating it under basal conditions. Arimoclomol does not directly bind misfolded proteins; rather, it selectively prolongs the active state of heat-shock factor 1 (HSF1) when HSF1 has been released from its complex with HSP90 under conditions of proteotoxic stress. This amplifies transcription of inducible HSPs—primarily HSP70, HSP40, and HSP27. Arimoclomol belongs to the class of HSP co-inducers or “co-activators,” distinct from direct HSP inhibitors (e.g., geldanamycin) or HSP mimetics (e.g., celastrol).

Therapeutic History  
1. Preclinical and Clinical Development in Protein-Aggregation Diseases  
 • Neurodegenerative disease models: Arimoclomol has been tested in vitro and in vivo in models of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), spinal bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), and inclusion-body myositis (IBM). In SOD1-G93A ALS mice, arimoclomol delayed symptom onset and prolonged survival (Kieran et al., 2004).  
 • Inclusion-body myositis: A phase II clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) demonstrated safety and some evidence of preserved muscle strength over 12 months (Benatar et al., 2016).  
 • Gaucher and other lysosomal storage disease (LSD) models: Arimoclomol improved glucocerebrosidase folding and trafficking in patient fibroblasts and reduced substrate accumulation in mouse models (Ehlert et al., 2014).  

2. Use in Ophthalmic or RPE-Related Disorders  
 • No published reports to date have specifically evaluated arimoclomol in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, several groups have documented HSP70 dysregulation in RPE cells under oxidative or lipofuscin-mediated stress (Mitter et al., 2014; Ferrington et al., 2016).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Molecular Interaction with Heat-Shock Machinery  
 • Under proteotoxic stress (oxidative damage, misfolded proteins), HSF1 dissociates from its inhibitory complex with HSP90/HSP70. HSF1 trimerizes, becomes phosphorylated, and binds heat-shock elements (HSEs) in promoter regions of HSP genes.  
 • Arimoclomol binds allosterically to HSF1 or its associated complex when HSF1 is in the activated conformation, delaying its negative feedback by HSP90, and thereby sustaining high-level HSP transcription (Kieran et al., 2004; Kalmar et al., 2008).  
 • Resulting up-regulation of HSP70, HSP40, and small HSPs enhances protein folding capacity, prevents aggregation, and promotes clearance of damaged proteins via ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kalmar & Greensmith, 2009).

2. Impact on Autophagy and Lysosomal Function

 • Upon treatment of stressed RPE cells, arimoclomol should selectively amplify HSP70 and HSP40 expression. Increased HSP70 will:  
   – Enhance folding and prevent aggregation of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagy regulators.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Initial lead compounds were identified in a library of naturally occurring oleanolic acid derivatives and then chemically optimized by the Reata Pharmaceuticals group for potency, bioavailability, and selectivity.  
• Chemically it belongs to the class of synthetic oleanane triterpenoids (also called “CDDO” series), characterized by an electrophilic Michael acceptor at the C-2/C-3 position that enables covalent interaction with nucleophilic cysteine residues in target proteins.  
• The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).  

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Assay  
Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
1. Nrf2 in RPE: Human and murine RPE express basal Nrf2 at rest and upregulate it under oxidative challenge (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Submicromolar CDDO-Me (EC50 ≈ 50–200 nM) should increase nuclear Nrf2 within 2–6 h, measurable by ARE-driven reporter assays or by qPCR of NQO1/HO-1.  
2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.  
3. Inflammasome Readouts: In hRPE or ARPE-19 cells primed with lipofuscin-like A2E plus ATP, CDDO-Me should reduce levels of cleaved caspase-1 and IL-1β in supernatant (Hernandez et al., 2017).  
4. Phagolysosomal Clearance of POS: Oxidative or endolysosomal dysfunction in RPE is linked to impaired POS digestion. Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.

• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.

The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-971432 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule agonist with high selectivity for sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor subtype 5 (S1PR5). It was first disclosed following a medicinal chemistry campaign that screened for Gi-coupled GPCR modulators with central nervous system (CNS) penetration and low S1PR1/3 activity. Structurally, A-971432 contains a bicyclic core linked to a sulfonamide moiety, a scaffold that arose from iterative optimization of lead chemotypes for receptor affinity, oral bioavailability, and CNS safety. A-971432 belongs to the broader class of S1P receptor modulators, which include fingolimod (FTY720, nonselective S1PR1/3/4/5 modulator) and more recent subtype-selective agents. In general, S1P receptor agonists have been deployed primarily for immune-modulation (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and neuroprotection.

Therapeutic History  
• S1PR-targeted drugs have clinical precedent in MS (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod) by sequestering lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid organs via S1PR1 functional antagonism.  
• A-971432 itself has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication but has been characterized in rodent models of neuroinflammation (e.g., experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, EAE). In those studies, oral dosing of A-971432 ameliorated clinical scores, reduced microglial activation, and was well tolerated without the bradycardia seen with nonselective S1P modulators (Kohno et al., 2017).  
• No published reports describe use of A-971432 or any selective S1PR5 agonist in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, nonselective S1P analogs (e.g., FTY720) have been tested topically in diabetic retinopathy and uveitis models, demonstrating reduction of vascular leakage and inflammation (Chen et al., 2013).

• S1PR5 is a GPCR that couples predominantly to Gi/o proteins. Ligand binding triggers Gαi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, release of Gβγ subunits, and downstream activation of small GTPases, notably Rac1.  
• Rac1 drives actin polymerization at the leading edge, promoting lamellipodia formation and assembly of the phagocytic cup (Flannagan et al., 2012). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, Rac1 activation is a critical step in outer segment phagocytosis (Lee et al., 2008).  
• Recent work has shown that engagement of S1PR5 on RPE enhances phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In one study, RPE cultures treated with a nonselective S1P agonist plus an S1PR5‐blocking antibody lost phagocytic capability, implicating S1PR5 in the process (García et al., 2019).  
• A-971432 binds S1PR5 with low nanomolar affinity (Ki ∼2 nM) and shows >50‐fold selectivity over S1PR1–3, limiting unwanted immunosuppression or vascular effects mediated by other subtypes (Kohno et al., 2017).

• Cytoskeletal Remodeling: Enhanced lamellipodial ruffling and phagocytic cup formation can be visualized by phalloidin staining, and quantitated by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) imaging (Lee et al., 2008).  
• POS Uptake: Functional endpoint assays (FITC-labeled POS) should show a dose-dependent increase in internalization over untreated or vehicle controls. This may rescue phagocytosis deficits in RPE derived from AMD donors or in models of oxidative stress that impair cup formation (Khandhadia et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a mechanistic deficit in dry AMD—reduced RPE phagocytosis of POS—a core driver of outer retinal atrophy.  
• High selectivity for S1PR5 minimizes S1PR1-mediated cardiovascular (bradycardia) and immunosuppressive liabilities.  
• Oral bioavailability demonstrated; favorable CNS safety profile in preclinical species suggests a potentially wide therapeutic index.  
• Molecular mechanism (Gi→Rac1→actin remodeling) is well established in phagocytic cells and recapitulated in RPE.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability is uncharacterized. Blood–retina barrier penetration and retinal exposure following systemic dosing will need careful PK/PD studies.  
• Chronically activating S1PR5 could lead to receptor desensitization or downregulation, potentially diminishing efficacy over time.  
• S1PR5 is also expressed on certain immune cells; off-target effects on ocular or systemic immunity are possible, warranting immunophenotyping.  
• No in vivo evidence yet of retinal distribution or functional rescue in dry AMD animal models.

Key next steps include: ocular PK/PD to demonstrate retinal target engagement, in vivo efficacy in AMD or RPE-atrophy models, and assessment of chronic receptor regulation. If these hurdles can be cleared, A-971432 (or an optimized ocular formulation) merits advancement as a first-in-class phagocytosis-enhancing therapy for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB216763 is a small-molecule, ATP-competitive inhibitor of glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β). It was first reported by Sato et al. (2000) following high-throughput screening of a chemical library for compounds that elevate β-catenin signaling. Chemically, SB216763 is a maleimide derivative bearing a 3-benzylamino substitution; its core scaffold mimics ATP’s adenine moiety, allowing it to occupy the GSK-3β nucleotide-binding pocket with nanomolar affinity (IC₅₀ ∼ 34 nM for GSK-3β, ∼ 75 nM for GSK-3α). As a member of the ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor class, SB216763 and related maleimide inhibitors have been broadly used in basic research to dissect Wnt/β-catenin pathways, autophagy regulation, and neuroprotective signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Investigations:  
  – Neuroprotection: Multiple groups have used SB216763 in rodent models of cerebral ischemia, Parkinson’s disease models, and Alzheimer’s disease cell systems. In these contexts it showed anti-apoptotic effects, protected against oxidative stress, and activated pro-survival β-catenin and Nrf2 pathways (through indirect cross-talk).

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct GSK-3β Inhibition  
   • SB216763 binds competitively at the ATP-binding site of GSK-3β (and to a lesser degree GSK-3α), preventing phosphorylation of canonical substrates.  
   • Well-characterized substrates include β-catenin (phospho-Ser33/37/Thr41), TFEB (phospho-Ser142/Ser138), and multiple glycogen-metabolizing enzymes.

   • β-Catenin Stabilization: By blocking GSK-3β–mediated phosphorylation, SB216763 prevents β-catenin ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Accumulated β-catenin translocates to the nucleus, partners with TCF/LEF transcription factors, and upregulates Wnt target genes (Ring et al., 2003).

   • Autophagy Induction: Beyond TFEB, GSK-3β inhibition can indirectly modulate mTORC1 activity and AMPK signaling, further promoting autophagosome formation and autophagosome–lysosome fusion.

•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). •  Native CFH Function

  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. •  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1). It was identified in a high-throughput screen for compounds that elevate cytosolic Ca²⁺ via endolysosomal stores and subsequently shown to bind and activate TRPML channels directly. Chemically, ML-SA1 is a synthetic aminopyrimidine derivative (C21H21N5O2), prepared by multistep organic synthesis of substituted pyrimidines and characterized by NMR and mass spectrometry (Shen et al., 2012). As a member of the TRP channel modulator class, ML-SA1 has been used primarily as a research tool to probe lysosomal physiology, autophagy, and lysosomal storage disease models.

Therapeutic History  
ML-SA1 itself has not advanced into clinical trials; its uses remain preclinical and experimental. Key applications include:  
 • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).  
 • Neurodegeneration studies: In neuronal culture and iPSC-derived neurons from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models, ML-SA1 enhances autophagy, reduces protein aggregates, and improves cell viability (Wang et al., 2016).  
 • No reports to date describe ML-SA1 in ocular models or in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Its pharmacology in ocular tissues, particularly the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), remains untested.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct TRPML1 Activation  
   • ML-SA1 binds the cytosolic domain of TRPML1, inducing a conformational shift that opens the lumen-facing channel pore (Shen et al., 2012).  
   • This triggers Ca²⁺ efflux from the lysosomal lumen into the cytosol at micromolar potency (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.6–1.5 µM).  

2. Downstream Signaling to TFEB  
   • Elevated cytosolic Ca²⁺ near lysosomal membranes activates the Ca²⁺/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • Calcineurin dephosphorylates TFEB on serine residues (S142, S211), releasing TFEB from 14-3-3 proteins and allowing its translocation into the nucleus.  
   • Nuclear TFEB binds CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) elements in promoters of lysosomal and autophagic genes (e.g., LAMP1, CTSD, CTSB, MCOLN1), upregulating their transcription.

3. Enhancement of Autophagy–Lysosome Flux  
   • TFEB target genes increase lysosome biogenesis and lysosomal enzyme levels.  
   • ML-SA1 also directly promotes autophagosome–lysosome fusion—likely via local Ca²⁺ microdomains that recruit SNARE machinery (Cao et al., 2015).  
   • Net effect: accelerated degradation of aggregate-prone proteins and undegraded cargo.

TRPML1 (MCOLN1) mRNA and protein are present in human RPE cells and cell lines (ARPE-19) (Zhang et al., 2018). RPE lysosomes are critical for degrading photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In dry AMD, lysosomal dysfunction and impaired autophagy contribute to accumulation of lipofuscin and drusen (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Mitter et al., 2014), making TRPML1 a rational target.

In an RPE cell culture model challenged with POS or A2E (a lipofuscin precursor):  
 • ML-SA1 should increase lysosomal Ca²⁺ release, trigger TFEB nuclear translocation (verify by immunofluorescence or Western blot for dephospho-TFEB), and upregulate CLEAR network genes (qPCR for LAMP1, CTSD).  
 • Increased lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D assay) and enhanced autophagic flux (LC3-II turnover assays ± bafilomycin).  
 • Accelerated clearance of POS or A2E deposits—measured by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assays or A2E quantification.  
 • Reduced lipofuscin-like autofluorescence over time.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistically grounded: directly addresses lysosomal Ca²⁺ signaling and TFEB activation, pathways shown to be deficient in AMD RPE.  
 • Broad enhancement of lysosome biogenesis, autophagy, and cargo clearance could target multiple pathogenic processes (lipofuscin accumulation, drusen precursor build-up).  
 • Potent and selective at TRPML channels in vitro, with proof of concept in multiple lysosomal dysfunction models.

Weaknesses and Risks

Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). •  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. 1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).

   • Electrophilic Michael acceptor groups in CDDO-Im covalently modify reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) in Keap1.    • Recent studies indicate cross-talk between Nrf2 and TFEB (the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis).    • Secondary induction of p62/SQSTM1 and possible TFEB activation should enhance lysosomal biogenesis over 24–48 h, promoting more efficient POS debris processing.  
   • Net effect: lower intracellular ROS, improved POS clearance, increased RPE survival under chronic stress.

Strengths  
   • Potent, well-characterized Nrf2 inducer with proven target engagement in multiple cell types at low nanomolar levels.

   • No direct data in dry AMD or RPE-specific disease models—needs orphan disease modeling (e.g., NaIO3-induced RPE atrophy, aged Ccl2−/−/Cx3cr1−/− mice).  
   • Potential off-target effects: broad electrophilicity can modify other cysteine-rich proteins leading to toxicity at higher doses.  
   • Chronic dosing considerations: pro-proliferative or pro-survival signaling could be deleterious if unregulated in the long term.  
   • Ocular delivery route: systemic dosing may not achieve sustained therapeutic levels in the retina without side effects; local (intravitreal or periocular) formulation and tolerability must be established.

Iptacopan (also known as LNP023) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of complement factor B (FB), discovered initially by high-throughput screening at Achillion Pharmaceuticals and subsequently optimized by medicinal chemistry (structure-based design around a 2,4-dihydrobenzo[1,4]oxazin scaffold). Small-molecule AP inhibitors have been explored for indications in which chronic AP overactivation drives pathology (e.g., paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy).

Therapeutic History  
– Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH): Iptacopan is in late-stage clinical trials (Phase III) for PNH, where oral FB inhibition reduces hemolysis and transfusion needs with a favorable safety profile (No significant infections or thromboses).  
– C3 glomerulopathy, IgA nephropathy: Early-phase studies demonstrated reduced glomerular C3 deposition and improved proteinuria.

Mechanism of Action  
– Molecular target: Factor B is the serine protease zymogen that, upon binding to C3b, is cleaved by factor D into Ba (regulatory fragment) and Bb (catalytic subunit). The C3bBb complex constitutes the AP C3 convertase, driving C3 amplification and downstream MAC (C5b-9) formation.  
– Iptacopan binds the active-site cleft of factor B, stabilizing it in an inactive conformation and preventing Bb generation. Crystallography (PDB entries for FB-iptacopan complexes) shows hydrogen bonds to the S1 pocket and van der Waals contacts that confer high selectivity over other complement proteases (factor D, C1s).  
– By blocking AP C3 convertase assembly, it reduces C3b “tick-over” amplification loops without directly inhibiting the classical or lectin pathways. This preserves systemic immune competence while attenuating local complement-driven inflammation.

– RPE and choroidal endothelial cells are known to synthesize FB and other complement components (Anderson et al., 2010; Bora et al., 2005). Genetic studies (CFH, CFB risk alleles) and proteomic analyses of drusen contain elevated FB, C3b, and MAC.
