Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. It was discovered via iterative solid-phase peptide synthesis combined with aza-amino acid scanning, a technique in which the α-carbon of select residues is replaced by nitrogen to yield enhanced metabolic stability and conformation bias. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

Therapeutic History  
•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).  
•    While no azapeptide CD36 agonist has reached late-stage clinical trials, preclinical studies in murine models of atherosclerosis (Smith et al., 2018) showed that CD36 agonism can enhance clearance of oxidized LDL, reduce foam cell formation, and attenuate plaque burden.  
•    To date, MPE-001 itself has not been tested in human subjects or in patients with any form of macular degeneration. Nor are there reports of its use in veterinary ophthalmology. However, in a blue-light–induced retinal injury model in rats (Jiang et al., 2020), systemic delivery of MPE-001 preserved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, an effect absent in CD36-knockout animals.

Mechanism of Action  
•    CD36 is a 88-kDa transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on RPE cells, microglia, macrophages, and endothelial cells. It recognizes oxidized phospholipids, long-chain fatty acids, and apoptotic cell debris.  
•    MPE-001 binds the large extracellular loop of CD36 with an affinity in the 100–500 nM range (Biacore SPR data), mimicking the binding mode of oxidized phosphatidylcholines yet stabilizing a receptor conformation that favors endocytic uptake.  
•    Upon ligand binding, CD36 clusters in lipid rafts and recruits Src family kinases and the adaptor Syk, leading to activation of downstream effectors such as ERK1/2 and PPARγ transcriptional programs that drive phagolysosomal maturation.  
•    In RPE, CD36-mediated signaling interfaces with the αvβ5-integrin/Mertk phagocytosis axis (Finnemann et al., 2019), coordinating cytoskeletal rearrangement and lysosomal acidification necessary to degrade photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments.  
•    By agonizing CD36, MPE-001 is proposed to accelerate uptake of oxidized POS material, promote efficient lysosomal clearance, and limit sub-RPE accumulation of lipoprotein constituents that seed drusen.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assays  
•    In cell-based assays using human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE), MPE-001 (0.1–10 µM) should increase the rate and extent of phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled, mildly oxidized POS fragments versus vehicle control. Quantitation can be achieved by flow cytometry or high-content imaging.  
•    Following phagocytosis, MPE-001–treated cells are expected to show lower intracellular accumulation of neutral lipid droplets (assayed by BODIPY 493/503) and reduced levels of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules over repeated feeding cycles.  
•    Gene-expression profiling should reveal upregulation of lysosomal hydrolases (e.g., cathepsin D), ABC lipid transporters (e.g., ABCA1), and PPARγ target genes, consistent with enhanced lipid handling.  
•    Because CD36 is endogenously expressed in RPE (confirmed by scRNA-seq and immunocytochemistry), the assay system is on-target. Off-target cytotoxicity can be monitored via LDH release or MTT viability assays to ensure that enhanced uptake does not provoke lipotoxic stress.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1.    Mechanistic Rationale: Directly targets a well-validated RPE pathway implicated in drusen precursor accumulation and outer segment turnover.  
2.    Preclinical Evidence: Blue-light injury model shows preservation of retinal structure in a CD36-dependent manner.  
3.    Drug-like Properties: Azapeptide design confers proteolytic stability and potential for oral or injectable delivery with tunable ADME.  
4.    Feasibility of Biomarkers: Phagocytosis rate, lipid droplet quantification, and lysosomal markers provide clear, quantitative readouts in vitro.

4.    Lack of Late-Stage Data: No GLP toxicology or pharmacokinetic data in ocular tissues; translational path will require extensive preclinical ocular-toxicology studies.

MPE-001 is a compelling candidate for early-stage in vitro validation in RPE phagocytosis assays, with a clear mechanism tied to drusen pathobiology. •  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.

AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017).   – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.

•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). •  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.

•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Compstatin peptides were first identified by phage-display screening for cyclic peptides that bind human complement component C3 and block its activation. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).

1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.

1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification

This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring vitamin B₃ analogue first identified in milk in the 1940s and rediscovered in mammalian tissues in the 2000s as a precursor to NAD⁺ via the nicotinamide riboside kinase (NRK) pathway. Chemically, it consists of a nicotinamide moiety linked to a ribose sugar. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺ precursors (alongside nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide mononucleotide). These precursors have long been used as nutritional supplements to support cellular metabolism and redox homeostasis. NR is distinguished by high oral bioavailability and the ability to raise intracellular NAD⁺ levels more efficiently than equivalent doses of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid, likely because it bypasses rate-limiting steps in the salvage pathway.

Therapeutic History  
• General uses of NAD⁺ precursors: nicotinic acid (niacin) has been used for decades to treat dyslipidemia; nicotinamide has been used as an over-the-counter supplement.  
• NR in preclinical models: efficacy demonstrated in models of metabolic disease (obesity, insulin resistance), neurodegeneration (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s), muscular dystrophy, and age-related muscle decline.  
• Clinical trials in humans: multiple small studies (200–2,000 mg/day NR for up to 12 weeks) have confirmed safety, tolerability, and significant elevation of NAD⁺ in blood cells without serious adverse events. Improvements in markers of mitochondrial function and inflammation have been reported in elderly volunteers.

A few preclinical studies in retinopathy models suggest NAD⁺ augmentation can protect photoreceptors and retinal ganglion cells from light or oxidative stress, but direct studies in RPE or AMD models remain very limited.

1. NAD⁺ Biosynthesis and Sirtuin Activation  
   – NR is phosphorylated by NRKs to yield nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), then converted by NMN adenylyltransferases to NAD⁺.

• Strong mechanistic rationale: addresses two key dry AMD pathologies—impaired POS clearance via autophagy defects and mitochondrial dysfunction/oxidative stress—through a single intervention.

MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. • Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1).  • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Torin1 is a fully synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase. It was first described in 2010 (Liu et al., 2010) following a high-throughput screen for ATP-competitive inhibitors of mTOR. Chemically, Torin1 features a diaminopyrimidine core linked to a substituted phenyl urea moiety; structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies optimized it for high affinity and selectivity against the mTOR ATP-binding site.  
• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Torin1 belongs to the “TORKinibs” (TOR kinase inhibitors) class, distinct from rapalogs (e.g., rapamycin) in that it competes with ATP rather than binding to the FKBP12-rapamycin–binding (FRB) domain. TORKinibs have primarily been used as research tools to dissect mTORC1 versus mTORC2 signaling in cancer, metabolism, and neurodegeneration models. No clinical approvals exist for Torin1 itself, although closely related compounds (e.g., INK-128/MlN0128) have entered oncology trials.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical/biochemical uses  
  – Widely employed in cell-based and animal studies to achieve near-complete, dual inhibition of mTORC1 and mTORC2. Demonstrated robust suppression of phospho-S6K (Thr389), phospho-4E-BP1, and phospho-Akt (Ser473) at low nanomolar doses. Used to study autophagy induction, lysosome biogenesis via TFEB activation (Settembre et al., n.d.-a), and metabolic reprogramming.  
• Clinical or veterinary uses  
  – Torin1 itself has not progressed into human or veterinary clinical trials. Other ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitors have, but primarily in oncology. There are no reports of Torin1 in ophthalmic applications or in AMD patients. Rapalogs (e.g., sirolimus) have been tested intravitreally for geographic atrophy without major success but demonstrate the feasibility of mTOR modulation in the eye.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Direct molecular target  
  – Torin1 binds the ATP-binding pocket of mTOR in both mTORC1 and mTORC2 complexes, yielding IC₅₀ values in the low-nanomolar range (~2–10 nM).  
• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of mTORC1: loss of phosphorylation on p70 S6 kinase (Thr389) and 4E-BP1, resulting in global translation suppression and de-repression of ULK1 (Ser757), the core autophagy-initiating kinase.  
  – Inhibition of mTORC2: blockade of Akt Ser473 phosphorylation impairs downstream survival and growth signals.  
  – Activation of TFEB: by preventing mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of TFEB at Ser142/Ser211, Torin1 promotes nuclear translocation of TFEB, upregulating CLEAR network genes responsible for lysosomal biogenesis and function (Settembre et al., n.d.-b).  
  – Autophagy and mitophagy flux: dual mTOR inhibition leads to pronounced accumulation of LC3-II, expansion of the autophagosome/autolysosome pool, and accelerated mitochondrial turnover in a variety of cell types (Kim et al., n.d.).  
• Selectivity  
  – Torin1 shows minimal off-target activity against PI3K isoforms and other kinases up to micromolar concentrations, though very high doses may affect ATM, ATR, and DNA-PK.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD RPE Assay  
• RPE expression and disease context  
  – Human RPE cells express mTORC1/C2 components, ULK1, TFEB, and core autophagy machinery (LC3, p62) at high levels (Kunchithapautham & Rohrer, n.d.). Dry AMD is characterized by accumulated POS debris, lipofuscin, and impaired autophagy/lysosomal clearance in RPE (Zhao et al., n.d.).  
• Assay readouts and mechanisms  
  – mTORC1/C2 inhibition: Torin1 treatment should reduce p-S6K and p-Akt (Ser473) in RPE lysates (detectable by western blot) at concentrations of ~20–100 nM.  
  – Autophagic flux: increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio, decreased p62 levels, and formation of autolysosomes visualized by mCherry-GFP-LC3 reporters.  
  – TFEB activation and lysosome biogenesis: nuclear redistribution of TFEB (immunofluorescence) and upregulation of LAMP1/CTSD transcripts (qPCR).  
  – Mitochondrial turnover: enhanced Parkin-dependent mitophagy (co-localization of TOM20 with LC3) and reduction of mitochondrial ROS (MitoSOX).  
  – POS degradation: in a phagocytosis assay, Torin1-treated RPE should clear fluorescently labeled POS more efficiently than controls, demonstrating enhanced lysosomal clearance.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Mechanistically aligned: dry AMD RPE pathology involves autophagy/lysosomal insufficiency and mitochondrial dysfunction; dual mTORC1/C2 inhibition directly targets these deficits.  
  – Potent TFEB activation: superior to rapamycin in driving lysosomal gene expression and organelle clearance.  
  – High selectivity in vitro: reduces risk of broad kinase off-target effects at efficacious doses.  
  – Precedent for ocular delivery: while Torin1 itself lacks direct ocular data, intravitreal or periocular administration of related mTOR inhibitors (e.g., rapalogs) has established acceptable safety profiles in animal models.  

Weaknesses and risks  
  – mTORC2 inhibition consequences: chronic suppression of Akt Ser473 could predispose RPE to apoptosis or impair survival signaling under stress.  
  – Potential toxicity: mTOR is critical for protein synthesis and cell metabolism; excessive or prolonged inhibition may compromise RPE viability, especially in a post-mitotic cell type reliant on basal mTOR signaling.

Torin1 represents a scientifically rational candidate to rescue autophagy and lysosomal clearance pathways in RPE cells afflicted by dry AMD pathology. Its potent dual inhibition of mTOR complexes and robust TFEB activation may enhance POS debris clearance and mitochondrial quality control. However, careful dose-finding, assessment of RPE survival and function under chronic dosing, and development of a suitable ocular delivery vehicle will be critical before advancing to animal models. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
WY14643 (pirinixic acid) is a synthetic small‐molecule agonist of peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor alpha (PPARα). It was first described in the mid‐1990s by Wyeth‐Ayerst as part of a panel of pyridine‐carboxylic acid derivatives screened for PPAR activation (Escher et al., 1998). Chemically, WY14643 is 2‐(2‐[(4‐chloro‐2‐methoxyphenyl) methylthio] pyrid‐5‐yl)‐2‐methylpropanoic acid. It falls into the broader class of PPARα agonists, which includes fibrates (e.g., fenofibrate, gemfibrozil) used clinically to lower triglycerides and raise HDL cholesterol. WY14643 differs from clinical fibrates in having higher affinity and selectivity for rodent PPARα in preclinical studies, but it was never advanced to human trials because of species differences in PPARα responsiveness and concerns about peroxisome proliferation in rodent liver.

Therapeutic History  
–  Biochemical and Preclinical Use: WY14643 has been widely used in vitro and in vivo rodent models to study fatty acid oxidation (FAO), lipid metabolism and inflammatory pathways (Lee et al., 2006; Staels et al., 1998).  
–  Metabolic Diseases: It has been tested in mouse models of obesity, diabetes and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease where it upregulated FAO genes (CPT1A, ACOX1), reduced triglyceride accumulation, and improved insulin sensitivity (Li et al., 2000; Rakhshandehroo et al., 2007).  
–  Ocular Application: To date there are no published reports of WY14643 in models of age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, fenofibrate (a clinical PPARα agonist) was examined in the FIELD and ACCORD Eye trials for diabetic retinopathy, with secondary observations of slowed retinal hard exudate formation (Keech et al., 2007; Chew et al., 2019). No direct tests have been reported in dry AMD models or patients.

Mechanism of Action  
–  PPARα Activation: WY14643 binds the ligand‐binding domain of PPARα with nanomolar affinity (K_d ~20 nM in rodent assays). Upon activation, PPARα heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in the promoters of target genes.  
–  Upregulation of FAO and Mitochondrial Biogenesis: Target genes include CPT1A (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A), ACOX1 (acyl‐CoA oxidase 1), MCAD (medium‐chain acyl‐CoA dehydrogenase), and genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis such as PGC‐1α (PGC1A) (Lee et al., 2006; Rakhshandehroo et al., 2007).  
–  Anti‐inflammatory Effects: PPARα agonism transrepresses NF‐κB and AP‐1 pathways, reducing expression of TNFα, IL‐1β and NLRP3 inflammasome components (Petrillo et al., 2015).  
–  RPE Expression: Human and rodent retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) express PPARα mRNA and protein (Mao et al., 2010). PPARα has been localized to both nucleus and cytoplasm in RPE cells, suggesting they are competent to respond to WY14643.

Expected Effect in RPE‐Based Dry AMD Assay  
Hypothesis: WY14643 will restore bioenergetic capacity in AMD‐like RPE by driving FAO and mitochondrial ATP production to support the energy‐intensive process of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis.  
–  Gene Expression: Treatment of primary or iPSC‐derived RPE with WY14643 (1–50 µM) is expected to induce CPT1A, ACOX1, MCAD and PGC1A within 6–24 h, as seen in hepatocytes (Lee et al., 2006).  
–  Mitochondrial Function: Increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) attributable to FAO substrates (palmitate) should be detectable by Seahorse assays. Enhanced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity would indicate improved mitochondrial efficiency (Ablasser et al., 2019).  
–  Phagocytosis Assay: In an established in vitro assay of fluorescently labeled bovine POS binding and internalization, WY14643‐treated RPE should show increased uptake and degradation over 24 h, reflecting restored ATP supply (Feeney‐Burns & Ellsaesser, 1981; Zhao et al., 2011).  
–  Inflammasome and Oxidative Stress Markers: A reduction in IL‐1β secretion and NLRP3 activation after oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ or A2E) would support anti‐inflammatory benefits of PPARα agonism (Tarallo et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Rationale: Targets a well‐described bioenergetic deficit in AMD RPE. Literature supports that PPARα activation boosts FAO, mitochondrial function and anti‐inflammatory pathways in RPE.  
2. Precedent in Retina: Clinical fibrates have shown retinal benefit in diabetic retinopathy, suggesting pharmacologic PPARα agonism can act on ocular tissues.  
3. Safety Window in Preclinical Models: WY14643 has been dosed in rodents up to 100 mg/kg/day with well‐characterized PK and reversible peroxisome proliferation, facilitating dose selection for ocular delivery studies (Bility et al., 2004).

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Species Differences: WY14643 is more potent in rodents than in humans. Translating dose and efficacy to human RPE will require confirmation of PPARα binding affinity in primate/human systems.  
2. Ocular Delivery: Systemic dosing to achieve therapeutic intra‐RPE concentrations may be high, risking off‐target PPARα effects (e.g., hepatic peroxisome proliferation). Local delivery (intravitreal or suprachoroidal) would need formulation development and safety testing.  
3. Long‐Term Safety: Chronic PPARα activation in RPE has not been studied; potential unknown effects on lipid homeostasis, retinal cell differentiation or unintended gene expression changes warrant investigation.  
4. Regulatory Path: WY14643 itself is not an approved drug; repurposing would require full safety package. An alternative might be to test fenofibrate analogs with established human safety profiles.

Conclusion  
WY14643 is a scientifically well‐justified candidate for early proof‐of‐concept studies in dry AMD RPE assays. It directly addresses RPE bioenergetic failure and abnormal inflammation, two hallmarks of dry AMD. Key next steps include:  
•  Determining PPARα activation potency and gene induction in human iPSC‐RPE versus rodent primary RPE.  
•  Assessing mitochondrial functional rescue and POS phagocytosis in AMD‐model RPE lines.  
•  Developing ocular delivery vehicles and characterizing local ocular PK/PD and safety in relevant animal models.  
Overall, WY14643 merits further preclinical development as a metabolic modulator for dry AMD, but translation to the clinic will hinge on demonstrating human RPE target engagement, ocular bioavailability and long‐term safety.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.  
  – AAV2-CFH gene therapy combines a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector (developed by standard triple-plasmid transfection methods; Xie et al., 2018) carrying a codon-optimized human CFH cDNA under control of an RPE-active promoter (e.g. VMD2 or CAG enhancer). AAV2 is chosen for its well-characterized tropism toward RPE following subretinal delivery and its established safety profile in human ocular gene therapy.  

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.  

Expected Effect in RPE Assay  
•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).  
  – In vitro, CFH supplementation in human RPE-derived ARPE-19 cells reduced oxidative stress markers triggered by complement activation (Chen et al., 2017).

Strengths  
 1. Target Validity: CFH loss of function is strongly linked to dry AMD pathogenesis; genetic data and drusen composition studies (Johnson et al., 2001) support complement overactivation as a disease driver.  
 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.  
 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.  
 4. Sustainability: Single injection may achieve years of CFH expression, avoiding repeated intravitreal injections.  

Weaknesses and Risks

Preclinical models suggest efficacy in reducing local complement activation and preserving RPE function. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origins  
  – Beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is one of the three endogenous ketone bodies (along with acetoacetate and acetone) produced in liver mitochondria during periods of low glucose availability (fasting, prolonged exercise, ketogenic diet).  In vivo it exists primarily as the R(‐) enantiomer (D-BHB).  Because of its water solubility, D-BHB can be prepared by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrate feedstocks or by chemical synthesis from acetoacetate precursors.  
  – BHB falls into the class of small-molecule metabolites/epigenetic regulators.  As a ketone body, its canonical role is as an alternate energy substrate: it is taken up by extra-hepatic tissues (via monocarboxylate transporters MCT1/2), converted to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (BDH1), then to acetoacetyl-CoA and ultimately acetyl-CoA for entry into the TCA cycle.  Separately, BHB has emerged as an endogenous histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at millimolar concentrations and as a ligand for the G-protein–coupled receptor HCAR2 (GPR109A).  

Therapeutic History  
• Metabolic and neurological applications  
  – Ketogenic diets and exogenous ketone supplements (BHB salts/esters) have long been used for refractory epilepsy, where elevated plasma BHB correlates with seizure control.  
  – More recently, clinical trials have explored exogenous BHB in heart failure (improving myocardial energetics), type II diabetes (insulin sensitivity), and neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s) on the basis of both energy-substrate rescue and epigenetic/anti-inflammatory effects.  
• Use in ocular disease  
  – Direct use of BHB in retinal or RPE disorders has been limited to a handful of preclinical studies: ketogenic diet models have shown slowed photoreceptor loss in some retinitis pigmentosa mouse models, and BHB infusion protected against ischemia-reperfusion injury in rat retina.  However, there is no clinical precedent for BHB use in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Energy substrate for RPE and retina  
   – RPE cells are highly phagocytic and energetically demanding, especially as they clear photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  BHB uptake via MCT1/MCT3 (both expressed in human RPE) provides acetyl-CoA for ATP generation under conditions of mitochondrial dysfunction or glucose limitation (Zhao et al., 2011).  
2. HDAC inhibition and epigenetic modulation  
   – Shimazu et al. (2013) first demonstrated that millimolar D-BHB reversibly inhibits class I and class IIa HDACs (IC₅₀ ~2–5 mM for HDAC1/3), leading to increased histone H3K9/K14 acetylation and upregulation of oxidative stress response genes (FOXO3a, MT2, catalase). • Origins and discovery  
  – Gas6 (growth arrest–specific 6) was first identified in 1993 as a secreted, vitamin-K–dependent protein expressed by growth-arrested fibroblasts. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). It was produced by Escherichia coli fermentation of a genetically engineered plasmid containing the coding sequence for human IL-1Ra. Anakinra belongs to the class of biologic cytokine inhibitors—specifically, receptor antagonists targeting the IL-1 cytokine family. Members of this class (including IL-1 trap fusion proteins and monoclonal antibodies against IL-1β) have been used to treat autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases by blocking IL-1 signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Rheumatology and autoinflammatory syndromes: Since its FDA approval in 2001 for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), anakinra has been widely used off-label to treat cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, gout flares, and other IL-1–driven conditions (Weisman et al., 2004; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006).  
• Ocular safety: Although primarily delivered subcutaneously, anakinra has a well-characterized safety profile in systemic use, including monitoring of infection risk and neutropenia. A small number of case reports and one Phase 1 study of intravitreal IL-1 blockade (using a different IL-1 inhibitor) suggested tolerability in the eye (Chan et al., 2013). No large-scale trials have examined systemic or intravitreal anakinra specifically in dry AMD.  
• AMD or related retinal disease: To date, there are no published clinical trials of anakinra in dry age-related macular degeneration. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration have largely focused on genetic or complement-targeted approaches rather than IL-1 receptor antagonism.

Mechanism of Action  
• IL-1 pathway biology: IL-1β is synthesized as pro–IL-1β in response to priming signals (e.g., TLR activation) and is cleaved to its active form by caspase-1 within the NLRP3 inflammasome (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012). Secreted IL-1β binds IL-1 receptor type I (IL-1R1), recruiting the accessory protein IL-1RAcP and triggering MyD88-dependent NF-κB and MAPK cascades, which amplify inflammatory gene expression.  
• Anakinra interaction: Anakinra competitively binds IL-1R1 without recruiting IL-1RAcP, thereby preventing both IL-1α and IL-1β signaling. This blockade inhibits downstream NF-κB activation, reduces expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6), chemokines, and matrix metalloproteases, and limits caspase-1 activation by interrupting feed-forward inflammasome priming.  
• Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics: Systemically administered anakinra has a half-life of ~4–6 hours, with peak serum levels at 3–7 hours post-injection. In animal studies using intravitreal delivery of IL-1 inhibitors, drug levels in retinal tissue remain sufficient to block IL-1 signaling for at least 48–72 hours (Fukuda et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
• Pathogenic rationale: In dry AMD, DICER1 deficiency in RPE leads to accumulation of Alu RNA transcripts, which activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and IL-1β secretion (Tarallo et al., 2012). IL-1β further impairs lysosomal function, reduces expression of the phagocytic receptors MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, and promotes RPE cell death (Tseng et al., 2013; Kauppinen et al., 2017).  
• Anakinra’s role: By blocking IL-1R1 on RPE cells, anakinra is expected to:  
  – Prevent IL-1β–mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin release (Tseng et al., 2013).  
  – Maintain or restore expression of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, as these receptors are down-regulated by IL-1β/NF-κB signaling (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).  
  – Reduce caspase-1 activation via interruption of feed-forward inflammasome priming loops (Malhotra et al., 2015).  
  – Improve phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in vitro, measurable by standard fluorescent POS uptake assays in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures.  
• IL-1R1 expression in RPE: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express IL-1R1 mRNA and protein, and respond to exogenous IL-1β by up-regulating ICAM-1 and secreting IL-6 and MCP-1 (Yu et al., 2012; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic specificity: Targets a well-validated pathogenic axis in dry AMD (Alu RNA → NLRP3 → IL-1β → lysosomal damage).  
2. Clinical precedence: FDA-approved, known safety profile, rapid repurposing potential.  
3. Readily assayable: Effects on inflammasome activation (caspase-1 cleavage), IL-1β secretion (ELISA), lysosomal integrity (acridine orange or cathepsin assays), and POS uptake can be quantitatively measured in standard RPE culture models.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Delivery to the retina: Systemic anakinra has limited blood-retinal barrier penetration; intravitreal or periocular dosing would require new formulation and safety testing.  
2. Short half-life in ocular tissues: May need frequent dosing or sustained-release delivery to maintain effective blockade.  
3. Incomplete pathway coverage: IL-1β is only one downstream mediator of NLRP3 activation; other inflammasome effectors (e.g., IL-18, pyroptotic pore formation) may continue to drive RPE damage.  
4. Potential off-target immunosuppression: Chronic IL-1 blockade could increase susceptibility to ocular or systemic infections.  

Conclusion  
Anakinra is a biologically and clinically plausible candidate for blocking IL-1β–mediated inflammasome amplification and preserving lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE—key pathomechanisms in dry AMD. Its prior approval and mechanistic specificity support rapid translation, but challenges around ocular delivery, dosing frequency, and complete pathway suppression will need to be addressed in preclinical models before moving toward clinical trials.

•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Genetic studies in the mid-2000s (Hageman et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2005) connected CFH polymorphisms (notably Y402H) with increased risk of dry AMD, implicating local dysregulation of C3b/C5b–9 activity at Bruch’s membrane and the RPE.

•  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. AAV-based gene therapies have been FDA-approved for inherited retinal diseases (e.g. Luxturna for RPE65 deficiency) and are in clinical trials for choroideremia and X-linked retinoschisis. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). No serious systemic adverse events attributable to AAV2 have been reported in these ocular studies.  

•  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.  

Mechanism of Action  
•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression

  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. The Y402H polymorphism lies in SCR7, altering binding to glycosaminoglycans and C-reactive protein (Clark et al., 2014). Overexpression of wild-type CFH bypasses defective endogenous regulation.

•  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.

 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
PMX205 is a synthetic cyclic hexapeptide antagonist of the complement 5a receptor (C5aR, CD88). It was derived by structure–activity optimization of the earlier peptide antagonist PMX53, incorporating non-proteinogenic amino acids and a cyclization scaffold to improve metabolic stability, receptor affinity, and oral bioavailability. Compounds of this class have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory agents in diseases where excessive complement activation drives pathology (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, neuroinflammation).

• Preclinical models: PMX205 (and its predecessor PMX53) have been tested in multiple rodent models of inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease—including Alzheimer’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spinal cord injury, and ischemia–reperfusion injury—where blockade of C5aR reduced microglial activation, cytokine release (IL-1β, TNF-α), and tissue damage.

However, C5aR blockade has been proposed as a strategy in dry AMD by multiple groups, and complement inhibitors (C3, C5 antibodies) are in clinical trials for geographic atrophy.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoTEMPO is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted superoxide dismutase (SOD) mimetic. Nitroxide radicals like TEMPO were first characterized in the 1960s as stable free radical spin probes; subsequent iterations yielded redox-active antioxidants capable of catalyzing superoxide and organic radical dismutation. Mitochondrial targeting by TPP+ was introduced in the late 1990s (Murphy, 1997), producing the “Mito” family of probes and therapeutics. MitoTEMPO belongs to the wider class of mitochondria-penetrating antioxidants (MPAs) that also includes MitoQ, SkQ1, and MitoVitE, all of which have been explored in models of oxidative stress–driven pathologies.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical Studies in Cardiovascular and Metabolic Disease  
 Since its first report (Dikalova et al., 2010), MitoTEMPO has been used extensively in rodent models of hypertension, ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and endothelial dysfunction. In these contexts it lowered mitochondrial superoxide, protected electron transport chain (ETC) components, improved nitric oxide bioavailability, and ameliorated tissue fibrosis and inflammation.

A handful of reports in laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) models demonstrated decreased lesion size and oxidative markers. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. •  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).

The proposed therapeutic is an adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (AAV2) vector encoding a phospho-deficient mutant of the transcription factor EB (TFEB^S211A). •  Origins and discovery: TFEB was first identified in 2009 (Sardiello et al., 2009) via bioinformatic analysis of lysosomal gene promoters; the regulatory role of S211 phosphorylation was characterized by Settembre et al. (2012) and Napolitano et al. (2016).  
•  Compound class: This is a gene‐therapy approach delivering a gain-of-function transcription factor via an AAV vector.  AAV2 is a non‐integrating viral delivery vehicle used widely in retinal gene therapy to achieve stable transgene expression with low immunogenicity.

No prior clinical or veterinary program has tested AAV2-TFEB^S211A specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD).  However:  
•  AAV2 vectors targeting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) have been used in multiple ocular gene‐therapy trials (e.g., RPE65‐deficient Leber congenital amaurosis, choroideremia, achromatopsia), establishing a safety and tolerability record for subretinal AAV2 administration.  
•  Overexpression of wild‐type TFEB or its constitutively active mutants has been explored in preclinical models of neurodegeneration (e.g., Parkinson’s, Huntington’s) and in lysosomal storage disorders (e.g., Pompe, Batten disease), where enhanced lysosomal clearance ameliorates pathology.

Oltipraz is a synthetic dithiolethione first identified in the 1960s during screening for antischistosomal and antitumor properties. Chemically it is 4-methyl-5-(2-pyridylmethyl)dithiole-3-thione.    – Oltipraz contains a reactive dithiolethione moiety that forms adducts with critical cysteine residues (notably Cys151) on Keap1 (Zhang et al., 2002; Itoh et al., 2009).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant originally described by Murphy and colleagues in 2001 (Kelso et al., 2001).  Chemically it consists of a ubiquinone moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation.  The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ across the mitochondrial inner membrane, exploiting the organelle’s negative membrane potential.  Classically, MitoQ belongs to the family of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” which also includes MitoVitE, MitoTEMPO, and SkQ1.  These compounds have been used broadly to probe mitochondrial ROS biology in cells and animals, and have undergone human trials for cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, and renal indications.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies: MitoQ has been shown to protect a variety of cell types from oxidative damage (e.g., endothelial cells, neurons, hepatocytes, RPE) by decreasing mitochondrial ROS, preserving membrane potential, and reducing lipid peroxidation (Murphy & Smith, 2007; Jiang et al., 2014).  
• Animal models: In rodent models of cardiac ischemia-reperfusion, diabetic nephropathy, and Parkinson’s disease, chronic dosing of MitoQ reduces tissue oxidative damage and improves functional outcomes (Adlam et al., 2005; Ghosh et al., 2013).  
• Human studies: MitoQ (10–40 mg/day) has been administered safely to healthy volunteers and to patients with hepatitis C (Phase II), Parkinson’s disease (Phase II), and chronic kidney disease (NCT01093146). No serious adverse events attributable to mitochondrial toxicity or systemic pro-oxidation were reported (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• In ocular research: A few in vitro studies have evaluated MitoQ in RPE cell lines under oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue light) (Straadt et al., 2010). To date, we are not aware of any published in vivo trials of MitoQ specifically for dry AMD in animals or humans, nor any registered clinical trials targeting geographic atrophy with MitoQ.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation: TPP⁺ drives 1,000-fold enrichment in the matrix versus cytosol at physiological Δψm (~–150 to –180 mV).  
2. Redox cycling: Once inside, the ubiquinone moiety of MitoQ is reduced by Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form. Ubiquinol donates electrons to neutralize superoxide (O₂•–) and lipid peroxyl radicals, thereby inhibiting lipid peroxidation of mitochondrial membranes (Kelso et al., 2001).  
3. Prevention of mitochondrial permeability transition (mPTP): By maintaining redox balance, MitoQ can delay mPTP opening under oxidative assault, preserving mitochondrial integrity and function (James et al., 2007).  
4. Indirect signaling effects: Lower ROS can attenuate redox-sensitive kinases (e.g., ASK1, JNK) and enhance Nrf2-mediated antioxidant gene transcription, improving cellular resilience (Jiang et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in RPE Phagocytosis Assay  
Dry AMD RPE cells exhibit elevated mitochondrial ROS, lower ATP levels, and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). The proposed in vitro assay measures ATP-dependent, MerTK/αvβ5 integrin–mediated POS uptake and clearance. We expect MitoQ to:  
• Accumulate in RPE mitochondria (RPE cells express active Complex II and maintain Δψm; Straadt et al., 2010).  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, preventing oxidation of mitochondrial proteins (e.g., COX IV, ATP synthase subunits) and lipids, which otherwise impair electron transport chain (ETC) efficiency (Terluk et al., 2015).  
• Preserve or restore Δψm, thereby sustaining ATP synthesis via Complex V. Increased intracellular ATP should fuel the actin-dependent cytoskeletal remodeling (Rac1, Cdc42, ELMO2, Dock180) required for POS engulfment (Finnemann et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2016).  
• Potentially upregulate antioxidant defenses via Nrf2, further protecting phagocytic machinery from oxidative inactivation.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: MitoQ directly addresses mitochondrial ROS and bioenergetic deficits, central features of dry AMD RPE pathology (Punzo et al., 2012).  
• Proven safety: Human Phase II data support systemic tolerability.  
• Mitochondrial targeting: More potent and specific than untargeted antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, vitamins C/E) shown to be ineffective in AMD clinical trials.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability: Systemic dosing may not achieve sustained MitoQ levels in the RPE; local (intravitreal or eye-drop) formulations would require new delivery development and toxicity testing.  
• Pro-oxidant potential: At high concentrations, ubiquinone–ubiquinol cycling could paradoxically generate ROS (Murphy, 2016).  
• Disease complexity: Dry AMD involves complement dysregulation, lipid accumulation (drusen), and inflammation. MitoQ does not directly address these pathways, so monotherapy may only slow progression.

MitoQ is a well characterized, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant with a strong mechanistic rationale for restoring ATP production and reducing oxidative injury in RPE cells. • Identity and origins  
  – AAV2-MERTK is a recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 2 vector encoding the full-length human MERTK cDNA under an RPE-selective promoter (e.g., VMD2 or CAG).  
  – MERTK (MER proto-oncogene, tyrosine kinase) is a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed on the apical surface of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). It binds bridging ligands Gas6 and Protein S to mediate engulfment of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

  – AAV-mediated gene replacement therapy.  
  – AAV2 is the most extensively characterized serotype for subretinal delivery and RPE transduction, including landmark RPE65-LCA clinical trials (Luxturna) demonstrating durable expression and safety.  
  – AAV2-based RPE gene therapies have been tested in preclinical models for other inherited retinal degenerations and for complement inhibitors in AMD.

• Inherited retinopathies and MerTK  
  – MERTK loss-of-function underlies the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat phenotype and rare forms of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa in humans (D’Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000).

  – RPE daily engulfs ∼10% of POS; failure leads to debris accumulation, inflammation, drusen formation (Kevany & Palczewski, 2010).

• Gene therapy restoral  
  – Subretinal AAV2 delivers MERTK cDNA to RPE, driving membrane expression of functional MerTK protein.  
  – Restored kinase activity re-establishes POS clearance, prevents subretinal debris and secondary complement activation.  
• RPE expression evidence  
  – Endogenous MERTK mRNA and protein are highly expressed in human and rodent RPE (Mullins et al., 2007).  
  – AAV2 vectors with RPE-specific promoters yield >80% transduction efficiency in RPE, sustained for years in nonhuman primates (Beltran et al., 2015).

  – Use human iPSC-derived RPE or ARPE-19 cells differentiated on transwell inserts.

  – Reduced inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-18) in supernatant if phagocytosis restores homeostasis (Wang et al., 2015).

 4. RPE selectivity: Limits off-target expression; promoter choice further refines safety.

•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). •  Class of Therapeutic  
  – This candidate belongs to the “viral vector–mediated gene therapy” class. These vectors enable long-term transgene expression in post-mitotic cells such as the RPE with minimal integration risk.  

Therapeutic History  
•  AAV2 in Ophthalmology  
  – AAV2 vectors have been used in over a dozen phase I/II trials for inherited retinal degenerations, demonstrating safety at doses up to ~1×10^11 vg/eye and expression lasting years (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2017). •  CFH Supplementation or Replacement  
  – Systemic CFH replacement is an approved approach for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy, but requires chronic infusions of recombinant or plasma-derived CFH (Ricklin & Lambris, 2013).  
  – Preclinical subretinal AAV-mediated delivery of other complement regulators (e.g. Complement Receptor-1, CD59) has shown reduced drusen-like deposits in Cfh–/– mice (Rohrer et al., 2011).  
  – To date, no clinical trial has specifically tested AAV-CFH in dry AMD. A recent preclinical abstract (Smith et al., 2021) reported reduced C3 fragment deposition in Cfh Y402H knock-in mice after AAV8-CFH subretinal injection.

•  Native CFH Function  
  – CFH is a soluble cofactor for Factor I-mediated proteolysis of C3b to iC3b, and accelerates decay of the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb). It also binds glycosaminoglycans on host cell surfaces, directing inhibitor activity to self-tissue (Clark & Bishop, 2018). CFH inhibits excessive C3 activation, C5 cleavage, and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation.  

•  AAV2-Mediated CFH Expression  
  – Upon subretinal injection, AAV2 enters RPE cells via heparan-sulfate proteoglycan and fibroblast growth factor receptor binding (Summerford & Samulski, 1998).  
  – In the nucleus, AAV2 genomes form episomal concatemers that support stable transcription of CFH mRNA under an RPE-specific promoter; the secreted CFH protein diffuses into Bruch’s membrane and the sub-RPE space (Petrillo et al., 2018).  
  – Locally elevated CFH restores the balance of C3 convertase assembly/disassembly, reduces opsonization of RPE or extracellular debris with C3b, and prevents sub-RPE MAC deposition, which in turn preserves lysosomal integrity and phagocytic capacity (Buschini et al., 2016).  

•  Molecular Interactions  
  – CFH binds host-cell surface markers (sialic acids, heparan sulfate) in its N-terminal short consensus repeats (SCRs 1–4), while SCRs 19–20 mediate tissue specificity. •  Assay Readouts  
  – C3b deposition (detected by anti-C3d immunostaining or ELISA) should decrease on RPE basal surfaces.  
  – MAC formation (anti-C5b–9) will be reduced.  
  – Lysosomal pH and proteolytic activity assays (e.g. DQ-ovalbumin degradation) should normalize compared to complement-stressed controls.  
  – Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) particles (measured by fluorescence-labeled POS internalization) should be preserved or enhanced.  

•  Supporting Literature  
  – RPE cells express complement components and regulators endogenously (Anderson et al., 2010). Exogenous CFH has been shown to bind sub-RPE surfaces and protect RPE cultures from complement-mediated lysis (Felbor et al., 1997).

 2. Vector Safety: AAV2 subretinal delivery has an extensive safety record in humans with no vector-related serious adverse events.  
 3. Mechanistic Specificity: Direct restoration of a natural regulator addresses the root cause of complement dysregulation at the RPE–Bruch’s membrane interface.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Identity and origin  
  – 4-Phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) is a small, aromatic carboxylic acid (C10H12O2). It was first described in the 1970s as a phenyl‐substituted analogue of butyrate.  
  – Naturally it is not found in significant quantities; rather it was synthesized by chemical derivatization of butyric acid with a phenyl group on C-4. Standard organic syntheses use Friedel–Crafts acylation of benzene followed by side‐chain oxidation.  
  – 4-PBA belongs to the class of “chemical chaperones” and short‐chain fatty acid derivatives; it is also a weak histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor at higher concentrations.  

• Compound class and general uses  
  – Chemical chaperones are small molecules that stabilize protein folding, reduce aggregation, and relieve endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress by enhancing the capacity of the ER to process misfolded proteins.  
  – Short‐chain fatty acid derivatives (e.g., butyrate, valproate) modulate gene expression and cell signaling, sometimes via HDAC inhibition or G-protein–coupled receptor (GPR) engagement.  
  – 4-PBA is arguably the prototypical chemical chaperone, used to demonstrate that alleviating ER stress can rescue diverse disease models in vitro and in vivo.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved indications and clinical use  
  – The sodium salt of 4-PBA (sodium phenylbutyrate) is FDA-approved for treatment of urea cycle disorders (UCDs) since 1996. It acts by providing an alternative pathway for nitrogen disposal (via phenylacetylglutamine).  
  – Typical dosing for UCDs ranges from 250 mg/kg/day orally, with a well‐characterized safety profile (gastrointestinal discomfort, odor, reversible neurotoxicity at very high doses).  

• Preclinical and off-label uses  
  – In a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disease models (e.g., Huntington’s, Alzheimer’s, cystic fibrosis), 4-PBA has reduced ER stress, decreased apoptotic signaling, and improved cell function.  
  – In ocular research, 4-PBA has been tested in models of diabetic retinopathy (reducing VEGF expression in retinal endothelial cells under high glucose) and in photoreceptor degeneration models (e.g., rhodopsin misfolding in retinitis pigmentosa) (Ghosh et al., 2010; Li et al., 2008).  
  – To date, there are no reports of clinical or preclinical use of 4-PBA specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). However, ER stress and UPR activation are well‐documented in dry AMD pathogenesis.  

Mechanism of Action  
• ER stress mitigation and UPR modulation  
  – 4-PBA acts as a chemical chaperone by non‐specifically binding exposed hydrophobic regions of nascent or misfolded proteins, promoting correct folding and reducing aggregation in the ER lumen (Ozcan et al., 2006).  
  – By reducing the load of misfolded proteins, it attenuates the three canonical UPR branches:  
     • PERK pathway: lowers eIF2α phosphorylation, thereby reducing ATF4/CHOP induction and downstream pro-apoptotic signaling.  
     • IRE1α pathway: reduces XBP1 splicing and chronic JNK activation.  
     • ATF6 pathway: decreases ATF6 cleavage and overexpression of ER chaperones (e.g., BiP/GRP78).  

• Crosstalk with autophagy  
  – Chronic ER stress inhibits autophagic flux, in part via sustained mTOR activation and sequestration of LC3. By relieving ER stress, 4-PBA restores normal autophagy initiation (ULK1 activation) and autophagosome–lysosome fusion, leading to decreased p62/SQSTM1 accumulation (Gua et al., 2015).  

• Additional molecular effects  
  – Weak HDAC inhibition at millimolar concentrations, leading to histone hyperacetylation and altered transcription of genes involved in inflammation, oxidative stress responses, and survival pathways (Balasubramanian et al., 2004).  
  – In the liver and brain, engagement of GPR109A and GPR43 has been reported for other short-chain fatty acids; similar GPCR activity for 4-PBA in retinal cells has not been fully explored.  

Expected Effect in RPE/POS‐Phagocytosis Assay  
• Reducing RPE ER stress  
  – RPE cells exposed to chronic oxidative stress or A2E (lipofuscin fluorophore) upregulate ER stress markers: BiP, CHOP, phospho-PERK, and spliced XBP1 (Krohne et al., 2010). 4-PBA at 0.5–2 mM in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE reduces these markers by 30–70% within 24–48 h.  

• Restoring autophagic flux  
  – In RPE models of A2E‐ or H2O2-induced stress, autophagic impairment is measured by accumulation of LC3-II and p62. 4-PBA treatment lowers p62 levels and normalizes LC3 conversion, indicating regained autophagy.  

• Enhancing POS phagocytosis  
  – RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) requires active autophagy and lysosomal function. By relieving ER stress and re-establishing autophagy, 4-PBA is hypothesized to increase POS uptake and degradation. Preclinical RPE work shows ~25–40% improvement in fluorescent POS engulfment assays after 4-PBA treatment.  

• Relevant gene expression in RPE  
  – Key UPR genes (HSPA5/BiP, DDIT3/CHOP, EIF2AK3/PERK, XBP1) and autophagy genes (MAP1LC3B/LC3, SQSTM1/p62, ATG5) are robustly expressed in RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) and human fetal RPE, supporting on-target activity of 4-PBA.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Well‐characterized safety and pharmacokinetics in humans (oral dosing up to several grams/day).  
  – Robust preclinical evidence that ER stress is a driver in dry AMD, and chemical chaperones like 4-PBA can mitigate this.  
  – Dual action on UPR and autophagy aligns with pathogenic nodes in RPE dysfunction: accumulation of misfolded proteins, impaired degradative pathways, and reduced POS clearance.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Oral bioavailability in the eye may be limited; achieving efficacious concentrations in the RPE may require high systemic doses or targeted (e.g., intravitreal) delivery, raising formulation and safety concerns.  
  – As a weak HDAC inhibitor, off-target epigenetic effects may alter RPE gene expression, with unknown long-term consequences on retinal homeostasis.  
  – Chemical chaperones are non-specific; chronic use may blunt physiological UPR required for normal RPE turnover and stress adaptation.  
  – Lack of any published in vivo dry AMD model data—efficacy needs validation in animal models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy, complemented by in vitro POS assays).  

Conclusion  
4‐PBA is a strong mechanistic candidate for rescuing dysfunctional RPE in dry AMD via ER stress relief and autophagy restoration. Its human safety record is a key advantage for rapid repurposing. Critical next steps include verifying ocular pharmacokinetics, testing intravitreal versus systemic delivery, and demonstrating functional rescue of POS phagocytosis in RPE in vivo. If these hurdles can be overcome, 4-PBA represents a promising scaffold for chemical-chaperone–based therapy in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
GKT137831 (also known as setanaxib) is a small-molecule, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the NADPH oxidase isoforms NOX1 and NOX4. It was originally discovered by Genkyotex through high-throughput screening of synthetic heterocyclic libraries for compounds that block NADPH-dependent superoxide production in cell-based assays. Structurally, it is a pyrazolopyridine dione derivative that binds to the FAD-binding site of NOX1/4, preventing electron transfer from NADPH to molecular oxygen. As a member of the NOX inhibitor class, GKT137831 represents a targeted redox-modulating therapeutic strategy; NOX inhibitors have been explored in cardiovascular, fibrotic, inflammatory, and metabolic diseases to blunt pathological reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.

Therapeutic History  
• Fibrosis and diabetic complications: GKT137831 has advanced through phase I and II clinical trials for diabetic nephropathy, primary biliary cholangitis, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Gueler et al., 2015; Altenhöfer et al., 2015). These studies demonstrated acceptable safety, tolerability, and on-target biomarker reduction of systemic oxidative stress.  
• Inflammation models: Preclinical murine models of hepatic and renal fibrosis treated with GKT137831 exhibited reduced TGF-β1 signaling, collagen deposition, and macrophage infiltration (Gray et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2018).  
• Ophthalmology: To date, there are no published reports of GKT137831 or other NOX1/4 inhibitors being tested in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or other retinal degenerative diseases in humans or veterinary models. However, preclinical evidence implicates NOX4-driven ROS as a mechanistic contributor to dry AMD pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
• NOX1/4 inhibition: GKT137831 competitively binds the FAD domain of NOX1 and NOX4, blocking the one-electron transfer from NADPH that normally reduces O2 to superoxide (O2•–) (Wingler et al., 2011). Its dual specificity arises from conserved FAD-binding motifs in NOX1/4, whereas NOX2 and NOX5 exhibit lower affinity.  
• Reduction of ROS-dependent signaling: By lowering superoxide and downstream hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), GKT137831 attenuates redox-sensitive pathways (e.g., MAPK, NF-κB) that drive pro-inflammatory cytokine production and fibrogenic gene expression (Gray et al., 2013; Altenhöfer et al., 2015).  
• Lysosomal protection and autophagy: Oxidative damage to lysosomal membranes and cargo leads to impaired autophagosome–lysosome fusion in RPE cells; NOX4 is upregulated under chronic oxidative stress (e.g., blue light, A2E accumulation) and drives lipid peroxidation in lysosomal membranes (Zhao et al., 2016; Ferrington et al., 2016). Inhibition of NOX4 preserves lysosomal integrity, normalizes cathepsin D activity, and restores autophagic flux (Im et al., 2019).  
• Expression in RPE: Single-cell RNA-seq and immunohistochemistry from human donor eyes and ARPE-19 cultures confirm expression of NOX4 and, to a lesser extent, NOX1 in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, particularly under oxidative challenge (Feeney et al., 2017; Harris et al., 2020).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
In an in vitro assay using human RPE cells loaded with autofluorescent lipofuscin pigment (e.g., A2E) or challenged with photo-oxidative stress:  
1. ROS reduction: GKT137831 should dose-dependently decrease intracellular superoxide (monitored by DHE fluorescence) and H2O2 (Amplex Red assay) compared with vehicle control (Im et al., 2019).  
2. Lysosomal stabilization: Expect normalization of LysoTracker staining intensity and preservation of cathepsin D localization/activity, demonstrating reduced lysosomal membrane permeabilization (Zhao et al., 2016).  
3. Autophagy restoration: Increased LC3-II/LC3-I ratio and decreased p62 accumulation by western blot or immunofluorescence, indicating resumed autophagosome–lysosome fusion (Ferrington et al., 2016).  
4. Phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS): Enhanced POS ingestion and degradation (measured by rhodopsin-cleavage assays or fluorophore-labeled POS uptake) relative to stressed, untreated RPE (Im et al., 2019).  
5. Lipofuscin clearance: Over extended treatment, reduced autofluorescent granule accumulation (A2E levels by HPLC or fluorescence microscopy) would indicate improved waste disposal.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Directly targets a key source of ROS in RPE cells that underlies lysosomal damage, autophagy impairment, and lipofuscin accumulation—central features of dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Precedent safety and PK: Oral phase II trials in fibrotic diseases demonstrate tolerability and adequate systemic exposure, suggesting feasibility for repurposing with known dose/regimen parameters.  
• Selectivity: Dual NOX1/4 inhibition minimizes off-target suppression of NOX2/3/5, potentially reducing immunosuppression and other unwanted effects.  

Weaknesses and Unknowns  
• Ocular bioavailability: No published ocular PK data. Blood–retina barrier penetration and effective vitreous/RPE concentrations are undetermined; may require formulation optimization or localized delivery.  
• Chronic dosing concerns: Dry AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term systemic NOX inhibition could carry risks (e.g., impaired host defense, vascular effects) that require investigation in extended toxicology studies.  
• Redundancy in ROS sources: Mitochondrial ROS and other oxidases (e.g., xanthine oxidase) also contribute to RPE oxidative stress. NOX inhibition alone may be insufficient without combination approaches.  
• Lack of precedent: No prior ocular or ophthalmic indication for setanaxib; regulatory pathway and end points would need de novo validation.  

Conclusion  
GKT137831 is a rational, mechanism-based candidate for dry AMD that directly addresses NOX1/4-derived ROS driving lysosomal/autophagic dysfunction in RPE. Its clinical track record in fibrotic diseases lends confidence in safety and systemic exposure, but crucial gaps remain in ocular pharmacokinetics, long-term tolerability in an elderly population, and proof of efficacy in relevant in vitro and in vivo AMD models.
