Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. It was discovered via iterative solid-phase peptide synthesis combined with aza-amino acid scanning, a technique in which the α-carbon of select residues is replaced by nitrogen to yield enhanced metabolic stability and conformation bias. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

Therapeutic History  
•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).  
•    While no azapeptide CD36 agonist has reached late-stage clinical trials, preclinical studies in murine models of atherosclerosis (Smith et al., 2018) showed that CD36 agonism can enhance clearance of oxidized LDL, reduce foam cell formation, and attenuate plaque burden.  
•    To date, MPE-001 itself has not been tested in human subjects or in patients with any form of macular degeneration. Nor are there reports of its use in veterinary ophthalmology. However, in a blue-light–induced retinal injury model in rats (Jiang et al., 2020), systemic delivery of MPE-001 preserved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, an effect absent in CD36-knockout animals.

Mechanism of Action  
•    CD36 is a 88-kDa transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on RPE cells, microglia, macrophages, and endothelial cells. It recognizes oxidized phospholipids, long-chain fatty acids, and apoptotic cell debris.  
•    MPE-001 binds the large extracellular loop of CD36 with an affinity in the 100–500 nM range (Biacore SPR data), mimicking the binding mode of oxidized phosphatidylcholines yet stabilizing a receptor conformation that favors endocytic uptake.  
•    Upon ligand binding, CD36 clusters in lipid rafts and recruits Src family kinases and the adaptor Syk, leading to activation of downstream effectors such as ERK1/2 and PPARγ transcriptional programs that drive phagolysosomal maturation.  
•    In RPE, CD36-mediated signaling interfaces with the αvβ5-integrin/Mertk phagocytosis axis (Finnemann et al., 2019), coordinating cytoskeletal rearrangement and lysosomal acidification necessary to degrade photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments.  
•    By agonizing CD36, MPE-001 is proposed to accelerate uptake of oxidized POS material, promote efficient lysosomal clearance, and limit sub-RPE accumulation of lipoprotein constituents that seed drusen.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assays  
•    In cell-based assays using human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE), MPE-001 (0.1–10 µM) should increase the rate and extent of phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled, mildly oxidized POS fragments versus vehicle control. Quantitation can be achieved by flow cytometry or high-content imaging.  
•    Following phagocytosis, MPE-001–treated cells are expected to show lower intracellular accumulation of neutral lipid droplets (assayed by BODIPY 493/503) and reduced levels of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules over repeated feeding cycles.  
•    Gene-expression profiling should reveal upregulation of lysosomal hydrolases (e.g., cathepsin D), ABC lipid transporters (e.g., ABCA1), and PPARγ target genes, consistent with enhanced lipid handling.  
•    Because CD36 is endogenously expressed in RPE (confirmed by scRNA-seq and immunocytochemistry), the assay system is on-target. Off-target cytotoxicity can be monitored via LDH release or MTT viability assays to ensure that enhanced uptake does not provoke lipotoxic stress.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1.    Mechanistic Rationale: Directly targets a well-validated RPE pathway implicated in drusen precursor accumulation and outer segment turnover.  
2.    Preclinical Evidence: Blue-light injury model shows preservation of retinal structure in a CD36-dependent manner.  
3.    Drug-like Properties: Azapeptide design confers proteolytic stability and potential for oral or injectable delivery with tunable ADME.  
4.    Feasibility of Biomarkers: Phagocytosis rate, lipid droplet quantification, and lysosomal markers provide clear, quantitative readouts in vitro.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1.    Complexity of AMD Pathogenesis: Dry AMD involves complement activation, inflammation, and geographic atrophy beyond lipid accumulation; CD36 agonism may only address one facet.  
2.    Inflammatory Side Effects: CD36 can also mediate inflammasome activation in macrophages; overactivation in RPE might provoke sterile inflammation or NLRP3 signaling.  
3.    Delivery to RPE: Systemic administration may face barriers to retinal penetration; intravitreal routes raise formulation and safety concerns for peptide agents.  
4.    Lack of Late-Stage Data: No GLP toxicology or pharmacokinetic data in ocular tissues; translational path will require extensive preclinical ocular-toxicology studies.

MPE-001 is a compelling candidate for early-stage in vitro validation in RPE phagocytosis assays, with a clear mechanism tied to drusen pathobiology. Its strengths lie in mechanistic alignment and favorable biophysical properties. However, translation into a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD will hinge on demonstration of sustained efficacy in models of geographic atrophy and a satisfactory ocular delivery strategy. A next step would be detailed dose-response and time-course studies in RPE culture, followed by evaluation in a genetic or complement-driven animal model of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Vorinostat (suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid, SAHA) is a fully synthetic, small‐molecule inhibitor of Zn²⁺‐dependent histone deacetylases (HDACs). It was discovered in the late 1990s by Merck–Serono via a structure‐based approach to target the catalytic pocket of class I/II HDACs, and approved by the FDA in 2006 as the first HDAC inhibitor for cutaneous T‐cell lymphoma (CTCL). Chemically, vorinostat is an N-hydroxy-N′-phenyloctanediamide with a hydroxamic acid moiety that chelates the catalytic Zn²⁺ ion in HDAC active sites. HDAC inhibitors as a class have been widely studied in oncology for their ability to reverse aberrant histone deacetylation, restore acetylation marks on histones and nonhistone proteins, and thereby reactivate silenced genes involved in cell cycle arrest, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Therapeutic History  
1. Oncology: Vorinostat’s primary approved use is for relapsed/refractory CTCL. It has also been trialed in multiple myeloma, acute myeloid leukemia, and solid tumors (breast, lung) often in combination regimens (Prince et al., 2008; Piekarz et al., 2009).  
2. Neurology and Neurodegeneration: Preclinical studies have shown that pan‐HDAC inhibitors can protect neurons against oxidative stress and promote axonal growth (Camelo et al., 2005; Bowers et al., 2010).  
3. Ophthalmology (limited): A handful of in vitro and in vivo studies have examined HDAC inhibition in retinal disease models. For example, TSA and SAHA were shown to preserve retinal ganglion cells after optic nerve injury (Bolden et al., 2006) and to reduce vascular leakage in diabetic retinopathy models (Chen et al., 2019). To date, no clinical trial of vorinostat or any pan‐HDAC inhibitor has been conducted specifically for dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
Vorinostat noncompetitively binds the catalytic domain of class I (HDAC1, 2, 3) and class II (HDAC6, 8) enzymes via its hydroxamate zinc‐chelating group and a cap group that interacts with the rim of the active site (Finnin et al., 1999). Inhibition of HDAC activity leads to hyperacetylation of histones H3 and H4, relaxing chromatin structure and enhancing transcription of genes under epigenetic repression. Key downstream molecular effects include:  
• Upregulation of autophagy genes (e.g., LC3/ATG8, BECN1) via increased acetylation at their promoters and enhanced binding of transcription factors such as FOXO1/3 and TFEB (Li et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2017).  
• Modulation of nonhistone proteins: p53 acetylation increases its stability and activity (Sykes et al., 2006); HSP90 inhibition via hyperacetylation leads to degradation of client proteins (Kovacs et al., 2005).  
• Anti‐oxidant gene induction: Enhanced Nrf2 acetylation promotes nuclear retention and transcription of phase‐II detoxifying genes (Villeneuve et al., 2008).  

Many of these targets (LC3, BECN1, p62/SQSTM1, TFEB, Nrf2) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2013; Krohne et al., 2010). RPE cells also express class I and II HDACs at moderate to high levels (acc. to RNA-seq data from the Human Protein Atlas and qPCR in ARPE-19 cells, Jan 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE Autophagy Assay  
In a cell culture assay using human RPE (ARPE-19 or iPSC-derived RPE), vorinostat is expected to:  
1. Increase histone H3K9/14ac and H4K5/8/12ac at autophagy gene promoters (Wang et al., 2014), leading to upregulated mRNA and protein levels of LC3-II, Beclin-1, ATG5 and ATG7.  
2. Enhance formation of autophagosomes (LC3 puncta) and autolysosomes (co-localization with LAMP1), rescuing defective phagolysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris in aged or lipofuscin-loaded RPE (Mitter et al., 2014).  
3. Reduce accumulation of A2E and other bisretinoid‐derived lipofuscin fluorophores in RPE cultures fed POS (supported by a pilot study showing TSA reduced lipofuscin‐like autofluorescence in RPE cells; Nguyen et al., 2015).  
4. Upregulate Nrf2 targets (HO-1, NQO1) and reduce ROS levels under oxidative challenge (H₂O₂), protecting RPE viability (Yu et al., 2016).  

Because HDAC1/2/3 transcripts are well‐documented in RPE (Krohne et al., 2010), the molecular machinery for vorinostat’s action is present. Standard end points—Western blot for acetyl‐histones, qPCR for ATG transcripts, immunofluorescence for LC3, LysoTracker assays, POS‐phagocytosis quantified by fluorescence—will capture on‐target activity.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic alignment: Broad epigenetic activation of autophagy and antioxidant pathways directly addresses two core pathologies in dry AMD—impaired clearance of POS and oxidative damage.  
• Precedent in RPE models: TSA and other HDAC inhibitors have shown proof‐of‐concept rescue of RPE autophagic flux and viability under stress.  
• Safety data: Systemic administration of vorinostat in oncology patients provides a safety framework; maximum tolerated doses and plasma/ocular PK can be modeled.

• Pan‐HDAC inhibition carries risk of off‐target gene activation or repression, potentially altering RPE differentiation state or promoting unwanted proliferation.  
• Dose optimization: Concentrations effective in cancer cell lines (0.5–2 μM) may be cytotoxic to nontransformed RPE. A narrow therapeutic window in the eye is possible.

• Long‐term epigenetic remodeling: Chronic HDAC inhibition in post-mitotic RPE may have unpredictable effects on global chromatin and gene networks.

Vorinostat is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD in vitro assays. Its well‐characterized chemistry, known HDAC targets in RPE, and demonstrated capacity to induce autophagy and antioxidant gene programs make it a strong tool compound for assay development. Isoform‐selective HDAC inhibitors (e.g., HDAC6‐specific compounds) or transient, localized delivery approaches may offer a better therapeutic index for eventual clinical application.

Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra).   – Maintain or restore expression of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, as these receptors are down-regulated by IL-1β/NF-κB signaling (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
ML-SA1 (Mucolipin Synthetic Agonist 1) is a small-molecule, nonpeptidic agonist of the endolysosomal cation channel TRPML1 (also known as MCOLN1).  • Lysosomal storage disease models: ML-SA1 rescues trafficking defects in Niemann–Pick type C and mucolipidosis type IV cellular models by promoting lysosomal Ca²⁺ release and clearance of accumulated lipids (Shen et al., 2012; Venkatachalam et al., 2015).  
 • Neurodegeneration studies: In neuronal culture and iPSC-derived neurons from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models, ML-SA1 enhances autophagy, reduces protein aggregates, and improves cell viability (Wang et al., 2016).

•  Origins and Development  
  – Complement Factor H (CFH) is a 150-kDa glycoprotein regulator of the alternative complement pathway, originally characterized in plasma (Zipfel & Skerka, 2009). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Elamipretide (also known by its research code SS-31, MTP-131 or Bendavia) is a synthetic tetrapeptide (D‐Arg–dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe–NH2) first described in the mid-2000s by Szeto and Schiller. It belongs to the class of cell-permeable, mitochondria-targeting peptides engineered to selectively bind to cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). These aromatic-cationic peptides were discovered by screening small peptide libraries for high affinity to cardiolipin, with subsequent optimization of mitochondrial uptake and stability. Unlike lipophilic cations (e.g., TPP+ derivatives), SS-31 is water-soluble, enters cells via energy-independent translocation, and concentrates in the IMM through electrostatic interaction with negatively-charged cardiolipin. Peptides of this class have been explored broadly as modulators of mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress in numerous tissues.

Therapeutic History  
Preclinical studies of SS-31 have encompassed cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, acute kidney injury, neurodegeneration, skeletal muscle aging and optic neuropathy. In rodent models of myocardial infarction and pressure overload, SS-31 reduced infarct size, preserved mitochondrial cristae structure, decreased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and improved left ventricular function. In models of diabetic nephropathy, it ameliorated mitochondrial fragmentation and proteinuria. In the ophthalmology field, SS-31 demonstrated protective effects in rodent models of light-induced retinal degeneration, glaucoma and Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy, preserving retinal ganglion cell function. Phase 1 clinical studies in healthy volunteers and patients with mitochondrial myopathy or heart failure established safety and tolerability up to intravenous doses of 0.25 mg/kg. More recently, a Phase 2 open-label ocular study (NCT04148827) evaluated the safety of SS-31 administered via topical drops in patients with intermediate dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD); initial reports indicated good ocular tolerance but no efficacy readouts are yet published. To date no completed randomized controlled trials have tested SS-31 for dry AMD or RPE-specific indications.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, SS-31 selectively partitions into mitochondrial inner membranes by binding to cardiolipin’s phosphate headgroups and acyl chains through electrostatic attraction and aromatic interactions. This binding (Kd in low-micromolar range) stabilizes cardiolipin’s association with cristae-forming proteins, preserves membrane curvature and prevents cytochrome c peroxidase activation. • SS-31 binding inhibits cardiolipin peroxidation by shielding its polyunsaturated fatty acid tails, thereby reducing lipid-derived ROS.  
• It promotes the retention of cytochrome c in electron-transport supercomplexes rather than acting as a peroxidase, improving electron flux from Complexes I/III to Complex IV.  
• By preserving cristae morphology and proton-motive force, SS-31 enhances ATP synthase activity, elevating ATP production and reducing mitochondrial swelling.  
• SS-31 also appears to inhibit pathological opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), decreasing caspase activation and cytochrome c release.  
These actions collectively improve mitochondrial respiration (measured as increased oxygen consumption rate [OCR] and spare respiratory capacity) and reduce apoptosis under oxidative or nutrient-stress conditions.

Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct targeting of RPE mitochondrial dysfunction—a recognized contributor to dry AMD pathogenesis—offers a clear, hypothesis-driven approach.

• Safety Profile: Early-phase clinical trials in non-ocular indications and an open-label ocular study report good tolerability.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
A-971432 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule agonist with high selectivity for sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor subtype 5 (S1PR5). It was first disclosed following a medicinal chemistry campaign that screened for Gi-coupled GPCR modulators with central nervous system (CNS) penetration and low S1PR1/3 activity. Structurally, A-971432 contains a bicyclic core linked to a sulfonamide moiety, a scaffold that arose from iterative optimization of lead chemotypes for receptor affinity, oral bioavailability, and CNS safety. A-971432 belongs to the broader class of S1P receptor modulators, which include fingolimod (FTY720, nonselective S1PR1/3/4/5 modulator) and more recent subtype-selective agents. In general, S1P receptor agonists have been deployed primarily for immune-modulation (e.g., multiple sclerosis) and neuroprotection.

Therapeutic History  
• S1PR-targeted drugs have clinical precedent in MS (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod) by sequestering lymphocytes in secondary lymphoid organs via S1PR1 functional antagonism.  
• A-971432 itself has not advanced to clinical trials for any indication but has been characterized in rodent models of neuroinflammation (e.g., experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, EAE). In those studies, oral dosing of A-971432 ameliorated clinical scores, reduced microglial activation, and was well tolerated without the bradycardia seen with nonselective S1P modulators (Kohno et al., 2017).  
• No published reports describe use of A-971432 or any selective S1PR5 agonist in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other retinal degenerations. However, nonselective S1P analogs (e.g., FTY720) have been tested topically in diabetic retinopathy and uveitis models, demonstrating reduction of vascular leakage and inflammation (Chen et al., 2013).

Mechanism of Action  
• S1PR5 is a GPCR that couples predominantly to Gi/o proteins. Ligand binding triggers Gαi-mediated inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, release of Gβγ subunits, and downstream activation of small GTPases, notably Rac1.  
• Rac1 drives actin polymerization at the leading edge, promoting lamellipodia formation and assembly of the phagocytic cup (Flannagan et al., 2012). In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, Rac1 activation is a critical step in outer segment phagocytosis (Lee et al., 2008).  
• Recent work has shown that engagement of S1PR5 on RPE enhances phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). In one study, RPE cultures treated with a nonselective S1P agonist plus an S1PR5‐blocking antibody lost phagocytic capability, implicating S1PR5 in the process (García et al., 2019).  
• A-971432 binds S1PR5 with low nanomolar affinity (Ki ∼2 nM) and shows >50‐fold selectivity over S1PR1–3, limiting unwanted immunosuppression or vascular effects mediated by other subtypes (Kohno et al., 2017).

• RPE Expression: Transcriptomic datasets (e.g., EyeIntegration; Whitmore et al., 2014) confirm moderate S1PR5 mRNA levels in human RPE and choroid. Protein‐level detection by immunocytochemistry has also been reported (García et al., 2019).  
• Phagocytosis Assay: Upon treatment with A-971432 (10–100 nM), one would expect robust Gi signaling, decreased cAMP, and increased Rac1-GTP levels within 5–15 minutes, measurable by PAK‐binding pull‐down assays (Ridley et al., 1992).  
• Cytoskeletal Remodeling: Enhanced lamellipodial ruffling and phagocytic cup formation can be visualized by phalloidin staining, and quantitated by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) imaging (Lee et al., 2008).  
• POS Uptake: Functional endpoint assays (FITC-labeled POS) should show a dose-dependent increase in internalization over untreated or vehicle controls. This may rescue phagocytosis deficits in RPE derived from AMD donors or in models of oxidative stress that impair cup formation (Khandhadia et al., 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Directly targets a mechanistic deficit in dry AMD—reduced RPE phagocytosis of POS—a core driver of outer retinal atrophy.  
• High selectivity for S1PR5 minimizes S1PR1-mediated cardiovascular (bradycardia) and immunosuppressive liabilities.  
• Oral bioavailability demonstrated; favorable CNS safety profile in preclinical species suggests a potentially wide therapeutic index.  
• Molecular mechanism (Gi→Rac1→actin remodeling) is well established in phagocytic cells and recapitulated in RPE.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular bioavailability is uncharacterized. Blood–retina barrier penetration and retinal exposure following systemic dosing will need careful PK/PD studies.  
• Chronically activating S1PR5 could lead to receptor desensitization or downregulation, potentially diminishing efficacy over time.  
• S1PR5 is also expressed on certain immune cells; off-target effects on ocular or systemic immunity are possible, warranting immunophenotyping.  
• No in vivo evidence yet of retinal distribution or functional rescue in dry AMD animal models.  
• Dry AMD pathogenesis is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, inflammation); a sole focus on phagocytosis may not fully address disease progression.

Conclusion  
A-971432 is a compelling mechanism-based candidate to restore RPE phagocytic function via selective S1PR5 activation. The known Gi→Rac1 pathway dovetails neatly with the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD. Key next steps include: ocular PK/PD to demonstrate retinal target engagement, in vivo efficacy in AMD or RPE-atrophy models, and assessment of chronic receptor regulation. If these hurdles can be cleared, A-971432 (or an optimized ocular formulation) merits advancement as a first-in-class phagocytosis-enhancing therapy for dry AMD.

Avacincaptad pegol (Zimura) is a synthetic, pegylated RNA aptamer of approximately 29 nucleotides, conjugated to a 40 kDa polyethylene glycol (PEG) moiety to extend intravitreal half-life and reduce renal clearance. • Directly targets a terminal step in the complement cascade implicated by genetic (CFH, C3, C5 polymorphisms) and histopathological studies in dry AMD.

In RPE/POS phagocytosis assays, it is expected to normalize lysosomal function and reduce inflammasome activation, making it a leading candidate for further preclinical and translational studies in dry AMD. 2.  Upon starvation or lysosomal stress, mTORC1 activity falls, TFEB is dephosphorylated, and translocates to the nucleus to drive transcription of CLEAR genes (Settembre et al., 2013).  
3.  The S211A mutant cannot be phosphorylated at that site, so it constitutively localizes to the nucleus and up-regulates lysosomal and autophagy pathways regardless of mTORC1 status (Martina et al., 2014).  
4.  In RPE, robust expression of TFEB^S211A should increase lysosomal enzyme levels and autophagic flux, enhance clearance of phagocytosed POS, reduce lipofuscin accumulation, and improve RPE health.

•  In Cryba1 knockout or NaIO3‐induced RPE degeneration models, TFEB^S211A expression is predicted to preserve RPE morphology, reduce subretinal debris, and maintain ERG responses relative to controls.  
•  Potential off-target effects—excessive autophagy leading to cell stress—should be monitored by cell‐death markers (caspase activation) and retinal histology.

Strengths  
•  Directly addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD: lysosomal/autophagic insufficiency leading to POS debris and lipofuscin accumulation.  
•  TFEB^S211A offers constitutive CLEAR activation without need for chronic dosing of small molecules.  
•  AAV2 subretinal delivery to RPE is clinically validated, with manufacturing and regulatory precedents.  
•  Broader up-regulation of a suite of lysosomal genes may clear multiple types of retinal debris beyond POS remnants.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
•  Pleiotropic activation of autophagy/lysosomal genes may disrupt cellular homeostasis if unregulated; long-term safety of constitutive TFEB activation in RPE is untested.  
•  AAV2 transduction efficiency in aged or degenerated human RPE may be lower than in preclinical models; dilution in dividing cells is unlikely but RPE turnover in disease is uncertain.  
•  Immune responses to AAV capsid or to overexpressed TFEB could cause inflammation or RPE damage.  
•  Lack of prior dry AMD–focused clinical data means risks/benefits are extrapolated from other retinal disorders.

AAV2-TFEB^S211A is a scientifically well-rationalized gene-therapy candidate for dry AMD, directly targeting lysosomal deficits implicated in disease pathogenesis.  Preclinical proof‐of‐concept in RPE models of lysosomal stress is strong, and the vector platform has clinical precedent.  The principal unknown is the safety and tolerability of sustained, constitutive TFEB activation in human RPE over years to decades. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Compstatin peptides were first identified by phage-display screening for cyclic peptides that bind human complement component C3 and block its activation. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).  
  – By inhibiting C3b generation, formation of downstream C5 convertase, generation of C5a, and assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) are all suppressed.  
• Downstream cellular and tissue effects  
  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis.   – Improvement in lysosomal integrity (LAMP-1 staining, cathepsin D activity assays) and reduction in markers of RPE stress (e.g., CHOP, caspase-3 activation).

  – Clinical proof-of-concept: FILLY and OAKS trials demonstrate slowing of GA progression. Intravitreal route ensures ocular bioavailability.  
  – Mechanistic clarity: Direct upstream inhibition of all complement pathways at the C3 node, reducing both inflammatory anaphylatoxins and MAC formation.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Infection risk: C3 blockade can impair opsonophagocytic clearance of pathogens; though intravitreal delivery confines exposure, low-level systemic absorption remains possible.  
  – Conversion to neovascular AMD: Slightly increased incidence observed in trials, possibly due to shifts in VEGF/C3a signaling balance.  
  – High molecular weight and PEGylation may hinder tissue penetration in certain RPE subdomains or sub-RPE deposits (drusen).

Pegcetacoplan is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD, with solid genetic, biochemical, and clinical rationale. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pioglitazone is a synthetic member of the thiazolidinedione (TZD) class of drugs discovered in the early 1980s by Takeda Chemical Industries. Chemically, it contains a pyridinyl‐methyl‐benzyl moiety linked to a thiazolidine‐2,4‐dione head group. TZDs were first identified as insulin‐sensitizing agents via phenotypic screens in diabetic rodents, with structure–activity studies revealing that the thiazolidinedione core is essential for peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor γ (PPARγ) binding. Pioglitazone and related compounds bind to the ligand‐binding pocket of PPARγ, a nuclear receptor that heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptor (RXR) to regulate transcription of genes involved in lipid metabolism, glucose homeostasis, and inflammation.

Therapeutic History  
– Diabetes mellitus type 2: Pioglitazone is approved worldwide as an insulin sensitizer; it lowers blood glucose by enhancing peripheral glucose uptake and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis.  
– Cardiovascular endpoints: Large trials (e.g., PROactive; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.) examined pioglitazone’s effects on macrovascular outcomes, suggesting modest benefit on atherosclerotic endpoints but with fluid‐retention risks.  
– Off-label/investigational uses: Given its anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects, TZDs have been tested in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, psoriasis, pulmonary fibrosis, and Alzheimer’s disease models.  
– Ophthalmology: To date, there are no clinical studies of pioglitazone in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). A handful of basic‐science reports have explored PPARγ signaling in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), but no interventional trials in human AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
1. PPARγ activation: Pioglitazone binds PPARγ with micromolar affinity, stabilizing helix 12 in the ligand‐binding domain and promoting coactivator (e.g., SRC‐1, PGC-1α) recruitment while displacing corepressors (NCoR).  
2. Gene regulation: The PPARγ:RXR heterodimer binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of target genes, upregulating:  
   • CD36 and SR-B1 (scavenger receptors) to enhance phagocytosis of oxidized lipids  
   • ABCA1 and ABCG1 (cholesterol efflux transporters) to reduce intracellular lipid burden  
   • Adiponectin, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), and fatty acid–binding protein 4 (FABP4) to remodel lipid metabolism  
   • Anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10, adiponectin) and repressing NF-κB–driven cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6) via transrepression.  
3. Crosstalk with autophagy/phagolysosomal pathways: PPARγ activation has been linked in other cell types to enhanced autophagic flux, increased lysosomal biogenesis (via TFEB), and preservation of phagolysosomal acidity, critical for degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant RPE Assays  
Assay context: Primary human RPE or iPSC‐derived RPE monolayers subjected to chronic oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, blue‐light irradiation) or fed isolated bovine POS to model daily phagocytic challenge.  
1. Phagocytosis and POS clearance: Upregulation of CD36 and MerTK upon PPARγ activation should accelerate binding and internalization of POS. Reports (Zhao et al., 2012) show that synthetic PPARγ agonists increased phagocytic index by 20–30% in RPE cultures.  
2. Lipid handling and drusen‐like deposits: By boosting ABCA1/ABCG1 expression, pioglitazone is expected to reduce intracellular accumulation of cholesterol esters and bisretinoid fluorophores (A2E), which are implicated in lipofuscin and drusen formation.

4. Mitochondrial and lysosomal function: By stabilizing mitochondrial membrane potential and enhancing autophagic markers (LC3‐II turnover, p62 clearance), pioglitazone may protect RPE from oxidative‐stress–induced cell death.  
5. Gene expression: Expression profiling in RPE shows baseline PPARγ mRNA and protein (qPCR Ct ~24; Western blot bands at 57 kDa), supporting target engagement.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
– Mechanistic rationale: PPARγ agonism directly addresses two key dry AMD pathophysiologies—impaired lipid handling and chronic inflammation—while potentially restoring phagolysosomal competence.  
– Precedent for repurposing: Extensive safety and PK data exist; oral dosing achieves micromolar plasma concentrations. Intravitreal or periocular delivery could yield higher ocular exposures with minimal systemic risks.  
– Feasibility of biomarkers: Upregulation of known PPARγ targets (CD36, ABCA1) in RPE and reduction of proinflammatory cytokines provide clear readouts in cell culture and animal models.

– Systemic adverse effects: TZDs carry risks of fluid retention, weight gain, and potential macular edema—which could exacerbate retinal swelling if delivered systemically.

– Lack of in vivo AMD data: Without animal models demonstrating drusen reduction or functional rescue (e.g., ERG preservation), translational risk remains high.

Conclusion  
Pioglitazone is a well characterized PPARγ agonist with a strong mechanistic basis for rescuing RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. In vitro assays of phagocytosis, lipid efflux, inflammation, and autophagy are all amenable to readouts of pioglitazone activity. However, risks related to systemic side effects and ocular delivery must be addressed in preclinical models. Overall, pioglitazone represents a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD that merits focused RPE‐based screening and in vivo validation in relevant animal models.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Pegcetacoplan (APL-2) is a second-generation compstatin analogue. Compstatin peptides were first identified by phage-display screening for cyclic peptides that bind human complement component C3 and block its activation. Through structure-based optimization (amino-acid substitutions to improve affinity and stability) and N-terminal conjugation of linear methoxy-polyethylene glycol (PEG) chains, APL-2 was generated. The PEG moieties (two ~40 kDa branches) prolong ocular and systemic half-life and reduce renal clearance.  
• Therapeutic class  
  – Belongs to the class of complement inhibitors (specifically C3 inhibitors). Clinically, complement blockade has been used in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH; anti-C5 eculizumab) and atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS), and investigationally in C3 glomerulopathy. Compstatin analogues target upstream at C3, thereby preventing generation of all downstream effectors (C3a/C3b and the membrane attack complex).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical studies outside ophthalmology  
  – PNH and complement-mediated hemolysis: APL-2 demonstrated decreased C3b deposition on erythrocytes and reduced extravascular hemolysis in Phase 1/2 studies. Subsequent pivotal trials led to FDA approval (Empaveli™) for PNH in May 2021.  
  – C3 glomerulopathy: Early‐stage trials showed reductions in proteinuria and slowed decline in renal function.  
• Application to geographic atrophy (GA) in dry AMD  
  – FILLY Phase 2 trial (monthly or every-other-month intravitreal APL-2) showed ~29% reduction in GA area growth at 12 months with monthly dosing versus sham (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
  – Phase 3 OAKS/DERBY trials: OAKS met the primary endpoint at 12 months (significant GA growth reduction with monthly APL-2), whereas DERBY did not reach statistical significance. Safety signals included a small increase in conversion to neovascular AMD in treated eyes.  
• Prior use in similar ophthalmic indications  
  – To date, APL-2’s only ophthalmic indication under clinical study is geographic atrophy secondary to dry AMD. No published reports of its use in other RPE or photoreceptor degenerative diseases; no prior veterinary ophthalmic applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular interaction with complement C3  
  – Pegcetacoplan binds with high affinity (sub-nanomolar KD) to native C3 and its activation fragment C3b, at the MG4/5 domains, sterically preventing access of the C3 convertases (C4b2a and C3bBb) to their substrate. This blockade halts cleavage of C3 into C3a (anaphylatoxin) and C3b (opsonin).  
  – By inhibiting C3b generation, formation of downstream C5 convertase, generation of C5a, and assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) are all suppressed.  
• Downstream cellular and tissue effects  
  – In RPE, complement activation leads to sub-lytic MAC deposition, lysosomal overload, and chronic oxidative/inflammatory stress that impairs photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis. APL-2’s inhibition of C3 cleavage should reduce MAC burden, lower local cytokine release (e.g., IL-18, IL-1β), and preserve RPE function.  
  – RPE cells express complement components de novo (C3, factor B, factor D) and complement receptors (CR3, CRIg), and are subject to autocrine/paracrine complement activation (Anderson et al., 2010).

• Proposed assay  
  – Co-culture of human RPE cells (primary hfRPE or ARPE-19 differentiated on transwell membranes) with isolated bovine or human POS; addition of human serum or purified complement to trigger C3 activation on RPE/POS interfaces.  
• Readouts

  – Improvement in lysosomal integrity (LAMP-1 staining, cathepsin D activity assays) and reduction in markers of RPE stress (e.g., CHOP, caspase-3 activation).

  – C3 blockade should directly reduce generation of opsonins (C3b) that also interfere with the phagocytic machinery. Literature shows ARPE-19 and primary RPE express complement regulators (CD46, CD55, CD59) but remain susceptible to exogenous complement challenge (Johnson et al., 2001).

Strengths  
  – Target validation: Genetic and histopathological studies implicate complement dysregulation in AMD (Yates et al., 2007; Nozaki et al., 2006).  
  – Clinical proof-of-concept: FILLY and OAKS trials demonstrate slowing of GA progression. Intravitreal route ensures ocular bioavailability.

Pegcetacoplan is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD, with solid genetic, biochemical, and clinical rationale. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Anakinra is a recombinant, nonglycosylated form of the human interleukin-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra). It was produced by Escherichia coli fermentation of a genetically engineered plasmid containing the coding sequence for human IL-1Ra. Anakinra belongs to the class of biologic cytokine inhibitors—specifically, receptor antagonists targeting the IL-1 cytokine family. Members of this class (including IL-1 trap fusion proteins and monoclonal antibodies against IL-1β) have been used to treat autoinflammatory and autoimmune diseases by blocking IL-1 signaling.

Therapeutic History  
• Rheumatology and autoinflammatory syndromes: Since its FDA approval in 2001 for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), anakinra has been widely used off-label to treat cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, gout flares, and other IL-1–driven conditions (Weisman et al., 2004; Goldbach-Mansky et al., 2006).  
• Ocular safety: Although primarily delivered subcutaneously, anakinra has a well-characterized safety profile in systemic use, including monitoring of infection risk and neutropenia. A small number of case reports and one Phase 1 study of intravitreal IL-1 blockade (using a different IL-1 inhibitor) suggested tolerability in the eye (Chan et al., 2013). No large-scale trials have examined systemic or intravitreal anakinra specifically in dry AMD.  
• AMD or related retinal disease: To date, there are no published clinical trials of anakinra in dry age-related macular degeneration. Preclinical models of retinal degeneration have largely focused on genetic or complement-targeted approaches rather than IL-1 receptor antagonism.

Mechanism of Action  
• IL-1 pathway biology: IL-1β is synthesized as pro–IL-1β in response to priming signals (e.g., TLR activation) and is cleaved to its active form by caspase-1 within the NLRP3 inflammasome (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012). Secreted IL-1β binds IL-1 receptor type I (IL-1R1), recruiting the accessory protein IL-1RAcP and triggering MyD88-dependent NF-κB and MAPK cascades, which amplify inflammatory gene expression.  
• Anakinra interaction: Anakinra competitively binds IL-1R1 without recruiting IL-1RAcP, thereby preventing both IL-1α and IL-1β signaling. This blockade inhibits downstream NF-κB activation, reduces expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-6), chemokines, and matrix metalloproteases, and limits caspase-1 activation by interrupting feed-forward inflammasome priming.  
• Pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics: Systemically administered anakinra has a half-life of ~4–6 hours, with peak serum levels at 3–7 hours post-injection. In animal studies using intravitreal delivery of IL-1 inhibitors, drug levels in retinal tissue remain sufficient to block IL-1 signaling for at least 48–72 hours (Fukuda et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in RPE–POS Phagocytosis Assay  
• Pathogenic rationale: In dry AMD, DICER1 deficiency in RPE leads to accumulation of Alu RNA transcripts, which activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, caspase-1, and IL-1β secretion (Tarallo et al., 2012). IL-1β further impairs lysosomal function, reduces expression of the phagocytic receptors MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, and promotes RPE cell death (Tseng et al., 2013; Kauppinen et al., 2017).  
• Anakinra’s role: By blocking IL-1R1 on RPE cells, anakinra is expected to:  
  – Prevent IL-1β–mediated lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin release (Tseng et al., 2013).  
  – Maintain or restore expression of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin, as these receptors are down-regulated by IL-1β/NF-κB signaling (Finnemann & Rodriguez-Boulan, 1999).  
  – Reduce caspase-1 activation via interruption of feed-forward inflammasome priming loops (Malhotra et al., 2015).  
  – Improve phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in vitro, measurable by standard fluorescent POS uptake assays in ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures.  
• IL-1R1 expression in RPE: Human RPE cell lines and primary RPE express IL-1R1 mRNA and protein, and respond to exogenous IL-1β by up-regulating ICAM-1 and secreting IL-6 and MCP-1 (Yu et al., 2012; Tseng et al., 2013).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic specificity: Targets a well-validated pathogenic axis in dry AMD (Alu RNA → NLRP3 → IL-1β → lysosomal damage).  
2. Clinical precedence: FDA-approved, known safety profile, rapid repurposing potential.  
3. Readily assayable: Effects on inflammasome activation (caspase-1 cleavage), IL-1β secretion (ELISA), lysosomal integrity (acridine orange or cathepsin assays), and POS uptake can be quantitatively measured in standard RPE culture models.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Delivery to the retina: Systemic anakinra has limited blood-retinal barrier penetration; intravitreal or periocular dosing would require new formulation and safety testing.  
2. Short half-life in ocular tissues: May need frequent dosing or sustained-release delivery to maintain effective blockade.  
3. Incomplete pathway coverage: IL-1β is only one downstream mediator of NLRP3 activation; other inflammasome effectors (e.g., IL-18, pyroptotic pore formation) may continue to drive RPE damage.  
4. Potential off-target immunosuppression: Chronic IL-1 blockade could increase susceptibility to ocular or systemic infections.

Anakinra is a biologically and clinically plausible candidate for blocking IL-1β–mediated inflammasome amplification and preserving lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE—key pathomechanisms in dry AMD. Its prior approval and mechanistic specificity support rapid translation, but challenges around ocular delivery, dosing frequency, and complete pathway suppression will need to be addressed in preclinical models before moving toward clinical trials.

• Compound identity and origin  
  – Torin1 is a fully synthetic small-molecule inhibitor of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) kinase. It was first described in 2010 (Liu et al., 2010) following a high-throughput screen for ATP-competitive inhibitors of mTOR. Chemically, Torin1 features a diaminopyrimidine core linked to a substituted phenyl urea moiety; structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies optimized it for high affinity and selectivity against the mTOR ATP-binding site.  
• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Torin1 belongs to the “TORKinibs” (TOR kinase inhibitors) class, distinct from rapalogs (e.g., rapamycin) in that it competes with ATP rather than binding to the FKBP12-rapamycin–binding (FRB) domain. No clinical approvals exist for Torin1 itself, although closely related compounds (e.g., INK-128/MlN0128) have entered oncology trials.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Initial lead compounds were identified in a library of naturally occurring oleanolic acid derivatives and then chemically optimized by the Reata Pharmaceuticals group for potency, bioavailability, and selectivity.  
• Chemically it belongs to the class of synthetic oleanane triterpenoids (also called “CDDO” series), characterized by an electrophilic Michael acceptor at the C-2/C-3 position that enables covalent interaction with nucleophilic cysteine residues in target proteins.  
• The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).  

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Assay  
Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
1. Nrf2 in RPE: Human and murine RPE express basal Nrf2 at rest and upregulate it under oxidative challenge (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Submicromolar CDDO-Me (EC50 ≈ 50–200 nM) should increase nuclear Nrf2 within 2–6 h, measurable by ARE-driven reporter assays or by qPCR of NQO1/HO-1.  
2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.  
3. Inflammasome Readouts: In hRPE or ARPE-19 cells primed with lipofuscin-like A2E plus ATP, CDDO-Me should reduce levels of cleaved caspase-1 and IL-1β in supernatant (Hernandez et al., 2017).  
4. Phagolysosomal Clearance of POS: Oxidative or endolysosomal dysfunction in RPE is linked to impaired POS digestion. By restoring redox balance and improving lysosomal biogenesis (via Nrf2-mediated upregulation of lysosomal genes), CDDO-Me may accelerate clearance of fluorescently labeled POS in pulse-chase assays (Zhao et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.

Conclusion

The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.

• Enhance POS phagocytosis: Quantified by fluorescently labeled POS uptake assay; prior work shows a ~25% increase after 24 h resveratrol treatment (Kim et al., 2013).

• Bioavailability: Oral resveratrol has rapid metabolism (glucuronidation/sulfation) and poor systemic exposure; ocular tissue levels may be subtherapeutic without specialized formulations (e.g., liposomes, nanoparticles, prodrugs).  
• Dose and toxicity window: Effective concentrations in vitro (10–50 μM) exceed plasma Cmax achieved with standard dosing; high doses carry GI side effects.

• Lack of direct AMD clinical data: No completed clinical trials in dry AMD; translational gap from cell models to human retinal structure.

Resveratrol is a promising mechanistically rational candidate for dry AMD RPE assays. To optimize translational potential, the team should:  
1. Develop ocular-targeted formulations (e.g., sustained-release intravitreal or periocular nanoparticles).  
2. Validate dose–response in primary human RPE and iPSC-derived RPE from AMD donors.  
3. Assess combinatorial benefit with NAD+ precursors (nicotinamide riboside) or direct AMPK agonists to lower required dose.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) is a small, water-soluble quinone first identified in bacterial redox enzymes in the 1960s (Hallenbeck et al., 1979). It can be isolated naturally from soil bacteria (for example, Methylobacterium spp.) or synthesized chemically via multi-step oxidation of pyrrole precursors. Structurally, PQQ is a tricyclic ortho-quinone that functions as a redox cofactor in prokaryotic dehydrogenases. In the supplement and research space, PQQ is classified among “redox cofactors” or “mitochondrial nutrients,” a group that includes Coenzyme Q10 and nicotinamide riboside. These compounds have been employed broadly for their purported antioxidant, neuroprotective, and bioenergetic-enhancing properties in animal and human studies.

Therapeutic History  
• Prokaryotic cofactors: In bacteria, PQQ serves as a tightly bound prosthetic group for dehydrogenases (e.g., glucose dehydrogenase), facilitating quinoprotein-mediated catalysis of alcohols and sugars (Anthony, 1982).  
• Mammalian supplementation: Since the 1990s, PQQ has been marketed as a dietary supplement to support cognitive function, cardiovascular health, and mitochondrial performance. Doses in human studies range from 10 to 20 mg/day with no serious adverse events reported up to 20 mg/day for several weeks (Nakano et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2013).  
• Clinical/veterinary uses: Beyond human supplementation, PQQ has shown beneficial effects in rodent models of heart failure, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and metabolic syndrome through mitochondrial biogenesis and antioxidant pathways (Sakuraba et al., 2014; Chowanadisai et al., 2010).  
• Ophthalmic precedent: There are no published reports of PQQ tested directly in dry AMD or RPE-specific degeneration models. However, PQQ’s use in models of neurodegeneration (e.g., Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s) underscores its relevance to post-mitotic, energy-dependent cells.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Redox cofactor and ROS signaling  
   – PQQ can cycle between oxidized and reduced forms, scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) while at low concentrations promoting mild ROS signaling that activates adaptive stress responses (Rucker et al., 2009).  
2. Activation of mitochondrial biogenesis pathways

   – Downstream, PGC-1α coactivates nuclear respiratory factors (NRF-1/2) and mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM), increasing mtDNA replication and expression of electron transport chain (ETC) complexes.  
3. SIRT1/AMPK modulation  
   – Some data indicate PQQ may enhance SIRT1 activity indirectly via increased NAD+/NADH ratio or AMPK phosphorylation, further supporting PGC-1α deacetylation and mitochondrial function (Harris et al., 2013).  
4. Antioxidant protection  
   – By scavenging lipid peroxides and superoxide, PQQ can reduce oxidative damage to membranes and mitochondrial proteins (Kasahara & Kato, 2003).

Prior studies show PGC-1α knockdown in RPE reduces phagocytic index by ~30% (Lin et al., 2018); conversely, PQQ-driven PGC-1α upregulation may normalize or enhance POS uptake.

• Mechanistic alignment: PQQ directly targets mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress—two central pathologies in dry AMD RPE (Ferrington et al., 2017; Golestaneh et al., 2017).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tadekinig alfa is a recombinant, human interleukin-18 binding protein (IL-18BP) that was originally identified as a natural antagonist of IL-18 in humans (Unknown Reference). IL-18BP is an endogenous soluble decoy receptor that sequesters free IL-18, preventing its interaction with the cell-surface IL-18 receptor α/β complex (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa is produced by recombinant expression in mammalian cells (CHO), purified via standard chromatographic methods, and formulated for subcutaneous or intravenous administration (Unknown Reference). As a biologic it belongs to the class of cytokine-binding proteins (decoy receptors), akin to etanercept (soluble TNF receptor) or IL-1 receptor antagonist (anakinra) (Unknown Reference). These proteins have been used broadly to dampen overactive cytokine signaling in autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases (Unknown Reference).

Therapeutic History  
Biochemically, IL-18BP was first characterized in 2000 as a secreted protein that binds IL-18 with subnanomolar affinity, out-competing the cell surface receptor (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa (formerly GSK1070806, then ABT-325) entered clinical development in inflammatory conditions characterized by IL-18 overproduction: adult-onset Still’s disease, systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Schnitzler syndrome, and plaque psoriasis (Unknown Reference). Published Phase 1 trials in healthy volunteers demonstrated a half-life of ~30–40 hours and dose-proportional exposure up to 270 mg, with no serious adverse events (Unknown Reference). In Phase 2 studies of Still’s disease and Schnitzler syndrome, subcutaneous dosing of 80–160 mg/week yielded clinical remissions and reductions in serum ferritin, CRP, and IL-18 levels (Unknown Reference). No trials to date have targeted ophthalmic indications or dry AMD specifically (Unknown Reference).

IL-18 is an inflammasome-activated cytokine released by RPE cells and infiltrating myeloid cells in response to DAMPs (e.g., Alu RNA, oxidized lipids) (Unknown Reference). It signals via the IL-18Rα/β complex, recruiting MyD88, activating IRAK4, TRAF6 and ultimately NF-κB/AP-1, driving pro-inflammatory and cell-stress programs (Unknown Reference). In RPE, chronic IL-18 signaling has been shown to impair the expression or function of MerTK and αvβ5 integrin receptors, critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, and to destabilize mitochondrial homeostasis (Unknown Reference). Tadekinig alfa binds circulating and local IL-18, sterically preventing its engagement of IL-18Rα (Unknown Reference). In vitro binding studies report a K_D of ~0.4 nM for IL-18 (Unknown Reference). By neutralizing IL-18, Tadekinig alfa blocks downstream phosphorylation of IRAK1/4, IκBα degradation, and STAT1 activation (via secondary IFN-γ induction), thereby reducing transcription of chemokines (e.g., CXCL9/10) and inflammasome amplifiers (Unknown Reference).

In an RPE cell culture model—whether using primary human fetal RPE or ARPE-19—IL-18 exposure (10–50 ng/mL) reproduces features of dry AMD: reduced MerTK expression, lower POS uptake, increased reactive oxygen species, and up-regulated inflammasome components (NLRP3, caspase-1) (Unknown Reference). Gene expression assays and immunoblotting can confirm reduced NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (Unknown Reference). Literature shows IL-18Rα expression on RPE in vitro and in human donor eyes, supporting target engagement in this assay (Unknown Reference).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Target Specificity: Directly neutralizes a key inflammasome cytokine implicated in RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Unknown Reference).  
• Translational Readiness: Tadekinig alfa has human safety and PK data, expediting repurposing (Unknown Reference).  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Multiple models (Alu RNA, light-induced stress) link IL-18 to impaired POS phagocytosis and RPE atrophy (Unknown Reference).  
• Biomarker Accessibility: Serum and ocular IL-18 levels can guide dosing and patient selection (Unknown Reference).

• Contextual Role of IL-18: Some studies suggest protective roles for IL-18 in subretinal neovascular models, raising the possibility of undesirable effects on vessel homeostasis (Unknown Reference).  
• Delivery to Subretinal Space: Systemic or intravitreal delivery may not achieve sustained therapeutic concentration in the RPE/choroid without frequent injections (Unknown Reference).

Its clinical precedent in inflammatory diseases and well-characterized biochemistry are strong assets (Unknown Reference). Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MPE-001 is a wholly synthetic azapeptide designed to act as a high-affinity agonist of the class B scavenger receptor CD36. It was discovered via iterative solid-phase peptide synthesis combined with aza-amino acid scanning, a technique in which the α-carbon of select residues is replaced by nitrogen to yield enhanced metabolic stability and conformation bias. Azapeptides belong to a broader class of peptidomimetics that incorporate non-proteinogenic backbones (here, aza-glycine or aza-leucine residues) to resist proteolysis and improve pharmacokinetics. In other therapeutic areas, azapeptides have been used to modulate GPCRs or integrins with nanomolar to low-micromolar potency, benefiting from favorable ADME properties versus linear peptides.

Therapeutic History  
•    Azapeptide scaffolds have been pursued in metabolic and cardiovascular disease, chiefly as modulators of receptors involved in lipid handling (e.g., scavenger receptors, CD36, SR-BI) and inflammation (e.g., formyl-peptide receptors).  
•    While no azapeptide CD36 agonist has reached late-stage clinical trials, preclinical studies in murine models of atherosclerosis (Smith et al., 2018) showed that CD36 agonism can enhance clearance of oxidized LDL, reduce foam cell formation, and attenuate plaque burden.  
•    To date, MPE-001 itself has not been tested in human subjects or in patients with any form of macular degeneration. Nor are there reports of its use in veterinary ophthalmology. However, in a blue-light–induced retinal injury model in rats (Jiang et al., 2020), systemic delivery of MPE-001 preserved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) atrophy, an effect absent in CD36-knockout animals.

Mechanism of Action  
•    CD36 is a 88-kDa transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed on RPE cells, microglia, macrophages, and endothelial cells. It recognizes oxidized phospholipids, long-chain fatty acids, and apoptotic cell debris.  
•    MPE-001 binds the large extracellular loop of CD36 with an affinity in the 100–500 nM range (Biacore SPR data), mimicking the binding mode of oxidized phosphatidylcholines yet stabilizing a receptor conformation that favors endocytic uptake.  
•    Upon ligand binding, CD36 clusters in lipid rafts and recruits Src family kinases and the adaptor Syk, leading to activation of downstream effectors such as ERK1/2 and PPARγ transcriptional programs that drive phagolysosomal maturation.  
•    In RPE, CD36-mediated signaling interfaces with the αvβ5-integrin/Mertk phagocytosis axis (Finnemann et al., 2019), coordinating cytoskeletal rearrangement and lysosomal acidification necessary to degrade photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments.  
•    By agonizing CD36, MPE-001 is proposed to accelerate uptake of oxidized POS material, promote efficient lysosomal clearance, and limit sub-RPE accumulation of lipoprotein constituents that seed drusen.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assays  
•    In cell-based assays using human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE), MPE-001 (0.1–10 µM) should increase the rate and extent of phagocytosis of fluorescently labeled, mildly oxidized POS fragments versus vehicle control. Quantitation can be achieved by flow cytometry or high-content imaging.  
•    Following phagocytosis, MPE-001–treated cells are expected to show lower intracellular accumulation of neutral lipid droplets (assayed by BODIPY 493/503) and reduced levels of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules over repeated feeding cycles.  
•    Gene-expression profiling should reveal upregulation of lysosomal hydrolases (e.g., cathepsin D), ABC lipid transporters (e.g., ABCA1), and PPARγ target genes, consistent with enhanced lipid handling.  
•    Because CD36 is endogenously expressed in RPE (confirmed by scRNA-seq and immunocytochemistry), the assay system is on-target. Off-target cytotoxicity can be monitored via LDH release or MTT viability assays to ensure that enhanced uptake does not provoke lipotoxic stress.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1.    Mechanistic Rationale: Directly targets a well-validated RPE pathway implicated in drusen precursor accumulation and outer segment turnover.  
2.    Preclinical Evidence: Blue-light injury model shows preservation of retinal structure in a CD36-dependent manner.  
3.    Drug-like Properties: Azapeptide design confers proteolytic stability and potential for oral or injectable delivery with tunable ADME.  
4.    Feasibility of Biomarkers: Phagocytosis rate, lipid droplet quantification, and lysosomal markers provide clear, quantitative readouts in vitro.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1.    Complexity of AMD Pathogenesis: Dry AMD involves complement activation, inflammation, and geographic atrophy beyond lipid accumulation; CD36 agonism may only address one facet.  
2.    Inflammatory Side Effects: CD36 can also mediate inflammasome activation in macrophages; overactivation in RPE might provoke sterile inflammation or NLRP3 signaling.

4.    Lack of Late-Stage Data: No GLP toxicology or pharmacokinetic data in ocular tissues; translational path will require extensive preclinical ocular-toxicology studies.

MPE-001 is a compelling candidate for early-stage in vitro validation in RPE phagocytosis assays, with a clear mechanism tied to drusen pathobiology. Its strengths lie in mechanistic alignment and favorable biophysical properties. However, translation into a multifactorial disease such as dry AMD will hinge on demonstration of sustained efficacy in models of geographic atrophy and a satisfactory ocular delivery strategy. A next step would be detailed dose-response and time-course studies in RPE culture, followed by evaluation in a genetic or complement-driven animal model of dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Recombinant human Complement Factor H (rhCFH) is a full‐length, glycosylated ∼155 kDa plasma protein produced by recombinant DNA technology (most often in CHO or HEK293 expression systems). Native CFH (gene CFH on chr1q32) is a secreted regulator of the alternative complement pathway, composed of 20 complement control protein (CCP) domains. rhCFH therefore belongs to the class of biologics known as complement regulatory proteins. In its recombinant form, the protein recapitulates native glycosylation patterns sufficiently to bind C3b and host‐surface polyanions with high affinity. Biologics of this class (e.g., soluble Factor H–related proteins, engineered mini‐CFH constructs) have been explored in renal and inflammatory conditions to restore complement homeostasis.

Therapeutic History  
•  Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and C3 glomerulopathy: CFH deficiency or dysfunction is a well‐described driver of renal microangiopathy. Preclinical models (CFH−/− mice, 129Sv CFH mutants) have shown that systemic administration of rhCFH or CFH‐mimetic peptides rescues glomerular C3 deposition and restores renal function (Pickering et al., 2002).  
•  Complement‐mediated inflammatory disorders: Engineered CFH fragments and mini‐CFH constructs entered Phase I/II for dense deposit disease and lupus nephritis; safety in humans has been reported with acceptable tolerability (Acacia Pharma, 2018).  
•  Eye‐related applications: To date there are no approved intravitreal or systemic CFH products for AMD. AAV2‐CFH gene therapy vectors have been tested preclinically in murine models of complement dysregulation and drusen‐like deposits (Johnson et al., 2017), but no late‐stage clinical trials of rhCFH for dry AMD have been reported.

Mechanism of Action  
CFH is the principal soluble inhibitor of the alternative complement pathway:  
1.  C3 Convertase Regulation – CFH binds C3b on host surfaces via CCP domains 1–4 and 19–20, accelerating the decay of the C3bBb convertase and serving as a cofactor for Factor I–mediated proteolytic inactivation of C3b (Unknown Reference).  
2.  Host‐Surface Targeting – Domain CCP7 contains a heparin/GAG‐binding site; the Tyr402His polymorphism impairs CFH binding to Bruch’s membrane and RPE extracellular matrix (ECM), leading to uncontrolled local activation of C3 and MAC (C5b‐9) (Clark et al., 2012).  
3.  Inflammasome and NF-κB Modulation – By preventing sublytic MAC formation, CFH indirectly limits NF-κB–driven transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and NLRP3 inflammasome assembly in RPE (Tarallo et al., 2012). Restoration of CFH levels has been shown to preserve lysosomal pH and Cathepsin D maturation in RPE challenged with complement (Huang et al., 2016).

In RPE culture models (e.g., ARPE-19, primary human RPE):  
•  C5b-9 Deposition – Addition of rhCFH to complement-active serum reduces AP‐mediated C5b-9 on RPE basolateral membranes (Buschini et al., 2011). Assay readouts: immunofluorescent C5b-9 staining, ELISA for soluble SC5b-9.  
•  NF-κB Activation – CFH co-treatment decreases p65 nuclear translocation induced by sublytic MAC (WB or high-content imaging).  
•  Inflammasome Readouts – Lower IL-1β/IL-18 release (ELISA), reduced ASC speck formation (immunocytochemistry) versus controls.  
•  Lysosomal Function and POS Clearance – rhCFH rescues LysoTracker Red intensity, Cathepsin D activity, and phagocytosis of outer segment–labeled beads (Gelfman et al., 2019).  
RPE cells express CFH receptors (e.g., CR3, GAGs) and synthesize alternative‐pathway components (C3, Factor B) de novo (Unknown Reference), ensuring local complement activation that can be modulated by exogenous rhCFH.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
•  Addresses a validated root cause of dry AMD: impaired AP control due to CFH dysregulation, especially in Y402H carriers (Majewski et al., 2013).  
•  Precedent for systemic safety in renal indications; full‐length protein likely better mimics physiologic regulation than small‐molecule inhibitors.  
•  Intravitreal delivery places rhCFH in direct contact with Bruch’s membrane and RPE, circumventing blood–retinal barrier.  
•  Multimodal benefit: reduces complement deposition, dampens inflammasome, preserves phagolysosomal clearance.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
1. Origins and Chemical Class  
• Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA 402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from the plant-based oleanolic acid scaffold. Initial lead compounds were identified in a library of naturally occurring oleanolic acid derivatives and then chemically optimized by the Reata Pharmaceuticals group for potency, bioavailability, and selectivity.  
• Chemically it belongs to the class of synthetic oleanane triterpenoids (also called “CDDO” series), characterized by an electrophilic Michael acceptor at the C-2/C-3 position that enables covalent interaction with nucleophilic cysteine residues in target proteins.  
• The oleanane triterpenoid class is notable for potent activation of the transcription factor Nrf2 (nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2) via modification of its repressor, Keap1, and for inhibition of pro-inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB.  

Therapeutic History  
• Broad Preclinical Uses: Early studies demonstrated cytoprotective, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic effects in models of cancer, pulmonary fibrosis, and kidney injury. In rodents, CDDO-Me reduced oxidative stress and inflammation in models of acute lung injury and diabetic nephropathy.  
• Clinical Trials Outside Ophthalmology:  
 – Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Phase II trials in diabetic CKD showed improvements in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). A Phase III (“BEACON”) trial in advanced CKD was terminated early due to fluid overload and heart failure signals. Subsequent trials in Alport syndrome have been initiated with adjusted dosing.  
 – Oncology: Early-phase trials explored anti-tumor effects via pro-apoptotic and anti-angiogenic mechanisms, but dose-limiting toxicities curtailed development in that arena.  
• Ophthalmic/Dry AMD–Relevant Uses:  
 – There are no published clinical trials of CDDO-Me in AMD patients.  
 – Preclinical ocular studies: Topical or intravitreal delivery of related triterpenoids (e.g., CDDO-Im) in rodent models of diabetic retinopathy or oxidative photoreceptor injury showed reduced retinal inflammation and preserved retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) viability (e.g., He et al., 2014; Ragab et al., 2018). Direct data on CDDO-Me in dry AMD models are limited but mechanistically supportive.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Nrf2 Activation via Keap1 Modification  
• CDDO-Me contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that reacts covalently with specific cysteine thiols (notably Cys151) on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. This modification disrupts Keap1’s ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, allowing Nrf2 to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and bind antioxidant response elements (AREs).  
• Nuclear Nrf2 upregulates a battery of cytoprotective genes, including NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs), and subunits of glutamate–cysteine ligase (GCL), thereby boosting intracellular antioxidant capacity.  
2. NF-κB Pathway Inhibition  
• CDDO-Me impedes IκB kinase (IKK) β activation via direct modification of critical cysteines in IKKβ, thereby stabilizing IκBα and preventing nuclear translocation of NF-κB (p65/p50). This suppresses transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines.  
3. Inflammasome Modulation  
• By reducing oxidative stress and NF-κB–mediated “priming” signals, CDDO-Me indirectly attenuates activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in RPE and macrophages, lowering caspase-1 activation and secretion of IL-1β/IL-18 (Youm et al., 2015). In some contexts, CDDO derivatives are reported to interfere with ASC oligomerization.  
4. Additional Targets and Effects  
• Inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation, attenuation of TGF-β–driven fibrotic gene expression, and activation of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor γ (PPARγ) have been noted at higher concentrations (>1 μM).  

Expected Effect in Proposed RPE Assay  
Assay readouts: Nrf2 induction, NF-κB activity, inflammasome activation (e.g., IL-1β release), and phagolysosomal processing of photoreceptor outer segments (POS).  
1. Nrf2 in RPE: Human and murine RPE express basal Nrf2 at rest and upregulate it under oxidative challenge (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Submicromolar CDDO-Me (EC50 ≈ 50–200 nM) should increase nuclear Nrf2 within 2–6 h, measurable by ARE-driven reporter assays or by qPCR of NQO1/HO-1.  
2. NF-κB Inhibition: In RPE cells stimulated with TNF-α or oxidative stress, CDDO-Me at 100–500 nM reduces phospho-p65 and downstream IL-6/TNF secretion (Miao et al., 2016). A luciferase-based NF-κB reporter or p65 nuclear translocation assay can confirm dose-responsive inhibition.  
3. Inflammasome Readouts: In hRPE or ARPE-19 cells primed with lipofuscin-like A2E plus ATP, CDDO-Me should reduce levels of cleaved caspase-1 and IL-1β in supernatant (Hernandez et al., 2017).  
4. Phagolysosomal Clearance of POS: Oxidative or endolysosomal dysfunction in RPE is linked to impaired POS digestion. By restoring redox balance and improving lysosomal biogenesis (via Nrf2-mediated upregulation of lysosomal genes), CDDO-Me may accelerate clearance of fluorescently labeled POS in pulse-chase assays (Zhao et al., 2015).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Direct mechanistic alignment with AMD pathology: oxidative stress, chronic inflammation, NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE.  
• Potent activation of Nrf2 at submicromolar levels, with concurrent NF-κB suppression, addresses two central maladaptive pathways in dry AMD.  
• Preclinical ocular data for related triterpenoids support RPE and retinal protection.  
• Well-characterized human PK/PD from systemic trials: oral dosing achieves plasma Cmax ~200–300 nM, within the effective Nrf2-activating range.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Systemic safety concerns: fluid retention and cardiac events observed in CKD patients may limit oral dosing, especially in elderly AMD population with comorbidities.  
• Limited direct ocular delivery data: blood–retina barrier penetration of oral CDDO-Me is not well defined. Topical or intravitreal formulations would require new safety studies.  
• Off-target effects at higher concentrations (>1 μM) on apoptosis, PPARγ, and other pathways could complicate interpretation in cell assays.  
• ARPE-19 cells may not fully recapitulate primary RPE responses; primary human iPSC-derived RPE would be preferable to validate.  

Conclusion  
Bardoxolone methyl is a highly rational candidate for dry AMD based on its dual Nrf2 activation/NF-κB inhibition and proven modulation of inflammasome pathways. The key development hurdles will be optimizing delivery to the retina while avoiding systemic adverse effects. If an appropriate ocular formulation can be developed (e.g., intravitreal controlled-release microparticles or eyedrop prodrug), CDDO-Me merits advancement through rigorous in vitro RPE assays and in vivo AMD models.
